## 10.891 Docker on a ring box drops the failover; the plan says so

ml350 runs Docker (read on the box: `dockerd` up, `br_netfilter` loaded,
`/proc/sys/net/bridge/bridge-nf-call-iptables` 1). With that switch on, a
frame crossing a bridge from one port to another passes every table's IP
forward chain, and Docker leaves `ip filter/FORWARD` dropping by policy.
With -01 as the ring's root (10.889), ml350 is the box the path between
-01 and -03 goes through once their cable is cut, so the failover would be
dropped there -- on the one day it is needed, and silently.

Measured in `make hull-storage-ring`, with ml350 given br_netfilter, the
switch and a dropping `ip filter/FORWARD` (the hwsim image gains
`nftables` for it): before the cut every box reached the others; after it,
-01 and -03 did not reach each other or ml350 for the 281-291 s the rig
waited. Nothing of netcfgd's can fix that from its own table -- the
strictest verdict across tables wins (0294) -- and the per-bridge
`nf_call_iptables` only adds to the global switch, it cannot exempt one
bridge from it.

So the plan says it. The observation keeps, beside the neighbouring filter
chains, the forward chains whose policy drops (`forward_droppers`, as
`family table/chain`) and br_netfilter's two switches (absent where the
module is not loaded); and every bridge with two ports or more, when a
dropping chain of a family whose switch is on exists -- or the document's
own `forward` drops -- gets a warning naming the chain and the remedy:
`iptables -I DOCKER-USER -i BRIDGE -o BRIDGE -j ACCEPT`, or the switch set
to 0. The rig now checks ml350's plan says it, inserts that remedy in
nft's words, and the ring heals in 13-14 s as before. `plan_input_test`
holds the four cases (warned; not with the switch off; not for the other
family's chain; not with nothing dropping).

For the holder's boxes: ml350 needs that DOCKER-USER rule (or the switch
off) before the ring is relied on, and any other box that comes to run
Docker the same. Whether Docker's own containers need the switch on is
Docker's question; the rule is the narrower change.

Once, in the run without the remedy, ml350's first jumbo ping to -01 was
lost before any cut -- not forwarded traffic -- and reached after it; it
did not recur with the remedy. Unexplained, seen once.

## 10.890 Taken over from ifupdown, a Devuan box mounted no network filesystem at boot

The takeover rigs (10.884, 10.886) switch within one boot and never boot
again, so they never saw where netcfgd lands in the boot. Read from the
images after the switch: `networking` gone from rcS (`K09`), `mountnfs.sh`
at `S09` in rcS, and netcfgd at `S01` in **rc2** -- its script said
`Default-Start: 2 3 4 5` and `Required-Start: $remote_fs`. rcS runs whole
before rc2, so everything in it that wants the network ran before netcfgd
existed, and `$remote_fs` *is* the network filesystems, which cannot wait
for the thing they need.

**Worse, nothing mounted them at all.** With `ASYNCMOUNTNFS` at its
default, Devuan's `mountnfs.sh` only waits for NFS under /usr and /var; the
mounting is `/etc/network/if-up.d/mountnfs`, which ifupdown runs as each
interface comes up, once the last `auto` one is up. netcfgd runs no
if-up.d hook. So a box switched from ifupdown would boot with every NFS
and `_netdev` line in its fstab unmounted. ml350's one such line today (-03's
home) is `noauto`, mounted on demand and untouched by this; any line without
it -- the NAS mount made automatic -- is what it would have hit. ml350's
other if-up.d hooks (resolvconf, ethtool, openvpn, bridge, wpasupplicant)
act on `interfaces` stanzas, which the translated documents carry instead.

Two ways to fill the facility were measured and refused. `$network` is
`+networking +ifupdown` in /etc/insserv.conf, and a second definition in
/etc/insserv.conf.d is not merged: Devuan's OpenRC reads LSB headers
through `lsb2rcconf`, which reads the same files, and run on a header
with `$network +netcfgd` in insserv.conf.d it still expanded `$network`
to `networking ifupdown` alone. Providing the name `networking` would
make netcfgd and ifupdown's script two providers of one name, which
insserv refuses while both are installed.

So netcfgd takes `networking`'s slot by its own name. Its script starts in
rcS (`Default-Start: S`, `Required-Start: $local_fs`, `Should-Start: udev`,
`X-Start-Before: mountnfs`; dbus dropped, being rc2's and only
netcfgd-nm's), and a new `netcfgd-wait-online` -- the systemd unit's
counterpart -- runs after it and before mountnfs: `ncfg wait-online 30`,
then what the if-up.d hook's `do_start` does (rpcbind and nfs-common where
an NFS line needs locking, `mount -a` of the network types and of
`_netdev`, between `pre_mountall` and `post_mountall`). It never fails the
boot. Under OpenRC the switcher now puts a script whose header says
`Default-Start: S` in `boot`, where Devuan's OpenRC had `networking`,
rather than `default`, which runs after everything in `boot`; and it
enables netcfgd-wait-online without starting it, as it does the systemd
unit.

Held by both rigs: after the switch netcfgd, then netcfgd-wait-online,
then mountnfs in rcS (sysv-rc), or both in `boot` (OpenRC), and running
netcfgd-wait-online mounts a `_netdev` tmpfs line in fstab, standing in for
NFS. `tests/live/select.sh` checks the runlevel and the enable-not-start.
A real boot is not in either rig: hull machines run their payload as the
boot, so what is checked is the order insserv and OpenRC computed and the
script doing its part, not a cold boot end to end.

## 10.889 The storage ring heals around a cut cable; a bridge takes `max_age`

The holder chose the bridged storage net (2026-11-21: "bridged, possibly
with STP"), settling 10.887's open question. Spanning tree is not optional
in it: three boxes with two ports each, cabled box to box, close a ring,
and with `stp = false` the rig's boxes lose each other (10.887). So each
box bridges its two ConnectX-3 ports with STP on.

A ring is cabled for its redundancy, so `make hull-storage-ring` now cuts a
cable -- both ends of a forwarding segment down, as a pulled cable drops
carrier at both -- and every box must reach the other two again. **The cut
measured is the hard one**: the segment the box holding the blocked port is
not on. That box loses no link of its own, so classic spanning tree (the
kernel's; RSTP needs mstpd) unblocks its port only once the root's
information there has aged out, then listens and learns. At the kernel's
`max_age` of 20 s that took 28 to 30 s; a cut beside the blocked port took
8 to 9. Half a minute is an NFS stall the holder would notice.

**So a bridge takes `max_age`**, in seconds like its other timers, through
every layer `hello_time` goes (document, observed record, plan comparison,
apply, renderer, witnesses -- a minor bump), refused outside the kernel's
6 to 40 at compile time. 802.1D wants `2 x (forward_delay - 1) >= max_age
>= 2 x (hello_time + 1)`; at `forward_delay = 4` and the default hello of
2 that is exactly 6, and the ring heals in 13 to 16 s, which the rig now
holds to 20. -01, the NAS, takes `priority = 4096` so it is the root: both
its links forward and the port that blocks is on the ml350 -- -03 cable,
which carries neither box's NAS traffic; the rig checks that too.

Each box's storage section is then

    device eth2 { mtu = 9000 }
    device eth3 { mtu = 9000 }
    device br-storage {
    	mtu = 9000
    	bridge {
    		members       = ["eth2", "eth3"]
    		stp           = true
    		forward_delay = 4
    		max_age       = 6
    		priority      = 4096	# on dl180g6-01 only
    	}
    }
    interface eth2 { config = "null" }
    interface eth3 { config = "null" }
    interface br-storage { config = "10.1.0.X/24" }

with the port names whatever mlx4_en gives the ConnectX-3 once its ports are
in Ethernet mode, which is the boxes' setup and not netcfgd's.

During the suite run for this change `node_store_trouble.sh` failed its
recovery check once ("when it has room the line goes") and passed three of
three alone: it waits 60 s for a pressure that comes down a step per 30 s,
which is tight under the suite's load. Nothing here touches it; noted as
intermittent, not explained.

**`make packaging` had been red since 10.885, and I had not run it.** Its
privilege gate named `over` and `max_age` as keys nobody had classified
(both ordinary: one narrows what a drop matches, the other is a timer like
`hello_time`), and its form gate named `over` as a member the GUI's
firewall dialog neither read nor declared -- so saving any rule in the
firewall tab rewrote the document without the SSH guard, leaving its
drop to match every new connection. The client reads `over`, the dialog
shows it as "only over" and writes it back, and `firewall_load` loads a
guard, saves unchanged and compares; it fails with the dialog's write
line removed.

## 10.888 The plan offers the whole-machine remedy that works on this machine

On the Devuan rig (10.884) `ncfg plan`'s warning that ifupdown also holds
the interfaces led with a systemd drop-in -- `mkdir -p
/etc/systemd/system/netcfgd.service.d` and a `systemctl daemon-reload` --
on a machine systemd does not run, with `netcfgd_select.sh` in the last
sentence. And for ifupdown it was wrong under systemd too: the drop-in
conflicts with NetworkManager, systemd-networkd, connman, wpa_supplicant
and ModemManager, never with ifupdown's `networking`.

The message offers one whole-machine remedy now: the drop-in where systemd
runs and the contender is one it conflicts with, the switcher otherwise.
`ncfg_contender_describe_on` takes whether systemd runs, so
`contention_test` asks both ways: NetworkManager under systemd names the
drop-in, without systemd the switcher and not the drop-in, and ifupdown the
switcher even under systemd.

## 10.887 The coming storage net, bridged in a ring, simulated

The holder's boxes are to get ConnectX-3s in Ethernet mode, two ports each,
cabled box to box with no switch (system-notes, 2026-11-20); whether each
box bridges its two ports or routes a subnet per link was the holder's, and
was settled bridged on 2026-11-21 (10.889). Both shapes are things netcfgd already expresses -- a `bridge` with
`stp`, or addresses and `routes` per port -- so this measures the one that
can go wrong: the bridged ring, ml350 to -01 to -03 and back, where spanning
tree must block one port or every broadcast circles for ever.

`make hull-storage-ring`: three vms, two segments each forming the ring,
each running `ncfg apply` with its two ports in `br-storage`, STP on,
`forward_delay = 4`, MTU 9000 on the ports and the bridge, and its 10.1.0.x
address. Every box reaches the other two with an 8972-byte ping that may
not fragment, a second plan has nothing to do, and across the ring exactly
one port blocks. With `stp = false` the boxes fail their check and nothing
blocks. virtio-net stands in for mlx4, and the machines run the host's
kernel: hull's microvm kernel has no bridge module, which was the first
run's failure.

The document each box needs, for the holder's choice of a bridge (10.889
adds `max_age` and the NAS's priority to it):

    device eth2 { mtu = 9000 }
    device eth3 { mtu = 9000 }
    device br-storage {
    	mtu = 9000
    	bridge { members = ["eth2", "eth3"]; stp = true; forward_delay = 4 }
    }
    interface eth2 { config = "null" }
    interface eth3 { config = "null" }
    interface br-storage { config = "10.1.0.X/24" }

with the firewall's NFS rules naming `br-storage` where they name `ib0`
today.

## 10.886 Taking over ml350's shape: OpenRC under sysvinit

10.884's rig on the desktop's shape: `make hull-takeover-openrc` boots the
same payloads on a Devuan excalibur image with OpenRC as the rc system under
sysvinit, as ml350 runs (10.845), so the boot and the switch go through
`/etc/runlevels`. `nas.sh` tells the two apart by `/run/openrc` and checks
OpenRC's runlevels there rather than `/etc/rc?.d`, which nothing reads.

**It found the switcher leaving ifupdown enabled.** Under OpenRC
`netcfgd_select.sh` stood a script down with `rc-update del SCRIPT
default`, but Debian's `networking` says `Default-Start: S`, so OpenRC has
it in `boot`: the delete failed quietly, the script stayed enabled, and at
the next boot ifupdown would have configured ml350's interfaces beside
netcfgd. It deletes the script from every runlevel `rc-update show -v`
lists it in now. `tests/live/select.sh`'s stand-in `rc-update` answers
`show -v` as such a machine does, and its check -- `networking` out of
`boot` -- fails with the old line and passes with the new. Both rigs pass,

## 10.885 A firewall rule can count per source: `over`

The one rule of the servers' `rules.v4` with no translation (10.884): an
SSH chain whose iptables `recent` match dropped an address's ninth new
connection within 900 s. `over = "8/15m"` on a `drop` or `reject` makes it
match a source address's packets only past that rate, counted per source;
kept in the model as `"8/900s"`, written back as that, and part of the
rule's digest only where set, so no earlier digest moves.

**In the kernel it is nftables' meter**: a set per family in netcfgd's
table (`over-<digest>-4` and `-6`, flags `timeout` and `eval`, keyed on the
source address), and per family a rule loading the source address and
updating the set with a `dynset` that carries a `limit` -- packets, rate
COUNT per window, burst COUNT, inverted so it matches over the rate. The
bucket holds COUNT and refills COUNT per window, so the COUNT+1st of a
burst is the first dropped and a persistent source gets one try per
window/COUNT after; an entry idle for a window expires. That is near
enough to `recent --hitcount 9 --seconds 900` to guard the same door,
and is said in the example as what it is.

**Two things it needed beyond the rule.** The transaction's audit admits a
`NEWSET` now, only in netcfgd's table and only named `over-`. And the
reader decodes the `dynset` back into the rate, because the planner
compares the installed table with the document by decoding both: a rule it
could not read was "somebody's hand edit" on every pass.

Only in `input` and `forward`, and only on `drop` or `reject`: in `output`
the source is this host, and an `accept` past a rate lets in what the rate
is for. A rule naming addresses counts in the families they name; one
naming none counts in both.

Verified: `nft_test` (two meters and two rules, each read back as
`8/900s`, the transaction passing the audit; an IPv4 source making it one
of each; the rate in the digest), red with the reader answering one more
than written; `lower_test` (kept as `8/900s`, refused on an accept, in
output and when unreadable; the renderer refusing a rate it cannot write,
which its extreme-value sweep found); `render_test` round trip; in a
namespace, `over = "3/1m"` on port 22 opening three connections and
dropping the next three, with `ncfg plan` converged after; and `make
hull-takeover`, the guard dropping the same burst after netcfgd took over
as iptables did before.

## 10.884 Taking over dl180g6-01: simulated, and what it needs

The holder asked (2026-11-20) whether netcfgd can go onto the servers now
and take over from what configures them. Their state was captured by the
system-notes tree that day (its `~/claude`): every box Devuan, sysvinit as
pid 1 -- sysv-rc on the DL180s, OpenRC on ml350 -- classic `ethN` names
pinned by udev, `eth0` by DHCP from ifupdown's `isc-dhcp-client` against a
router reservation on a /16, the storage link `ib0` (QLE7340, IPoIB,
10.1.0.x/24; connected mode and MTU 65520 set by hand and not yet kept), and
iptables-persistent loading a `rules.v4` from `rcS.d`: INPUT DROP,
established, `lo`, ping, NFS only on `ib0`, an SSH chain with a `recent`
brute guard (9 new in 900 s, ml350 exempt), and `rules.v6` accepting
everything. **Live takeover waits**: a 16 TB copy -03 -> -01 runs over
`ib0` on runtime-only state, and -01 gets a fresh install afterwards, the
natural point for netcfgd (system-notes, 2026-11-20).

**Simulated in `make hull-takeover`**: a Devuan excalibur vm booting real
sysvinit with sysv-rc, configured from -01's own `interfaces` and
`rules.v4` (`ib0` written as `eth1`: a vm has no InfiniBand), beside a
router leasing the reserved address and probing from the LAN, from the
admin desktop's address and from the storage net. Phase A is the box as it
is; phase B installs netcfgd as the package does, gives it the translated
document (`tests/hull/takeover/netcfgd.conf`), retires iptables-persistent
by hand and runs `netcfgd_select.sh netcfgd`. **76 checks pass**: the
lease moves to netcfgd's DHCP client with no `dhclient` left, the storage
address stays, iptables holds nothing, the start links are netcfgd's alone,
and from outside the same matrix holds -- ping, ssh on both nets, NFS and
mountd on the storage net only -- with UniFi open for the NAS role and,
because netcfgd's table is `inet`, IPv6 filtered where `rules.v6` left it
open (ICMPv6 accepted, or neighbour discovery breaks).

Found on the way, and fixed or open:

- **Under sysvinit the daemon's log went nowhere**: `start-stop-daemon
  --background` with no output. The first run took no lease and nothing
  said why. The script writes `/var/log/netcfgd.log` now with `--output`,
  asked for only where `start-stop-daemon --help` names it, since beowulf's
  dpkg (still on -01's current install) has no such option and would
  refuse to start netcfgd. OpenRC's script and procd already kept it.
- **A hand install without `/usr/libexec/netcfgd/dhcpcd-hook` takes no
  lease**, and the log says exactly that. The package and `make install`
  place it; the rig had missed it.
- **The firewall handover is by hand**: netcfgd leaves another program's
  table alone, so `netfilter-persistent flush` and `update-rc.d
  netfilter-persistent disable` are steps of the takeover, and
  `netcfgd_select.sh` does not do them. What makes a forgotten step
  visible is `ncfg plan`, which names iptables-nft's tables filtering beside
  netcfgd's -- and named them `filter/INPUT` twice, IPv4's and IPv6's, since
  the chain record carried no family. It names `ip filter/INPUT` and `ip6
  filter/INPUT` now, as `nft list` does; the rig checks both.
- **The switcher named the `dhclient` it ended as left by "networkmanager"**
  when ifupdown had started it: the sweep walks NetworkManager first and
  both start dhclient. It credits a manager now only where its init script
  or unit is installed, and says "whichever manager started it" otherwise;
  what it sweeps is unchanged. The rig checks the sentence.
- **The SSH guard had no translation**: the firewall language had no
  per-source rate limit. **Settled by 10.885**, `over`; the rig checks the
  guard in phase B as in phase A.
- **IPoIB's connected mode is not modelled**, and nothing here has
  InfiniBand to test a native setting on, so the translation is a `pre_up`
  hook writing `connected` to `/sys/class/net/ib0/mode` and setting the MTU
  with `ip`. **Not `device ib0 { mtu = 65520 }`**: a plan sets a device's
  MTU before `pre_up` runs (measured, `ncfg plan` on a dummy `ib0`), IPoIB
  refuses 65520 in datagram mode, and a failed `link.set_mtu` stops the rest
  of the plan -- so `ib0` would never come up. Unverified on the card; the
  first live install is its test.
- **The translated documents for -01, -03 and ml350**, each compiling,
  went to the system-notes tree's inbox (`~/claude`, 20261120T2017Z) with
  the steps for -01's fresh install: a DHCP client netcfgd drives
  (`dhcpcd-base`), iptables-persistent retired, `netcfgd_select.sh`, from
  the BMC's serial console. **One check only the real network can make**:
  netcfgd's dhcpcd sends a DUID client identifier where `dhclient` sent
  none, so a router keying a reservation on client-id rather than MAC would
  lease -01 another address.
- hull's microvm kernel has no `nf_tables`, so the rig's machines run
  `(tuning (vm (profile full)))`, the host's kernel and modules.

## 10.883 The GUI follows a dark desktop, and has Help and About

M8's desktop half, against the list the holder set 2026-11-20 of what a
new GUI in this workspace carries without being asked. Three of it were
missing here:

- **A dark palette on a dark desktop.** Qt hands a TDE or LXQt session its
  light palette, so the window glared white there. `main.cpp` calls
  `qtkit_follow_desktop` once the application exists, except in the TUI;
  `NETCFGD_GUI_THEME=dark` or `light` overrides a desktop that says
  neither. Without QtDBus, so the freedesktop portal is not asked -- the
  desktop's own files and Qt's colour scheme are.
- **Help, holding About**, as hydra, beerssh and fuzzypickles have it: the
  version and the copyright line, the address escaped so
  `QMessageBox::about`'s rich text keeps it.
- **An accessible name on the one control with no visible text**, the
  machine box on the toolbar. The GUI has no icon-only button; its
  controls are in form rows, which name them by their labels.

**qtkit is a pinned copy, not a submodule** -- `gui/vendor/qtkit`, qtkit
`ed18c25`, six files -- because qtkit has no remote: a submodule nobody
else could clone would be a broken checkout. **Open, and the holder's:
publishing qtkit**, after which this becomes the submodule the rule
describes, by replacing the directory.

Verified: the GUI builds with it; `gui/tests/about_menu` (offscreen) finds
Help and About, reads the box's text with the address escaped, and the
machine box's accessible name. qtkit's own suite is what holds its theme;
nothing here drives a dark desktop through the GUI.

## 10.882 netrescue: a gateway that drops pings is still a gateway

Reachable meant a default gateway answering an echo, so under a router
that drops pings netrescue climbed for ever on a network that worked --
listening, forcing, rebinding -- and the listening rung would have put a
second address, picked from what it heard, beside the port's own lease in
the same pool. Two changes. **After an unanswered echo, a completed ARP
entry for the gateway counts** (`ncfg_rescue_arp_resolved` over
`/proc/net/arp`, flags `ATF_COM` and a hardware address not zero): a
router has to answer ARP to route at all, and the echo just sent made the
kernel ask. The report says "(by ARP; it drops pings)". **And a port with
an IPv4 address other than the fallback is not listened on**: its network
has already said what it is.

Verified: `rescue_test`'s ARP cases (complete, incomplete, zero hardware
address, absent); `tests/live/rescue.sh`'s phase 1b, a gateway **in a
namespace of its own** leasing an address and ignoring echoes
(`icmp_echo_ignore_all`), reached at rung 1 by ARP; then with its ARP off
and the neighbour table flushed, the ladder climbs and says it is not
listening on the port with a lease, which keeps only its lease. With
both changes disabled the phase goes red on all three. 35 checks.

## 10.881 `ethtool`'s ring sizes are applied, on virtio-net over PCI

The next fields of 10.877's shape, parsed and applied by nothing:
`rx_ring` and `tx_ring`. Built the same way -- `RINGS_GET` and `RINGS_SET`
in `c/src/sys/ethtool.c`, the observed link's `rx_ring`, `tx_ring` and
their maxima, `link.set_rings` (the fifty-fourth op, disruptive since most
physical drivers reset the NIC to resize, optional since a refusal leaves
the ring as it was) planned by `ncfg_plan_rings`. A ring already the size
asked is left out of the set; a size past the device's maximum is warned
about and not asked for, since the driver would refuse it every pass.
`wol` is now the one field of the block applied by nothing.

**virtio-net resizes a ring only with queue reset, which a microvm does not
have.** The first rig run had `ethtool -G` itself answer `ENOENT`, the same
as netcfgd, on a NIC whose device sat on `LNRO0005`, virtio-mmio: hull's
default vm is a microvm on its own kernel. `(tuning (vm (profile full)))`
makes it q35 on the host's kernel, virtio-net on PCI, where QEMU 10 offers
queue reset; the rig now runs that way, and the link modes pass there too.

Verified: `link_modes_test`'s ring cases (the set leaving an unasked ring
out rather than sending zero, the reply with its maxima, a grown ring with
its inverse, a size past the maximum warned, a ring already right left, a
link with no rings warned); `make hull-link-modes`, now 15 checks, the
rings shrunk to 128 each and read back by `ethtool -g` in the guest -- the
hwsim image carries `ethtool` for that, a reader that is not netcfgd's --
and a second plan with nothing to size: VERDICT ok, and red with the
encoder sending twice the receive size. A diagnostic that called
`ethtool -G` in the rig was taken out once it had answered: it set the
rings itself, and hid the second-plan check in the sabotaged run. Both
witnesses moved, a minor bump.

## 10.880 netrescue answers to NAME.local

The proposal's "always reachable on a direct cable: IPv6 link-local kept on
every port, plus an mDNS announcement". The link-local half was already so
(10.876 checks the kernel's address stays); this is the name. netrescue
answers A and AAAA questions for `--name`.local (`rescue` by default) on
every port, over IPv4 and IPv6, between its two-second looks at the machine
rather than in a thread. **IPv6 is the family that always works on a direct
cable**: a link-local address is on every port the moment it is up, where
an IPv4 one is only on the port the fallback is on. A question is answered
on the port it arrived on, with that port's own addresses, since another
port's are unreachable from where the asker is. One from a port other than
5353 is a legacy resolver's and is answered to it with its ID (RFC 6762
6.7); the rest go to the group, with the cache-flush bit and a two-minute
TTL, as RFC 6762 says of host records. It answers and does not announce or
probe for its name: a rescue box is one host, and two on one cable would
both answer, which is a nuisance and not a hazard.

`ncfg_rescue_mdns_answer` is the only code reading those bytes, as root,
from anybody on the link, so it is pure, tested, and the fifteenth fuzz
target (`fuzz/mdns_query`): names with compression pointers are followed
only backwards and at most eight times. Two minutes, 9.2 million runs,
clean.

Verified: `rescue_test` (A, AAAA without case, ANY with the second record
by pointer; another name, a response, a cut question, a self-pointing
name and an answer too large for its buffer all refused);
`tests/live/rescue.sh`'s fourth phase, a neighbour **in a namespace of its
own** asking from a random port over both families and from 5353 as a
responder would: 10.0.0.250, the port's link-local address, and the group
answer. A neighbour in netrescue's own namespace was the first try, and
its IPv4 question was never answered: the kernel drops a packet arriving
on a port from an address the namespace holds, as a martian, and IPv6 does
not -- a test artifact, recorded so nobody reads it as a responder fault.
Not answering the legacy resolver turns the phase red.

## 10.879 netrescue rebinds a NIC's driver, and says what the kernel said

The proposal's "reload NIC drivers and log firmware errors", built as
**rung 5**, the last: for every port still without a carrier,
`ncfg_rescue_rebind` follows `PORT/device` and its `driver` link and writes
the device's own name -- a PCI address, `virtio11` -- to the driver's
`unbind` and then its `bind`. That is a module reload for one device,
without touching the others the module drives or needing `modprobe`. The
two writes have nothing between them, since a device left unbound is a port
gone until reboot. Then three seconds of `/dev/kmsg`, read from where it
stood before the first rebind, are searched by `ncfg_rescue_kmsg_complaint`
for records naming the driver or the device and saying something went wrong
-- firmware, fail, error, timeout, reset -- and up to ten are reported; or
that the kernel said nothing troubled; or that the log could not be read.
The document at rung 5 is rung 4's: the rebind is netrescue's own act.

Verified: `rescue_test` against a sysfs tree of real links (unbind then
bind with the device's name; a device with no driver and a port with no
device refused with a sentence) and the log matcher; `make hull-rescue`, a
vm whose segment NIC netrescue is told has no carrier while its `device`
link is the real one, so the ladder climbs through the forcing rungs on
virtio-net to rung 5 and rebinds `virtio11` through the real sysfs:
VERDICT ok, the device bound to `virtio_net` again and `eth1` back **with a
new ifindex**, which is the evidence the device really went and came back
-- "bound again" alone would also be true of a rebind that did nothing.

**Open now**: PPP on a serial console, the proposal's last rung (the
name is 10.880); and the stick itself, which is the consumer's.

## 10.878 netrescue listens: an unknown network learned from its ARP

The proposal's rung 4, built as **rung 2**: on a port with a carrier and no
lease, netrescue listens to ARP for `--listen` seconds (15 by default), and
`ncfg_rescue_learn` reads the traffic -- the /24 most of it is in, and its
busiest address as the gateway, since every host asks for its gateway and
the gateway asks for every host. It takes the highest address in
.200-.250 nobody was heard using or probing for (DHCP pools usually start
low), confirms it with an RFC 5227 probe (`ncfg_rescue_address_free`:
sender 0.0.0.0, so no cache learns an address that is not yet taken; an
answer, or another host's probe for the same address, means taken, and the
next is tried), and the next document carries it with a default route
through the gateway. **Before the forcing rungs**, which are now 3 and 4,
because it disturbs nothing and serves the ports they do not: the ones with
a carrier. What was learned is written at every rung after, and forgotten
when its port loses its carrier.

**Listening time does not count against the rung's wait**: found by the
live test, which reached the gateway one rung late because the four
seconds spent listening had already used rung 2's four-second wait.

A /24 is a guess -- right on almost every network a rescue meets and never
wider than the truth; DHCP traffic would say the real mask and is not read
yet, nor is IPv6's router advertisement, which the kernel acts on itself.

Verified: `rescue_test` (learning from a LAN's traffic with link-local
noise and a probe in it, a taken address passed over, too little traffic
saying nothing; the learned address and route compiling at a later rung);
`tests/live/rescue.sh`'s third phase, a far end at 10.46.0.1 asking for its
neighbours and holding .250 without being heard using it: netrescue names
the gateway by its traffic, finds .250 taken by its probe, takes .249, and
reaches the gateway at rung 2. A probe that never finds anything taken
turns that phase red.

## 10.877 `ethtool`'s autoneg, speed and duplex are applied

**They parsed, compiled and were applied by nothing** -- the plan said so
in `warn_unapplied` -- because the encoder for `ETHTOOL_MSG_LINKMODES_SET`
was held back until it could meet a driver: a veth refuses every link-modes
set, and every netlink defect this project has shipped was found by a real
kernel rather than by a careful encoder (`ethtool.h`). netrescue's forcing
rungs (10.876) were the first consumer to need them. **virtio-net is the
driver**: it takes speed and duplex with autonegotiation off, and a hull vm
has one, so no hardware was needed.

Built: `ncfg_ethtool_link_modes_get_request`, `_set_request` and `_merge`
in `c/src/sys/ethtool.c`; the observed link carries `autoneg`, `speed` and
`duplex`, asked of every link beside its offloads and absent where it will
not say; `link.set_link_modes`, the fifty-third op, planned by
`ncfg_plan_link_modes` in `c/src/plan/offload.c`, disruptive (the PHY
retrains) and optional (a driver that will not force leaves the link
negotiating, and the rest of the plan goes on). `wol` and the ring sizes
are still warned about as applied by nothing.

**What is compared depends on what is wanted.** With autonegotiation off,
speed and duplex are the setting and are compared. With it on, the speed
the kernel reports is what the two ends agreed, so only `autoneg` is
compared -- comparing the rest planned a carrier-dropping set on every pass,
and the unit test's sabotage of exactly that goes red.

**A forced NIC with no carrier cannot say its speed** (a physical one
reports `SPEED_UNKNOWN`; virtio does not), which would have left the
planner a choice between never converging and never changing it -- the
second stopping netrescue's 1000-to-100 rung on precisely the ports it is
for. The executor writes `<run>/link_modes/<iface>` after a forced set,
WireGuard's record precedent, and `ncfg_observe_link_modes_recorded` uses
it only where the kernel said autoneg off and gave no speed; a kernel
answer always wins. Measured only in the unit test: no NIC here reports
`SPEED_UNKNOWN` while forced, so the record's live half waits for a real
one.

**And a wrong name in every generic netlink refusal through the executor.**
`ncfg_netlink_send_batch` named a refused request by its message type read
as rtnetlink, which on a generic netlink socket is the family's runtime id:
ethtool's was 22 here, so a refused link-modes set read "RTM_GETADDR
failed". `ncfg_netlink_request_from` already corrected this and the batch
path did not; it does now, for ethtool, WireGuard and nl80211 sets alike.

Verified: `c/tests/link_modes_test.c` (the messages, the merge, the record,
six plans; sabotaging the autoneg-on rule and the kernel-wins rule each
goes red); `make hull-link-modes`, a vm forcing its segment NIC to 100/full
and 1000/full read back through sysfs rather than netcfgd's own netlink,
converging, writing the record, and refusing "negotiate" without stopping
the address -- VERDICT ok, and red with the encoder sending ten times the
speed. Both witnesses moved, a minor bump: `observed.json` gained the
three fields, `plan.json` the op.

## 10.876 netrescue: a ladder of documents, for a box nobody configured

**Asked for by the holder** (2026-11-20, building a USB rescue stick for the
HP G6 servers: "netrescue sounds like something we should have in netcfgd
instead and include that when it's finished"), and proposed through the
inbox by the system-notes tree, whose stick is the first consumer
(`~/claude/rescue/build-rescue-usb.sh`, Devuan, sysvinit). The proposal's
seven rungs and its rejected alternative -- a local language model -- are
recorded in [0326](doc/decision/0326-netrescue-is-a-ladder-of-documents.md),
which is the design: **a fourth name of the multi-call program that writes
one netcfgd document per rung and runs its own netcfgd on it**, climbing
when no default gateway answers an echo by the rung's deadline.

**Built, step one**: `c/src/rescue/rescue.c` (which links are ports, the
document for a rung, the gateways from `/proc/net/route`, the echo) and
`c/src/main/rescue_main.c` (the loop, the child daemon, the report on
standard output, `DIR/netrescue.log` and with `--console` on
`/dev/console`). Rung 1 is DHCP on every port and 10.0.0.250/16 on the
first with a carrier, kept there while it has one; rung 2 listens on ports
with a carrier and no lease (10.878); rungs 3 and 4 force the ports with
no carrier to 1000/full and 100/full; after rung 4 it starts again, asking
the forced ports to negotiate. Ports are taken again every
two seconds, so a USB adapter or a tethered phone plugged in later is a
port at the next tick. `--for` bounds a run from inside, which is what the
test uses.

Verified: `c/tests/rescue_test.c` compiles every rung's document with the
compiler the daemon runs (a quoted speed and a radio taken for a port both
turn it red); `tests/live/rescue.sh` gets a lease through netrescue's own
netcfgd from busybox udhcpd across a veth, reads the default route, has
the gateway answer at rung 1 with the fallback and the kernel's IPv6
link-local address both on the port, then with no server climbs every
rung, keeps the fallback, and goes round. The ports there come from a
sysfs directory the test writes, because a veth has no `device` and is
rightly not a port.

**The forcing rungs are applied since 10.877**, which built what they write:
until then `ethtool`'s `autoneg`, `speed` and `duplex` parsed and were
applied by nothing.

**Open, and the stick's builder's to answer: PPP on a serial console.**
The proposal's last resort turns a BMC's serial-over-LAN into a slow IP
link, and to do it netrescue would have to take a tty from whatever owns it
-- the stick's getty on `ttyS0` and `ttyS1`, and the kernel's console
output, either of which corrupts PPP's frames. So it is a choice between a
serial login and a serial network, made per machine, with a timing
question beside it: after how many rounds of the ladder. **Best guess,
unbuilt:** opt-in, `--serial-ppp TTY`, started only after a full round
with no gateway, the stick's inittab leaving that tty without a getty.
Testing it needs `pppd` in a vm image, which the hwsim image lacks. The
driver rebind is 10.879 and the name 10.880. **The stick needs a DHCP client netcfgd drives** --
dhcpcd or busybox's udhcpc; its isc-dhcp-client is not one -- and should
not also run ifupdown on the same ports. **Ready to try on the stick**
(2026-11-20, after 10.880): the consumer was told so, with what it needs,
in its inbox (`~/claude`, 20261120T1752Z). What an HP G6's own NICs do
under it is that run's to find.

Two findings from building the stick, recorded as the proposal gave them:
ifupdown's `allow-hotplug /eth*=eth` pattern stanza does not answer the
boot script's or udev's `ifup eth0` ("ifup: unknown interface eth0",
measured under a hull pc boot 2026-11-20), where explicit per-name stanzas
do; and on a box with no COM2 an inittab getty on `ttyS1` respawns too
fast and prints on the console every five minutes, so the stick gates each
serial getty on `/proc/tty/driver/serial` showing a UART.

## 10.875 A report directory another account owns is read as untrusted

`report_writer` (10.863) gives a tunnel's report directory to the account a
daemon such as charon drops to -- Alpine's `ipsec` -- and root netcfgd reads
what is in it on every observation. It read with a plain `open`, so two things
that account could place there reached root:

- **a FIFO blocked the reader for good**: reproduced, `ncfg plan` over a run
  directory holding one in `reported.d/ipsec0/` was still waiting when a
  five-second timeout killed it, and the daemon reads the same files. The
  account a network-facing IKE daemon runs as could stop netcfgd.
- **a link was followed**, pointing root's read at any file on the machine;
  what the reader then keeps is only `address=`, `dns=` and the other
  report keys, but the read itself is the boundary crossed.

Report files are read with `ncfg_host_read_regular` now: `O_NOFOLLOW` and
`O_NONBLOCK` on the open, so neither a link nor a FIFO's missing writer is
waited on, then `fstat`, and nothing but a regular file is read; anything else
is skipped like an unreadable file. `ncfg_host_read_file` is unchanged for the
files root's own directories hold, where a link -- a `conf.d` file linked in
-- is ordinary. `c/tests/state_test.c` places a FIFO and a link beside a real
fragment under an alarm: only the fragment is read; with the plain open back,
the test dies on its alarm.

**And what the account writes inside a file is fuzzed now**:
`fuzz/interface_report`, the fourteenth target, asserts every kept value is a
string with no newline and no blank at either end, and every route has a
destination. Its first two minutes found the reader inconsistent with itself:
`trim` treats `\r` as a blank and `parse_route` split only on space and tab,
so a `\r` between a route's words stayed inside the destination -- a route the
planner would then refuse, so nothing worse, but a CRLF report losing routes
for it. Routes split on `\r` too; the input is in the corpus as
`regress-route-cr.txt`, and the next two minutes, 1.9 million runs, were clean.

The other two places netcfgd hands something to another account were read for
the same shape and already hold: a caller's document is created `O_EXCL |
O_NOFOLLOW` in a directory checked to be the caller's alone, and the control
socket gets only its group.

## 10.874 A router hands its network to netcfgd, held until confirmed

The aim is to take over cleanly from the manager a machine has, on procd as
on the other three, and on a router the switcher could not: it knew no
netifd and no procd, the OpenWrt packages did not ship it, and it undoes
nothing when the new manager brings up no network -- "nothing here has been
undone" -- which on a machine with a console is a message and on a router
with none is a lockout. 10.746 rejected taking netifd down on install for
that reason, and left which manager a router keeps to its operator.

So on procd, `netcfgd_select.sh netcfgd` is held, as commit-confirm holds an
apply (0163): netifd is stopped and left enabled, netcfgd started and not
enabled, and the switch recorded in `/var/run/netcfgd-select.pending`, on
tmpfs. `netcfgd_select.sh confirm` disables netifd and enables netcfgd;
without it, a watcher started with the switch -- HUP ignored, the terminal let
go, so the session a switch cuts does not take it along -- switches back when
the window ends, 120 s by default, `--confirm=N` to change, `--confirm=0`
for a switch made at once. A reboot inside the window comes up on netifd,
since nothing was disabled. **A new switch supersedes one that waits**: it
stops the watcher, drops the record and goes on. The first version refused it,
and the holder pointed out what that breaks: the switch back is the commonest
thing to want inside the window, and a script that runs `netcfgd_select.sh
netifd` -- or `none`, on removal -- would have failed for two minutes. Back to
netifd it is made at once, since netifd is still enabled; the same switch
again starts its window afresh. Each watcher acts only on a record carrying
its own token, so one a supersede failed to stop cannot wake and undo a newer
switch. **And it cannot fall back to the unconfirmed state it superseded**,
which the holder asked next: a held switch disables nothing, so until
`confirm` the last confirmed manager is the only one enabled, and every
switch computes its fallback afresh as that one. The same switch again, or a
switch to a third manager, falls back to netifd, never to the unconfirmed
netcfgd; only `confirm` or `--confirm=0` makes an unconfirmed manager stick.
The other rc systems are unchanged: their machines have a console.

`netifd` is a manager the switcher knows, as `/etc/init.d/network`, stood
down ahead of ifupdown, whose sweep takes every udhcpc not netcfgd's and on a
router would take netifd's own while netifd still ran. **procd's `stop`
returns before the process has gone**, measured: netifd still ran when the
switcher went on to start netcfgd, which reads a live netifd as holding its
interfaces. So on procd it waits, up to ten seconds, for procd to list the
service as not running.

`make hull-openwrt-select`, on the 128 MB OpenWrt 25.12 vm with stock netifd:
the held switch, a switch back inside the window made at once and left alone
by the first window's watcher, the same switch again, the window ending unconfirmed with
netifd back and netcfgd gone and nothing disabled, a confirmed switch that
outlasts its window, and the switch back. `tests/live/select.sh` (the
systemd paths, 50 checks) and the select gate pass unchanged. With the
watcher's switch-back made a no-op, the unconfirmed window goes red.

**Open: one failure not explained.** In the first run with the supersede, the
last step -- `netcfgd_select.sh netifd --confirm=0`, with nothing pending --
was reported failed, and the console line carrying it was torn, so its exit
status is not known. Its verdict, which holds the switcher's own output on a
failure, was overwritten by the next run before it was read. Five runs since,
27 of 27 each. Reading that path under `set -eu` found nothing that fails
transiently (`run` swallows a failed `kill`). Non-reproduction is not a
verdict on it; the next failure's `select:` lines are what to read.

## 10.873 `ncfg` waits for a daemon that is starting

Asked in the seconds after the daemon starts, before its node is open
(10.872), `ncfg` said "cannot reach the daemon at .../netcfgd.sock" -- a
socket a daemon with a node never binds (10.738) -- and that the daemon "has
to be running", while it was. A button script (`ncfg pair request`, 0320) or
a hotplug hook at boot is in exactly that window.

Now, where nothing answered and nothing ran but the run directory's
`netcfgd.lock` is held, `ncfg` waits up to ten seconds for the fuzznet face
or the control socket to appear and asks again; if neither does, it says the
daemon is running and has opened neither. A run directory nobody holds fails
at once, as before, and a request that may have run is never sent twice.

**Only a request that would otherwise fail waits.** `ncfg status` and `plan`
do the work themselves where no daemon answers, and they fall back at once as
they always did. The first version waited for them too, and
`c/tests/node_ram_host.sh` caught it: its daemon's fuzznet face is a socket
named elsewhere, never in the run directory, so `ncfg status` there had always
fallen back -- and now spent ten seconds first, past the test's own timeout.

**Whether the lock is held is read from `/proc/locks`, not by taking it.**
A shared lock taken to find out, however briefly, is one a daemon starting at
that moment meets with its non-blocking exclusive lock, and it would refuse to
start ("another netcfgd is running"). An unprivileged caller can read
`/proc/locks` and stat the 0600 file, so the answer does not depend on who
asks. `c/tests/ncfg_waits.sh` holds the lock with `flock(1)`: alone, `ncfg
reload` fails at once; held with nothing opening, it fails after ten seconds
naming the running daemon; held and then taken over by a real daemon, the
question asked during the hold gets the daemon's answer.

## 10.872 An IPsec tunnel runs on OpenWrt 25.12 under procd

`make hull-openwrt-ipsec`: the router is the guest's root namespace on
`hull-openwrt`'s image, with netcfgd's package and OpenWrt's own strongSwan
6.0.7, each under procd, and the far end a second charon in a network
namespace. The connection is an operator's `conf.d` file naming the hook the
package ships, with no `report_writer`. All twelve checks hold: OpenWrt's
`swanctl` service loads the file, its charon is uid 0, netcfgd makes ipsec0
with the if_id, `ncfg tunnel up` brings the child up, the hook writes the
report and the daemon puts `10.98.0.1/32` and `10.99.0.0/24` on ipsec0 by
itself, a ping is answered and counted leaving by ipsec0, and `ncfg tunnel
down` takes the address away.

What getting there found, each worth knowing on a router:

- **The OpenWrt packages did not carry the hook** (`59b0dd35`): they are
  built by `tool/openwrt_apk.sh` and `tool/ipk.sh`, not `make install`, so a
  router following doc/first-run.md section 11 named a command that was not
  there. Nor the example configuration (`3969461a`).
- **`strongswan-minimal` is not enough on 25.12.** charon needs its SHA-1
  hasher to start at all, and IKE fails `KDF_PRF with PRF_HMAC_SHA2_256 not
  supported` -- key derivation failed -- without `strongswan-mod-kdf`, which
  strongSwan 6 made a plugin and minimal does not pull in. An operator
  installs `strongswan-minimal strongswan-swanctl strongswan-mod-kdf` (the
  rig's list is minimal's, less `stroke`, plus vici and kdf).
- **The daemon answers `ncfg` a few seconds after procd starts it** on a
  machine this small, while its node opens; asked earlier, `ncfg` reported
  it missing. `ncfg` waits for it now (10.873); the rig still waits for
  `ncfg status` first, so its checks do not depend on that.

What the rig is not: strongSwan's files are unpacked with `apk extract`,
because OpenWrt's `strongswan` package depends on kmod packages for a kernel
the vm does not run -- the host's IPsec modules go in instead, as
`hull-openwrt`'s dummy does. The tunnel is split, so the vm's own uplink is
never routed into it; the full tunnel and the peer pin are
`tests/ipsec/e2e.sh`'s, in Alpine. 256 MB, not 128, for the far end's charon.

The control: the package built with an empty script for the hook leaves the
report unwritten, and the address, the route, the ping and the count on
ipsec0 go red -- four of twelve; "the virtual IP goes" passes there only
because it never came.

## 10.871 The window brings an IPsec tunnel up

`ncfg tunnel up|down` (10.864) had no control in the GUI, so a person who
uses the window and not a terminal could configure a tunnel and never connect
it. The devices tab now has `bring up` and `take down`, enabled on a row
whose document kind is `xfrm` and on nothing else -- by the document's kind,
which is what the daemon judges as well, since a tunnel the document does not
describe names no connection to ask for. They send `tunnel_set` through a new
`ncfg_client_tunnel_set`, which shares `radio_set`'s request builder: the two
requests carry the same two members. What the window says is what it asked,
not that the tunnel is up; the tunnel's addresses in `links` say that.
The TUI has them too, being these widgets (gui/project.md section 7a).

**The same for OpenVPN and WireGuard: the tier is decided by 0327; the mechanism is the holder's.** `tunnel_set`
answers only an `xfrm` device. netcfgd runs those two tunnels itself, so
"take it down" from the `wifi` tier would be that tier writing the
interface's `enabled`, as `radio_set` writes a `device` block -- precedent
for yes. It widens what the `wifi` tier may write, which sat inside the
deferred permission overhaul, so it was asked rather than built. **0327
answers it**: the `laptop` tier is defined as what a person at their own
machine needs, the VPN on and off among it. Until answered, neither has an
on/off control in `ncfg` or the window short of editing the file.

**Why it is not built, measured 2026-11-21.** Two things stand between the
tier and the switch, and the first is a language decision. *A drop-in cannot
change one key of an interface*: a second `interface wg0` block must say
`override`, and `override` replaces the block wholesale (merge.c, section 3)
-- so the radio's shape, a drop-in of its own written whole and removed
whole, has no `interface` to write without restating the operator's. The
options, each a change to the configuration language: (a) a block of its own
per interface, `switch wg0 { up = false }`, which a drop-in `tunnel-wg0`
holds as `radio-wlan0` holds a `device` block; (b) an explicit key-level
form, `amend interface wg0 { enabled = false }`, which section 3's rule
against *silent* last-wins does not forbid but which no block has had; (c) a
`global` list such as `held_down = ["wg0"]`, in one netcfgd-owned file
rewritten whole as `ncfg control set` writes `00-control`. (a) is the
recommendation: it is the radio's pattern, needs no read-modify-write, and
removing the file restores the operator's word. *And `enabled = false` only
takes the link down* (`plan_disable` in plan/link.c): a WireGuard link down
carries nothing, which is off; an `openvpn` daemon keeps running and keeps
its session behind a down `tun`, so "off" for OpenVPN also has to stop the
backend. Until the language question is answered, neither has an on/off
control short of editing the file.

On the devices tab rather than a tab of its own: the row is the tunnel's,
and a VPN tab with one kind in it would be the first of several kinds nobody
has asked to be gathered. `gui/tests/tunnel_buttons` drives it against a real
daemon and a recording swanctl; with the kind check removed and the up button
emptied, three of its nine checks fail.

## 10.870 Debian's strongSwan loads `conf.d` too, under systemd only, as root

0325 left open whether Debian's and OpenWrt's packages load
`/etc/swanctl/conf.d` as Alpine's does. Debian 13 (strongSwan 6.0.1),
measured in a `debian:trixie-slim` container from the packages themselves:
`charon-systemd` ships `strongswan.service`, which runs
`swanctl --load-all --noprompt` after start and on reload, and
`strongswan-swanctl`'s `swanctl.conf` ends `include conf.d/*.conf` -- the
same shape. The unit orders itself after `network-online.target`, which
`netcfgd-wait-online.service` provides.

Two differences matter to an operator:

- **There is no sysvinit or OpenRC script** in any of the four packages. On a
  Debian without systemd -- this host is one -- nothing starts a
  swanctl-loading charon, and the IPsec tunnel needs a service script of the
  operator's until Debian ships one. Not netcfgd's to fill: 0324 keeps
  running charon the init system's.
- **charon stays root.** Started in the container, `/usr/lib/ipsec/charon` ran
  as uid 0 with only `CAP_NET_ADMIN` effective, where Alpine's switches to the
  `ipsec` account. Its updown writes into root-owned `/run/netcfgd` as the
  owner, so `report_writer` is left out on Debian -- the case
  `doc/first-run.md` section 11 already names.

**OpenWrt 25.12.6 loads `conf.d` too, beside a file it writes from UCI.**
From its x86_64 packages (strongSwan 6.0.7), fetched and unpacked with the
tree's apk 3: `swanctl` is built with `/etc/swanctl` as its directory, and
`/etc/swanctl/swanctl.conf` ends with `include conf.d/*.conf` and
`include /var/swanctl/swanctl.conf`. The second is what the procd service
`swanctl` writes from UCI (`/etc/config/ipsec`), whose options include
`if_id` and `updown`; `--load-all` reads both, so an operator's `conf.d` file
works as 0325 says, and UCI is a second way to write the same three lines.
**Its charon stays root**, seen running since (10.872): uid 0 under procd.
The binaries had said so first -- the literal `ipsec` that Alpine's charon
carries for the account it switches to is in neither OpenWrt's `charon` nor
its `libcharon`.

## 10.869 `loop_test`'s roam check waits ten rounds, not two

The C suite failed one check once, "three joins are one roam", while
`make live-alpine` was building in a container beside it; alone,
`loop_test` passed thirteen runs of thirteen. The check gave the loop two
rounds, each bounded by its tick, for datagrams a fake supplicant sends from
another thread, so a loaded machine could end both before they arrived. What
it checks is that the joins come out as one roam, not how quickly another
thread is scheduled: ten rounds now, still stopping at the first that reports
one. Not reproduced under load on purpose -- the reading is from the code and
the one failure, which is recorded as such.

## 10.868 A report writer named for an existing tunnel takes effect at once

10.863 made the report directory with the device, so naming a `report_writer`
for a tunnel already up waited for the device's next remake while its updown
went on writing nothing. `ncfg_apply_report_dirs` prepares the directory for
every existing XFRM device that names one, and runs where the daemon adopts a
document and where a one-shot apply begins; a failure is said and does not
stop the document. Measured both ways in a namespace: a device made without
the key, the key added, and a one-shot apply with nothing to plan made the
directory; a daemon started on an existing device made it at start.
`tests/live/ipsec_report.sh` holds the one-shot case.

## 10.867 An IPsec tunnel authenticated as a commercial VPN is, measured

`tests/ipsec/eap.sh`: `fulltunnel.sh`'s full tunnel with the server proven by
an RSA certificate from a CA made with strongSwan's `pki`, and the client by
EAP-MSCHAPv2 against `eap_id = probe-user` and a password in strongSwan's
secrets, trusting the CA -- the shape of the holder's PrivadoVPN profile. In
Alpine 3.21 with strongSwan 5.9.14: the server's certificate verified, "EAP
method EAP_MSCHAPV2 succeeded", the child came up, the shipped `ipsec-updown`
reported the virtual IP, the default route and the peer, and pings through
`ipsec0` were answered before and after an IKE and a CHILD rekey. So the
authentication a provider hands out changes nothing on netcfgd's side, as 0325
expected; the guide says so now rather than that it was not run. Its first
attempt made ed25519 keys and `pki --pub` would not read them; RSA is what the
probe uses.

## 10.866 `ncfg tunnel up|down`: strongSwan asked from netcfgd

10.864's design, built. The `xfrm` block gains `connection` and `child`, and a
request `tunnel_set` (`interface`, `activate`, `radio_set`'s two members) asks
the daemon to run `swanctl --initiate --child <child> --ike <connection>` or
`--terminate --ike <connection>`. In the `wifi` tier, beside joining a
network: a device name and up or down, no configuration text (0117). **Started
detached and not waited for**: an initiate waits for IKE, and every request is
answered on the loop's thread (0111), so the answer is the protocol's `ok` and
what comes of it arrives as the tunnel's report. Refused by name for a device
that is not an `xfrm` one, for a block naming no connection (or, for up, no
child), and where `swanctl` is not installed; `NCFG_SWANCTL` names another
program, as `NCFG_OPENVPN` does. `ncfg tunnel up|down IFACE` is the client.

`tests/live/ipsec_report.sh` runs the daemon with a `swanctl` that records what
it is asked: up asks for the child of the connection, down terminates the
connection, and a device that is not a tunnel is refused naming it; with
`--child` dropped from the up command, the check fails. The socket witness
gains the request's line (69 now), the document witness the two keys -- an
addition each, minor under 0020; both keys classified ordinary; `proto_test`,
`authorize_test` and `idempotence_test` carry the kind. The guide's section 11
says how. The first version answered with a sentence where the protocol wants
JSON, and the client said "a number with no digits at byte 0" -- the live test
is what caught it.

## 10.865 The container tiers unpack the sources rather than copy the tree

`make live-alpine` and `make live-container` ran `cp -a /src /work` inside the
container, and the tree is 3.2 GB with its build output -- hull's images, the
GUI's Android builds, `.git` -- while a container's writable layer is the
host's `/`, at 94% on ml350g6-01 (10.862's probe met it first and was killed).
Now the recipe makes `dist/live-src.tar` of what git knows -- tracked files,
every submodule's, and untracked ones nothing ignores, 58 MB -- with
`--no-recursion` so a submodule's directory entry cannot bring its build output
back, mounts it, unpacks it, and removes it after the run whatever the result.

Measured on `live-alpine`: unpacked, built, 85 scripts run, the tar removed.
Two failed, and neither was the copy. `select.sh` failed eighteen checks
because the Alpine image has no `/etc/init.d` for its sysvinit and OpenRC passes
(10.842, 10.845) to mount a tmpfs over, so their namespace died and every
count read zero; those passes now run only where `/etc/init.d` exists, saying
so where it does not. `c_supplicant_settings.sh` failed because Alpine 3.21's
wpa_supplicant refuses the `SAE` and `FT-` key managements -- that image's
build, recorded and not changed here.

## 10.864 Bringing a tunnel up from ncfg: what it needs to know, measured

0325 left `ncfg` unable to bring a tunnel up or down. Before the design:
does `swanctl --initiate --ike <connection>` bring the connection's children up
with it? Measured on `tests/ipsec/fulltunnel.sh`'s setup in Alpine 3.21:
**no** -- "initiate completed successfully" and no CHILD_SA; and
`--terminate --ike <connection>` took everything down. So bringing a tunnel
up needs the child's name, and taking it down only the connection's.

The design that follows, not built: the `xfrm` block gains `connection` and
`child` -- what `swanctl --initiate --child <child> --ike <connection>` and
`--terminate --ike <connection>` take -- and a typed request (0117's shape: no
configuration text, a device name and up or down) runs those two as root, in
the `wifi` tier beside joining a network, since connecting the VPN is the same
kind of act for a person at their own machine. A new request kind is an
addition to the frozen socket protocol, a minor bump (0020), with its witness
line and ledger row. Waits on nothing but the work.

## 10.863 netcfgd gives a tunnel's report directory to charon's account

10.862's open step. `device ipsec0 { xfrm { if_id = 7; report_writer = "ipsec" } }`:
when netcfgd makes the device it makes `reported.d/ipsec0/` and gives it to
that account (`chown`, mode 0755), so a charon that runs its updown as
`ipsec` -- Alpine's, measured -- can write that interface's addressing and
nothing else. Named rather than guessed, because the account is the
distribution's build choice. Resolved from `/etc/passwd` as a file, as
`tun { owner }` is, and refused by name where there is no such account rather
than falling back to root. Privileged, as `tun { owner }` is
(`NCFG_PRIV_PRINCIPAL`): it hands a device's state to a principal.

`tests/ipsec/e2e.sh` with the key and no hand-made directory, in Alpine 3.21
with netcfgd built for musl: the directory is `ipsec`'s, the updown writes the
report, netcfgd applies the virtual IP, the tunnel's default and the peer's
pin, two packets leave by `ipsec0` and are answered before and after both
rekeys, a second plan is empty, and the teardown restores the uplink's routes.
Without the key the same run wrote no report (10.862). In a namespace, an
account with no entry fails the create naming it.

A `report_writer` added to a device that already exists is prepared when the
document is taken up rather than at the device's next remake (10.868).

## 10.862 netcfgd and strongSwan in one run, and the account charon's updown runs as

`tests/ipsec/e2e.sh` builds netcfgd for musl inside Alpine 3.21 and runs the
full tunnel of `fulltunnel.sh` with netcfgd doing its part: it makes the XFRM
interface, the shipped `ipsec-updown` writes the report, and `ncfg apply` takes
the virtual IP, the tunnel's default route and the peer's pin from it. Then:
the internet host routes by `ipsec0` and two packets are counted out of it,
pings are answered before and after an IKE and a CHILD rekey, a second plan
has nothing to do, and terminating the tunnel empties the report and the next
apply puts the routes back as they were -- `default via 198.51.100.1 dev c0`
and nothing else.

**Only with the report directory handed to charon's account by hand**, and
that is the finding. On Alpine charon runs the updown as `ipsec` (uid 100)
with no capabilities, measured by a trace in front of the hook -- so in
netcfgd's root-owned run directory `mkdir -p reported.d/ipsec0` fails, and
the hook, which exits 0 whatever happens so as never to disturb charon, wrote
nothing. The earlier probes passed only because their run directory did not
exist yet and `/tmp` let anyone create it. Before that was understood, two
runs reported success they had not earned: the pings were answered OUTSIDE
the tunnel, because the server answers there too -- the script counts packets
on `ipsec0` and names the device now.

**Settled since, by 10.863** (`report_writer`), and hardened by 10.875; what
follows is what this entry said while it was open. The account is
the distribution's choice (Alpine builds charon to drop to `ipsec`; whether
OpenWrt's and Debian's run it as root is unmeasured), so it is named rather
than guessed -- an `xfrm` key such as `report_writer = "ipsec"`, privileged,
with netcfgd making `reported.d/<interface>/` that account's when it makes
the device, so the account can write that interface's addressing and nothing
else. The alternative is netcfgd reading charon's SAs as root
(`swanctl --list-sas`), which needs no account and polls; 0324 set it aside.
Also: the first run of this copied the whole 3.2 GB tree into the container,
whose writable layer is the host's `/` at 94%, and was killed short of filling
it; it copies the C build's 81 MB of sources now.

## 10.861 strongSwan's service loads the connection; netcfgd owns the device (0325)

10.857 planned for netcfgd to load the operator's file with `swanctl`. Measured
first, in Alpine 3.21 with `openrc`: the `charon` service runs `swanctl
--load-all` after starting charon, and `swanctl.conf` includes `conf.d/*.conf`;
it needs `net`, which netcfgd's OpenRC script provides. So
[0325](doc/decision/0325-strongswans-own-service-loads-the-connection-and-netcfgd-owns-the-tunnel-device.md):
the connection and its secrets live in `/etc/swanctl/conf.d/`, strongSwan's
service loads them, and netcfgd loads nothing into charon -- a second loader of
one directory would be a second owner of one charon. netcfgd's part is the
device, its addressing and the peer's pin, and the file binds itself to it with
three lines: `if_id_in`, `if_id_out`, `updown`. The EAP secret is strongSwan's,
not an `@secret:`. OpenWrt's and Debian's services are not measured.

**What is open for IPsec now**: bringing a tunnel up and down from `ncfg` (a
typed request running `swanctl --initiate`/`--terminate`, for the wifi tier);
netcfgd and strongSwan in one run, which wants a hull guest with `swanctl`;
and `install_virtual_ip = no` in charon's settings, which is the operator's to
set and which the guide will have to say.

## 10.860 netcfgd pins a full tunnel's peer to the uplink

10.859 measured that a full tunnel carries nothing unless its peer has a host
route by the uplink. Now the report says who the peer is -- `peer=`, written by
`ipsec-updown` from `PLUTO_PEER`, the contract's "unknown keys are ignored"
letting the writer add it before any reader -- and netcfgd pins it.

**On the uplink, in the uplink's own route list.** When `ncfg_plan_routes_for`
builds an interface's routes it also appends, for every report it acts on that
takes the default route and names a peer, a host route to that peer by the
best-metric default route of the peer's family that is not itself such a
tunnel's -- read from the kernel, since an uplink's default is very often a
DHCP client's and not the document's -- where that route is on this interface.
One list for the forward pass and the teardown (the function's own rule), so
when the tunnel goes down and its report stops taking the default, the pin is
no longer in the list and is withdrawn like any route the document dropped.

`tests/live/ipsec_report.sh` against the kernel: with `default via 192.0.2.1
dev up0 metric 100` installed as a DHCP client would, a full-tunnel child's
report puts `default dev ipsec0` in and `198.51.100.1 via 192.0.2.1 dev up0`
beside it; `ip route get` sends the peer by `up0` and everything else by
`ipsec0`; a second plan has nothing to do; down, the pin goes and the uplink's
own default stays. With the pin switched off, the live check fails.
`plan_reported_test` holds it without a kernel, and a report with no peer
pins nothing. The observed witness carries `peers`: a field added, minor.

Not covered: an uplink netcfgd does not manage -- the pin is planned in the
uplink's own list, so an interface outside the document gets none, and the
tunnel then carries nothing as before. The netcfgd binary here is glibc and
the strongSwan probe's container is musl, so the two have met through the
report and the measured route shape rather than in one run; hull's Alpine or
OpenWrt guests are where they meet.

## 10.859 A full tunnel needs its peer pinned to the uplink, measured

10.858's open question, answered by `tests/ipsec/fulltunnel.sh` in Alpine 3.21
with strongSwan 5.9.14: all of IPv4 into the XFRM interface, the peer reached
only by a default route (host addresses and `onlink` routes, since a
container's `/proc/sys` is read-only and nothing in it forwards), the shipped
`ipsec-updown` writing the report, and what netcfgd does with it done by hand --
the virtual IP on `ipsec0` and `default dev ipsec0` at metric 50, under the
uplink's 100.

- **Without a route to the peer, IKE works and the tunnel carries nothing.**
  The peer resolves to `dev ipsec0`; both an IKE and a CHILD rekey completed
  with no retransmits -- charon's own packets get out -- while pings through
  the tunnel went unanswered: the ESP packets to the peer route back into
  `ipsec0`.
- **With `198.51.100.1/32` by the uplink, added first, it all works**: pings
  answered before and after both rekeys.

So a tunnel whose report carries a default route needs a host route to its
peer by whatever reached the peer before -- which netcfgd, not charon, has to
install, since netcfgd puts the default route there. The updown command knows
the peer (`PLUTO_PEER`). Next: the report gains `peer=`, which the contract's
"unknown keys are ignored" lets the writer add first, and netcfgd pins it.

Also found: **charon runs the updown command with an environment of its own
making**, so `NCFG_RUN_DIR` set where charon started never arrives -- the probe's
report went under charon's own `/run`. The command now takes a run directory
after the interface; the default is right on a real machine.

## 10.858 IPsec, step three begins: the updown command writes the report (0324)

`packaging/hooks/ipsec-updown`, installed as `libexec/netcfgd/ipsec-updown`.
A child of the operator's `swanctl.conf` names it with the interface --
`updown = /usr/libexec/netcfgd/ipsec-updown ipsec0`, beside `if_id_in` and
`if_id_out` -- and charon runs it on the child's way up and down. On
`up-client` it writes `reported.d/ipsec0/<child>`: the virtual IP as a host
address (`PLUTO_MY_SOURCEIP`, or every `PLUTO_MY_SOURCEIP4_n`/`6_n` where
several were given), the far side's subnet as a route (`PLUTO_PEER_CLIENT`,
`0.0.0.0/0` spelled `default`), and any nameservers charon was given
(`PLUTO_DNS4_n`/`6_n`). On `down-client` it empties the fragment. **A fragment
per child, not the single file**: one interface can carry several child SAs,
and with one file each replaces the last -- measured, the sabotage below. An
interface name that is not one, or walks a path, writes nothing.

With `interface ipsec0 { config = "reported" }` that is all it takes today:
`tests/live/ipsec_report.sh`, in a namespace and in `make live`, drives the
command with the environment the probe recorded for two children, applies,
and finds the XFRM interface with the virtual IP and both subnets routed into
it; one child down takes its route and leaves the other's, both down take the
address. With the command writing the single file instead, five checks fail.

**Measured since, by 10.859, and built in 10.860**: a full tunnel needs its
peer pinned to the uplink, and netcfgd pins it. What follows is what this
entry said while it was open. The holder's PrivadoVPN
profile sends all of IPv4 through the tunnel, which reports `route=default` on
`ipsec0` -- and IKE's own packets to the peer must still leave by the uplink,
not into the tunnel they are negotiating. Whether charon's socket bypass
policies keep them out with an XFRM interface, or a host route to the peer is
needed, is for the probe with `remote_ts = 0.0.0.0/0`.

## 10.857 IPsec, step two: strongSwan's half, measured (0324)

0323 left the IKE half to measurement, and this host's strongSwan has no vici
and no `swanctl`, so `tests/ipsec/probe.sh` measures it in Alpine 3.21
(strongSwan 5.9.14): two namespaces, a charon each, IKEv2 with a pre-shared
key, a virtual IP from the server's pool, the client's child SA on step one's
XFRM interface by `if_id`. The SAs carry `if_id 0x7`; charon puts the virtual
IP on `ipsec0` with `install_virtual_ip_on`, or with `install_virtual_ip = no`
reports it over vici and installs nothing -- and placed from outside, as
netcfgd will, the far side answers through the tunnel either way.
`tests/ipsec/twin.sh`: two charons in one namespace, and the second cannot
bind IKE's port. And a child's `updown` command is handed the virtual IP, the
`if_id` and the peer's subnets (`PLUTO_MY_SOURCEIP`, `PLUTO_IF_ID_IN`,
`PLUTO_PEER_CLIENT`) on `up-client`.

So [0324](doc/decision/0324-netcfgd-drives-the-machines-charon-and-places-the-virtual-ip-itself.md):
netcfgd drives the machine's one charon and does not run its own, and each
tunnel's virtual IP reaches its interface through the interface report, which
an updown command netcfgd ships writes -- the operator's child names it beside
the `if_id` lines it needs anyway. No vici client is needed to read anything.
Still to measure: an EAP secret handed over vici rather than written in the
file, which needs a server certificate in the probe. Step three builds
netcfgd's side: the updown command (10.858) -- and, it turned out, not the
loading, which strongSwan's own service does (10.861).

Found on the way, and worth the next person's time: `swanctl.conf` takes no
`;` between keys -- `local { auth = psk; id = srv }` loads as one value and the
whole connection is discarded ("invalid value for: auth"); a relative
`include` in a `strongswan.conf` named by `STRONGSWAN_CONF` resolves against
that file's directory, so charon loaded no plugins and aborted; and a
policy-based server's replies need some route to a device before its policy
takes them.

## 10.856 IPsec, step one: the XFRM interface (0323)

The holder, 2026-11-14: if nothing else is left, do IPsec. [0323](doc/decision/0323-an-ipsec-tunnel-is-an-xfrm-interface-and-the-swanctl-file-is-the-operators.md)
gives the shape: a route-based tunnel, an XFRM interface netcfgd makes, so the
tunnel is an interface like every other; strongSwan driven through `swanctl`,
the connection file the operator's as the `.ovpn` is (0046). This is the
first step, and the one that does not wait on the IKE half.

`device ipsec0 { xfrm { if_id = 7 } }` makes `ip link add ipsec0 type xfrm
if_id 7`: a new device kind, `xfrm`, with one required non-zero key (the kernel
refuses 0, and an IKE connection reaches the device only by the same id).
**The id is observed and compared**: it is fixed at creation, and a device with
another id binds to no SA the connection makes -- up, addressed, carrying
nothing -- so an edited or foreign id is a remake, as a VLAN's id is (0059).
Observed as `xfrm_if_id` on the link, read from `IFLA_XFRM_IF_ID`.

Checked: `lower_test` (an id required, 0 refused); `plan_kind_test` (another
id is a delete and a create naming `xfrm.if_id`, the same id nothing);
`tests/live/links.sh` against the kernel (created with `if_id 0x7` and its
address, edited to 8 and remade with the address back, then nothing to do).
With the comparison removed, both the unit check and the live one fail. The
schema witnesses gain a `k-xfrm` device and the observed field: a variant and
a field added, a minor bump (0020). `bare_ifb`'s size assertion moved to 616.
The suite's own coverage caught two more: the document reader took `if_id = 0`,
which renders a profile the compiler then refuses (its range starts at 1 now),
and the ledger's `link.create`-per-kind witness had to move by hand, as it is
written to. `if_id` is classified ordinary (`tool/privilege-ordinary.txt`):
making a tunnel device is configuring the network, as a VLAN's id or a VRF's
table is.

**Next**, in 0323's order: measure strongSwan's half in a container (Alpine
has `swanctl` and the vici plugin; this host has neither) -- whether netcfgd
runs its own charon, how a virtual IP reaches the interface, and where the
EAP secret goes.

## 10.855 A process any user can start is not evidence of a network manager

10.848 to 10.850 believe connman, iwd and a manager dhcpcd from their processes
-- a name, and for iwd and dhcpcd a command line. **Any local user can start a
process called `iwd`, `connmand` or `dhcpcd`** with whatever command line they
like, and a believed claim makes the supplicant's guard decline to start Wi-Fi
on the radio. So an unprivileged user could switch netcfgd's Wi-Fi off with a
renamed `sleep` -- for connman wherever `/etc/connman` exists, which it does
after a takeover has stopped connman; for iwd and dhcpcd anywhere. Found by
asking who controls each input the new readers trust, which is the question
the fuzz target for them started from.

Now those three are believed only when the system runs them: the process owned
by root, or for dhcpcd by dhcpcd's own user (`dhcpcd`, or `_dhcpcd`), which is
what its manager runs as under privilege separation. A fixture's fake `/proc`
belongs to whoever made it, so the owner of `/proc` counts as root; on the
machine that is root. NetworkManager, networkd and netifd are unchanged: their
claim is a file only root writes, and a process is asked only whether that
file's writer still runs -- networkd as its own user -- so a spoofed one can at
most keep a stale root-written claim alive.

## 10.854 The router test's resolver step waits for the line it checks

`hull-malta` failed at load 30 in `restart.sh`'s resolver step: the wait for
netcfgd to rewrite `lan4.conf` was `grep -q '192.168.7.1'`, which the range's
`192.168.7.100` already matched, so it ended at once ("after 0 s") and the
check ran mid-reload with the file still offering `.53`. The wait and the check
now share one pattern, anchored at the line's end and written for `grep -E`,
since BusyBox's grep on OpenWrt is musl's regex, where `\|` in a basic
expression is not to be relied on; checked against both file states with GNU
grep and with BusyBox in `alpine:3.21`.

## 10.853 `network_arrives.sh` waits for the disable it then reads

At load 33 `make live` failed three checks after `DISABLE [DISABLED] HomeFiber`:
`ncfg status` ran a fixed second later and read the radio before the disable
had reached it, while the script run alone passed. The status path touches
none of this day's contention work. It now waits, bounded by the script's own
`awaits` at fifteen seconds, for status to name HomeFiber, and the checks read
the status taken after; a disable that never shows still fails them. Three runs
alone, all 22.

## 10.852 A sandbox that cannot read pid 1's namespace is not on the host

`make live` after 10.851 failed eight checks in `tui.py`: the plan and events
panes missing, apply's window never shown. The same tree at the start of the
day passed under the same load (45), so it was today's. Inside `unshare -rn`
the TUI's own plan asked the contention check, which asks whether the host's
`/run` is about this namespace by comparing ours with pid 1's -- and pid 1's
`ns/net` cannot be read from a child user namespace, and an unreadable one was
read as "ours". So this host's running connman claimed the test's interface,
and the warning filled the panes. The reading predates 10.848; the new
contenders made it visible.

A root netcfgd can always read pid 1's namespace, and an ordinary user on the
host cannot and is in the machine's namespace all the same, so for both the
answer stays "ours". The process that cannot read it and is not on the host is
one in a child user namespace, so that case is decided by `/proc/self/uid_map`:
the first user namespace maps all of uid space onto itself (`0 0 4294967295`)
and nothing else does. `tui.py` passes; with the decision forced to "ours", the
new check fails.

## 10.851 A fixture's run root takes the machine's `/etc` out of the question

`make live` after 10.848 failed three checks in `network_arrives.sh`: the
daemon never joined the network it was asked to. The script names a fixture
run root (`NCFG_RUN_ROOT`), which switches off the namespace question -- and
`/proc` and `/etc` stayed this host's, where connman runs and `/etc/connman`
exists. So the new connman read claimed the fixture's simulated radio, and the
supplicant guard declined to start a supplicant on it.

The product was not wrong -- unset, a netcfgd in another namespace asks
nothing -- but a named run root is a fixture, and the machine's `/etc` is not
part of it. Now naming one, in the daemon and in `ncfg plan`, sets `etc_root`
to none, so connman, dhcpcd and netifd are not asked; and iwd, judged from a
