process's options rather than a file, is asked only where `etc_root` is given,
as the three that describe the machine as a whole. `network_arrives.sh`: 22 of
22. An unnamed run on this host still warns that connman and ifupdown hold
`eth0`.

## 10.850 A dhcpcd running as a manager is a contender, and ifupdown-ng is ifupdown

The shape of 10.848 and 10.849 once more: dhcpcd started with no interface is a
whole network manager -- Raspberry Pi OS's until bookworm, and many minimal
installs' -- taking every interface its configuration does not leave out. It
contends with the dhcpcd clients netcfgd starts per interface, and nothing
here read it.

**Told apart from netcfgd's own by its title**, because dhcpcd retitles itself
and its arguments are gone. Measured with dhcpcd 10.1 in a namespace: the
manager is `dhcpcd: [manager] [ip4]`, one started on an interface `dhcpcd: d0
[ip4]`, and the helpers of either `dhcpcd: [privileged proxy] ...`; before 10
the word was `[master]`. netcfgd starts dhcpcd only on an interface, so a
manager is never netcfgd's. Its claim is every interface but the loopback that
`/etc/dhcpcd.conf`'s `denyinterfaces` does not match and, where
`allowinterfaces` appears, that it does -- fnmatch patterns separated by spaces
or commas, as dhcpcd.conf(5) gives them; Docker's own advice for Raspberry Pi
OS is `denyinterfaces veth*`, which is the case. The remedy is that key. An
unreadable `/proc` finds no manager: the title is the only evidence.

`contention_test` holds a manager with `denyinterfaces`, an older `[master]`
with `allowinterfaces`, and a per-interface dhcpcd that is not one; with the
configuration or the title not read, two checks fail each.

**And ifupdown-ng, Alpine's default `networking`**, which 10.843's ifupdown
read missed: it keeps `/run/ifstate` rather than `/run/network/ifstate`, with
lines `d0=d0 1 explicit`. Measured in `alpine:3.21` with ifupdown-ng installed:
`ifup -a` wrote `lo` and `d0`, `ifdown d0` took its line away. Both files are
read now, the name before `=` the claim in each.

## 10.849 iwd is a contender for radios, read from its command line

The same shape a third time: a daemon that takes interfaces unless told not
to, which no check here read. iwd holds every wireless interface unless started
with `-i LIST` (`--interfaces`, only these) or `-I LIST` (`--nointerfaces`, all
but these), each a comma-separated list of fnmatch patterns; it keeps no state
file, so its command line is the claim. It uses no wpa_supplicant control
socket, so the supplicant guard -- "a socket netcfgd did not bind" -- could not
see it, and netcfgd would start its own supplicant on a radio iwd was driving.

A contention claim now says whether it is a radio (`link->wireless` where the
plan and the daemon build claims; always, where the supplicant's start asks),
and a running `iwd` claims the radios its options leave it, read from
`/proc/<pid>/cmdline` with the value joined (`-iwlan0`, `--interfaces=...`) or
following. A cmdline that cannot be read keeps the guard. An unreadable `/proc`
names no pid, so iwd is not asked then -- unlike the file-backed daemons there
is nothing else to read, and the socket check still stands. The remedy is
`--nointerfaces` for that radio, or stopping iwd. `contention_test` holds no
options, `-I` with a pattern, `--interfaces=` and a joined `-i`.

## 10.848 connman is a contender, read from what its configuration leaves it

10.843 left connman out because it keeps no per-interface state outside D-Bus.
But what it holds is settled by its configuration, as netifd's is: **every
interface it has a technology for, except names starting with an entry of
`NetworkInterfaceBlacklist`** in `/etc/connman/main.conf`, whose default is
connman's own list -- vmnet, vboxnet, virbr, ifb, ve-, vb-. Not `veth` and not
`docker`, which is exactly why connman on ml350g6-01 numbered docker's veth
from 169.254 and gave it a default route.

So with `connmand` running, an interface netcfgd is configured for and the list
does not spare is connman's claim; the remedy is adding it to the list and
restarting connman. The loopback is never one, and **only the Ethernet-like kinds are**: connman
decides by the kernel's device type and gives no technology to a bridge,
WireGuard, VXLAN or VRF device -- the first probe on ml350g6-01 reported
`docker0`, which connman had left unnumbered while it numbered docker's veth.
So a claim now carries its link's rtnetlink kind, and connman's are physical,
veth, VLAN, bond and macvlan: an allowlist, because a kind missing from it
costs a warning not given, and one wrongly on it a warning about a fight that
is not happening. Where `/proc` cannot be read -- which makes every daemon
"running", the guard's direction -- `/etc/connman` has to exist as well, or a
machine that never had connman would be told it does.

On ml350g6-01, probed with this code against its own `/run`, `/proc` and
`/etc`: connman holds `eth0` and `eth2` (it raised the idle ports), not
`docker0`; ifupdown holds `eth0`.

`contention_test` holds the default list with a bridge among the claims, a configured one (spaces and a
commented line aside), a stopped connman and a machine with no `/etc/connman`;
with the list read as sparing everything, three fail.

## 10.847 `ncfg pair open` restarts the daemon on a router too

The same lens -- **a path written for systemd alone** -- run over the C's own
calls of `systemctl`: `ncfg pair open` (10.726) writes `conf.d/remote.conf` and
restarts the daemon, since the tiers and the port are read at start, and it did
so only where `/run/systemd/system` exists. A router has no systemd, and the
appliance is exactly where pairing is for (0320), so there it printed "Open,
once netcfgd restarts" and left the port closed until something else restarted
it. Now, without systemd, `/etc/init.d/netcfgd restart` -- which procd's
`rc.common`, OpenRC and this tree's sysvinit script all answer -- and still
only for the machine's own daemon (default run directory, as root).

Held on the router tier: `tests/hull/malta/guest.sh` runs `ncfg pair open`
against netcfgd under procd and asks for a new process serving `0xBBDA`.

The other `systemctl`s in messages (`daemon/wifi.c`, `supplicant/launch.c`)
tell somebody to stop NetworkManager and its supplicant; they are advice, not
an action, and name the case they were written for, so they stay.
`doc/first-run.md` gained the sysvinit install target in step 4 and, in section
8, `netcfgd_select.sh netcfgd` as the whole of the takeover without systemd.

## 10.846 A missing interface names the card port that explains it

ml350g6-01's `/etc/network/interfaces` configures `ib0` while both ConnectX
ports run Ethernet, and the plan said only "ib0 is configured but no such
device is present". The observation already held the card's ports (10.586);
the warning now uses them: a missing `ib*` name where VPI ports run Ethernet
says so and names their interfaces (`eth2, eth3` here), and a missing
Ethernet name where a port runs InfiniBand names that port and points at
`ncfg status`, which says how to switch it. With no card ports the warning is
the bare one. `plan_setting_test` holds all three; with the reason switched
off, two fail.

And `ncfg plan` now takes the contention seam the daemon already read,
`NCFG_RUN_ROOT` and `NCFG_PROC`: run bare, `tests/live/c_warnings.sh` read this
host's `/run` and gained "ifupdown also manages eth0" the day 10.843 landed.
Under `make live` it runs in its own network namespace, where the check stands
aside, so only a bare run saw it; the script names an empty run root now.

## 10.845 The switcher asks which rc system runs, not which is installed

Running `netcfgd_select.sh --dry-run netcfgd` on ml350g6-01 as the user, after
10.842, previewed a switch that stopped connman and disabled nothing. Two
causes, and the second corrected 10.842 itself.

- **An ordinary user's PATH has no `/usr/sbin`**, where `update-rc.d` and
  `rc-update` live, so the preview -- the command the postinst tells a person
  to try -- never showed the disabling root's run does. The script appends
  `/usr/sbin:/sbin` to PATH now.
- **This machine boots by OpenRC under sysvinit**: `/etc/init.d/rc` is
  OpenRC's wrapper, `/run/openrc` is live and the services are in
  `/etc/runlevels/default`, while `/etc/rc?.d` holds links nothing reads.
  Debian and Devuan package OpenRC beside sysv-rc, so `rc-update` being
  installed says nothing about which one boots -- and choosing by it, as the
  switcher did, edits runlevels nothing reads on a sysv-rc machine with the
  package beside it. It now asks `/run/openrc`, which OpenRC writes when it
  runs. `tests/live/select.sh` runs the sysv-rc pass with `rc-update` on PATH
  and asserts none of it is called, and the OpenRC pass asserts no
  `update-rc.d`; with the old choice, the sysv-rc pass fails 14 checks.

And a race made noise: the process scan read `/proc/<pid>/comm` with
`< file 2>/dev/null`, which opens the file before stderr is redirected, so
every process that exited during the walk printed an error -- dozens on a
loaded machine. The redirections are the other way round.

On ml350g6-01 the dry run now reads `rc-service connman stop`, `rc-update del
connman default`, the same for `networking` and `dhcpcd`, and nothing else.

## 10.843 ifupdown is a contender, and the remedy has a sysvinit half

10.842's survey, read once more for the shape of its fault -- **a check that
covers some of the managers it means to cover** -- found a second instance.
`ncfg_contenders_find`, which warns when another daemon manages an interface
netcfgd is configured for, read NetworkManager, systemd-networkd and netifd. On
ml350g6-01 ifupdown holds `eth0` through its `dhclient`, and a netcfgd
configured for `eth0` planned DHCP on it and said nothing of the second client.

Now ifupdown is read from `<run>/network/ifstate`: `ifup` writes
`PHYSICAL=LOGICAL` and `ifdown` takes the line away, and the physical name is
the claim, mapped or bare. **No process is checked**, unlike the other three:
ifupdown has no daemon, and the file is in `/run`, so a boot clears it. The
remedy is `ifdown` and the stanza out of `/etc/network/interfaces`, since an
`allow-hotplug` stanza brings it back otherwise. The machine-wide advice, which
named only systemd's drop-in, now also names `netcfgd_select.sh netcfgd` for a
machine without systemd -- 10.842's fix.

Run against this machine: the plan for `eth0` now warns "ifupdown also manages
eth0". `contention_test` gains five checks; with the read disabled, two fail.
connman was left out here, as publishing no per-interface state outside D-Bus;
10.848 reads it from its configuration instead, as netifd is read. The switcher stands it down.

## 10.842 ml350g6-01 against netcfgd: what it has, and the switcher's sysvinit half

**Asked by the holder 2026-11-13: is everything this machine and its network do
supported by netcfgd already?** Read from the machine, read-only, and planned:
a configuration describing it, `ncfg plan` against the live kernel as the user.

What it runs: Devuan 6, kernel 6.12, sysvinit as pid 1 and **OpenRC as the rc
system** -- `/etc/init.d/rc` is OpenRC's wrapper and the services are in
`/etc/runlevels/default`; the `/etc/rc?.d` links are present and not what boots.
This entry first read those links and called it plain sysvinit; 10.845 corrects
it. `eth0` takes DHCPv4
from 10.0.0.1, by ifupdown's `dhclient`; `eth1` (onboard) and `eth2`/`eth3` (the
ConnectX-3 Pro, both ports Ethernet, RoCE device `rocep5s0`) are up with no
carrier and nothing configured. `/etc/network/interfaces` also has `ib0`
static 10.1.0.5/24, which does not exist: the ports run Ethernet (10.586).
Alongside: **connman, running too**, which owns `/etc/resolv.conf` through its
DNS proxy on 127.0.0.1 and ::1, gave docker's veth a 169.254 address and a
default route, and keeps a profile directory for every veth it has ever seen --
11,796 under `/var/lib/connman`, most of them the live suites' veths. dhcpcd's
init script is enabled at boot and not running. docker (`docker0`), libvirt
(its `default` network not autostarted), VirtualBox, nftables and
netfilter-persistent at boot (`/etc/nftables.conf` begins `flush ruleset`, in
rcS, before any runlevel-2 service), OpenVPN with PrivadoVPN profiles and
nothing autostarted, strongSwan with one IKEv2 EAP connection `auto=add`,
avahi, ntpsec, opensm, iwpmd, Bluetooth, ofono and dundee, hostapd's script
with no configuration. No Wi-Fi interface.

**Served by netcfgd today:** `eth0`'s DHCP (planned as `dhcp4`, nothing else
wanted); the resolver file connman writes now (`write_resolv_conf`, or
dnsmasq/unbound); docker's, libvirt's and VirtualBox's own interfaces and
tables, which netcfgd leaves as foreign and does not touch (0318; `docker*`,
`veth*`, `virbr*` out of connectivity); the ConnectX's port types, read and
reported (10.586); an OpenVPN profile as an `openvpn` device (0046); the
sysvinit script (10.183). The leftover `bond0`, `dummy0`, `ifb0/1` and the
tunnel devices are the modules' own defaults from loading, not configuration.

**Not served, each already a decision:** IPsec -- strongSwan's IKEv2 client --
is 0036's end stage, not built; netcfgd would leave strongSwan running as it
is. Asked whether to start it now, the holder, 2026-11-13: not wanted right
now. IPoIB (`ib0`) is not being built (10.586), and nothing here needs it.
Setting a port's type is 10.586's open half. opensm, iwpmd, NTP and mDNS are
not networking configuration and stay their own daemons.

**The fault, and it was netcfgd's: a takeover without systemd went by the
switcher's own names, and under sysv-rc did not last past a reboot.**
`netcfgd_select.sh` -- what the deb's postinst runs -- used `rc-update` where
it was installed, and otherwise only *stopped* `/etc/init.d/<name>`, in both
cases with `<name>` the switcher's own word for the manager. So everywhere
without systemd ifupdown was asked for as `ifupdown`, where Debian's and
Alpine's script is `networking`, and was never stood down -- its `dhclient`
kept `eth0`; NetworkManager is `network-manager` on Debian, so the same; and
the dhcpcd service was left alone. On this machine, OpenRC, connman went out
of the runlevel correctly. **On sysv-rc it was worse**: connman was stopped
and stayed enabled, so it came back at the next boot beside netcfgd, and
netcfgd was started and **never given boot links** -- the deb keeps
dh_installinit out -- so after a reboot it did not start, while the postinst
said the others were "stopped, disabled and masked".

Now: `script_of` names each manager's script as Debian, Alpine and Gentoo spell
it, and whichever exists is acted on. Without systemd, standing one down is
its stop and `update-rc.d NAME disable` (or `rc-update del` under OpenRC), and
selecting one is `update-rc.d NAME defaults` and `enable` before its start.
The radios and tools follow the same path (dhcpcd's script stops with
`dhcpcd -x` and no interface, which dhcpcd(8) applies to the master only, so
netcfgd's per-interface clients stay); `none` stops netcfgd's script; the
postrm's purge removes its links; and the postinst says "masked" only where
systemd runs. `tests/live/select.sh` gains 20 checks in a namespace with stub
init scripts and a stub `update-rc.d`, and 4 for OpenRC; with the old script,
13 of them fail.

**What the machine would need from its holder to move**, if it ever does:
`netcfgd_select.sh netcfgd` stops connman and ifupdown now and keeps them
down; the `ib0` stanza goes with ifupdown; and connman's 11,796 profile
directories are connman's to clear (`/var/lib/connman/ethernet_*_cable`), which
nothing here does. Not done: this is the holder's working machine, and a
switch is theirs to make.

## 10.841 On the router: the guest bridge comes up, and the plan stops saying it will not

10.839's guest network was added to `tests/hull/malta/bridge.sh`, run on both router
tiers: a bridge `brguest` whose port is a VLAN `guest10` on a veth `zport`, the VLAN's name
sorting before its parent's. **On OpenWrt 25.12 the daemon did all of it** -- created the
VLAN after its parent, raised `zport`, then `guest10`, then the bridge, and addressed it --
and the plan then said `nothing to do`. Two things were wrong around it:

- **The plan said the opposite.** `warn_inert_devices` told `guest10` and `zport` "has a
  `device` block and no `interface` block, so nothing is planned for it" while the same plan
  created and raised them, as it had told the LAN bridge's ports all along (seen in 10.833's
  first runs, unread). A person reading `ncfg plan` on that router would be told their guest
  network does nothing. The warning now skips what netcfgd raises -- a port, or the parent
  of something it raises -- through `ncfg_plan_device_is_raised`, the rule 10.839 raises
  by. **The first version also skipped every virtual kind, and silenced 0186's radio**:
  `plan_wifi_test` and `c_warnings.sh` caught it, and it was narrowed to the raised alone.
  `plan_kind_test` checks the guest chain draws no such warning, and fails with the skip off.
- **The step's own check read nothing**: it used `ip -br`, which OpenWrt's BusyBox `ip` does
  not have. It reads `/sys/class/net/*/flags` now.

## 10.840 Teardown in stack order: a VLAN before its parent

**The other direction of 10.839's lens.** With the document emptied, a VLAN `zvlan` on a
dummy `apar` was torn down in the kernel's order: `apar` deleted first, the kernel took the
VLAN with it, and `link.delete zvlan` failed, so `ncfg apply` reported a stop on a machine
that had reached exactly what the document asked. `teardown_links` now deletes deepest
first, following each observed link's `parent` (bounded at eight), the reverse of
creation's parent first. Measured in a namespace: the VLAN, then its parent, both `ok`.
`plan_kind_test` holds it, from an observation listing the parent first.

## 10.839 A guest bridge on a VLAN: created out of order, and its parent left down

**Derived from 10.833 and 10.835's shape, one level deeper**: a router's guest network is
a bridge whose port is a VLAN on a port, `device brguest { bridge { members = ["guest10"]
} }` on `guest10`, a VLAN of `lan0`, neither with an `interface` block. Run in a namespace,
**three faults, one behind the other**:

- **Created out of order, under `ncfg apply` too.** The device walk creates in name order,
  and `guest10` sorts before `lan0`: the VLAN was created first, failed "lan0 is not an
  interface this kernel knows", and the apply stopped there. 10.835's own check had a VLAN
  named `vlan10` on `lan0`, which the alphabet put in order -- it passed by luck. **A parent
  the document makes is now created first**, inside `ncfg_plan_link_creation`, and the
  child's creation waits on it; the walk's own rule 1, "every link created before anything
  references it", now holds whatever the names.
- **The parent left down.** 10.835 raised a parent only where the device on it had an
  `interface` block; `guest10` is only a bridge's port. A parent is raised now where what
  rides on it is raised by netcfgd -- an interface, a port, an `ifb`, or something that
  carries one, followed down -- and raised before the device on it, which waits on it.
- **The daemon dropped the parent's actions**: 10.833's rule looked one level up, to
  `guest10`, which has no block. It follows the chain now, to the first device with one.

**Measured** in the namespace: the daemon brings the bridge, the VLAN and its parent up
within a second of the config changing, and the plan is then empty; `ncfg apply` creates
the parent first. `plan_kind_test` (order and raising) and `reconcile_test` (the chain)
cover each: creation-first off, the old interface-only rule, and the chain stopped at one
level each turn its check red. **The first version of the planner test passed with its fix
removed**: its fixture listed the parent first, and a document read from JSON keeps the
order given, so the walk never met the fault; it lists the devices by name now, as a
compiled document has them.

## 10.835 A VLAN's parent, the same shape: dropped by the daemon, and left down by the plan

**Derived from 10.833's shape**: a link the document names only inside another device's
block. A bridge's ports were one; a VLAN's, a VXLAN's, a macvlan's, a tunnel's or a PPPoE
session's `parent` is the other. Run against a daemon in a namespace -- `lo` configured,
then `device lan0 { kind = "dummy" }`, a VLAN 10 on it and `interface vlan10 { config =
"192.168.10.1/24" }` appended while it ran -- it showed two faults, one behind the other:

- **The daemon dropped the parent's creation**, as it had the ports': `link.create
  failed: lan0 is not an interface this kernel knows`, on every pass. The VLAN's
  `link.create` carries no dependency edge on its parent's, so 10.833's walk could not
  bring it along; the membership rule could. `ncfg_reconcile_restrict`'s helper is
  `asked_for_by` now -- a bridge's or bond's members and the five kinds' parents -- and
  `reconcile_test` has the VLAN case.
- **And the plan never brought the parent up**, under the daemon or under `ncfg apply`:
  `link.up failed: ... Network is down (ENETDOWN)`, the kernel refusing to raise a VLAN
  over a down parent. `ncfg_plan_device_up` was deliberately narrow -- a port or an `ifb`
  -- so that a `device eth9 { mtu = 9000 }` with no interface block stays down. It now
  also raises a device that carries one the document configures: the parent of a VLAN,
  VXLAN, macvlan, tunnel or PPPoE device that has an `interface` block. The narrow case is
  kept, and `plan_kind_test` checks both halves: the parent raised, a dummy carrying
  nothing left down. **PPPoE is in the list on purpose**: a router whose WAN Ethernet has
  no block of its own, under netcfgd alone with nothing else raising it, had a session
  that could never start; the armsr rig never met it because `guest.sh` raises the NIC.
  A mesh point's parent is a radio, which the radio pass raises, and is left out.

**Measured**: the same namespace, the fix in -- the VLAN up with its address a second
after the append, no error in the daemon's log, and the plan `nothing to do`. Each rule,
disabled alone, turns its test red.

## 10.833 A bridge over ports with no `interface` block was never put up by the daemon

**Asked by the holder, 2026-11-13: "what needs a real router? can't you use hull?"** --
after a run had ended saying the router side had nothing left short of real hardware.
That was not checked against what hull can emulate, and checking found a fault in the
router guide's own example.

**The fault.** `doc/first-run.md` section 10 has a person write `device br-lan { bridge {
members = ["lan1", "lan2", "lan3", "lan4"] } }` and `interface br-lan { ... }`, the ports
having no `interface` block -- they are DSA ports, the bridge is what is configured. No
rig had run that: their LANs were a single veth, and wider.conf's bridge had one dummy
port and served nothing. `tests/hull/malta/bridge.sh`, run on both router tiers, makes
the guide's LAN over four veth ports and asks hosts on two of them for leases; the bridge
never came up. netcfgd's own log said why:

    not reconciled in isolation: link.up on brlan needs action 5, which belongs to
    another interface

The daemon applies a configuration change, a drift repair and its passes through
`ncfg_reconcile_restrict`, which keeps an action only where its interface reconciles --
and `ncfg_reconcile_reconciles` answers no for an interface the document does not name,
"a plan can only carry an action for it if something else in the document asked for
it". The members' `link.create`, `link.set_master` and `link.up` are on links the
document names only inside the bridge, so they were dropped, and every bridge action
that depends on them with them. A one-shot `ncfg apply` takes the whole plan, which is
why a hand test passed and the daemon did not. **So a router configured as the guide
says got its bridge only from the first explicit apply**, and lost it to any change the
daemon had to make itself.

**The fix takes the comment at its word**: something did ask -- the bridge -- and it
needed two halves, found in that order on armsr. **A port goes with its bridge**: an
action on a link the document names only as a member of a bridge or bond, with no
`interface` block of its own, is reconciled by the bridge's interface's policy. That alone
is what keeps the ports up once the bridge exists, when no dependency edge points at them
any more -- the first fix, without it, brought the bridge, its address and its server up
and left the four ports down, so the hosts had no carrier. **And what a wanted action
depends on comes with it**: a backwards walk from every wanted action takes in the
actions it depends on that are on a link with no `interface` block -- a veth's
`link.create`, which is no member of anything. A link with an `interface` block keeps its
own `on_drift` either way, and a `report` there still holds the bridge back, named.
`reconcile_test` has both halves, transitively through two members, a port with its own
`report`, and a link nothing asked for still left alone; disabling either half turns its
checks red.

**Measured on `hull-armsr`**, the fix in: the bridge with all four ports, its address and
its server within a second of the document changing; a lease each for hosts on `port1`
and `port3` (192.168.8.108 and .247 from 192.168.8.1); each host's SLAAC address from the
bridge's /64, the third of the delegated /56; and the plan after it `nothing to do`.
Before it, the same step on the same rig: no ports in the bridge, no leases, and the plan
still wanting every member's action. The step's waits are 120 s, and the guest's cap
went from 1200 s to 1800 s (malta's from 900 s to 1200 s) for the time the step adds on
an emulated CPU a loaded host slows several times over.

### What does need a real router, then

Measured against the rigs (`hull-armsr`, `hull-malta`, and the hwsim, roaming, mesh,
WDS, regulatory and width rigs), what hull cannot give is short and specific:

- **Vendor Wi-Fi drivers and their firmware** (mt76, ath10k/ath11k): hwsim runs
  mac80211, hostapd and wpad faithfully, and has none of a driver's quirks -- DFS channel
  availability checks, offloaded scanning, a firmware crash and recovery.
- **The switch chip.** A DSA port is a netdev like the veths here, so the bridge and its
  VLAN filtering are exercised; what is not is the same configuration offloaded into the
  switch (switchdev), and the chip's own limits -- its VLAN table, its CPU port's tagging.
- **Hardware flow offload**, a MediaTek PPE (0319); the software flowtable is emulable.
- **Line rate**: whether a two-core Cortex-A53 forwards and translates a gigabit WAN is a
  measurement of that CPU, not of a TCG emulation of it.
- **Real flash and a real bootloader**: armsr's root is an initramfs, so sysupgrade's keep
  list and restore are tested and a write-out to JFFS2 or UBIFS across a power cut and a
  U-Boot boot are not.

Everything else a person configures on a router in the guide is in reach of hull, and
the bridge over four ports, with its server and a delegated /64, is the step that was
missing from it. **A small router's memory is too, and is now what armsr runs in**: the
guest went from 256 MB to 128 MB, the floor of what 25.12 still builds for, and the whole
rig -- the bridge, PD, PPPoE, WireGuard, the stock restarts, sysupgrade -- passes there,
with the root an initramfs in that same RAM, which a real router keeps in flash.

## 10.830 fuzznet ed93497: the local verb is `rrpc`, not `call`

fuzznet's stage 3 (its sec 1087, f37ae02) gave a voice or video call CMD 18 and a STATUS
CMD 19 and retired family 2; the commit after (sec 1088, 21c2478) renamed the local verb
for a registered procedure `rrpc NAME [at HOST|estate|group=NAME] [ARGS]`, and `call` is
answered as unknown (inbox 20261113T0305Z). netcfgd builds none of the stage-3 bytes; the
rename is what touches it. **Every line the client writes to fuzznetd's socket for a
netcfgd procedure** -- `ask`, `askpart`, `status`, `events`, `eventlog`, `hosts` and `do`,
in `client/ncfg_fuzznet.c` -- now opens `rrpc`, and so do the node tests that type them by
hand and the comments naming them. A client at this pin cannot ask a fuzznetd from before
21c2478, nor an old client a new one, so a desktop's `ncfg` and its fuzznet move together,
which they do: both are this binary.

Pinned at ed93497, fuzznet's head, so the four commits after the rename (streams and file
references under their own CMDs, a call answered on another of the user's hosts, the hex
codec and distance helpers moved out of the core) come with it. **Size: unchanged**,
2,600,016 bytes, inside the budget 10.829 set.

**Measured:** the full C suite at this pin, the node, fleet and fuzznet-line tests among it.
And the router tier, since two pins had moved without one: `make hull-armsr` -- the arm64
package built with OpenWrt's toolchain against musl, installed by apk on 25.12.6 under
procd -- `VERDICT ok`, the stock services restarted, `dns_forward` and `range6` beside the
stock dnsmasq, and sysupgrade's keep-and-restore all as 10.821 to 10.828 left them.
`make hull-malta` too, big-endian MIPS with the radio half the armsr image lacks: `VERDICT
ok`, a station on netcfgd's access point and `ncfg wifi status` reading it, the same stock
restarts, and the package through apk and sysupgrade.

## 10.829 fuzznet b54490a: every host-to-host message's first byte moved

fuzznet split its family 2 into CMD categories (its sec 1085, stage 2; inbox
20261113T0049Z): byte 0 of a message between hosts is now a CMD (`wire/cmd.h`), byte 1 a
SUBCMD, and an extension's remote requests arrive under `FZN_CMD_EXTENSION`, 20, where they
were family 2's 128 to 191. **Both ends must run the same fuzznet**, nothing reading the old
bytes: so a netcfgd at the old pin 364241c and one at this pin cannot ask each other
anything, and an estate's hosts are upgraded together, as they already had to be for
netcfgd's own vocabulary.

netcfgd keeps its SUBCMDs, 128 a request and 129 its answer, which fuzznet now lists by
owner in `node/types.h` as `FZN_TYPES_NETCFGD_REQUEST`/`_ANSWER`; `node.c`'s assertion
checks netcfgd's against those, where it checked a range that no longer exists, and
`serve_remote` reads and writes byte 0 as `FZN_CMD_EXTENSION`. Nothing else here builds
those bytes: fuzznet sends a request from the local `call` verb.

**Size: +94,984 bytes, all fuzznet's**, measured by building at both pins with netcfgd's
tree otherwise the same (2,505,032 and 2,600,016). 166 commits came with it -- calls with
relays and NAT traversal, the metric layer, binary STATUS replies -- all reachable from
the daemon netcfgd runs, so `--gc-sections` keeps them. The budget is raised with the
figure; netcfgd's own +21,896 since 11-07 had been inside the tolerance.

Stage 3 and the local verb's rename came the same day, and 10.830 took them.

**Measured:** the full C suite at this pin, exit 0, the node and fleet tests among it.

## 10.828 DHCPv4 is served where the dnsmasq has no DHCPv6

**Found by deriving the next lens from 10.827**: one part of the LAN's dnsmasq failing took
the whole server down, so the next question was which other part could. On `hull-armsr`,
2026-11-12, `lan4` given an IPv6 address and `range6 = "::100-::1ff"`: OpenWrt's stock dnsmasq
is built `no-DHCPv6` (its `--version` says so), it refused its whole file -- "bad dhcp-range at
line 13" -- and the LAN's DHCPv4 went with it, every pass logging `backend.start failed`. The
question the step was written to ask, whether odhcpd's port 547 collides, never got that far,
and cannot on the stock build; it waits for a dnsmasq with DHCPv6 there.

**The holder's word for 10.827 decides it**: serve what can be served and warn. When a
`dhcp_server` has a `range6`, the start asks the dnsmasq's `--version` first; one saying
`no-DHCPv6` gets the file without its DHCPv6 range and a `# dhcpv6 off:` line, read back as
the backend's `dhcpv6_off`, and every plan warns that the server serves no IPv6 addresses and
names `dnsmasq-full`, which has DHCPv6. Asked of `--version` rather than read from the
failure, because "bad dhcp-range" is also what a range wrong in itself would say, and the
compile-time options are a fact about the binary that cannot be mistaken for one.

As with the forwarder, the summary stays the document's and the server is not restarted to
try again: a different dnsmasq is a package change, and the range is tried at the next start a
changed `dhcp_server` block makes.

`dhcp_server_test.c`'s stand-in prints a `no-DHCPv6` `--version` and refuses a range6 as the
real one did; with the check removed its three checks go red. `plan_dhcp_server_test.c` holds
the warning and the plan that restarts nothing; `restart.sh` makes the change on both OpenWrt
tiers and asks for a v4 lease and the warning.

## 10.827 DHCP is served without a forwarder that cannot have port 53

**The holder's word, 2026-11-12: serve DHCP without the forwarder, and warn in the plan.**
That settles the question 10.825 left open. A `dhcp_server` with `dns_forward = true`, started
where another server holds port 53 on its address -- OpenWrt's stock dnsmasq on every router --
used to fail whole, so one feature that could not be had cost every host its address.

Now `ncfg_dhcp_server_start` reads dnsmasq's output when it fails, and where it says `Address in
use` it renders the file again without the forwarder and starts once more: `port=0`, no
records, no block lists, no `local=` for the domain, and -- where the block names no `dns` --
`dhcp-option=6` offering the interface's own address, which the server holding port 53 there
answers, as 10.825's `dns = [router]` does by hand. The file carries a `# forwarder off:` line
quoting dnsmasq; observation reads it into the backend's `forwarder_off`, and every plan warns
of it, saying what is not answered and what to do on OpenWrt.

**The summary line stays the document's**, so the plan sees nothing to change and does not
restart the server to try again: a retry on every pass would take the LAN's DHCP down every
five seconds, which is the fault being fixed. The forwarder is tried again when the
`dhcp_server` block changes. A second failure is DHCP's own and is reported as before.

**Rejected:** checking port 53 at plan time and planning DHCP alone from the start. dnsmasq's
own failure is the one witness that cannot disagree with dnsmasq -- `bind-dynamic` binds an
address as it appears, so a reading taken at plan time can be wrong a second later -- and the
plan still warns, one pass after the start, from what the file records.

`dhcp_server_test.c` has a stand-in dnsmasq that fails on `port=53` as the real one did; with
the retry removed its three checks go red. `plan_dhcp_server_test.c` holds the warning and the
plan that does nothing. `restart.sh` turns `lan4` to `dns_forward = true` beside the stock
dnsmasq on both OpenWrt tiers and asks for a lease, the DNS server it offers, and the warning.

## 10.826 IPv6 over a PPPoE session

**A DSL line's IPv6 arrives by DHCPv6 over the PPPoE session**, its delegated prefix above
all, and netcfgd's pppd options never asked for IPv6CP: no `+ipv6`, so `ppp0` had no
link-local address and no DHCPv6 client could ask over it. The options now carry `+ipv6`,
which OpenWrt's own PPPoE protocol passes by default; an ISP with no IPv6 rejects IPv6CP and
IPv4 carries on. `tests/live/ppp.sh` has a real pppd take the options, and `pppoe_test.c` holds
the text.

On `hull-armsr`, 2026-11-12: the concentrator's pppd is told `+ipv6` too, a second kea serves
its end of the session, and `pppoe.sh` turns `ppp0` to `dhcp6 pd_length 56` once it has
dialled: `ppp0` took a link-local from IPv6CP and a /56 was delegated over the session in 12 s.

**kea will not serve a point-to-point link as pppd numbers it**: the session's link-local is
`inet6 <ours> peer <theirs>`, and kea bound the peer's address and failed ("Failed to bind
socket ... to fe80::<peer>"), so it opened no socket at all. The rig gives the concentrator's
`ppp0` an ordinary link-local of its own, `fe80::1/64`, which kea binds. That is the rig's ISP,
not anything a router does.

## 10.825 The LAN's resolver on OpenWrt is OpenWrt's dnsmasq

**`dns_forward` cannot be had beside OpenWrt's stock dnsmasq, and failing it takes the LAN's
DHCP down too.** The stock dnsmasq runs `bind-dynamic`: it binds port 53 on every address the
router has as each appears -- measured, 28 sockets, `lan4`'s 192.168.7.1 among them. netcfgd's
dnsmasq for a LAN with `dhcp_server { dns_forward = true }` (0301) binds port 53 on that
interface too, so it would not start ("failed to create listening socket for 192.168.7.1:
Address in use"), and since one dnsmasq serves both, the LAN's DHCP went with it: every apply
logged `backend.start failed` for `lan4`. A first version of the check passed anyway -- the
stock dnsmasq answered the name at 192.168.7.1 -- until it was made to ask whose process held
the socket.

**What fits OpenWrt** is to leave the forwarder off and offer the router: `dns =
["<the LAN's address>"]`, which the stock dnsmasq answers. `restart.sh` checks exactly that on
both OpenWrt tiers -- the lease made with the router offered, and a name answered at it --
and the router guide says it.

**Settled by the holder in 10.827:** a forwarder that cannot bind no longer takes its
interface's DHCP down; the DHCP is served without it and the plan says why.

## 10.824 WireGuard on the router

**The VPN a router is most often asked for**, run where routers are. `hull-armsr`'s image
pins `kmod-wireguard` and the eight packages it depends on from 25.12.6's kmods feed --
the image carries none of them -- and `tests/hull/malta/wg.sh` installs them as a person
would, gives netcfgd a `wireguard` device with one peer, and pings the peer's tunnel
address. The peer is the outer machine across the ISP's link (`wg` there, from
`wireguard-tools`, which also makes both keys). 2026-11-12: `wg0` carried 10.99.0.2/24
after 1 s, the far end saw a handshake, and it answered through the tunnel at once. Nothing
in netcfgd needed changing; netcfgd speaks generic netlink to the module itself, so the
router needs no `wireguard-tools`, which the guide now says beside `apk add kmod-wireguard`.

## 10.823 What a DHCPv6 lease gives the uplink itself

**The next lens from 10.822: what else odhcp6c hands its script that the hook dropped.**
Two things, and on OpenWrt they reach every DHCPv6 uplink, delegated prefix or not, since
`ncfg_dhcp6_client` picks odhcp6c wherever it is installed: `ADDRESSES`, IA_NA's addresses,
which odhcp6c puts on no interface, so the uplink had no global address of its own; and
`RDNSS`/`RA_DNS`/`DOMAINS`, the ISP's resolvers and search list, which reached nothing.

The hook installs the addresses (`ip -6 addr replace`, recorded as `.<uplink>.addresses`
beside the router's record, and one that leaves the lease removed and no other) and writes
the resolvers and search list as the interface-report fragment `reported.d/<uplink>/odhcp6c`,
beside dhcpcd's `dhcpcd6` (0086), staged and renamed; a resolver both lists name is written
once. `dhcp_test.c` runs it through two addresses becoming one and two resolvers; on
`hull-armsr`, with kea handing out `dns-servers`, `isp6` carries 2001:db8:aaaa::100/128 and
its report `dns=2001:db8:aaaa::53`. `doc/interface-report.md` counts four writers now.

## 10.822 A router's IPv6 default route, from the ISP's advertisement

**Every netcfgd router given a prefix had no IPv6 default route.** An IPv6 default route only
ever comes from a router advertisement -- DHCPv6 has no router option -- and on a router
nothing took it: the kernel ignores advertisements on an interface that forwards unless
`accept_ra` is 2, and decision 0073 sets 2 only for an interface that asks for SLAAC; a WAN
written `config = "dhcp6 pd_length 56"`, as every document here writes it, does not. When a
prefix is delegated netcfgd's client is odhcp6c (0050), which hears the advertisement in
userspace and hands it to its script as `RA_ROUTES` -- and netcfgd's hook took only
`PREFIXES`. The delegation tests checked the LAN's address and never the way out. Measured
on `hull-armsr`, with radvd on the ISP's tap advertising a managed default router as an ISP
that delegates does: no default route on `isp6`, and `accept_ra` 0 there besides, netifd
having zeroed it on `eth0` before the rename.

**The hook now installs it**, as the udhcpc script installs IPv4's for the same reason --
the client has no configuration step of its own: the `::/0` entry of `RA_ROUTES` becomes
`ip -6 route replace default via <router> dev <uplink>`, the router recorded as
`.<uplink>.router` beside the prefixes (the reader skips a leading dot, 0113), and when an
advertisement names another router or none -- the ISP withdrawing it, or the lease going --
that route and no other is removed. `dhcp_test.c` runs the hook against a stand-in `ip`
through a router advertised, changed and withdrawn; matching on anything but `::/0` fails
four of its checks. On `hull-armsr`, 2026-11-12: `default via fe80::... dev isp6` at once,
with `accept_ra` still 0.

**0073's open item, answered by another mechanism than the one it foresaw.** It measured
`dhcpcd -6` handling advertisements itself and wrote that if some other client turned out to
depend on the kernel's own processing, its pass would grow the case. odhcp6c is that
client, but setting `accept_ra=2` would have fought netifd on OpenWrt, which zeroes it, and
the advertisement is already in hand in the script, where IPv4's gateway is handled too.

## 10.821 The stock services restarted under netcfgd

**What LuCI's "Save & Apply" does a dozen times a day**: `network`, `firewall` and
`dnsmasq` restarted. `tests/hull/malta/restart.sh`, on both OpenWrt tiers, restarts each in
turn and wants netcfgd's table, `lan4`'s address and its dnsmasq whole within 20 s, then
stops the firewall again as the guide says and asks for a lease on `lan4` with OpenWrt's own
dnsmasq running beside netcfgd's. 2026-11-12, `hull-armsr` and `hull-malta`: whole after
every restart, the table back 2 and 4 s after the second `firewall stop` (0318), and the host
leased an address from 192.168.7.1 with two sockets on port 67.

**Concluded first and wrong, kept so it is not concluded again:** the first version asked for
the lease straight after the restarts, got nothing, saw both dnsmasqs on 0.0.0.0:67 and read
it as the stock one taking the DISCOVER. Setting `dhcp.lan.ignore=1` took the stock socket
away and still no lease came -- because `firewall restart` had brought fw4 back, and fw4
rejects input on a device with no zone, a DHCP server's included, which the guide already
says and `ncfg plan` already warns of. With the firewall stopped the two dnsmasqs coexist: a
broadcast reaches both, and the stock one has no range for `lan4`.

## 10.820 A home behind the router, and the NAT `fw4 flush` took away

**A host behind the router, reaching past it**, which is what a router is for and what no
tier had shown. `hull-armsr`'s guest gains a third NIC, `home0` -- 192.168.9.1/24 and
`@pd:isp6/1=::1/64`, advertised by uradvd -- and the uplink `isp6` gains 192.0.2.2/24,
2001:db8:aaaa:ffff::2/64, `forwarding` and `nat = true`. The far end of `home0` is a tap the
outer machine moves into a network namespace of its own (after qemu has opened it: qemu
opens `ifname=` in its own namespace and makes a fresh tap if it is gone), and a prober
there pings the ISP's 192.0.2.1 and 2001:db8:aaaa:ffff::1 every five seconds while qemu
lives. IPv4 can only answer through the router's masquerade (nothing here routes to
192.168.9.0/24), IPv6 only from the delegated prefix (routed back via the router's
link-local). Both answered: IPv6 from 2001:db8:1234:1::/64 within seconds of the
advertisement, IPv4 -- **minutes later.**

**Why minutes: OpenWrt's `/etc/init.d/firewall stop` runs `fw4 flush`, which deletes every
nftables table on the machine**, and `restart` is a stop and a start. The guest stops it
before its WAN test, as the router guide told people to. netcfgd's table -- the NAT, the
port forward and its reflection -- was gone (0 lines), `ncfg plan` listed `nftables.replace`
as the repair, and no drift pass made it: a drift pass keeps an action whose interface
reconciles or whose op 0165 calls host-wide, and `nftables.replace` names no interface and
was not on that list. The NAT came back with the next edit of the document. Reproduced on
this host in seconds, under `unshare -rn`, with the netlink batch `fw4 flush` sends.

**And a second fault under it: `--no-apply-on-start` was never released in a daemon with a
node.** The release is asked of the requests a pass is handed, and since 0311 fuzznet's loop
answers every request through `ncfg_main_answer` and hands the passes none -- a trace showed
every pass with zero requests. So a daemon started held, as the first-run guide starts one,
repaired no drift whatever after its first apply: an address taken off an interface stayed
off. Decision 0318 adds `nftables.replace`, `rule.add` and `rule.del` to the host-wide list,
and an answered apply now releases the hold. Measured: the deleted table, a deleted policy
rule and a deleted address each back within one 5 s tick; nothing re-applied in 25 idle
seconds, 0165's measure of a rewrite loop. `tests/live/nat.sh` deletes the table under the
daemon and wants it back; each fix reverted alone turns that check red. The router guide now
says what stopping `firewall` does.

## 10.819 A LAN served by OpenWrt's own dnsmasq

**The router tiers had never served a LAN.** Their only dnsmasq was the one the guest runs
by hand as the WAN's ISP; `hull-dhcp-server`, which proves decision 0297's `dhcp_server`,
runs Debian's. `tests/hull/malta/lan.sh`, sourced on both OpenWrt tiers, gives a veth pair
netcfgd makes a `dhcp_server` block and has BusyBox's udhcpc ask on the far end, which is
no interface of the document's. 2026-11-12: on `hull-armsr` (25.12.6, arm64) and
`hull-malta` (25.12.0, big-endian MIPS) the stock dnsmasq -- built `no-DHCPv6`, which a
DHCPv4 LAN does not need -- leased an address in 192.168.7.0/24, its lease file held it, and
`ncfg status` showed it. Nothing in netcfgd needed changing.

## 10.817 Advertising on OpenWrt 25.12: uradvd

**OpenWrt 25.12 carries no radvd in any feed**, measured 2026-11-12 against every feed's
`index.json` for `aarch64_generic` (base, packages, routing, luci, telephony): `packages` has
`uradvd`, and nothing else sends router advertisements but odhcpd, which is stock. The stock
dnsmasq is built `no-DHCPv6` (its own log line in the guest), so it cannot either. So on the
routers this project is for, `advertise` had no daemon to hand the LAN to: radvd absent,
odhcpd refused by name.

**uradvd became a backend**, `backend = "uradvd"`, and `auto` takes it where there is no
radvd. Chosen over odhcpd because odhcpd is configured only through UCI's
`/etc/config/dhcp` -- the file the stock router's netifd world uses -- where uradvd, like
radvd, is one process per interface netcfgd starts and stops, so the lifecycle in `ra.c`
carries over: a record file under `<run>/radvd/<iface>.conf` holds its arguments one to a
line, and its path rides after `--` (where uradvd stops reading options) as the marker
`ncfg_process_pid_of` matches. uradvd neither detaches nor writes a pid file, so a shell
does both; its reload is a restart, there being no file to re-read, and the program to
restart is the record's `# started as` line, since a command line shows an interpreter
where the program is a script.

Read from `uradvd.c` at the commit 25.12 builds (1e64364d), not from its usage line:

- **`-p`, not `-a`.** Both make a prefix autonomous; `-p` also makes it on-link, which is
  radvd's `AdvOnLink on`. The package's own init script calls `-a` "off link". The first
  version of this backend wrote `-a` and its unit test asserted `-a` -- the test agreed
  with the code it was written beside, which is why `hull-armsr`'s `prefix.sh` asks a
  host on the LAN instead.
- **The default router lifetime is 0**, which tells hosts the router is no default
  gateway; radvd's is 1800. An unset `lifetime` is written as 1800, so one document
  means the same under either daemon.
- **No managed or other-config flag** (both sent as zero), **only /64 prefixes**, at most
  8 prefixes and 3 name servers: each refused under uradvd with its reason rather than
  advertised as something else.

Installing the package enables its init script (`S50uradvd`), which does nothing:
`/etc/config/uradvd` ships `enabled '0'`. The router guide says `apk add uradvd`.

## 10.816 PPPoE through OpenWrt's own pppd

**The other WAN most ISPs hand a router, and the one netcfgd drives through somebody else's
pppd.** `tests/live/pppoe-session.sh` dials Debian's; `hull-armsr` now dials OpenWrt 25.12's
own, pppd 2.5.2 with its `pppoe.so`, over the guest's second NIC to Debian's `pppoe-server`
on a tap in the outer machine (`tests/hull/malta/pppoe.sh`, sourced where the payload says
there is a concentrator). It dials: `ppp0` has IPCP's 10.64.0.100, the name server the
server pushed reaches netcfgd's report, the report carries no address (0047), and taking the
device out of the document takes `ppp0` and pppd with it. Nothing in netcfgd needed
changing -- `plugin pppoe.so` and `nic-<parent>` are what 2.5.2 takes.

What the rig needed: the outer machine on the host's kernel (`(tuning (vm (profile
full)))`), since hull's own has no tun and ppp is modules there; `kmod` in the image to load
`tun`, `ppp_generic` and `pppoe`; and the concentrator's pppd given a log file, without
which an LCP timeout on the router's side was the only evidence -- the server's pppd had no
`ppp_generic` to run on. pppd reports one pushed server as both DNS1 and DNS2, so the report
names it twice.

## 10.815 A delegated prefix on OpenWrt, and three faults in the rig on the way

**What a router on a DHCPv6 ISP is for, run where routers are.** `hull-armsr` gives its
guest a virtio NIC on a tap in the outer machine, where kea-dhcp6 delegates from
2001:db8:1234::/48 at /56 as `tests/hull/delegation/isp.sh` does, and `tests/hull/malta/
prefix.sh` (sourced where the payload says there is an ISP) has OpenWrt's own odhcp6c ask
for a prefix under netcfgd and procd -- with nobody typing `ncfg apply` when it arrives --
number a LAN out of it, and advertise it with uradvd (10.817) to `host6`, the far end of a
veth pair and no interface of the document's, which has to take an address from the
delegated network and the router as its default route.

**It works, on OpenWrt 25.12.6 arm64, 2026-11-12:** kea delegated 2001:db8:1234::/56 in
11 s, the daemon numbered `lan6` 2001:db8:1234::1/64 two seconds later with no apply asked
for, and `host6` took 2001:db8:1234:0:...:a121/64 by SLAAC and a default route via `lan6`'s
link-local, from uradvd. That is decision 0009's router story end to end on the release and
architecture routers will have.

**The prefix never came, and the client was right to refuse it.** With odhcp6c verbose
(`-l7`) every SOLICIT drew an ADVERTISE it parsed with IA_NA and IA_PD and, a second later,
one it parsed with IA_NA alone, after which it solicited again, for ever. A capture on the
ISP's tap showed both ADVERTISEs carrying the /56 -- and every lifetime `pltime:3600
vltime:600`. The kea configuration set `valid-lifetime` to 600 and left the preferred
lifetime at kea's default of 3600, and RFC 8415 has a client discard a prefix whose
preferred lifetime exceeds its valid one: odhcp6c does (`dhcpv6_parse_ia`, `if
(entry.preferred > entry.valid) continue`). So the first candidate held no prefix, PD in
`try` mode fell to `none`, the second ADVERTISE's IA_PD went unread, and the transaction
restarted. All three kea configurations -- this one, `tests/hull/delegation/isp.sh` and
`tests/live/delegation.sh` -- now set `preferred-lifetime` to 300. The check is not new
(25.12.0's odhcp6c has it), and `hull-delegation`'s Debian CPE passes with the same
configuration; that rig's ISP runs trixie's kea where this one runs bookworm's 2.2, which
offered 3600 here, so the likely difference is kea's default -- likely, not measured. Either
way an offer whose preferred lifetime exceeds its valid one is not one a client may take.

**Tried first and wrong, kept so it is not tried again:** odhcp6c before 25.12.5 does read
16 bytes past each IA of an ADVERTISE (fixed by b6f0c70f5f, 2026-06-03), and that fitted the
symptom; moving the tier to 25.12.6 changed nothing, and the capture showed why. The tier
stays on 25.12.6, the release a router flashed today runs.

The rig's own faults, each of which read as a fault of netcfgd's for a run:

- **A stale console passed a run.** The verdict volume outlives a run, and a qemu that
  never started -- the tap it was given missing -- left the previous run's GUEST-END and
  two `VERDICT ok` in `/verdict/console`, which the payload read as this run's. Both qemu
  payloads (armsr, malta) now empty the console first and call a qemu that did not leave
  cleanly bad. Seen red: the next run, with no tap, read `VERDICT bad`.
- **An edited spec ran the old image.** `hull_image` built an image only when its ref was
  missing, so kea added to `hull.conf` booted an image without kea (10.602's hwsim had no
  hostapd the same way). It now keeps the spec's hash in `$(HULL_SPEC_DIR)` and rebuilds
  when it moves; a ref with no stamp is taken as current, so adopting it rebuilt nothing.
  The two delegation rigs carried their own copy of the old check and call it now.
- **Renaming by MAC renamed the bridge.** netifd's `br-lan` takes its port's MAC, so the
  guest's rename-by-MAC renamed the bridge to `isp6` and left the NIC down with no carrier;
  it matches only devices with a `device` link now.

And the outer machine runs the host's kernel (`(tuning (vm (profile full)))`): hull's own
has no tun, and `tun` is a module on the host's, loaded with `kmod`, which the image now
carries. virtio-net's option ROM is turned off (`romfile=`), there being no `ipxe-qemu`.

## 10.814 The router tier on arm64: `hull-armsr`

**The routers coming are mostly arm64 on OpenWrt 25.12**, and every router tier so far was x86
or big-endian MIPS. `make hull-armsr` runs the same two documents on OpenWrt 25.12.0's
`armsr/armv8` initramfs kernel under `qemu-system-aarch64 -M virt -cpu cortex-a53`: the shared
payload (`tests/hull/openwrt/payload.sh`: apk install, procd, the fuzznet store, respawn,
reload) and hull-malta's `guest.sh` (vlan, bridge, route, nftables, netifd beside it, a DHCP
WAN under busybox udhcpc, the package taken out and put back through sysupgrade's keep list).
Its image pins 25.12.0's kernel (25.12.6's since 10.815), the aarch64 musl toolchain (gcc
14.3.0), the dummy and veth module packages and apk-tools 3.0.2, all by sha256; the package arch is `aarch64_generic`.
It is not in `make hull`, like the other qemu tiers. First run, 2026-11-12: both verdicts ok,
the node key the same across a respawn and across the restore.

**armsr's image has no wireless stack** -- no cfg80211, wpad or iw in its manifest -- so the
radio half of `guest.sh` moved into `tests/hull/malta/radio.sh`, which `guest.sh` sources
unless the payload carries `/payload/no-radio`, whose text is printed as the reason. hull-malta
still runs it, and was rerun after the split: the station joins `bigend`, both verdicts ok.

## 10.813 A package OpenWrt 25.12 installs

**The holder agreed (2026-11-12) to build apk-tools from source**, which 10.812 left with them.
`make apk-tools` fetches Alpine's apk-tools 3.0.2 once into `build/apk-tools`, saying so,
checks it against the pinned sha256 of its tarball, and builds it out of tree with meson --
the docs, help, lua, python and tests left out, nothing installed. `tool/openwrt_apk.sh` then
makes the apk-v3 package of the files `tool/ipk.sh` lays down -- the static program, `ncfg`,
the procd script, the sysupgrade keep list -- with no scripts, so installing enables and
starts nothing (10.750). `make openwrt-apk OPENWRT_ARCH=... CC=...` is the person's way to
it, and the router guide says so.

Two things it had to get right that nothing would have said:

- **Owners.** `mkpkg` records each file's owner by name from the build directory, which is
  the builder's own; run under `unshare -r`, where that user is uid 0, the package says root.
- **Modes.** A builder's umask of 002 made what the package creates group-writable -- the
  keep list 0664, every directory 0775 -- in this package and in `tool/ipk.sh`'s alike. Both
  set `umask 022` now. The first guess, that a package carrying `/etc` as 0775 would loosen
  the router's own, was tested and is wrong for apk: with the umask taken out, `/etc` stayed
  0755. So the tier asks for the keep list's mode instead, which the same sabotage does change.

`hull-openwrt` on 25.12 installs it with the guest's own `apk add --allow-untrusted
--no-network` and asks apk and the files: listed, the program root's, the keep list
`-rw-r--r--`, nothing in `/etc/rc.d`, nothing running; then every procd check as before; then
`apk del` takes the program and init script and leaves the person's configuration. BusyBox there
has no `stat -c`, which the first version of the mode check asked for.

**`hull-malta` is on 25.12 too**, big-endian MIPS on OpenWrt's own kernel: its image pins
25.12's kernel, toolchain (gcc 14.3.0) and the dummy and veth module packages, and builds the
same pinned apk-tools, which also unpacks those modules. It had to move: it runs the x86 tier's
payload, which now installs with apk, so the first commit of this left it broken on 24.10.
Three things it met. **apk will not add a package from a file to a root in RAM**, malta's
initramfs, without `--force-non-repository` -- a reboot would lose it -- and a router's flash
root, like the x86 tier's block one, does not need it, so only malta says so. **Its own steps
deleted the files under apk** and then added the package again, which apk, still listing it,
did not reinstall; it removes with `apk del` now. **And procd's stop returns before the
process has gone**, so a count straight after a quick remove and add read the leaving daemon
as one the install had started; it waits, bounded, as the shared payload does.

**What no tier runs now: the `.ipk`.** `tool/ipk.sh` stays for 24.10, whose security updates
end in 2026-09, and nothing exercises it; the guide keeps its opkg lines for that release. The
package is unsigned: a feed with a key is the holder's, as 10.750 left the `.ipk`'s.

## 10.812 OpenWrt 25.12: netcfgd runs under its procd, and has no package it can install

**OpenWrt 25.12.0, stable since 2026-03, replaced opkg with apk** (apk-tools 3), and 24.10's
security updates end in 2026-09 -- so the routers expected next will most likely run 25.12.
`hull-openwrt` moves to `docker.io/openwrt/rootfs:x86-64-25.12.0` and passes every check
there: procd starts netcfgd and respawns it with the same node key, an edit alone, an edit
as it respawns and a `reload` each apply, a stop holds. The verdict now names the release
that ran, since the image is `netcfgd/openwrt` whatever its base and a store holding one built
from 24.10 would keep running it.

**The package does not reach it.** 10.750's `.ipk` is opkg's, and 25.12 installs apk-v3
packages -- not Alpine's v2 `.apk` either, which `packaging/alpine` makes. Making one needs
apk-tools 3's `mkpkg`, which OpenWrt's own apk 3.0.2 is built without (asked of the 25.12
image). Building apk-tools 3.0.2 from Alpine's source here was refused by this session's
permission check, as code from outside; the other road is the OpenWrt SDK. **The holder's**,
being a build dependency fetched from outside. Until then a router on 25.12 takes netcfgd as
a copied static binary and the procd script, which is what this tier does.

**And a figure that looked alarming and is the rig's:** about 3 MB available while netcfgd
runs, on 25.12 and on 24.10 alike (2.8 MB), netcfgd itself 5.8 MB resident in both. The tier
runs the host's Debian kernel in 128 MB, which leaves 88 MB; OpenWrt's own kernel on malta
left 51 MB of 118 (10.751). So it says nothing about a router, and malta is the tier to read
memory from.

## 10.811 A long hook path pushed udhcpc out of the "no DHCP client" sentence

`make live` on 428a4c75, run with a TMPDIR longer than `/tmp`, failed `exec_refused.sh`'s
"and accounts for udhcpc": the sentence for a machine with no usable DHCPv4 client ends at
"would use this o". The three clients' reasons share one error of `NCFG_ERROR_MAX`, 512
bytes, and the reason for a client installed in the sbins but not on PATH spent about 230 of
them explaining why netcfgd searches PATH alone -- so a hook path of ordinary length, such as
a packaged one, left no room for the last client's reason, which is the one 0182's case asks
the sentence to carry. The explanation is `backend_internal.h`'s to give; the sentence now
says where the client is, that it is not on PATH, and that an init's PATH would find it.
`exec_refused.sh` passes with the long TMPDIR.

## 10.810 After a sleep, the DHCP clients are asked to renew

**The wired half of the lid, which the radio could not ask.** 10.809's station re-asked for
its lease because its association dropped and the supplicant's reconnect said so. A wire
keeps its carrier across a suspend -- a dock, a cable -- so nothing tells the client that the
lease it holds ran out while it slept. `tests/live/suspend.sh` now gives the station a veth
to a second dnsmasq in the access point's namespace, same two-minute lease, and samples the
dock every second for 150 s after the wake.

**Measured before the change: held stale.** The dock kept its address for 103 s after the
wake, though dnsmasq's lease had run out during the 150 s sleep; at 104 s it dropped it, and
at 112 s it had one again, from a fresh request. A DHCP client's timers run on
CLOCK_MONOTONIC, which stands still while the machine is suspended, so a lease is held until
the client's own clock reaches its end -- for up to a whole lease, and the address is one the
server is free to give to somebody else meanwhile. The register asked whether "a lease that
expired during the suspend is renewed or silently stale"; on a wire, it was silently stale.

**So the daemon notices a sleep and asks.** Each pass compares CLOCK_BOOTTIME less
CLOCK_MONOTONIC -- the confirm window's measure (10.665) -- with the last pass's; grown by two
seconds or more is a sleep, logged under `power`, and the reconcile world's new `slept` seam
is called. The daemon's answers it by asking every DHCP client of netcfgd's on an interface
the document names to renew, in both families: `ncfg_dhcp_renew` runs `dhcpcd -4|-6 -n IFACE`
where dhcpcd's control socket says the client is netcfgd's -- `-n` starts a dhcpcd where none
runs, so only then -- and sends SIGUSR1, the renew both clients take, to the udhcpc or
odhcp6c whose pid netcfgd recorded.

**`-n`, rebind, and not `-N`, renew, which was tried first and measured wrong.** With `-N` the
dock's dhcpcd sent its REQUEST at the wake and dnsmasq, the lease gone, answered NAK "lease not
found" -- five times; dhcpcd, renewing, never acted on one, retrying until its own clock ended
the lease at 111 s, exactly as with no ask at all. The server's log, now in the rig's
diagnostics, is what showed it. `-n` starts the interface again from its saved lease, and with
it the dock was leased again 4 s after the wake with no second without an address. A client not running, or not netcfgd's, is left alone.
NetworkManager does the same on resume; it is the one thing about a resume nothing else
brings.

`reconcile_test` fixes the sleep through the confirm module's seam: the first pass and a
pass without sleep say nothing, a pass after 150 s calls `slept` once with 150; with the call
taken out of the pass two checks fail. The rig asks that the dock has a lease granted after
the wake within 30 s of it, which the run before the change -- 112 s -- fails.

## 10.809 The lid, measured: the window pauses, the station rejoins, the lease renews

**hull answered 10.773** (its note 20261111T0501Z, recorded here and deleted): since hull
f741a47 a machine with `(sleep true)` and `(projection block)` -- a block root, block volumes
only -- does the guest's own suspend: S3 woken by the guest's RTC alarm or `hull wake ID`,
S4 to a swap disk hull gives it, CLOCK_BOOTTIME ahead of CLOCK_MONOTONIC by the time asleep.
Its three causes for 10.773's guest never returning were virtio-fs refusing to suspend,
virtio-9p resuming with a dead root, and a vsock reset that the agent took for its host gone.
s2idle is not woken yet; `mem` is, and the hwsim guest's `mem_sleep` is `deep`.

**The rig moved to images.** `make hull-suspend` builds, without root, `repo.img` (the two
binaries, `suspend.sh`, the dhcpcd hook and the payload, by `mkfs.ext4 -d`), the host
kernel's modules once per release, and a fresh `verdict.img` the guest writes and the host
reads back with `debugfs`. Two things are worked around rather than fixed here. hull at
fede285 roots a stored image on qemu as composefs whatever the machine says, and then refuses
composefs under a block projection, so `(sleep true)` cannot take a stored image at all;
signalled to hull (its inbox 20261111T1210Z), and until it is answered the Makefile names the
image's checkout in hull's store as a `dir:` source in a generated `run.conf`. And the hull
binary netcfgd's `HULL` names was built on 2026-11-05, before the sleep work; the runs below
used hull's pushed fede285 built from `git archive` in a scratch directory, with a private
`XDG_RUNTIME_DIR` so that build's core ran them, `make hull-suspend HULL=...`.

**What a real 150-second S3 found**, the station joined to an access point on
`mac80211_hwsim`, leased by dnsmasq for two minutes, a 120-second confirm window open:

- **The confirm window paused** (10.665): the change still stood on waking and could be
  confirmed. The first run said otherwise, and it was the test's fault: it asked after
  waiting up to six minutes for the station and the lease, all awake, by which time a
  120-second window has rightly closed. The window is asked first now.
- **The rfkill watcher held**: a block after the resume was heard, and the radio came up
  again when the switch did.
- **The station did not come back at first, and it was not netcfgd.** It sat in `SCANNING`
  with an empty scan while the access point's side said `COMPLETED`, so the lease was not
  renewed either. **The control** -- `make hull-suspend SUSPEND_CONTROL=1`, the same radios
  and sleep with a plain `wpa_supplicant` as the station and no netcfgd -- failed the same
  way, and its diagnostics showed why: the access point's radio had sent two frames since the
  wake. mac80211_hwsim stops an access point's beacons across a resume. A laptop's access
  point is another machine that never slept; here it shares the kernel, so `suspend.sh` now
  restarts it on waking, as its power-on would, before asking the station anything. With
  that the control's station was back in 13 seconds.
- **Then, under netcfgd, every check passed**: associated again 13 seconds after the wake,
  the same as the plain supplicant; the lease that ran out asleep renewed (dnsmasq's expiry
  granted after the wake); the window still standing and confirmable; rfkill heard. So the
  register's four questions are answered for a station on a radio that survives a resume,
  and netcfgd adds no delay to the supplicant's own recovery.
- **No verdict file** in the first runs: the log stopped after the summary, the test's cleanup
  stuck in the kernel -- `ip netns delete` or `modprobe -r` on a radio the resume left odd,
  which even `timeout` cannot end, a process in D state ignoring the signal. They run in the
  background unwaited now, the machine being discarded anyway, and the payload runs the test
  under a timeout so a verdict is written whatever happens.

**The window's check was vacuous until a sabotage said so.** With the window made to ignore
the sleep (`deadline_of` returning the bare deadline), the run passed: the check was asked
within a second of the wake, before the daemon's next pass -- five seconds apart at most --
had looked at the window at all. It waits ten seconds now, two passes; the same sabotage then
fails both window checks and the log says `reverting ... (the window closed unconfirmed)`.

**Hibernation too**, `make hull-suspend SUSPEND_STATE=disk`: the guest writes its image to the
swap hull gives it, hull starts a new qemu on the same disks (its core log says so), and
every check passes -- the window, the station, the lease, rfkill. **But hull restores at
once**, so the guest was asleep three seconds, not 150: this says netcfgd and the station
come through a hibernate and restore, and asks nothing about what expires while asleep, which
the S3 run does.

**hull fixed the stored image's refusal** (its note 20261112T0043Z, recorded here and deleted):
since hull 5772098 a block projection takes the image's checkout, and the root's ext4 is built
from a tar with the image's owners applied, so the guest's root files are root's as over 9p.
The Makefile's checkout workaround and its generated `run.conf` are gone; the rig runs
`hull.conf` as written and passes every check on hull's c7c7c6c. hull is looking at s2idle
next.

**What it does not say.** One radio driver, simulated, and one sleep length; s2idle not
being woken by hull yet; a hibernation that is held for a while; a station whose link netcfgd found down after the wake and put
up (`link.up ... was false`), which a real driver may or may not do. And the run takes about
twenty-five minutes, most of it hull building the block root, so it stays out of `make hull`
as 10.790 had it.

## 10.808 The hooks tab can start a hook

**The last of 10.778's list.** The hooks tab could open the editor of an interface that
already had a hook, and nothing else; with none, its note said a hook is added from the
links tab, `configure`, then hooks -- three places for the one thing the tab is named after.
`new hook...` asks which interface, from the machine's links, `lo` left out, opens that
interface's editor and presses the editor's own `new hook...`, so the form a person meets is
the one they would have reached by the long way. The hook still lives in the interface's
block, so there is still one form and one save, which is why the tab has no hook form of its
own. A hand-written interface opens read-only, as 10.778 has it -- asked only of an interface
that has a block, from the inventory as the links tab asks it: `written_by_hand` answers for
a block that exists and says yes of one that does not, so the first version opened every
unconfigured link read-only. `live_hooks_tab` found that, following the chain -- the question,
the editor, the form opened over it -- and closes each.

## 10.807 A missing credential can be stored from the credentials tab

**The credentials tab names the fault 10.796 now stops an apply for, and could not mend it.**
A network, access point or tunnel naming a secret nobody stored shows there as MISSING;
since 10.796 an apply someone asks for does not start over it, and the tab's note said
`ncfg secret set NAME` stores one -- a terminal, for the people the GUI is for. Its header
held that a GUI field would be a value in a process that did not need one, a position the
project left when the network and access point dialogs began storing what is typed (10.782)
and the device dialog joined them (10.805). So the decision was already taken elsewhere, and
this tab was the one place still obeying the old one.

`store...` is offered for a MISSING row with the `admin` tier, asks for the value in a
password field, and sends it to `secret_put` without `replace`. A stored one is not offered:
replacing goes through `forget` first, so a value nobody else has is never overwritten by a
click (0042). Nothing is read back, which is the half of the header that stands.
`live_secrets` writes a network naming a missing credential, stores it through the button,
and finds it stored. The apply dialog's "Nothing was applied" (10.799), when the failure is
a secret that was not found, now ends by saying the secrets tab can store it -- the daemon's
own sentence names `ncfg secret set`, which is the CLI's remedy and not this window's.

## 10.806 The GUI said "Run apply" for a change netcfgd makes by itself

Sixteen sentences, one after every save -- a device, a network, an interface, a rule, the
firewall, DNS, UPnP, the country -- said "Run apply to make the machine match it". That is
wrong in the ordinary case: a write reloads the configuration, and the next pass reconciles
it on every interface whose `on_drift` is `reconcile`, which is the default
(`ncfg_on_drift_default`); 10.783's access point was reconciled at once on its
save. A person told to run something that has already happened either does it for nothing
or concludes the save did not take. They now say netcfgd puts it in effect itself and that
`Apply...` shows anything it holds back -- an interface set to `report`, an action not
reconciled in isolation, a daemon holding with `--no-apply-on-start` -- which is where those
cases are explained. The DNS tab's "`ncfg apply` is what does it", inside a window with an
Apply button, points at the button, and so do its warning and the Bluetooth tab's note, which
named `ncfg plan` for what `Apply...` shows before anything is sent.

## 10.805 A VPN's password and a WireGuard key are typed in the device dialog

**From the help lines 10.804 left open.** The device dialog's private key and password
fields took only `@secret:NAME`, and their placeholders and refusals told a person to run
`ncfg secret set` in a terminal -- for a VPN password, a PPPoE login from the provider, a
WireGuard key `wg genkey` printed. 10.782 had already settled the shape for access points:
a typed credential goes to the store through `secret_put`, and the block names it. The device
dialog does the same now, under `wg-`, `ppp-` or `vpn-` and the device's name, before the
block is written so it never names a secret that is not there -- without `replace` first, and
when one is there the dialog asks, since a WireGuard key nobody else has cannot be got back
(0042; the add-network dialog's question). A reference still works, the
fields echo only while edited, and a WireGuard key is checked as 32 octets of base64 beside
the field, since netcfgd would only find out at apply. The old comment's worry -- inviting
somebody to paste a key into a configuration file -- does not arise: what is pasted never
reaches the file. `live_device_dialog` refuses a non-key, then stores a pasted key and a typed
PPPoE password and finds both in the store and named by the block, then saves the session with
another password: No keeps the stored one and writes nothing, Yes replaces it.

## 10.803 A name that cannot change no longer looks like a box to type in

**From 10.778's list: a renamed DNS record's read-only name field looks editable and says
nothing.** The shape was ten dialogs wide, not one: device, network, access point, mesh,
rule, link set, host list, block list, DNS record and Bluetooth each make the name or id
read-only when editing an existing block -- since it is what the block is called, and a
change would write a second one and leave the first -- and a read-only `QLineEdit` still
draws as an ordinary field. A person types, nothing happens, nothing says why.

`gui/src/fixed_name.h`'s `ncfg_fix_name` draws it on the window's colour without a frame,
as a label reads, keeps it selectable for copying, and says on hover that a rename is adding
one under the new name and deleting this one. Ten call sites, one helper, so the next dialog
with an identity field gets the same. `host_list_load` and `mesh_load` assert both halves;
with the frame left on, `mesh_load` fails.

## 10.802 After a delete, nothing is selected rather than the next row

**From 10.778's list: the selection moved to the next row after a delete.** Every tab is an
`ncfg_table_view`, and every refresh replaced its rows with `setRowCount` and new items,
which keeps the current row's *number*. Delete the second of three and the third became
current -- highlighted, and `selected_row()` answering for it -- so the tab's delete button
stayed live on an item nobody had chosen, one more press from going too. Every tab whose
buttons ask `selected_row()` or `selected_cell()` had it.

`show_rows` now keeps the choice on the item rather than the index: it remembers the chosen
row's first column, and after the refresh selects the row with it, wherever it moved, or
nothing when it is gone, then tells the view so its buttons follow. A first column that
repeats picks its first row, which is no worse than before. `gui/tests/table_selection.cpp`
states the cases; the old `show_rows` fails three of them.

## 10.801 A saved profile can be deleted

**From 10.778's list: no profile could be deleted** -- not from the GUI's profiles tab and
not from `ncfg`, though both could save one. A profile saved by mistake, or for a place
somebody no longer goes, stayed in the list for good unless somebody went to
`/etc/netcfgd/profile` by hand, which is what the GUI exists to spare a person.

`ncfg_profile_delete` takes only what `ncfg_profile_save` wrote: a directory under the
operator's `profile/` holding its `00-saved.conf` and nothing else. It refuses the profile in
use -- its selection would name a directory that is gone and the next load would fail; the
remedy is switching away, which is a decision about what the machine runs and not one a
delete should make -- one shipped with the machine, which has nothing of the operator's, and
one written by hand, which 9.4 keeps from clients. One already gone is success, as for
`config_delete`, so `profile_delete` is idempotent in `idempotence.c`'s table; `ncfg profile delete`
checks the list first so that a typo is still "no profile called".

**A new request, `profile_delete`**, at `admin` like `profile_save`, answered by the
daemon against the profile its running document has chosen. It is additive -- a client
older than this daemon never sends it -- and `doc/schema/socket.json` gains its line (68).
The GUI's profiles tab has `delete`, offered only for this machine's own profile that is not
in use, asked first. `tests/live/profile.sh` holds the refusals and the delete through a
running daemon; `gui/tests/live/live_profiles.cpp` presses the button, No then Yes, and
asserts the daemon's list.

## 10.798 A tunnel's credentials are asked before the first action too

**10.796's shape, looked for again: a credential resolved only by the action that needs it.**
The access point and the supplicant were not the only ones. A WireGuard private key is read
when the tunnel is configured, and a plan that creates a tunnel has no `wg.set_device` -- the
create carries the whole configuration (`finish_create`) -- so the key was found missing
inside `link.create`, after the link existed. Measured in a namespace before the change: an
apply naming a key nobody stored failed at `link.create`, and `wg1` was left behind with no
key, its address skipped.

The kernel executor's `ready` now asks the WireGuard arm, with the document and resolver that
arm is given: the private key for `wg.set_device`, each preshared key for `wg.set_peers`, and
both for a `link.create` of a tunnel. `c/tests/world_test.c` asks it about a stored key and a
missing one; `tests/live/c_wireguard.sh` applies a tunnel whose key was never stored and finds
no device and "not started" in the journal -- the check that failed before.
