**And OpenVPN's and PPPoE's passwords**, which are resolved differently: when the executor is
opened (`daemon_service.c`), where one that cannot be read is logged by name and its tunnel or
session gets no entry, so `backend.start` refused it -- when its turn came, after whatever went
before. `ready` now asks for the entry. `tests/live/openvpn.sh` applies a tunnel whose
password was never stored and finds "not started" in the journal, which it did not before.
The PPPoE half has no live run here (no pppd installed) and rests on the same lookup.

## 10.796 Atomic stops before it starts; best-effort does what it can

**The holder, 2026-11-11: "A plan that is atomic needs to stop if it is missing
pre-requisites, weren't we supposed to also have a non-atomic best-effort apply?"** Both were
decided in 0286 (10.544) and neither was built for one host: the executor ran actions in order
and stopped at the first failure, with everything before it done -- 10.783's radio left with
neither supplicant nor access point. Now `ncfg_apply_as` takes a mode.

- **An executor may say what an action needs before it runs**: `ready`, optional, beside
  `execute`. The kernel executor's asks for the secrets a `backend.start` will resolve -- an
  access point's passphrase and roaming key -- and whether a radio's networks can be written,
  which reads every referenced passphrase. A wired 802.1X port and a radio given to a mesh are
  configured from their own block and never read the networks, so they are left to their op.
  It answers from the store and touches nothing.
- **Atomic** asks every non-optional action first. One not ready fails with "not started:"
  and what it lacks, every other action is skipped, and the machine is not touched. A
  failure while running still stops the plan, as before.
- **Best-effort** runs what it can. An action not ready, or one failing while it runs, is
  `unmet`; whatever depends on it, directly or through others, is skipped saying which action
  it waited on; everything else runs. **And what exists only to make room for an action that
  cannot run is skipped too**: an action is skipped when it has dependants and every one of
  them is either not ready or itself skipped this way. That is what keeps 10.783's supplicant
  up -- the stop exists for hostapd's start, and doing it alone is the outage. An action
  nothing depends on is never skipped this way; it was planned for its own sake. The skip
  is said on the log at `warning`, beside the unready action's own `error`.

**Who gets which.** An apply somebody asked for -- `ncfg apply`, the GUI's apply, the CLI
in-process -- is atomic, because the person is there to read why it did not start. The
daemon's own passes -- drift repair, the pass at startup, a radio taken on, a revert -- are
best-effort, because nobody is waiting on them and holding back an unrelated rule for a
network block with no secret is the worse outage. That is 0286's rule that the mode follows
the change rather than the operator, read at host scale: what decides it is whether there is
somebody to answer.

**Not built: choosing the mode at the apply button.** 10.544 keeps the override, and
`ncfg apply --best-effort` is where it would go; it changes the request schema, so it waits
until somebody needs it rather than arriving with the engine.

`c/tests/world_test.c` asks the kernel executor about an access point with its passphrase
missing and then stored. `c/tests/apply_test.c` holds the four engine cases -- atomic with a prerequisite missing starts
nothing, best-effort skips what waits and runs the rest, a runtime failure takes its
dependants and nothing else, and the stop that serves only the unready start is not done --
and breaking either the preflight or the skip fails them. `tests/live/ap.sh` applies an access
point whose passphrase was never stored, in a namespace: the apply fails, the dummy device it
would have created first is not there, and `plan.last.json` says "not started" and names the
secret. With the preflight taken out the device is made and the journal names nothing.

## 10.792 An access point on a radio that is switched off waits for the switch

10.791's shape, looked for at once beside it. An access point on a radio whose rfkill switch
was set had its `backend.start` planned every pass, and hostapd failed it with "Failed to set
beacon parameters; Could not connect to kernel driver" -- nine times in forty seconds in a
hull guest, each one stopping the rest of the plan and none naming the switch. The access
point walk now plans nothing for a radio the observation reports blocked -- not the start,
and not the supplicant's stop that a change of role brings, since taking a station down for

already names the switch. Measured the same way after: no error in fifty seconds, and hostapd

## 10.791 A radio that is switched off is not brought up

Found by 10.790's rig on its first run, with the radio's rfkill switch set from sysfs. The
kernel refuses `link.up` on a blocked radio with ERFKILL, and a failed action stops the rest
of the plan: so with airplane mode on, every other change on the machine was skipped on every
pass, two error lines each time -- eight in fifteen seconds in the rig. `warn_blocked_radios`
already said netcfgd configures such a radio anyway and that it associates when the switch
comes back (0062: the block is somebody's act and is never undone); the bring-up was the one
part that did not follow it. The interface walk no longer plans `link.up` for a radio the
observation reports blocked, and the next observation after the unblock plans it -- the rig
watched the link come back. `plan_kind_test` holds both halves and fails with the condition
taken out.

## 10.790 A suspend rig, ready for the hull that can wake a guest

The holder has said hull will implement suspend and resume for testing (2026-11-11), which
is what 10.773 found missing. netcfgd's half is written now so the two meet without a round
trip: `tests/live/suspend.sh`, run by `tests/hull/suspend/hull.conf` through `make
hull-suspend`, measures the register's four questions on a real sleep. A station joined to an
access point on `mac80211_hwsim`, leased by dnsmasq for two minutes, with a confirm window of
120 seconds open over a change, suspends for 150 seconds -- so the lease and the window's
wall-clock deadline both run out asleep -- and is then asked: associated again within two
minutes, how long it took; the lease renewed (a dnsmasq expiry granted after the wake), not
held stale; the window paused, so the change still stands and can be confirmed (10.665); and
the rfkill watcher still hearing a block.

**The wake is the guest's own**, the RTC alarm and `/sys/power/state` that `rtcwake` uses,
so nothing in the rig is hull's syntax: hull's part is that the alarm wakes the guest and the
devices and shares survive, listed in its inbox (20261110T2300Z). Until then a run ends at the
target's timeout with "no verdict", which is that answer; it is not in `make hull`.
`SUSPEND_TEST=freezer` runs it as a check of itself, at the pm_test level this hull already
returns from -- labelled a rig check, since nothing expires in five seconds.

**The rig check found a fault on its first run**, and it was not in the rig: 10.791.
`make hull-suspend SUSPEND_TEST=freezer` passes every check now, labelled a rig check. The
rfkill check asks the daemon, through `ncfg wifi status` and the link coming back up, rather
than grepping its log -- the first version grepped for `rfkill` and the executor says
`RF-kill`.

policy, who may ask netcfgd for what, is outside what `admin` may write, so a tier cannot

## 10.785 A standing drift is announced once, not on every pass

From 10.778's list. The GUI walk's events tab held ninety-one identical lines -- `drift br0:
link.create: kind is <absent> but should be bridge` -- one per pass for as long as a bridge
waited for Apply, with whatever else had happened somewhere among them. The log line and the
`drift` hook already said a standing drift once, by the record in `/run`; the event every
client follows (`ncfg monitor`, the TUI, the GUI's events tab) said it every pass. The loop
now keeps a fingerprint of each drift it announced on the last pass -- interface, summary
and action -- and announces only one that is new or reads differently, so a drift starting,
changing or coming back after it cleared is still news. What stands is in the status and the
plan for a client that connects later. `reconcile_test` runs the same drift twice and asks

## 10.784 The plan's warnings are read rather than scrolled, and two dialogs open at their form's width

Two of 10.778's list, taken because they sit on the GUI's one promise -- show the plan before
changing anything. **The plan's warnings** were a strip a line and a half high whose message
column took the width of its longest sentence, so each warning was one cut line read by
scrolling sideways, in the apply dialog and the plan tab alike. The message and remedy columns
are capped and wrap now, each row as tall as its sentence, and a plan with nothing to do --
where the warnings are the plan -- gives them the room. `plan_notes`, a new probe, renders one
long warning and fails two checks with the change taken out.

**The interface and network dialogs** opened narrower than their forms, because a scroll
area asks for little width: the address fields read "192....", a routes column "ta", the
button after `remove` was cut, all under a horizontal scroll bar. Each is sized to its
form's width at construction now, capped by the screen, with a first screenful of height --
913 by 600 and 906 by 600 on Xvfb, every field readable, where they were 634 by 541.

## 10.783 A plan stopped what was running before it found the secret the replacement needed

**Measured in the GUI walk; closed by 10.796.** An access point `TestAP` on `radio0`, whose
passphrase reference named a secret nobody had stored, was saved while `radio0` was a station
joined to `HomeFiber`. The daemon reconciled at once: `backend.stop` took the supplicant down,
then `backend.start` for hostapd failed on `secret ap was not found`, and the radio was left
with neither -- the client connection lost by saving a dialog, until the access point was
deleted and the supplicant came back thirty seconds later. Secrets were resolved by the action
that needed them, at apply, and the executor stopped at the first failure with everything
before it already done.

The two ways this entry weighed -- ask every action before the first and run nothing, or skip
only what the missing secret holds back -- turned out to be 0286's two modes, already decided
(10.544) and never built at host scale. 10.796 builds both and says which caller gets which.

## 10.782 An access point or a mesh can be given a passphrase from the window

The walk could not make an access point with a passphrase at all: the dialog took only

secrets tab can forget a secret but not set one. The mesh dialog was the same. The network
dialog beside them had stored a typed passphrase through `secret_put` since 10.611, which is
the shape both now follow: checked as the supplicant will (8 to 63 printable octets), stored
first under the name the existing reference held or `ap-`/`mesh-` and the block's name with
what a secret name cannot carry made a dash, and the block given the reference -- so the
document still never holds a passphrase. Typed text is hidden; a reference, which is no
secret, is shown. `live_access_point` asked that a typed passphrase be refused and now asks

The walk added a hidden network with the passphrase `abc`: the block and the secret were

to do. `ncfg wifi add` has checked this since it was written; `wifi_add`, the socket verb the
tray and the window use, had not, and `add by hand` stores through `secret_put`, which no
