network dialog checks before it stores. `wifi_profile_test` and `live_network_dialog` hold
both.

## 10.779 A rule selector or a MAC that is no address is refused at compile, and a MAC in capitals is no drift

The walk saved a rule with `from = "300.1.1.1"` and a bridge with `mac = "zz:zz:zz"`; both
compiled. `rule_selector` passed text that was no address through untouched -- the Rust's
`unwrap_or`, so "a selector this build does not understand still reaches the place that can
say so" -- but that place is `kernel_rule.c`, which reads an address and nothing else, at
apply, after the actions before it had run. A device's `mac` was taken as any string, with
the same result in `kernel.c`. Both are refused at compile now, with the line, and the
document reader refuses the same for a document from the socket.

**Looking at the MAC found a worse fault beside it.** The plan compared a device's `mac`
with the kernel's text, and the kernel prints lowercase: a link at `02:aa:bb:cc:dd:ee` under
`mac = "02:AA:BB:CC:DD:EE"` was planned `link.set_mac` on every pass, measured in a
namespace -- a hardware address set again for ever under `on_drift = "reconcile"`. The
compiler writes it lowercase now and the plan compares without case, which also covers a
socket document. The document check accepts any spelling of a selector, because 10.200's
planner compares selectors as addresses for exactly that route; `plan_tc_test` said so when
a first version refused a non-canonical one. `lower_test` and `plan_kind_test` hold the
four; taken out together they fail five.

## 10.778 A hand-written block opens read-only, rather than refusing its save

**The window was walked whole for the first time**, every tab and dialog on Xvfb against a
scratch daemon, by a subagent that created, saved, reopened and deleted what each dialog
makes. Twenty-two findings came back; this is the first. Opening `configure` on `eth0`,
`radio0` or `HomeFiber` -- all three in the machine's own `netcfgd.conf` -- gave an editable
dialog that took every change and then refused Save with the compiler's "`interface eth0` is
already defined ... write `override interface eth0` to replace it". A client writes
`conf.d/interface-eth0.conf`, the name already exists, and nothing in the dialog said so
before the typing. So on a machine configured by hand, the GUI could edit nothing it found.

**The rule is not new**: design section 9.4 keeps hand-written blocks read-only to clients,
and 0030 enforced it for the NetworkManager shim by asking the filesystem whether the file
named for the block exists. `ncfg_connection::written_by_hand` asks the same of the daemon's
file list, for a block that exists; `hand_written.h` turns the dialog into a viewer -- Save
and Delete hidden rather than disabled, since a dialog re-enables Save as it validates, Cancel
named Close, and a sentence at the top saying where to change it. The interface, device,
network and access point dialogs ask, from the links, devices, hooks and wifi tabs. Not
offered: writing `override` from the GUI, which would be a client replacing what somebody
wrote by hand -- the thing 9.4 refuses. `live_config` holds the test and the dialog's shape,
and fails with `written_by_hand` answering false; seen on screen for `eth0`.

**The walk's findings not acted on**, kept so they are not found twice (10.784 to 10.789
have since taken the plan's warnings, the narrow dialogs, the repeated drift, the stale scan,
the profile offered twice, UPnP's order, the access tab's banner, the events' time and the
hooks tab saying where a hook is added -- the links tab, configure, then hooks): a
renamed DNS record's read-only name field looks editable and says nothing (~~fixed~~, 10.803); the selection
moves to the next row after a delete (~~fixed~~, 10.802); ~~no profile can be deleted~~ (10.801); the hooks tab
cannot itself start a hook (~~fixed~~, 10.808); and backticks (~~around names~~, 10.804),
`ncfg` commands and op names reach a person's eye in many help lines. Each is small, and
each is what a laptop's owner meets.

## 10.777 The tray said "offline" for a machine on a network, and was first seen running

**The tray had never been on a screen.** `tray.h` says as much: `create` returns nullptr
without a notification host, "which is every machine this has been built on", so its menu was
known only through the rules `tray_choices` checks. A sixty-line XEmbed system tray -- it
owns `_NET_SYSTEM_TRAY_S0` on Xvfb and docks what asks, the protocol TDE's own tray speaks --
put it there, against a scratch daemon over `fake_supplicant.py`. Docking, the menu, `Scan for
networks`, the `Connect to` list with strengths, joining a new network through the add
dialog (one `SELECT_NETWORK`), `Profile` and `Show window` all worked.

**The state line did not.** On HomeFiber with 192.0.2.20/24 and no default route it said
`offline`. The daemon names a primary link only where a default route runs, so that machine
is `local` with nothing to name -- and `line_for` returned "offline" for any empty label
before it looked at the rung, beside an icon drawn from the rung, which said otherwise. A
network that hands out no gateway, or a static address written without one, is that case;
and `requires = "address"` makes the same machine `routed`, which read as offline too. The
shared notice had the same blind spot and would have said "Connected to ." It now says
`connected, no default route` and `connected` where no link is named, and the notices drop
the name rather than leaving a hole. `tray_choices` and `client_test` hold both; with the old
`line_for` back, two fail.

**What still differs from nm-applet, by decision rather than fault:** the `Connect to` list
is empty until somebody chooses `Scan for networks`, because `tray.h` holds that nothing scans
on a timer or on the menu opening.

## 10.776 The wifi tab gives the scan the room

10.774's walk found the wifi tab's three tables stretched alike, so an 880 by 560 window
showed two of the six networks in range while the access points this machine offers -- none,
on most laptops -- held a third of the tab. Weighting them 3, 2 and 1 moved the scan to three
rows, since a stretch shares only the height a window has spare; a minimum of five rows for
the scan table is what showed five, and grows the window from 560 to 620 pixels, inside a
768-line screen. Seen on Xvfb against the walk's scratch daemon, before and after.

## 10.775 Signal as the strength a person reads, on NetworkManager's curve

The tray listed networks as `HomeFiber  (-53 dBm)`, and the wifi tab's column the same. A
laptop's owner has no sense of a dBm and every applet they have used draws bars from a 0-100
strength, so 10.774's walk recorded it and this changes it. `ncfg_signal_percent` in the
client library, beside the tray's other shared rules so the TDE tray can show the same, is
NetworkManager's `nm_wifi_utils_level_to_quality` -- 100 at -40 dBm, 0 at -100, linear and
truncated between -- because 10.399's oracle found the obvious `2 * (dBm + 100)` disagreeing
with a real NM by fifteen points at -53. The tray shows the percentage alone; the wifi tab,
being where somebody places an access point, shows `79%  (-53 dBm)`. `client_test` holds
the ends, the clamps, -53 as 79 and -70 as 50, and fails two with the linear formula. The
stations tab and the roam and steering settings stay in dBm: they are thresholds an operator
types, and those are dBm in hostapd and the supplicant alike.

## 10.774 Adding a network from the window joins it, as the tray does

Found by walking the desktop aim with the GUI on a screen (Xvfb, a scratch daemon over
`fake_supplicant.py`): picking a network in the wifi tab and pressing `add` wrote its block,
re-scanned and stopped. The machine stayed on the network it was on, and joining meant
finding the row again and pressing `join` -- a second step the tray dropped in 10.652, which
joins once the daemon has loaded the block. nm-applet, plasma-nm and GNOME's network panel
all connect on the one act, and nothing recorded argued for the window keeping two: a block
`wifi_add` writes from a scan row is a network the operator asked to use. The window's `add`
and `hidden network...` now join the same way, by SSID among the saved networks, twenty looks
half a second apart, and say so when the block is not loaded in that time. `live_wifi` adds
the open network in range through the button and asks that the daemon send the supplicant a
`SELECT_NETWORK`, read from the daemon's log, which `gui_wifi.sh` now names; with the join
taken out it fails.

**What else the walk showed, recorded rather than changed.** The window is the full
editor -- closer to nm-connection-editor than to an applet -- and the tray is the laptop
owner's way in, so the rest weighs less: the wifi tab prints the supplicant's own state word
(`COMPLETED`), which `ncfg_client.h` keeps on purpose so every tool names a state alike;
signal was in dBm where the three above draw bars (10.775 changes that); the scan table showed two rows (10.776 gives it five) while the
access points this machine offers, which a laptop rarely has, keep the most room; and the
links tab lists the kernel's fallback tunnels (`gre0`, `sit0`, `erspan0`) beside the
interfaces the machine uses. Each is a choice somebody could reasonably make the other way.

## 10.773 Suspend in a hull vm stops at the device step

The register's suspend item wants a lid measured -- a lease across the sleep, the
supplicant's association, the rfkill watcher -- and `tests/live/` cannot suspend the machine
it runs on. A hull vm can suspend its own kernel, so the hwsim image was tried. With
`/sys/power/pm_test` at `freezer`, both `freeze` and `mem` return after the test delay; at
`devices`, and in a real s2idle woken by the RTC, nothing more is heard from the guest: no
output, no write to its rw 9p volume, until the outer timeout. Whether the guest dies or only
its channels do is not established, since its console does not reach the host afterwards.
The guest's `rtc_cmos` routes its alarm through the HPET, a known way for an alarm not to
wake s2idle, and hull offers no kernel argument to change that. Signalled to hull with the
reproduction (its inbox, 20261110T1922Z). The register's "never been run" was already not
quite true: 10.338's afternoon is a resume on the holder's laptop, the radio dropping and
netcfgd carrying on, and that is all that has been watched.

## 10.772 A stop waited for the command line to empty, not for the process to go

`make hull-mips` on b838b06e failed one check nothing excuses, `service_test`'s *the stop
returns only once it has gone, so a start cannot meet it*, where 10.765's three runs had passed
it. The stops 10.649 and 10.661 made wait ask `ncfg_process_still`, which asked only whether the
pid's command line still carried the marker. **A process's command line goes empty part way
through its exit**: `exit_mm` releases the memory it is read from before `exit_files` closes the
descriptors and before `exit_notify` makes it a zombie. Measured on this machine: a parent
polling an exiting child's command line until it read empty found the child not yet reapable
2000 times in 2000. So a wait landing in that stretch said "gone" of a hostapd still holding its
control socket, and the 25 ms step made it rare rather than impossible -- a loaded guest is where
it showed. `ncfg_process_still` now also counts a process the kernel has marked `PF_EXITING`
and that is not yet a zombie, read from `/proc/<pid>/stat`; a zombie is still gone, as before.
Every stop that waits by pid gets it: hostapd, wpa_supplicant, radvd, openvpn, pppd. Four more
waited by re-reading the pid file, which asks the same command line through
`ncfg_process_pid_of` -- dnsmasq, miniupnpd, the DHCP clients (odhcp6c's release among them)
and avahi-autoipd -- and now follow the pid they signalled through `ncfg_process_still`, as
10.661 made the first five do.
`process_test` polls two hundred exiting children the way the stops do and asks that each be
reapable once it reads as gone; with the old rule put back it fails. That this is what the mips
run hit is inferred, not watched: it is the one way the check can fail with the stop reporting
success.

## 10.771 The polling watcher missed a file rewritten inside one clock tick

`make live` on d48f9fda failed two checks in `config_arrives.sh`'s mtime-polling run, after
the same commit had passed: a drop-in written broken was not reported within ten seconds, and
was reported only once the script touched `netcfgd.conf` afterwards. The fingerprint compared
mtimes, nanoseconds included, and the kernel stamps them from a coarse clock, so two writes
inside one tick of it leave the same mtime. `cat > file` is two writes -- the create empty,
then the content -- and a poll landing between them compiles an empty drop-in, which compiles,
and never sees the rest. Git met this as its "racily clean" index entries and settled it by
reading content; the fingerprint now carries each regular file's size and an FNV-1a digest of
its first megabyte, read on each tick only in the polling fallback and at startup.
`watch_test` puts the old mtime back after a fill and after a same-length rewrite, and both
fail with the digest taken out. **Not proven to be what the live run hit**: the daemon's log
cannot tell an empty compile from a late one. It is the one path that fits, and real either way.

## 10.770 `on_drift = "reconcile"` survives a save

The next case of 10.767's shape: the global drift policy was a plain enum with `reconcile` as
its fallback, and the renderer left `reconcile` out as the default, so a profile saved from a
configuration that chose it came back following whatever the default became. It is the one
whose default has already moved once (0132, from `report`), so the pin is worth having. It is
`ncfg_optint_t` now, read through `ncfg_on_drift_default()`; the renderer writes it where it
was written; an empty document no longer carries `on_drift_default` on the wire, and the client
shows absent as `reconcile`, as it does `networking`. The socket witness moved by that one key,
blessed; the schema version stays pinned (0038). A side effect worth having: a zeroed document
can no longer mean `report` by accident, which is why `ncfg_document_new` existed. 10.743's
answer stands for `networking`, `autoconnect` and the control blocks; the connectivity `ignore`
list is left as it is, its default being one an inheritor should follow when it grows.

## 10.769 A roam block pinned the values nobody wrote

The next case of 10.767's shape, found by looking for others: the compiler filled a roam
block's `signal`, `interval` and `slow_interval` with -70, 30 and 300, and the renderer wrote
all three whenever the block existed -- so the opposite failure the holder's rule names first.
A network that said only `roam { signal = -60 }` came back from `profile save` with
`interval = 30` and `slow_interval = 300` pinned, kept past any later change to either default.
The three are `ncfg_optint_t` now, the defaults `NCFG_ROAM_*_DEFAULT`, the supplicant's
`bgscan` built from `ncfg_roam_*()`, and the renderer writes what was given; an empty block is
still written, being a different document from none. `render_test` checks a signal-only block
pins neither interval, a block at every default keeps all three, and an empty one round trips;
writing all three again fails all three. Neither the GUI nor the client reads roam.

**The profile header said more than was true.** "A value equal to a default is left out" is
what 10.743 decided for `on_drift`, `autoconnect`, `networking` and the control and remote
blocks, whose model cannot tell a written default from none, and is no longer what happens to a
probe or a roam block. It says "what follows a default is left out" now, which holds for both.
Whether those others want the same treatment is the question the rule asks per setting -- when
the default changes, should this person get the new one? -- and for booleans whose defaults are
not expected to move, 10.743's answer stands.

## 10.768 A write is answered with the machine observed after it

`live_linkset` failed one run in four while 10.767 was being verified: it wrote two
`interface` blocks for links that do not exist and asked for the inventory at once, and the
inventory held neither. The inventory -- every link the machine has and every one the
document names -- lives in the observation, which `ncfg_daemon_state_reload` leaves alone
until the next pass. The write wakes that pass within milliseconds, so on an idle machine the
next request finds it done; under load (that run followed a rebuild of the GUI probes) the
client asked first. Six more runs did not fail, which is what a window that narrow does.

`wrote_configuration` now observes again and publishes, as a pass does, before the answer
goes -- for every writer that goes through it: `config put` and `delete`, `wifi add` and
`forget`, `profile set` and `save`. A failed observation keeps the previous one, as it does in
a pass.

**The live script written first proved nothing and was deleted.** It used `--poll-config` to
hold the pass off, and passed with the fix taken out: the write wakes a pass whichever way the
directory is watched. `answer_test` asks with no loop at all and a counting observer, so the
answer is the only thing that can observe: one observation per write with the fix, none
without it.

## 10.767 A probe's chosen default survives a save

Reported by claude-guidelines 2026-11-09, against the holder's rule of 2026-11-06 in
`working-practice.md` (*A config file records choices, not values*): a configuration keeps
"follow the default" apart from "this value, chosen", because somebody who picks today's
default does so knowingly and loses that intent when the default moves.

**What was wrong.** The compiler filled a probe's `interval`, `timeout`, `down_after`,
`up_after`, `hold_down` and `require_lease` with their defaults, and the renderer wrote each
only where it differed from one -- `render.c`'s own convention then, "a value equal to the
parser's default is not written". So `profile save` dropped `down_after = 3`, and the GUI's
interface dialog, which copied the rule and had no unset state, did the same on every Save.
Neither half could be fixed alone: both read the compiled document, which held values only.

**What it is now.** The six are `ncfg_optint_t` / `ncfg_optbool_t` in the model, optional in
the document, recorded by the lowering only where written; what the daemon acts on comes from
`ncfg_probe_interval()` and its five siblings, with the defaults as `NCFG_PROBE_*_DEFAULT`.
The renderer writes what was given whatever it equals. The client library reads -1 for "not
written". The dialog's lowest position on each control is "default (N)" and writes nothing --
0 for the interval and the counts, where 0 is not a legal value, and -1 for the timeout and
the hold, where 0 is -- and `require_lease` is a three-state box whose middle is the default.
`render.c`'s header states the rule the other way round now; the probe was the one block
whose numbers the compiler filled in, and the other renderer sites that compare with a
default compare with an enum's own "default" member.

The document's JSON changes only for a probe that left a value out, which no longer carries
it; one read from an older document has every value present and is kept as chosen, the safe
direction. 0038 pins the schema version until netcfgd ships, so no minor is bumped.

**Verified.** `render_test` keeps a probe written entirely at today's defaults through a round
trip, and fails both checks with the old rule put back; `lower_test` checks written apart from
left out; `live_interface_dialog` chooses `up_after = 2` -- today's default, which the old Save
dropped -- and fails its two checks with the old `!= 2` put back. `make check` exits 0, and
`gui_wifi.sh`'s thirteen live GUI probes pass. `live_linkset` failed one run in four on the
inventory not yet holding links just written, which this change does not touch (10.768).

## 10.764 A name with a colon was a command, for any `wifi`-tier caller

A secret reference is `@secret:PROVIDER:NAME` or `@secret:NAME`, read up to its first colon,
and `exec` runs its name as a command, as root. `ncfg_secret_name_usable` refused quotes,
slashes, dots and control characters and not a colon. Two routes from a `wifi_add`, which needs
only the `wifi` tier, wrote a name into a reference: the network's id becomes its passphrase's
`@secret:<id>`, and a certificate's name became `ca_cert = "@secret:<name>"` through
`stored_reference`, which asked no rule at all. So `wifi add --id exec:reboot` with a
passphrase, or an enterprise network naming its CA `exec:reboot`, configured a network whose
credential was `reboot`, run by the daemon at the next apply. The content gate never saw it:
it reads `config_put`, and this was the daemon writing configuration on a caller's behalf.

Fixed at the rule rather than at the routes: a colon is refused in every secret name, since
no name containing one can be referred to as itself anyway -- it would parse as a provider --
and `stored_reference` now asks that rule. `secrets_test`, `wifi_profile_test` (the id, which
the real installer checks) and `daemon_wifi_test` (the certificate, refused before anything
reaches the installer) each failed before and pass now.

**The cost, stated rather than found later:** a network whose SSID contains a colon can no
longer be added under its SSID as its label, and needs `--id`. The message says the colon is
why. Spelling the provider out (`@secret:file:<name>`) everywhere a reference is built would
have kept such labels, and meant changing the round-trip comparison and every place a
reference is matched as text -- more surface for a security fix than one rule.

Found by asking of today's other privilege fixes' shape (10.760, 10.761) where else a caller's
text becomes configuration without passing the content gate.

## 10.761 A block list's `file` chose where root's fetch writes

The second gap behind 10.760, and the one the gate could never have shown: it matches key
*names*, and `file` is privileged in `openvpn`, so `block_list { file }` read as classified.
It was ordinary. `ncfg block fetch` (0305) downloads each list's `url` and renames the
download onto its `file` at 0644 once it holds one name; an operator or a timer runs it, as
root. So a caller who is not root could name both -- `file = "/root/.ssh/authorized_keys"` and
a URL serving one hostname and one key -- and the next root fetch wrote it there.
`authorized_keys` ignores the line it cannot read.

**Privileged outside `NCFG_BLOCK_LIST_DIR` (`/var/lib/netcfgd/block`) and ordinary inside it**,
which is the certificates' shape: conditional on the value, where `@secret:` is ordinary and a
path is not. The directory is where the GUI offers to keep a list, so a desktop user keeps the
feature. Inside means no empty, `.` or `..` component after the prefix -- the string test alone
calls `/var/lib/netcfgd/block/../../../root/x` inside, and the test that says so failed when
the `..` arm was taken out. `url` stays ordinary: it chooses what goes into a file, and the
file is what is guarded.

Searched for the rest of the shape -- a key that takes an absolute path -- by every lowering
arm for `file`, `path`, `config`, `command` and the like: `openvpn { config, file }` and
`probe { command }` were privileged already, and `block_list { file }` was the one that was
not.

**A relative `file` is left to the compiler**, which refuses it as "not an absolute path". The
first version called it privileged, and `make gui`'s `block_list_load` -- "a relative file is
refused", expecting the compiler's sentence -- got one about root instead. It names nothing
root would open, and a typo deserves the message that says what is wrong with it.

## 10.760 `remote { agent }` was ordinary, so a client could open the remote socket

0127 lets a caller who is not root send configuration and refuses the productions that grant
more than configuring a network; `privileged[]` in `c/src/daemon/privilege.c` is the list.
`remote`'s three tiers were on it and `agent` was not. `agent` says which local principal may
hold the other end of the remote socket, and it sets that socket's mode and group (0159), so
`remote { agent = "any" }` from an admin-tier caller opened it to every local user -- each of
whom then reached whatever the remote tiers open. That is widening who may ask, which is what
`NCFG_PRIV_AUTHORIZATION` exists to refuse.

**Unclassified in both implementations, and found by porting the gate that should have
caught it.** The Rust's `privilege_gate.py` read the keys the compiler accepts out of
`match ... key.as_str()` arms, and the Rust lowered `agent` with an `if` -- so the gate never
saw the key and passed. The C kept the table and `authorize_test.c` pinned its rows, which
checks that no row is lost and never that a new key was looked at. Pointing the gate at the
C's lowering (10.759's open list) printed `agent` among 43 keys nobody had classified.

Fixed by the row and a case in `the_content_gate_refuses_each_privileged_production`, which
failed before the row and passes with it. The other 42 keys are the gate's port to classify.

## 10.759 The Rust is retired, and what `make live` said the day before

[0317](doc/decision/0317-the-rust-is-retired.md) is the decision, on the holder's word: retire
the Rust that blocks work or causes extra work. All of it did -- `make check` built the
workspace twice, every shared message was written twice or declared a difference -- and every
gate that read it read only it, measured before anything went. 106,000 lines, 166 files,
eleven make gates -- fmt, clippy, unsafe-policy, executor-policy, test, conformance, agree,
deny, cross, fuzz-rust, nm-containment -- and the nine Python gates 0317 lists.

**`make live` on dcbc20ee, the last run with the Rust in it:** 0 failures; 90 scripts passed;
the Rust test binaries 5, 31 and 17. Six skips, each needing real root, hardware or `nmcli`,
which 10.758's `vm-skipped` covers. It stops at `sandbox_writes.sh` refusing on this sysvinit
machine, by design and last for that reason; `vm-sandbox` runs it under systemd 257.

**What took the Rust's place in the live scripts** is in 0317. Two things went further than
replacing it. `c_wireguard.sh` reads the kernel with `wg` and compares the whole private key
the device holds against the store's, clamped, where the Rust reported only `key_matches`. And
`c/tests/shed_test` now runs in `make live` under `unshare -rn`: its own header says the drop
is observable only from a process with something to shed, `c-test` runs it as a person, and so
the C's privilege drop had never been asserted anywhere. The Rust's `netcfgd-sys` tests were
in `make live` for that reason and the C's equivalent was not.

**A sentence the C printed to operators went with it.** `ncfg_plan_warn_unbuilt` said "That is
not this port catching up: nothing acts on it in the Rust either" -- true and checked against
`crates/` while there were two, meaningless with one. It says "Nothing in netcfgd acts on it,
so there is nothing to wait for" now. Its negative checks in `plan_test.c` and
`plan_gaps_test.c` moved to the new words: left on the old ones they could never fail again.

**`c_daemon_answers.sh` showed that "answered" is not "reached".** With the comparison gone,
the first rewrite checked each verb got a non-empty answer, which the client gives with no
daemon running at all -- it observes and compiles for itself. A reload is the daemon's alone
(`cannot reach the daemon ... this command is answered by netcfgd` without one), so that is
the check that a daemon was there. The same run found `wifi add` now goes through the daemon
and succeeds in a namespace, where both daemons once refused it as "not a radio on this
machine".

**Open, from what went:**
- Five deleted gates held properties the C should hold and has no gate for: every `/etc` path
  written is one the systemd unit grants (`sandbox`), every op the planner can emit has an
  executor arm (`op`), every supplicant setting has a real one behind it
  (`supplicant_coverage`), every config key is classified for privilege (`privilege`), and no
  write failure is dropped silently (`write`). Each read `crates/` and never the C.
- Under `resolvconf` and `openresolv`, one interface's delivery runs the helper four times,
  twice with an empty `lo.netcfgd` record. Both implementations did it, so the comparison could
  not see it, and `c_dns_delivery.sh` now pins it. Read since: `dns.apply` and `dns.apply f0`
  each deliver every scope, global included, so the second delivery repeats the first.
  Redundant and idempotent; not worth a change on its own.
- `make live-container` now uses `debian:trixie-slim` rather than the Rust image, and the CI
  workflow's jobs build the C; neither has run since (the workflow is off, 2026-09-01).

## 10.756 A management command is one write

`hull-mips` at 364241c failed `openvpn_test` for the first time: *reads past the greeting*, on
a loaded machine. 10.573's shape again. `ncfg_openvpn_command` sent the command and then its
newline; a stand-in that read once took the first, answered and closed, and the second failed
a command that had worked. 10.573 made that survivable and taught one fixture to read to the
newline, and left the two writes and the other fixture. It is one write now, which is what a
line is, and so a peer has no gap to leave in. Two sends on a stream can arrive as one, so no
stand-in fails on demand; the test asks what the race depends on instead. `openvpn_test`
defines `send`, which the client then links to, and counts: one per command, ending in the
newline. With the two writes put back that check fails and the rest pass.

## 10.755 fuzznet 364241c: a removal a fork silently undid

Past 60934e20, fuzznet fixed what touches this tree's fleet: a group's fork made again only the
first 16 acts of a host it dropped, so a removal past those was silently undone (its sec 947,
20261107T1636Z), and it keeps such an act's time (sec 946). Three commits of notes and shares
at scale ride along; netcfgd holds no thousands of notes. No interface it calls changed. Its
full gates were still running when it said to take this pin, and it will say if they fail.

## 10.754 An access point restarted under its first station, on every boot

A pass of `hull-malta` read `wlan1 after 11 s: not connected`, with the handshake refused: *IE
in 3/4 msg does not match with IE in Beacon*. Then three passes passed, so it looked like a
flake, and it was not: **the station fell exactly once in every pass**, and the wait left at
the first sight of an association, so a pass depended on when it looked. The two IEs differ in
their last two bytes, `00 00` in the beacon and `0c 00` in the handshake, the replay counters
WMM sets. The access point had changed under the station.

10.748's `radio` kind did it. What hostapd is started with is read from the radio, a device
this plan makes has nothing to read yet, so it came up with no `ieee80211n`, and WMM follows
that; the next reconcile read the radio and restarted it to take them. On a stock OpenWrt
router, where netcfgd makes every wifi interface, that is each boot.

The plan now leaves the start to the reconcile that sees the radio, as a mesh point's
supplicant waits on its creation (10.687), and says so. `ncfg apply` in-process with no daemon
therefore needs a second run for that access point. `hull-malta` waits for a settled link with
the access point agreeing, and fails on any fall.

## 10.753 What a firmware upgrade keeps

The first-run guide has a person take a port out of `/etc/config/network` and give it to
netcfgd. `sysupgrade` keeps what is named, the image holds no netcfgd, and the package named
nothing: so an upgrade with settings kept would have left that port with netifd not holding
it and nothing else there, the configuration gone, and a new node identity for every paired
device to not know.

**The package now lists `/lib/upgrade/keep.d/netcfgd`, and the program is in that list.**
Keeping the configuration alone keeps a file nothing reads. A package reinstalled from a feed
afterwards was the other way, and it needs the network the upgrade has just taken. The program
is static, so the new image's libraries do not matter. The cost: what comes back is unknown to
opkg, so a later install needs `--force-overwrite`, which the guide says.

`hull-malta` archives what `sysupgrade -l` lists, deletes everything of ours, restores it as
an upgrade does, and starts: the start links are there and the node key is the same. `-l` and
not `-b`, which says *Cannot save config while running from ramdisk* on this image and exits 0
having written nothing. **Not run: a real flash**, which a kernel loaded by qemu has nothing to
write to, and the archive here is made by the test rather than by `sysupgrade`.

## 10.751 fuzznet 60934e20, and the first measure on a small machine

fuzznet took 10.740's finding to its default build: 1136 MB of bss to 434 MB, with the notes
view and six tables on the heap, and a reply past 68608 bytes, which never arrived, now
received (20261107T1029Z, 20261107T1108Z). netcfgd builds no reassembly slots of its own.
It asked for this tree's numbers, no small machine having run it. On OpenWrt's malta-be at
128 MB: bss 20.5 MB, netcfgd 4.7 MB resident, 51 MB of 118 available, and every tier passes.

## 10.750 A package for the router

netcfgd claimed to fit an OpenWrt router and had no way onto one but a copied binary.
`tool/ipk.sh PROGRAM ARCHITECTURE OUT.ipk` makes the `.ipk`, which is a gzipped tar of three
members and needs nothing of OpenWrt's build. **Installing configures nothing and starts
nothing**, the rule of the Debian and Alpine packages and sharper here: netifd is holding
the network, and there may be no console. With no `postinst` the init script stays out of
`/etc/rc.d` until a person enables it, which is the moment 10.746's warning is for.

`hull-malta` installs it with the real `opkg`, finds it listed, disabled and not running,
asks the installed `ncfg` for its version, and removes it. **Not a feed**: a package per
architecture wants the SDK and somewhere to publish, which is the holder's. Also here, unmentioned
in 402205ea's message: `dhcp_server_test`'s stand-in was stopped before its trap was set, the
race of 10.742's `autoip_test`, and now says when it is ready. `liveness_test` was the third of
that family: it waited for `timeout` and scanned while `timeout`'s child was still leaving.
**Three stand-ins, one shape, none of them netcfgd's**: a test that takes a process's arrival or
departure at one step's word, on a machine where steps had always been fast. An emulator is
slow enough to find them, which is `hull-mips` earning its keep beyond byte order.

## 10.749 What OpenWrt's hostapd does not answer

`ncfg wifi clients` said nothing was associated beside a kernel holding a station. OpenWrt
builds hostapd without the MIB commands, so `STA-FIRST` answers `UNKNOWN COMMAND`, which the
walk took for the end of it. **A false empty, and not only a wrong line of output**: the same
walk gives a deny list's prefix its stations to expand against. The station is now asked of
the kernel, by the `GET_STATION` dump mesh peers use, which any hostapd build answers, with
`authorized` read from its flags. Signal and counters are hostapd's and stay absent there.
**If the kernel will not say either, the list is `unread`**, 10.647's word for short, and never
"nobody".

## 10.748 `radio`: a router's interface is netcfgd's to make

**OpenWrt patches mac80211 to make no interface on a radio.** netifd makes them as it needs
them, so a stock router has `phy0` and no `wlan0`, `device wlan0` named nothing, and netcfgd
could make only a `mesh_point`, whose parent has to exist first. Without netifd, wifi on a router
needed a person with `iw`.

`device wlan0 { radio { phy = "phy0" } }` is a new kind, on `mesh_point`'s pattern: made over
nl80211, never remade by deletion, wanted before it exists. The difference is what names the
radio: `NL80211_ATTR_WIPHY`, read from `/sys/class/ieee80211/NAME/index`, as a phy's number is not
the digits of its name once a driver reloads. A station at first; hostapd or the supplicant makes
of it what it needs. **Named `radio` and not `wifi`**, as `wifi { }` already is the block
beside it saying how it is used. **Rejected: making the interface whenever an access point or a
network names a device that is not there**, which is a typo creating an interface, and needs
somewhere to learn the phy anyway.

**Measured on real OpenWrt** (`hull-malta`): no interface on either radio beforehand, netcfgd makes
both, and a station associates to an access point through the stock `wpad`.

**Which took one fix more**: `SET update_config 0` answers `FAIL` on `wpad`, built with no way
to write a configuration, and that stopped every apply on a stock router. 0015's pin has nothing
to pin there, so a `FAIL` goes on and only no answer at all still fails.

## 10.747 Two byte orders in one estate

A router in an estate is big-endian and its operator's laptop is not, and no two nodes of
different byte order had ever spoken. A wire fault of that kind cannot show on a machine of
either sort alone. `make hull-mips` now runs `node_fleet.sh` with the node built for the guest
and a MIPS fuzznetd and `ncfg` as the operator, after the same run all native as its control:
status, `ask`, an apply with a window, a configuration in pieces and `monitor --at`, all of it.
**It passes whole**, so fuzznet's wire and `ask` are byte-order clean. The node has to be the
native one, as qemu-user cannot observe.

## 10.746 The manager a stock router already has

`contention.c` knew NetworkManager and systemd-networkd, and every stock OpenWrt runs
**netifd**, which appeared once in this document, in passing. So the first install on a real
router would have put two managers on one interface in silence, which is the failure that file
exists to prevent, and `packaging/procd/netcfgd`'s `START=21` assumes they coexist.

netifd keeps no state file; it answers over ubus, and constraint 3 keeps a bus off the core's
path. **So the claim is its configuration**: `<etc>/config/network`, an `interface` section's
`device` or `ifname`, a `device` section's `name` or `ports`, with a running `netifd` as the
liveness, as for the other two. This is detection and imports nothing, so 0019 stands, and it
feeds what the others feed: the warning, and the refusal of a second supplicant.

**Rejected: `ubus call network.device status`**, the live answer, as a process per look on
the observe path and a word of netifd's protocol in the core. **Rejected: disabling netifd on
install**, as an installer that takes down the only network on a router with no console is the
lockout `confirm` exists to prevent. Which of the two a router keeps is the operator's, and
the remedy says how. Wireless is not read: `/etc/config/wireless` names radios and a
`wifi-iface`, and netifd's hostapd comes up under a name netcfgd would not have claimed.

`make hull-malta` is the witness: stock netifd, told of `eth0` by OpenWrt itself, and a document
naming the same device. netcfgd says `netifd also manages eth0`. **The fight is real, and the log
of that run shows it**: netifd took the new `eth0` into `br-lan`, and netcfgd answered
`link.unset_master master: <absent> (was br-lan)` two seconds later.

**A WAN port on DHCP works there too**, the commonest thing a router is told: OpenWrt's busybox
udhcpc under netcfgd took `192.168.77.50` from OpenWrt's dnsmasq in 6 s, across a veth netcfgd
made. The first run took nothing, and that was the stock firewall: it rejects input on a device
it has no zone for, which a DHCP server's socket is behind and a client's raw one is not.
**On a real router that is the operator's to arrange**, and `ncfg plan` already warns that other
nftables tables filter at the firewall's hooks.

## 10.743 A profile's header said the opposite of what it does

A saved profile told its reader it "says everything explicitly -- including things a
person would have left to a default", and the renderer omits every value equal to a
default. 10's list held that open for a person to settle, with both called defensible.
**The holder's rule of 2026-11-06, a config file records choices rather than values,
settles it**: an absent key is the choice to follow the default, and a written default
compiles equal to an absent one, so nothing later could tell it from a pin. Writing them
all is the direction that rule measures freezing every default at save time. The renderer
was right, and the sentence changes, in the C and the Rust alike.

## 10.742 A real big-endian kernel, and what it took to get one

10.741 left byte order open and said there was no cross compiler here. There does not
need to be: a hull guest can carry one, and OpenWrt publishes `malta-be`, a real kernel
and rootfs for a machine qemu emulates. Two tiers now, because each sees what the other
cannot:

- **`make hull-mips`**: the C suite as big-endian 32-bit MIPS under qemu-user, in a Debian
  12 guest, trixie having dropped the toolchain. 8758 lines read `ok`.
- **`make hull-malta`**: `tests/hull/openwrt/payload.sh` itself, on OpenWrt 24.10.4's
  `malta-be` kernel 6.6.110 in `qemu-system-mips -m 128`, under real procd, netcfgd built
  with OpenWrt's own toolchain and so against musl. `VERDICT ok`: start, respawn with the
  same key, the edit race, reload and stop, with addresses reaching `dummy0` over
  big-endian netlink. netcfgd resident at 4.6 MB, 52 MB available of 118. Everything
  fetched is pinned by checksum. Not in `make hull`, being two emulators deep.

**A second document goes where byte order can break**, after the router test: a vlan, a
bridge, a route, a port forward and firewall rules. Three witnesses that are not netcfgd's
word for itself: `/proc/net/vlan/config` reads `vlan10 | 10 | lan0`, `nft` reads `dport 443`
and `8443` where a swapped port would read 47873, and **`ncfg plan` then has nothing to do**,
which needs everything observed to compare equal to what was asked. All hold on big-endian.

**qemu-user answers `EOPNOTSUPP` for rtnetlink it cannot translate**, so `cli_apply_test`
and five scripts that need a machine cannot run in `hull-mips`. The verdict names them, and
excuses a section only if it also shows that limit; any other failure fails the run.
`hull-malta` is what covers that ground, for the paths its documents take; wifi is 10.748,
and the fleet between byte orders 10.747.

**What the suite found was nearly all the suite's own.** No byte-order fault in `src`:
every ioctl comes from the kernel's headers, and native integers were copied rather than
shifted, as `wire.h` asks. Tests carried x86 ioctl numbers and little-endian byte arrays:
`tun_test`, `rfkill_test`, `wire_test`, `observe_wireguard_test`. Two things were real:

- **`ncfg_supplicant_next_event` read `errno` after another syscall**: the deadline was
  put back between `recv` and the test, so a failed restore reported a harmless timeout
  or signal as a supplicant that had stopped answering. Saved straight after `recv`,
  which took all three of `supplicant_client_test`'s failures with it.
- **`autoip_test`'s stand-in raced its own scan**: until it execs, a forked child of the
  script recites the same markers, and an emulator is slow enough to be caught at it.
  Tested rather than argued: letting the child exec before the script exits took both
  failures. The real client is no shell, so this was the test's.

**Measured beside this, and needing nothing: an idle node does not wear flash.** Ten
minutes with the node serving changed no file in the store, which stayed at 76 KB. What
netcfgd writes, about 8 KB a second, goes to its run directory, which on a router is RAM.
The first attempt at this measured nothing: a scratch path too long for a unix socket
stopped fuzznet listening, so the store sat idle for the wrong reason. It was noticed
from a peak of 3.9 MB where a node reads 6, and redone asserting the socket first.

**And this answers 10.740's pressure question**: a real 128 MB OpenWrt has 44 per cent
of its memory available, where `hull-openwrt`'s guest, carrying a desktop kernel, has 8.

## 10.741 32-bit, which most routers are, had never been compiled

Everything here had only ever been built for a 64-bit machine, and the routers expected
next are as likely as not 32-bit ARM or MIPS. `gcc -m32` was on this machine all along.
**The tree did not compile**, and once it did the suite found the one fault that mattered:

- **`(long)UINT32_MAX` is -1 where `long` is 32 bits**, so `interface_index_of` in
  `apply/backend_ops.c` read `value > -1`, turned down every real index, and the refusal to
  start a second supplicant on a radio NetworkManager holds **failed open, in silence**: it
  has never worked on a 32-bit machine, and `contention_test` passed throughout, the
  fault being in the caller. `service_test` caught it. The bound is `INT32_MAX`, an ifindex
  being the kernel's `int`.
- **`sys/lock.c` kept milliseconds in a `long`**, which overflows on a 32-bit machine after
  24.8 days of uptime, a router having a quiet month. No test could see that, so it
  was found by reading for the shape of the first: every other clock helper widens first.
- **Two assertions stated an LP64 fact as a universal one**: `ifreq` is 32 bytes on 32-bit,
  so the tun request's length now comes from `sizeof(long)`, and the size of
  `ncfg_device_t` is held on x86-64 only. It is a reminder to whoever adds a field, and the
  figure is an ABI's: i386 and ARM do not even agree.

**A first guess was tested and was wrong**, and is worth keeping: 32-bit glibc's `readdir` failing
on ext4 offsets. `-D_FILE_OFFSET_BITS=64` changed nothing about that failure. The flags stay
regardless, with `_TIME_BITS=64`, in `LARGE_TYPES`, for what they do on a 32-bit glibc; they
do nothing on 64-bit or on musl, so OpenWrt never needed them.

`make c-32` runs the C suite as 32-bit: every check passes, 8840 lines reading `ok`. It is
not in `make check`, for the reason `c-san` is not. i386 is little-endian with 4-byte
`int64_t` alignment, so this says nothing of a MIPS router, big-endian and 8-byte: 10.742.

## 10.740 A program a router could not exec, and every gate green

fuzznet sizes its static tables for a person's thousands of notes and shares, and
netcfgd linked them with the services that use them switched off: 173 MB of bss in
`c/netcfgd`. **An untouched table costs no resident memory, so `make rss` passed and
fuzznet's sec 914 is right to call it address space. But the kernel promises a private
mapping before anything touches it**, and in its default mode refuses one larger than
RAM and swap together. So on a 128 MB router, measured in `hull-openwrt` with the
guest's memory cut:

    __vm_enough_memory: pid: 355, comm: netcfgd, bytes: 173522944 not enough
    procd: Instance netcfgd::instance1 s in a crash loop 6 crashes

The process dies at exec, before main, and `ncfg` dies with it, being one program.
There is no log line of netcfgd's to read. **Nothing here could have seen it**: `rss`
reads what is touched, `size` what is installed, and the one test that boots an OpenWrt
gave itself 512 MB, four times a router's memory, in a suite that exists because the
routers are next. fuzznet's message of 2026-11-06 (20261106T2010Z) named the risk for its
newer pin, which takes a full daemon to 1.14 GB, and that would have put the floor above
any small VPS as well.

**Fixed by naming the bounds, in every build** (`FUZZNET_BOUNDS`, `c/Makefile`): bss 173 MB
to 22 MB, fuzznet's bounds being `#ifndef` for this. Not an embedded variant of netcfgd:
these tables serve notes, shares, files and groups, which this node has off at build time
(10.702) on every machine, so a laptop gives up nothing either and one binary stays one
binary. The values are fuzznet's embedded ones, which `livecheck-embedded` holds.
**Two of its bounds were deliberately not taken**: `FZND_PULL_TARGETS_MAX` and
`FZND_SIBLING_TARGETS_MAX` stay at eight, being the estate's rounds, which a netcfgd node
does use. `PRESET=embedded-device` was rejected for the same reason, and because it also
turns the log file off and changes what the build reports itself as. Some bounds reach
headers, so `src/node` is compiled with them too.

`hull-openwrt` now runs at 128 MB and asks the program directly first, so this failure
names itself. It passes whole there: procd, respawn, the edit race, reload, stop. **The
same test, same memory, before the change: `VERDICT bad`, with the kernel line above.**
`make bss` holds the figure at 32 MiB, fuzznet's limit for its embedded build, in
`make check`, since `hull-openwrt` is not. 64 MB could not be measured: the host's kernel
panics there before init, which says nothing about netcfgd.

**The same run found an unbounded wait in that payload**, under a header saying every
wait was bounded: the race step spun on `pidof` with no count, so a daemon that never came
back held the vm until `HULL_TIMEOUT`. Counted now.

**This guest is tighter than a router, so read its pressure accordingly.** It runs the
host's Debian kernel: 88 MB of `MemTotal` from 128, 28 MB of that slab, about 7 MB
available beside a 5.6 MB daemon. fuzznet's ladder reads memory, so the node can reach
`scarce` here with an empty store, and netcfgd then says `fuzznet is in trouble`. That
report is true of this guest and not of a real router's kernel, measured in 10.742.

**One run in four read `procd started nothing`, and that was the test.** It came back on
the real kernel of 10.742, with the evidence this time: `after 0 s`, so the wait had ended
at once, on a pid that was not the one killed and was gone a moment later, and procd's real
respawn is in the log six seconds on. A fork of the daemon just killed can be seen by its
name for an instant. The payload now wants a pid that stays.

## 10.738 Two client roles, and a host daemon that lives with its clients

0314 is the decision. A client configures this machine through the root netcfgd and
holds nothing, or the person has joined and is a host of their own, whose key and store
are `ncfg host`'s. `ncfg node` and `ncfg nodes` became `ncfg host` and `ncfg hosts`, and
the phone's program `libncfghost.so`, on fuzznet's word that node no longer names
anything. `fzn_node_*`, `ncfg_node_*` and `node_*.sh` stay until a rename buys something.

**Only joining makes a host.** `--at`, `ncfg hosts` and a window's first look ask
`ncfg_fuzznet_user_host` for USE, which refuses a person with no store and says to
join; `ncfg join` alone asks MAKE. So a look no longer leaves a key behind.

**A flock is the count of clients.** Each holds `ncfg-clients.lock` shared, beside the
socket, from before it looks for the daemon until it exits. `ncfg host --while-held`,
which is what a client starts, tries it exclusively once a second from fuzznet's
`tick`, and stops the first time it wins. A socket of holders was the first
design and fails on `add join`, which restarts the process in place. Typed by hand
`ncfg host` takes no option and stays up.

**A remote apply may have no way back, and fuzznet may not fail (0316).** `apply --at
HOST --no-rollback HOST --reason TEXT` is the one remote apply with no window, logged as
an error on the target. `--confirm-within 0` had been getting past both of 0312's
refusals, which asked only that a value was present; `ask_test` fails with that restored.
The field is C's alone, as only an `ask` of another host reads it.

**A bad store, and what fuzznet does about it since its sec 917.** At e9b815a3 a read-only
store did not open: no node, no socket, no protocol, the case 0316 says must not exist. At
b81184c a host opens and works on one, and on a full one, writes held in RAM and flushed by
themselves when the disk returns. Rows held are lost by a stop. `get node` ends `pressure
STATE store disk|ram held N dropped N`, and that replaced the `statvfs` look here: every 10 s
from the tick, anything but disk and calm is an error in the log, said again hourly, a line
in `ncfg status` from `<run>/node-problem`, and `net-store-bad` then `net-store-ok` published
for another host, which `monitor --at`, the TUI and the GUI print as any `net-` subject.
Pressure comes down a step per 30 s, so the line outlasts the trouble by a minute or so.
`node_store_trouble.sh` holds it, and `node_ram_host.sh` runs every call netcfgd needs on a
read-only store with `netcfgd.sock` removed: `status`, `ask`, `askpart`, `hosts`, `eventlog`,
`get events`, `list peer` and the remote hop, an apply with its window among them. A store going read-only under a running daemon is not
staged, as the remount is refused while files are open for writing. A key that will not read
makes fuzznet's own daemon wait for it (its sec 920, no keyless mode, the holder calling it a
startup problem). netcfgd's `ncfg_node_open` still fails there, measured at 41eaf1a6: no node,
the own loop and `netcfgd.sock`, said in `ncfg status`, and every 5 s it tries again, starting itself over on the node when it opens, as a stop
holds. Set as `node_again_refresh`, after fuzznet's own wait for a key.

**A delegating odhcp6c could not be stopped, and only `vm-delegation` could see it.**
`ncfg_dhcp6_start` made `<run>/dhcp` and never `<run>/odhcp6c`, where it told the client
to write its pid; odhcp6c says nothing when that fails, so the one handle was missing.
udhcpc's start already made its own. `delegation.sh` also grepped wording the plan had
since changed. It passes in the guest now, a real kea to a real odhcp6c, and `dhcp_test`
holds the directory, as `vm-delegation` is not in `make check`.

**A daemon with a node binds no `netcfgd.sock` (0309).** The socket is only a no-node
daemon's now: one told `--fuzznet-dir ""`, or one whose node would not open. Binding it was
also what refused a second daemon on one run directory, so `<run>/netcfgd.lock` does.
`ncfg_cli_daemon_listening` took the socket for the daemon, so `ncfg` wrote the disk itself
beside a running one until it looked at fuzznet's too. The live scripts wait on `fuzznet.sock`;
`c_daemon_answers`, `control_exposure`, `log_shape` and `remote_tiers` are about the socket
and run with no node. Its code goes when nothing can reach that state: a node that will not
open at the start, and those four, and the Rust they compare against.

**The `rss` gate measured a daemon with no node too.** Its limit, 3644 KB, is for that, and
it stays on it with `--fuzznet-dir ""`. With a node the same daemon peaked at 6584 KB, 3064 of
it netcfgd's own. `make rss-node` holds that one, at 7040 KB: the observed peak of 6712 plus a band.

**`make live` tested a daemon nobody runs.** 41 of 42 live scripts started a daemon on a run
directory of their own, and such a daemon had no node, so they ran the own loop and
`netcfgd.sock` while every real machine runs fuzznet's. A daemon on any run directory has a
node there now (`<run>/fuzznet-store`, `--fuzznet-dir ""` for none), so they test what ships.
The first run of that found four things:
- **`cat > netcfgd.conf; ncfg apply` could remove every interface.** The own loop takes a
  configuration event ahead of a request in one round. fuzznet's calls a procedure before
  the tick, so an apply could be answered from a read taken as the file was truncated.
  `node_freshen` now takes what the outside loop has heard before any `ask` is answered.
  `nat.sh`, `rules.sh`, the shaping and ingress scripts all met it.
- **A wifi scan held the whole node deaf for up to ten seconds.** A procedure has to answer
  at once and the socket's thread had hidden the wait. A slow request now runs on a thread
  and `ask` answers `netcfgd is working on that; ask again`, which the client does for up to
  15 s, so `status` and the remote hop go on.
- **`NCFG_LOG` did not reach fuzznet.** It is passed as `--log-level` now, which governs its
  log file. Its stderr follows no level, told to fuzznet, so `log_shape.sh` runs with no node.
- **A stop takes about a second**, fuzznet's next pass. `restart.sh` allows two.

**A mesh_point's parent leaked on every reload.** `interface_kind_release` names each arm
that holds anything, and 5401de14 added `mesh_point` to the read and write tables and not
to it, so a daemon on a mesh router lost the name at each compile. LeakSanitizer named it in
five tests; the suite under ASan and UBSan is clean now, which is `make c-san`.

**`make live` ends at `sandbox_writes.sh` because that is its last step,** not because
anything is left behind it: `hwsim`, `association`, `pppoe-session` and `delegation` run
before it and skip without root. `make vm-sandbox` and `make vm-skipped` are what run
them. fuzznet's smallest host (its sec 912) reaches a daemon as an ordinary `call NAME`
from a paired peer, so nothing here changes for it.

**It stops at once, and for a while it did not (0315).** Stopping at once first made
every second `--at` hang 3 s with `the host did not answer`: fuzznet keeps a reply a few
seconds against resends (its sec 737), matched on sender, message number and bytes; a
new caller numbered from 0 on a new port; and since its sec 900 a match from another
address is dropped. So ten seconds of linger went in, and the fault went to fuzznet
(inbox 20261106T0215Z). Its sec 910, at a3d1fd9, begins a caller's numbers at a random
point, and the pin is at e9b815a3. With no linger and the test's wait removed, the first
`--at` after a restart fails at ba567ec2 and passes here, three runs of three. An `--at`
that starts a daemon takes 24 ms against 10 ms for one that finds it up, so the linger's
other reason, one daemon under a script, was worth nothing. `host_user.sh` now asks 40
times at spread moments across the stops: 0 unanswered here, 1 at ba567ec2. A client
meeting a stop waits for the lock, up to 500 looks, and starts another.

**fuzznet's presets (its sec 908) are at this pin and unused.** `preset`,
`preset_values` and `preset_revision` in the extension, `--preset=`, and a client's own
`local/client_config.h`, with names `rootd`, `userd`, `vault`, `ui-client` and
`one-shot-client`. It looks like the mechanism for the holder's profile system, but
fuzznet calls its values a first guess and the profile design is the holder's, so
nothing here takes it up yet.

**A cargo `target/` built from a worktree keeps that worktree's paths.** Sixty files in
`target/debug/deps` held `/tmp/claude-1000/wt-final`, gone since, because `env!` bakes in
`CARGO_MANIFEST_DIR` and cargo took them as fresh. `conformance` then reported the C
client's test binary as unbuilt beside the binary itself. Touching each crate's root
rebuilt them.

**`the node is waiting on a peer; ask again` is asked again,** for up to 4 s, in
`ask_again`: a daemon just started is usually in a round, and handing that on made a
cold `--at` fail. It refuses before anything runs, so a second asking is safe.
`fuzznet_line_test` holds this against a scripted socket; with the retry removed the
check fails.

**The first role's view of the estate is a procedure, `hosts`.** `peer` is not a grantable
subject, so a local user cannot ask root `list peer`; netcfgd asks it in-process and
hands it on under the `observe` tier, for a caller on this machine only. `ncfg hosts`
takes that for a person who has not joined, and their own daemon's list for one who has.
The fleet tab stays the second role's: its columns are each host's status, which only a
key can ask.

**A phone's daemon is started again whenever it has gone and the app is in front**
(`keep_up`), as Android kills a child of a backgrounded app and leaves the app. Behind,
it is left dead: a restart would be killed again, and what it holds is on disk. Seen on
the emulator: killed in front it was back within 4 s, killed behind it stayed gone, and
it came back when the app did.

**A renamed library survives in Gradle's intermediates and hangs the app blank.** With
`libncfgnode.so` left beside `libncfghost.so` the app drew nothing, with no error, and
Qt's main had returned; the store was never made. Five named copies under
`gui/build-android-*` had to go. Only a rename does this, and a clean tree never sees it.

**`ncfg join` and the first screen wait 15.5 minutes,** as a device now asks for 15.

**`ncfg pair confirm` holds whoever scans until the person at the terminal says yes,**
which answers the question of whether a scanned code is enough: the holder settled it
in fuzznet's sec 896 as both, and configurable. Plain `ncfg pair` sends no word, so the
host setting `invite/confirm` chooses, and it prompts all the same when one waits.

## 10.737 fuzznet's shape and terms, and what the next pin has to carry

From fuzznet's inbox message 20261106T0137Z and its sec 906, which reports the
holder's words; the holder had said here that it was coming.
**Terms.** A machine is the computer. A host is one user account's presence on it, the
unit of identity and authorisation, so several on a machine are normal. Daemons and
clients are processes of a host. "Node" now means only the English word, so this
document's "this user's host" and 0313's are the old usage. Root is the host holding
the estate's root key; vault is reserved, not a synonym.

**What this did to 10.734 and 10.735:** `ncfg node`, with a store and a key, is a
daemon of the user's host and not a client, and running that core inside a client would
have it write the disk. The holder settled it as two roles, 10.738.

**The repin, at ba567ec2** (f18ca13 or later, never 3f6b44b, which crashes on a tracked
write), done: `get events`, the setting `local/events`, and grants spelled `local:NAME`
and `local:@GROUP`. The `net-*` subjects stay. `any` has no read to grant, so such a
tier clears `local/events` and leaves those users on the control socket until fuzznet
has one; the node's own user needs no grant, which retires the root-by-number grant.
`node_second_user.sh` holds the stream as a real second uid at this pin.

Nothing to do for two of fuzznet's changes: no netcfgd verb takes a contact's name, so
`two contacts have that name` cannot reach us, and sec 897's SIGTERM is for a daemon
with no handler, which is `ncfg host` and not netcfgd's signal descriptor.

The phone's daemon links fuzznet's `make daemon-lib` and reads `make daemon-flags`, in
`gui/Makefile`, in place of a fragment read after fuzznet's Makefile for `FUZZNETD_LINK`.
At this pin the two links define the same 3109 symbols and differ by 16 bytes stripped.

## 10.736 One window, in a layout: what is a mode and what a device has

The holder: phone and desktop stay the same GUI, with minor differences by mobile or
desktop mode "like other GUI software here", and some things hardcoded, "the
non-existence of a local root node and prompting for remotes on mobile" (0313).

`gui/src/layout.h` keeps those two apart. `ncfg_layout` is how things are shown:
`--layout auto|desktop|mobile`, the device's by default, compiled in as
bbq-predictor's is. Today it decides one thing, the fit of 10.728, which left
`src/phone/` and now runs on any machine, so it can be tested with no phone.
`ncfg_device_has_local` is what is there at all, and no preference moves it.

**A phone's node box offered "this machine", which does not exist there.** It is
gone, and the fleet tab's test counts members rather than rows. `src/phone/` keeps
only what needs a phone: the camera, the first screen, the app's node.

## 10.735 Local by default, a host on asking

The holder: clients also connect to a remote netcfgd; on a phone that is the default
and only connection, on a desktop local is the default and remote "unusual but not
impossible". The transport was there (`--at`, `open_at`), but it stood on a node
nothing started. `ncfg_fuzznet_user_host` now starts `ncfg host` where a client asks
for a host, and `ncfg join CODE` does what the phone's first screen does. The window
has "Another host..." beside the node box until it has one, running `ncfg join`, and
starts the node at its own start where the user has a store, or after a reboot a
joined person would see this machine alone.

**The test is a connect and nothing more.** Asking `get prekey` was the first version:
it would take the one connection a test's fake serves, and it runs before every use.

Left up after its client, as this was first built, it was a user daemon in all but
name, and the holder wanted none: 10.738 replaced that. The reason first given here,
that a start costs a second, was never measured. On loopback a start is 13 ms, and the
rest of the 259 ms a cold `--at` took was this client's own 250 ms look.

## 10.734 `ncfg host`: netcfgd brings its own, and fuzznetd is a witness

The holder: all fuzznet software has its full function and coexists on the same files
and the same estate; fuzzypickles does not install fuzznetd, which is for testing that;
a client and a node are the same thing, hardcoded differently (0313). So every path here
that said "this user's fuzznetd" stood on a program nothing installs.

`c/src/node/user_host.c` is fuzznet's node with netcfgd's numbers, any free port, and
an empty extension, which is what makes it follow beside a face rather than exit.
`ncfg host` runs it from the binary already installed, and the app carries the same
file under a `main` of its own as `libncfghost.so`, linked against fuzznet's
`libfuzznetd.a`, as fuzzypickles links fzpd.

**The feared cost was the capability**, which fuzznet derives from service and product,
so a store opened under another product's number might have reached nothing.
Measured by `c/tests/host_user.sh`: joined as netcfgd, then served by fuzznetd under
fuzzypickles' number 2 on the same default store, `status --at` is answered by the
host, and `ncfg host` started beside it follows and becomes the face when it goes.

**`restart_argv` is the original command line**, or taking the claim would run `ncfg`
with fuzznet's options and no `node`.

## 10.732 `monitor` takes fuzznet's stream first

With 10.731 it costs nothing, so `ncfg monitor`, `ncfg tui` and the GUI's stream hold
fuzznet's first, and the control socket only for a caller it will not hold: under
`observe = "any"` until the holder's agreed right lands, past fuzznet's four, or on a
daemon with no node. Every request and stream a client makes now goes over fuzznet
first.

**What is left of 0309, which is all in this tree:**
- ~~`observe = "any"` needs fuzznet's held-stream right~~ -- not built there, and its
  direction is named users, so 10.739 serves that tier without one.
- A daemon with no node has the socket as its only way in. ~~A node that will not open
  should say so and stop, or keep this; that is the decision left.~~ **Answered by what
  was built (recorded 2026-11-12):** it says so, keeps the socket and the network, and
  tries the store again every few seconds, so a late mount does not leave the host
  unreachable (`open_node` and its retry in `c/src/main/daemon_main.c`).
- 42 live scripts and the unit tests wait on `netcfgd.sock` as "the daemon is up", and
  `doc/schema/socket.json` is the witness of what goes.

## 10.731 The events' detail has a home, so fuzznet's stream loses nothing

10.729's stream said an event's kind and nothing else. Its name field is 32 bytes, and
a summary or a compiler's diagnostics are sentences, so they could not ride on it. The
daemon now keeps its last 64 event lines, and a procedure of its own, `eventlog SINCE
FROM`, reads them by a cursor, paged and judged as `status` is. A reader that hears a
kind reads what happened since, and gets the lines the control socket would have
sent, whole: `{"response":"event","event":"reloaded","ok":true}` through fuzznet, to
the second user too. A procedure rather than a new control request: no schema or
vocabulary changes for something only the stream needs. A reader 64 behind has lost
the rest, and re-reads the status, as after any gap; if the read fails it still gets
the kind.

## 10.729 `monitor` over fuzznet, where the control socket is not there

fuzznet built held streams (its sec 899, asked from here): `get events`, for a
caller `local/events` lets read, hears what this daemon publishes as `net-...`.
The daemon writes that setting from the `observe` tier. `ncfg monitor` and the GUI's
stream take it when the control socket is gone, on the same descriptor to wait on.

It was the fallback at first, since fuzznet's event is a subject and no more; 10.731
gave the detail a home.

**A second real user is confirmed** by `c/tests/node_second_user.sh`: a user namespace
with subordinate ids gives real uids, so the user `observe` names holds the stream and
a third is refused `denied`, each judged by `SO_PEERCRED`. `ncfg tui`'s events pane
takes the stream too.

**Limits.** `any` has no `=r` (fuzznet's sec 883), so under `observe = "any"` only the
daemon's own user holds a stream, and everyone else stays on the control socket.
Asked of fuzznet, which parked it for the holder: `any` could take all four held slots
and shut a tray out, and it suggested a right that holds a stream and nothing else.
**The holder agreed, 2026-11-05**; fuzznet told, and its spelling awaited.

`node_serve.sh`: control socket hidden, `monitor --json` hears a reload.

## 10.728 A dialog fits a phone

Configuring a link from the emulator showed the dialog as the desktop's: narrower
than the screen, labels taking half of it, fields behind a scroll bar. Fixed once,
in `gui/src/phone/phone_fit.cpp`, by an event filter: a dialog shows full screen and
a form's labels go over their fields. The dialogs stay the desktop's, as gui/project.md
section 1 asks.

**A change made from the phone landed.** Saved in that dialog on the emulator, paired
by camera with a stock netcfgd with `admin` open: the host wrote

## 10.726 `ncfg pair open`: one step for who does not know what `remote` is

A closed machine answered `ncfg pair` with a sentence about the `global` block,
which is a dead end for the second of this project's three audiences. `ncfg pair
open` puts `conf.d/remote.conf`, with `observe` and `admin` open and a comment
saying how to close it, and on a machine's own daemon under systemd restarts it,
since the tiers and the port are read at the start. The window asks in words first.
It goes through the same `config put` as everything else, so a `remote` written by
hand elsewhere collides and is refused rather than overridden.

`node_remote.sh`: `ncfg pair open` against a running daemon, the file, and the port
at the next start. The restart branch is not reached in the test, by design: a run
directory of a test is not this machine's service.

## 10.724 The window can show the code too

The fleet tab has "Pair a phone...", for somebody who will not open a terminal. It
runs `ncfg pair` through what the access tab elevates with, and draws what that
printed (`gui/src/pair_code.cpp`), so the window needs no encoder and shows only the
code issued. Closing the dialog cannot signal a root child: it waits out its code,
ten minutes at most. Not run with a real `pkexec`; `phone_pair` holds the parsing,
read back through quirc.

## 10.723 One code: fuzznet's invite, and nothing carried back

fuzznet built what 10.720 asked for the same day (its sec 896, `30ca61f`). `ncfg
pair` now takes nothing: it asks `add invite delegable`, draws the `FZI1:` code,
and waits for a new member, up to the code's ten minutes. The phone gives it to
`add join`, and its key goes home sealed over the network. The prekey argument of
10.722 is gone, as it said it would be, and so is the file a card needed.

- **Whoever scans a code may join, with no word from the host's person.** fuzznet
  decided that and put it to the holder; `ncfg pair` says so beside the code. A
  device believes only a card signed by the key in the code, so a photographed code
  can join but cannot pose as the host.
- **It cannot be short.** About 150 characters, fuzznet's answer being that shorter
  needs a PAKE, which is not built. So the field for typing stays, for a phone with
  no camera, and QR is the way in.
- **The keyboard covered the field** at the foot of the screen, which the emulator
  showed; it sits under the status line now.

**Verified.** `node_remote.sh`: `ncfg pair` in a namespace, a device told only the
code joins, and that ends the wait. `phone_pair`: the view takes a real code from a
real host, ends in `paired`, and `get invite` is 0 after. On the emulator, the app's
node told the code joined a stock netcfgd on this machine's LAN address.

**Still not verified, and both want a phone:** a code read through a camera; and
the view's field by hand. `adb shell input text` put the first letter last, or
lost it, so the emulator's join was given to the node directly. Not run on arm64.

## 10.722 `ncfg pair`: the terminal displays, the phone scans

`ncfg pair` draws a code in half blocks,
black on white, since a dark terminal would otherwise invert it and quirc reads
no inverted code. The host's `net/address` is set first, from the source address
the kernel picks for the way out, or a card says nowhere. With no port held it says
what to open rather than draw a code nothing answers: a bind is the test, since
what counts is what the daemon read at its start, not what the file says now.

Root's, as fuzznet's `peer` is not grantable. It took the device's prekey until 10.723.

Verified: `c/tests/pair_draw_test.c` reads the drawing back module by module, on
an odd side, where the last line holds one row (dropping it failed its check);
`node_remote.sh` both refusal and card, in a namespace.

## 10.721 netcfgd has its numbers, and listens only where the config says

fuzznet assigned `FZN_PRODUCT_NETCFGD`, 3 (its `chain/service.h`), and `src/node/node.c`
holds `NCFG_FUZZNET_PRODUCT` to it at compile time. **The daemon now always gives
its node the numbers**, so a stock netcfgd has fuzznet's verbs and something can
pair with it; until now only the tests passed any.

**The port is another matter.** gui/project.md section 9 says a daemon listening
on a network is a thing this project has deliberately never had. So the node binds
UDP 48090 only where `global { remote }` opens a tier, which is closed by default
and is the one thing that already says a machine is reached from outside. Read at
the start, as the sockets are, so opening it takes a restart.

Rejected: always listening, since a member-only hop is still a new listener on
every laptop that installs this; and a separate switch, a second word for what
`remote` already says.

`c/tests/node_remote.sh`, each daemon in its own network namespace: the verbs
answer closed and open, the port is bound only when open. With the condition
removed, the closed case fails.

## 10.720 A phone pairs first, on a node of its own

The holder, 2026-11-05: on a phone, QR/code pairing is the first thing a person
does, since it is the main platform for this use, and it is not easy to move
files to a phone or share auth data between apps. That answers gui/project.md
section 9's two questions. **The code is the pairing and the discovery**: fuzznet's
card says where its sponsor is (its sec 671), so a phone needs no mDNS and no
typed address.

- **The phone's node**, `gui/src/phone/phone_host.cpp`: fuzznetd rides in the APK as
  `libfuzznetd.so`, built from the pin by `make -C gui android-node`, and the app
  starts it with `XDG_RUNTIME_DIR` in its own directory, so
  `ncfg_fuzznet_user_socket` and everything above it is the desktop's code.
  **No Android service**, which is where this differs from fuzzypickles: nothing
  arrives for this node, so it goes with the app.
- **The first screen**, `pair_view.cpp`: scan, or type. Nothing else is reachable
  until it is done. Back ends the app; the first version kept waiting with no
  window, and the emulator found it.
- **`allowBackup` is off** now that the app's storage holds keys, and the floor is
  API 28, fuzznet's.

**Asked of fuzznet** the same day: a join was two carries, the prekey out and the
card back, and a phone's prekey had no road to the host: 277 hex digits, no camera
on the host, no file. Built, 10.723; and netcfgd's product number, 10.721.

**Verified.** `gui/tests/phone_pair` on real nodes: a card's length of code read
back from its image, refusals, a fuzznetd started as the app starts it, the view
taking a card and ending in `paired`; three sabotages, each failed by its check.
On `Galaxy_Nexus_API_33`: the screen; the camera permission, opening and frames
through `-camera-back virtualscene`; and with the app's own node joined to a real
netcfgd at 10.0.2.2, **the window showing that machine's links**.

And after 10.721 and 10.722, a stock netcfgd with `remote` open, no fuzznet options
given: `ncfg pair` made the card, the emulator's node joined at this machine's LAN

**Not verified:** a code read through a camera, since the virtual scene was never
aimed at its poster; and the view's join on the emulator, since `adb shell input
