## 10.719 A supplicant that left by itself is noticed too

10.716 left the supplicant at "cannot tell", since its answer decides whether
the control socket is asked and `wedged.sh` holds that round with a planted
record and a fake carrying no mark. So wifi whose supplicant exited cleanly
stayed `running`, and nothing started it.

**The two cases differ on disk.** A wedged supplicant has its control socket
there, and one that left cleanly takes it along with its pid file. So: its mark
on a process is running; no mark and a socket is still "cannot tell", which keeps
`wedged.sh`'s round; none of the three is gone. One killed outright leaves its
pid file, so that arm is unchanged. A socket left by a crash keeps "cannot tell",
which is what it answered before.

## 10.716 A daemon that left by itself stayed `running` for ever

`ncfg apply` said `nothing to do` over an openvpn tunnel that was gone, and
nothing started it again. Any tunnel that exits by itself does this, and a
slow stop too. openvpn removes its pid file on the way out, and the liveness
pass read a missing file as "cannot tell" (34e8b045, wedged.sh), which kept the
record's `running`. A `kill -9` leaves the file, which is why the one check of
this, "netcfgd notices the tunnel is gone", passed.

**The rule stands for what it was written for, and these were outside its
premise.** "No handle means cannot tell" protects a live daemon from being
called dead for having no file, which took the supplicant out of its
`answering` round. openvpn, hostapd, the router advertisement daemon, the DHCP
server and miniupnpd have a handle: the mark `ncfg_service_backend_handle`
names, which adoption reads too. So they now answer as link-local does, always:
that mark on a process is running, and no file and no mark is gone.
`liveness_test` holds both halves for each, the live one first. Only openvpn's
was seen live; the other four rest on that test.

**How it was found.** `make live` failed "and is still running, which is the
window this is about" in `openvpn.sh`, every run. That control was doing its
job. The fake lingered 3 seconds and `OPENVPN_STOP_PATIENCE_MILLISECONDS` is
3000, so on the C the stop outlasted it and the section's window never opened:
its checks passed with nothing to test, the control alone saying so. How long
that had been so was not measured. It lingers 8 seconds now.

**The section changed with it.** The Rust did not wait for a stop, so its
replacement started inside the window. The C reports the stop as not done
(10.661), the record keeps the tunnel, and it is started once it has gone.

**The supplicant followed in 10.719.**

**And a filter hid a failed build while this was being done.** `grep ' error '`
does not match a compiler's `error:`, so `make` failed on a missing include,
the old binary stayed, and two runs of the test tested that. Judged by the exit
code since. Those two runs did show the check fail against the old code.

## 10.715 `make check` was measuring clang's fuzznet in a fresh tree

The `size` gate failed by 232 bytes at 2,454,928, while the same commit built
to 2,390,328 in the working tree. **The budget was not the fault, and raising
it would have hidden a wrong binary.**

The `clang` gate runs `make -C c syntax CC=clang`, and `syntax` needs the
fuzznet archive, so in a fresh tree it built fuzznet with clang. `.build-flags`
stamps this directory's objects and not fuzznet's, and fuzznet's Makefile does
not rebuild for a changed compiler. So every later gate linked clang's objects,
about 64 KB larger: `size`, and the suites too, ran a program no package
contains. A working tree escapes by having built with cc first, which is why
only scratch worktrees showed it, and it stayed under the ceiling until this
week's code.

It was read off the objects: `.comment` says clang. The first guess, `DEBUG=1`,
came from `accept_share` being present, a static function `-Os` inlines away,
and it was wrong.

`$(FUZZNET_LIB)` now keeps `.built-with` beside the objects, the compiler and
flags, and removes the objects when they differ. Run in that order, clang then
a plain build: rebuilt with GCC, 2,360,624 bytes. A build with nothing to do
leaves the archive untouched. A `make check` in a fresh tree pays for fuzznet
twice, about a minute. **`size-budget.txt` is unchanged.**

builds `gui/` unchanged as `se.vibes.netcfgd`, with `tool/android.mk`'s
vocabulary, and it starts on an emulator. **It does nothing useful yet**: a
phone runs no netcfgd and has no node, so the first screen says so, and that is
all this step claims.

- **Here and not in the root Makefile**, since `gui/` is where the window is

- **`client/` is compiled into the app**, three C sources, rather than a second
  archive per ABI.
- **Its own manifest**: without one the app was
  `org.qtproject.example.netcfgd_gui`. Its permissions are `INTERNET` and
  `ACCESS_NETWORK_STATE`, where Qt's marker would have asked for external
  storage.
- **The dialog is its own on Android.** The C layer's sentence names
  `systemctl`.

**What it needs next, in order:**

1. A node on the phone: built, 10.720.
2. Joining an estate: the screen is built, 10.720, and the holder answered how it
   should feel.
3. The fleet tab's child processes do not exist on a phone (10.710, 10.713). Its
   reads now run on a thread there, through `ncfg_fuzznet_status_at`, and the three

4. A window laid out for a phone. Forty tabs are a desktop's.

**Verified**, on `Galaxy_Nexus_API_33` (x86_64, API 33): installed, running as

## 10.713 The `fleet` tab acts: reload all, add to a group, seal a value

10.710 only looked. Three buttons now do what an operator does to many nodes:
`ncfg reload --at estate`, `ncfg hosts member`, and `ncfg secret seal`. They
are `ncfg`'s own verbs, run as child processes as the tab's reads are, so what
each refuses and prints stays in one place and the window never waits. The
last line of the answer sits under the table until the next action, which for
a reload is its count of nodes.

**The sealed value goes to the child's standard input.** On a command line any
user of the machine could read it in `/proc`. The probe sabotaged to pass it as
an argument fails. One action runs at a time, killed at two minutes, since
`--at estate` waits on every host's round.

Rejected: a push of one configuration to every node from here. `config put
--at estate` exists, but which file goes to which group is a design the window
does not have, and `beyond the simple case` is the holder's (0311).

**Verified:** `gui/tests/fleet_tab`, against the stand-in: each verb's argv,
the value on stdin and off argv, a refusal in `ncfg`'s words, and one action at
a time. The modal dialogs themselves are unexercised, offscreen or on a desktop.

## 10.712 Local requests go over fuzznet: `call ask` first, the control socket behind it

0309 says `ncfg` and the GUI speak fuzznet to the daemon, and only `status`
did. Every request from `ncfg` and from `client/`, so the GUI, the trays and
the NM shim, now goes as `call ask` on the daemon's fuzznet socket, in pieces
past one line. The control socket stays behind it, for a daemon with no node
and for what is listed below. Nothing above the transport changed: the same
line, judged by the same gate, answered by the same dispatcher (0312).

**A request is never sent twice.** `ncfg_fuzznet_ask_here` says whether the
daemon can have seen it. It falls back only where nothing can have run: no
node, nobody listening, or fuzznet refusing the call. Pieces count as nothing
run, since a staged request runs only when asked for whole. Sent and unanswered
is an error, and the client is marked broken. The obvious fallback, "fuzznet
did not answer, so try the socket", would have run an `apply` twice and armed a
second window.

**`ask` is granted to every tier's holder.** fuzznet calls a procedure for the
node's own user unless `local/permit/NAME` grants it, so a GUI user of a root
daemon would have been refused and fallen back: this change would have done
nothing on the machines it is for. `ask` and `askpart` are now granted to
`observe`, `wifi` and `admin`, each named once and root left out. That widens
nothing, because netcfgd's own gate judges each request behind the procedure.

**The wait is five minutes**, as long as an apply can take, against the two
seconds `status` gets.

**Staged pieces are wiped, and go when refused.** Every local client now
stages through `askpart`, so a long `secret_put` or a network with its
passphrase sits there. `part_clear` freed the bytes unwiped, and a request the
reader or the gate refused stayed staged for its minute. The refusal is tested
in `ask_test`. The wipe is by reading only: no test can see freed memory.

**Open, so newline-delimited JSON has not gone yet:**

- **`monitor` is a stream**, and 0312 does not carry one. fuzznet's held stream
  (10.729) carries the kinds, as a fallback; the detail still needs a home.
- ~~A tier of `any` has no grant~~ -- **built by fuzznet as sec 883**, 3b71a88:
  `any=x` lets every local user call a procedure, and is what such a tier
  writes now, for `status` as well. Signalled as inbox 20261104T2251Z.
- ~~**The client still connects to the control socket on open.**~~ It opens on
  fuzznet alone now, where the connect fails and fuzznet answers, with
  `client_test` holding both that and the old sentence for no daemon at all.
- ~~**raidcfgd reads the JSON socket**; the socket cannot go until it has moved.~~
  **It never did.** Written from a misreading of 0309's "adopted", and repeated in
  reports until read against its tree on 2026-11-05: raidcfgd copied the encoding for
  its own daemon's socket, and nothing in its code connects to netcfgd. Nothing outside
  this tree holds the socket up.

**Verified:**

- `client_test`, against fakes: taken over fuzznet, `call ask 0 REQUEST`
  on the wire, sent-and-unanswered an error, and the control socket hearing
  only the one request fuzznet refused. Sabotaged by retrying after a send: three
  checks fail.
- `node_serve.sh`, against a real daemon with its control socket renamed away:
  `plan`, `reload`, and a `config put` long enough for pieces all answer, so
  they can only have come through `ask`. The grants are read back.
- `node_answer_test`: each grant once, root's left out, a name that starts
  another kept apart, and `any` refused.
- `node_fleet.sh`; and live, now on this path: `c_daemon_answers`, `confirm`,
  `config_arrives`, `apply_race`, `remote_tiers`, `control_exposure`, `profile`.
  `make live` as a whole has not been run on it.

## 10.711 An operator's group verbs: `ncfg hosts member`, `ncfg secret seal`

10.709 left both as lines typed at fuzznet's socket, with a passphrase in the
line. `ncfg hosts member HOST GROUP` is `set setting host=HOST group/member
GROUP`. `ncfg secret seal GROUP KEY` is `set sealed`, on this user's own
fuzznetd, since it writes other hosts' cells.

- **The value is read as `secret set` reads one**, with the echo off or from
  standard input, and never from the command line. Every copy is wiped, the
  escaped form and the request line among them.
- **Sealing to nobody is a failure, not `ok 0 0`.** fuzznet keeps a copy for a
  later member, but every host's configuration would read the key as unset, so
  the sentence names `ncfg hosts member`.
- **`--at` is refused on `seal`**: it speaks for a group, and `--at` means one
  node. `secret` otherwise takes `--at`, so this is the one verb under it that
  does not.
- **Under `hosts` and `secret`, and no `group` word.** `hosts` is where a host
  is named and `secret` where a value is given. A group has nothing of its own
  here to list.

**Verified:** `tests/live/c_estate_secret.sh` runs both through the socket
`ncfg` finds for this user: sealing to an empty group refuses, naming a member
works, a bad group is refused, sealing reports one member, the apply carries,
and `wg` reads the key's public half back.

## 10.710 The `fleet` tab: every node at once

The node box visits one node at a time, so somebody minding ten routers had
to go to ten to learn which one was down. A `fleet` tab lists the estate's
nodes: the name a node gives itself, whether it answers, its connectivity
rung, its primary link and its links up. A double click or Open moves the
window there. It is only built where the estate has other members, because
somebody with one machine is who this window is for.

**Child `ncfg status --at KEY --json` processes, not `ncfg_connection`.** That
class waits on the window's thread, so one node off the air would freeze the
window for the length of the call, once per node. A child is waited for
without blocking and killed at 35 seconds. A thread in the client could not be
killed. Rejected for the same reason: moving the existing connection through
the nodes in turn.

- **At most four at once, and only while the tab is in front**, once a minute.
  A round in progress is not stacked behind by another.
- **Three rows that must not read alike**: `answering`, `refused:` for a node
  that is there and said no, and `no answer` for one that is not. The tab
  tells the second by `denied` on standard error, a string only the real
  program can vouch for, so `node_fleet.sh` asserts it with A's tier closed.
- **A node that stops answering keeps its name** and the time it last did,
  since "router-3, no answer" is the sentence wanted. `status --at estate` is
  no shortcut: it is refused, a `call` at many hosts bringing back only
  whether each one carried it out (10.708).

**Verified:** `gui/tests/fleet_tab`, against a stand-in `ncfg` on PATH: the
three states, a hung node killed by the view's own wait, the name kept, ten
nodes never more than four at once, a member leaving, no tab without an
estate, and Open. Sabotaged three ways: no cap, the name dropped, and no kill.
Each fails its check. `make hull` and a real desktop have not seen the tab.

## 10.709 Sealed group values as secrets: `@secret:estate:KEY`, built and live-tested

A fifth secret provider. `@secret:estate:KEY` is the fuzznet setting KEY in
force for this host: its own cell, else its group's, else the estate's, and a
value sealed to the host is opened. So a roaming key or mesh password an
operator sets once with `set sealed group=NAME KEY VALUE` reaches each access
point of the zone, and no other host can read it. `fuzznet` is pinned at
15b3b4f.

**A hook in the module, not the field 10.708 proposed.** That entry put a
function on `ncfg_secret_resolver_t`. There are five resolver sites, each
building its own resolver, and a site forgotten would read as a host with no
node. `ncfg_secret_estate_install` is one process-wide reader instead, which
`node.c` installs for the length of `fzn_daemon_main`. `secrets.c` still links
no fuzznet. It is safe because every resolution in the daemon runs on the
loop's thread, through the mailbox, and fuzznet's getter is safe there.
Moving a resolution onto another thread would break that.

**Three failures, and none of them is `NOT_FOUND`**, whose sentence sends a
person to `ncfg secret set`:

- no node in this process: `UNSUPPORTED`, saying so;
- none set here: `FAILED`, saying an operator of the estate sets it;
- sealed to a key this host lacks: `FAILED`, naming `ncfg hosts member`.

`ncfg secret list` skips these references, since its subject is the `secrets/`
directory and "referenced, not stored" would ask for a copy on disk. The
compiler refuses a KEY outside fuzznet's key grammar at the line that wrote
it. `@secret:estate:` is no privilege question beside `@secret:exec:`: it runs
nothing, and it reads what this host could read anyway.

**A member is a host an admin named, since fuzznet sec 879** (15b3b4f, inbox
20261104T2221Z). `set sealed` and the minute's reseal reach a host only when
its `group/member` is in force at an admin's or a root's rank and it stands. So
a new access point gets a roaming key when an operator says `set setting
host=KEY group/member zone1`, not when it says so itself, and the refusal
above names that verb. Its own word still places it for the group's plain
values. `ncfg hosts member` and `ncfg secret seal` say both (10.711). Sec 880 is
coming: copies held by other root and admin hosts, so a later member is served
once the sealer has gone.

**Beside a fuzznetd, netcfgd is a follower, and it reads through the face.**
The getter answered 0 there at first, so an estate secret read as "no value
here" on exactly the machines the holder wants running both. Signalled
(inbox 20261104T2229Z) and built by fuzznet as sec 882, 322f0d0: it asks the
face, whose node opens what is sealed, so no prekey secret reaches this
process. It can hold the loop up to 5 s, and -1 now also means the face did not
answer, which the refusal says.

**The Rust does not know this provider.** It is retired, and only C reads the
witness now: `doc/schema/document.json` carries `estate` on the PPPoE password,
and `frozen.rs` builds its own document. `NCFG_SCHEMA_MINOR` stays 1, as it
has for every variant since it was written.

**Verified:**

- `secrets_test`: the stand-in reader's value and key, all three failures, the
  reader leaving with the node, and the walk skipping the reference. Sabotaged
  twice: with the walk's skip off, and with the -1 arm off, each fails. The walk
  check passed vacuously at first, the fixture's count being 1; it is 2 now.
- `lower_test`, `render_test`, `document_test`: the key grammar, the round
  trip, the witness.
- `tests/live/c_estate_secret.sh`, in a namespace against fuzznet's real
  reader: an apply with nothing set refuses and says so. After `set sealed`,
  the store holds a box, the same apply carries, and `wg` reads back the public
  key of the sealed private key. The key is in no log and no output.

## 10.708 Propagation: `ncfg VERB --at estate|group=NAME`, built and live-tested

The design is in 10.707. A `do` procedure beside `ask` answers `ok` only
where the daemon carried the request out, so fuzznet's `call do at estate`
reports a refusing node as `failed` rather than `ok`. `ncfg VERB --at
estate|group=NAME` prints one row per host and a line of the form `C of N
netcfgd node(s) carried it out (A of T host(s) answered, U serving no
netcfgd)`. It exits 0 only where every netcfgd node carried the request out.
Reads are refused across many hosts, and `apply` needs a window.

**A host answering `unknown` serves no netcfgd, and is not a failure.**
fuzznet includes the calling host. An operator's own fuzznetd, B in the
fleet test, has no `do`, so it is always listed `unknown`. Counting it as a
failure would make every propagated command from an operator's machine
exit 1.

**The live failure first recorded here was the test, not the code.** It
was found with a debug print on `do`'s refusal. The open-tier check ran
after the test's revert, and A refused the reload correctly:
"this configuration was reverted away from and has not changed since; edit
it to try again". The check now runs before the revert. The closed-tier and
open-tier checks send the same request, so the two now differ only in the
tier.

**Verified:**

- `ask_test`: `do` answers `ok` for a carried request. It answers nothing
  for a request refused by the remote tier, for an operator's apply
  without a window, and for an error answer.
- `node_fleet.sh`: with A's admin tier closed, A is `failed` and the
  command exits 1. With it open, A is `ok` and the command exits 0, with
  B listed as serving no netcfgd. `status --at estate` is refused before
  anything is asked.

**Item 2 is built: 10.709.** fuzznet's getter is `fzn_daemon_setting_here`
(its sec 877, 513562d).

## 10.706 The rss band re-derived again: four runs in ten failed it unchanged

The `rss` gate failed this session's last full check at 3352 KB against 3328,
and on its own one run in three. The day's earlier full checks had read 3168
to 3344. **Ten back-to-back `make rss` runs** at load 4 read 3124 3124 3184
3204 3248 3248 3360 3360 3376 3380, so the band no longer covered the noise:
the failure at 252118af's check was the same gate, not a change.

- **What netcfgd allocates did rise**, and that is the part a ratchet is
  for. `RssAnon` read 396 to 400 KB in every run, against 324..328 when the
  band was last derived (2026-10-29). It was 400 already at this session's
  first check, so the rise is in the commits between, fuzznet's loop served
  by default among them (0311). It was not taken commit by commit, so no
  change is named as its cause.
- **The spread is not the first observation pass**, which was the guess.
  Sampled at 2 s and again just after the first observation, the two modes
  are already there at 2 s, and the pass adds 40..100 KB to each. What
  splits them happens earlier, and outside what netcfgd allocates.
  - A first attempt at that measurement read `timeout`'s own memory, since
    `$!` named the wrapper. It is said here because the numbers it gave,
    about 2 MB, looked like a finding.
- So, as 2026-10-29 did: the observed peak plus a band wider than the spread,
  3380 + 264 = **3644**, and still a ratchet. Three runs afterwards read
  3208 to 3360.

## 10.705 The events reader is fuzzed, and reads numbers as digits only

`ncfg_fuzznet_events_at` read another host's events inline, after its socket
call, where no fuzzer could reach. Its parsing is now
`ncfg_fuzznet_events_read`, given the unescaped text, and the new fuzz target
`events_list` holds it to its invariants: every subject kept is lower-case
letters and hyphens, NUL-ended inside its slot, and never more of them than
room.

- 25.7 million runs, clean. With the character check removed, the fuzzer
  finds a subject that would forge a printed line within seconds.
- **Two things the split tightened.** FIRST was read with a bare `strtoul`,
  which takes a sign or a space, so a hostile node's `-1` became a huge
  FIRST: only a false gap, but the page reader is digits only and this is
  now too. And text left after the last event is refused rather than
  ignored.
- The lens from that bug found nothing further. The members reader also
  uses `strtoul`, on this user's own fuzznetd's `list peer`, but a sign
  wraps its total past the 1,000,000 cap and is refused, and its FROM is
  checked against the one asked.

## 10.704 The GUI and TUI follow another node by its events cursor

10.698 to 10.700 refreshed a node's views every 15 seconds for want of an
event stream. 10.703 gave every node an events cursor, so both front ends
now read it every 5 seconds, and refresh only when it moved: a new event, a
gap, or a restart.

- **The GUI** (`ncfg_main_window::poll_node`). The first read learns where
  the node is, and each later one lists every event in the events tab as
  `WORD (on node KEY)`, by the whole key as `where()` gives it. Choosing
  another node resets the cursor. Where the cursor cannot be read, every
  third tick refreshes anyway, which is the old 15 seconds.
- **The TUI**, every 5 idle ticks, the same way into its events pane, with
  the 15-tick refresh left for when the cursor cannot be read.

The `node_menu` probe runs a fake fuzznetd on the probe's user socket that
answers two `call events`. `poll_node` twice lists `drift (on node KEY)`,
and without the listing the check fails. The pty check of 10.700 reads the
TUI's new sentence. **The TUI's listing of an event is not under test**:
nothing happens on A inside the pty's four seconds.

## 10.703 Another node's events: netcfgd publishes, and `ncfg monitor --at` reads a cursor

fuzznet carries no stream across the estate and plans none. Instead each node
keeps its last 256 published events, and its own procedure `events [FROM]`
reads them from a cursor (its `db35c7b`, sec 866). Two halves:

- **netcfgd publishes its events into fuzznet's.**
  - Every event goes through `ncfg_main_subscribers_tell`, which now notes
    its kind as a bit before its no-local-subscriber return, since another
    host may be reading.
  - The node's tick publishes the noted kinds through
    `ncfg_node_publish_event` as `net-observed`, `net-reloaded`,
    `net-drift`, `net-armed` and `net-resolved`. It has to be the tick,
    because fuzznet takes a publication from its `tick` only and an event is
    told from inside an answer too.
  - A kind added without a subject is a build error rather than an event
    that goes unpublished.
- **`ncfg monitor --at HOST`** polls that node's cursor every two seconds and
  prints each event as its word. A FIRST past the cursor is said as missed
  events, and a NEXT below it as a restart, both with "re-read its status".
  It runs until interrupted, and a call fuzznet cannot carry ends it.
  - The reader takes a subject of lower-case letters and hyphens only.
    That is held here, not trusted to the other host's fuzznet, since a
    subject is printed into `--json`, where a quote would forge a line.
  - A page with more events than room is said as a gap, because NEXT is
    already past them all.

**The scripted test first agreed with a wrong parser.** fuzznet's note gave
the answer as "`ok NEXT FIRST ...`, escaped". The parser and the scripted
answers in `fuzznet_line_test` both expected an inner `ok`, so the unit test
passed. The live check failed with `that node answered 1 1`: the escaped text
is `NEXT FIRST ...` (`fzn_node_events_since`), and the `ok` is the call's own.
Both are fixed, and the scripted answers are now copied from fuzznet's
writer, not from the note. **A fake written from the same reading as the
code it tests is one witness, not two.**

`node_fleet.sh`, in A's third start:

- `monitor --at A` runs in the background through B, and the 2.5 KB config
  put's reload shows up in it as `reloaded`;
- without the tick's publish, it never does, and the check fails.

`fuzznet_line_test` checks:

- a page read with its cursor;
- a quoted subject refused, which fails without the character check;
- an overfull page said as a gap.

The GUI and TUI node views followed in 10.704.

## 10.702 fuzznet's answers taken: its bound, its huge pages, its services off, and gc-sections

Two inbox messages from fuzznet, 2026-11-03 (`20261103T2225Z`, and one written
at 22:27 local under the reused name `20261103T1938Z`), answered four asks. The
pin moves to fuzznet `f1fdea6d`.

- **The bound a call's answer reaches its caller within** (fuzznet
  `3b8f055`, its sec 863) is `FZN_DAEMON_CALL_ESCAPED_MAX`, 1020 escaped
  bytes, here or across hosts. `node.c` used `FZN_REPLY_MAX - 5`, which is
  1019, so nothing on the wire changes. The constant names what the number
  is and moves with it.
- **Huge pages** (its sec 862): `fzn_daemon_refuse_huge_pages(argv)` refuses
  them, and where one was faulted before `main`, in the loop's large bss, it
  runs the program again once. A `prctl` here refused new ones and left that
  one resident. `main` calls it through `ncfg_node_refuse_huge_pages`, since
  only `src/node/` includes fuzznet, and `ncfg` takes it as the same
  program.
- **The consumer services are build options** (its secs 856, 860), and
  netcfgd's node is built with all four off. The flags reach fuzznet's `.c`
  files only, no header, so `src/node/` compiled with this tree's flags
  still agrees with the archive. Each removes that service's verbs and the
  node's own use of its data, while the estate's data is still carried and
  relayed, so a fuzzypickles host in the same estate loses nothing through
  this node.
- **`-ffunction-sections -fdata-sections` and `--gc-sections`**, as fuzznet
  links its daemons and asked a program linking its loop to do. `readelf`
  shows per-function sections in netcfgd's objects and fuzznet's (624 in
  `daemon.o`), so the collection reaches both.

Measured on the installed program:

| | file | text | bss |
|---|---|---|---|
| before | 2,492,936 | 2,110,913 | 31,051,928 |
| services off | 2,457,024 | 2,079,674 | 30,109,688 |
| and gc-sections | 2,383,200 | 2,017,634 | 26,420,472 |

`size-budget.txt` comes down to 2,383,200, as its own line said it would
when the services became options. The bss fell by 4.6 MB with it, which is
the resident gate's business.

**And another host's events** (fuzznet `db35c7b`, its sec 866): there is no
subscription across hosts and none is planned. Each node keeps its last 256
published events, and fuzznet's own procedure `events [FROM]` answers `ok
NEXT FIRST [SUBJECT NAME]...` from a cursor. Remote monitoring is built on
that next (go item 31) instead of polling the status.

## 10.701 The parsers of another host's bytes are fuzzed, and today's code sanitized

10.688 to 10.700 added three parsers that read another host's bytes, and they
are reached from the network:

- `ncfg_status_page_read`, which reads a node's page;
- `ask`'s `FROM REQUEST` and `@DIGEST`;
- `askpart`'s `TOTAL OFFSET DIGEST PIECE`.

Two targets join `FUZZ_TARGETS`, with seeds:

- **`status_page`**: a page read stays inside its own bytes, and pages
  joined end in a whole their digest names or in a refusal. The source
  answers the same bytes to every offset, which is the shape of most hostile
  answers.
- **`ask_args`**: every `ask` answer is a page that reads back as one, every
  `askpart` answer is one line of `ok`, `error` or `malformed`, and what is
  kept between calls is let go, which the leak checker holds it to. Several
  calls run from one state, so a staged request and a kept answer meet the
  next call. `daemon_ask.c` is the program's and in no archive, so the target
  names it as a source of its own.

Runs and controls:

- `status_page`: 15 million runs, clean. With the COUNT-is-the-bytes check
  removed, the fuzzer aborts on a page read outside itself within seconds.
- `ask_args`: 3 million runs, clean. With `askpart`'s piece bound removed,
  ASan reports a heap overflow in its `memcpy`.
- **Sanitizers over the rest:** `ask_test`, `status_page_test`,
  `fuzznet_line_test`, `node_answer_test`, `seen_test` and `mesh_peer_test`,
  then `node_fleet.sh` and `node_serve.sh` live, on an ASan and UBSan build
  (instrumentation confirmed with `nm`), with no report.

**And the fuzz archive had 10.690's stale-member hazard**, the third
`ar rcs` rule in this tree that never removed one. It is removed and remade
like the other two.

## 10.700 `ncfg tui --at HOST`

The TUI asks through `ncfg_cli_ask`, so `--at` (10.694) carried its panes
unchanged, and `tui` joins the carried commands. It had the GUI's two
hazards, met the same way:

- **Its events pane subscribed to this machine's socket**, which under
  `--at` would have listed this machine's events in a pane showing another
  node. It does not subscribe then, and the pane says that events are not
  carried from another node.
- **It refreshed the devices and plan panes every idle second**, which for
  another node is a call across the estate each second, possibly waiting on
  fuzznet's round. A node's panes refresh every 15 ticks instead, as the
  GUI's window does (10.699).

`node_fleet.sh` runs `ncfg tui --at A` in a pty: it is drawn, `e` shows the
events pane with its sentence, and `q` ends it, under the script's own read
deadline and `timeout`. Removing the `--at` branch fails the check, because
the pane then tries this machine's socket. The 15-tick throttle is not under
test.

## 10.699 The window moves between nodes: the node box

10.698's open half. The toolbar's node box lists this machine first, then
the estate's other members as this user's fuzznetd lists them (`list peer`,
10.692), by whole key, as `where()` names them. A user with no fuzznetd sees
this machine alone. Choosing one reopens the connection on it, the line above
the tabs follows, and the 15-second refresh starts for a node and stops for
this machine. The events tab already stops a stream of this machine's when a
node is shown (10.698).

- **A choice that cannot be reached puts the window back where it was**,
  connection and box alike, and says why in the status bar, rather than
  leaving a window unconnected that looks as if it moved.
- **The tray is this machine's, on a connection of its own.** It had sat in
  this machine's panel on the window's connection, so once the window could
  move to a router, the panel would have shown the router's state as this
  laptop's. Its menu, which joins and leaves networks and sets a profile,
  would have acted on the router's radio. `main` now opens a second
  connection for it on this machine's socket, whatever the window shows,
  before the window so that it outlives the tray, and the tray reopens it
  itself, since the window's refresh reopens only the window's. **This is
  checked by reading `main.cpp`, not by a probe**: a probe handing a tray a
  separate connection would only show that the tray keeps the pointer it was
  given.
- **Found by the probe, before anybody started it: the window crashed on
  every start.** The constructor builds the toolbar, node box included,
  before the timer further down, and following the node from the toolbar
  touched a timer not yet made. It is followed once the timer exists.

The probe `node_menu` builds the whole window offscreen, taking every source
but `main.cpp` with qmake's `files()` rather than a second copy of gui.pro's
list. It checks that:

- the box shows this machine and the node the window was opened on;
- the window refreshes on its timer;
- a choice of an unreachable "this machine" puts window and box back on the
  node.

Removing the put-back fails it, leaving the connection on no node at all.

## 10.698 The GUI on another node: `netcfgd-gui --at KEY`

Section 10's first next step names the GUI's verbs over `ask`. The client
library had every one of them on one function, `ncfg_client_request`. So a
client that asks a node, **`ncfg_client_open_at(KEY)`**, sends each request as
`call ask at KEY` through this user's fuzznetd, and the GUI's typed calls
work on another node unchanged.

- **A refusal is still a document**, as from the socket. Only a fuzznet
  that cannot carry the request marks the client broken, which is the GUI's
  cue to reopen.
- **It reopens the node, never this machine.** `ncfg_connection` reopened a
  broken connection by its socket path, and a node's path is empty, which
  the C layer reads as the default socket: this machine's daemon, while the
  window said the other node. That is exactly what `gui/project.md`
  section 4's rule exists to prevent, the operator unsure whose network
  they are changing. A node connection reopens by its key. `where()` names
  the node by its whole key, never an abbreviation another node could share.
- **No event stream from another node** (0312). The events tab says so
  rather than subscribing to this machine's stream, and the window refreshes
  on a 15-second timer instead, because otherwise nothing would tell its
  views the node moved. An earlier draft of the events tab's sentence said
  the views refreshed on their own. They did not: only events and the
  Refresh button refreshed them, and the timer is what made the sentence
  true. **The timer then made a second fault.** The window's refresh
  refreshes the events tab when it is showing, so the tab gained its line
  every 15 seconds. It is said once per node now. The tab also stops a
  stream of this machine's when a node is shown: it had returned early for
  a running stream before asking whether a node was open, which would have
  kept this machine's events under the other node's name once the window
  could move between them.
- `--at` and `--socket` together are refused, as two answers to which
  machine.

`client_test` checks that a node client:

- opens without connecting;
- names its node and has no socket path;
- answers a request through a fake fuzznetd;
- is left broken by a fuzznet that cannot carry the request.

Removing the node branch fails it. The GUI probe `node_connection` breaks a
node connection with no fuzznetd and reopens it, and it must still be that
node. Without the node branch in `reopen_if_broken`, the reopen fails, being
aimed at this machine's default socket. The probe also refreshes the events
tab three times on a node and finds one line, where without the once-only
rule it finds three.

**Not done yet:** a node menu in the window, from `ncfg hosts`'s list, so
the GUI can move between nodes without a restart.

## 10.696 A refused `seen` record is asked again a minute on, and said once

Found by deriving a lens from 10.695's bug, a limit taken from the wrong
one of fuzznet's bounds, and asking every line netcfgd sends to fuzznet
whether it fits 512 bytes. Most do. A `seen` record need not:

- `NCFG_SEEN_VALUE_MAX` is 256 bytes, and escaping can triple that.
- A lease's value carries the hostname the DHCP client chose, and option 12
  allows 255 bytes.

So a client with a long enough hostname makes a record fuzznet refuses,
`malformed a request is at most 512 bytes`. The recorder then asked it again
**every pass** and warned each time, because a refused record was never held.
That is a log any device joining the network could fill.

The retry was deliberate: `seen_test` asserted "asked again next pass, since
nothing was kept", because a refusal may lift once a permit is given or a
record trimmed. So it stays, but **a minute on**, the backoff the recorder
already uses when fuzznet is silent (`NCFG_SEEN_RETRY_SECONDS`), and the
warning is said once for each record and value. The held record carries
`refused`, so it is asked again sooner than a written one's daily refresh
but not every pass. A changed value is asked at once, as before. The
test's two checks of this, a refusal and a fuzznetd with no record store
that answers with its status line, now say the record is not asked the next
pass and is asked a minute on. Saying the warning once is counted rather
than asserted, because `seen_test` cannot capture the log: three warnings
for two rounds of three refused records, and six with the once-only rule
removed.

Not changed: what a record says. Cutting a client's hostname to fit would
write something the network did not say.

## 10.695 A request longer than a line goes in pieces: `askpart`

10.694's open limit. A request travels inside one fuzznet line, about 1 KB,
so a `config put` of a real configuration could not cross the estate.

- **`call askpart at HOST TOTAL OFFSET DIGEST PIECE`** stages it on the node,
  in order from 0, each piece answered `ok HAVE TOTAL`. Then **`call ask at
  HOST FROM @DIGEST`** runs the whole request under every rule of 0312: the
  same reader, the same gate, a page made once and kept, only a read made
  again.
- **Nothing new in fuzznet's grammar.** It is a second procedure beside
  `ask`, so fuzznet carries the pieces as it carries any call's arguments.
- **The node holds it for this caller only**, one request at a time, until
  it is whole and run or a minute has passed, and at most 256 KiB. Pieces out
  of order are refused, and so are joined pieces that are not the request
  their digest names. A staged request runs once, and its later pages come
  from its kept answer, which is filed under the same digest.
- The client splits any request past 360 bytes into 360-byte pieces
  (`client/ncfg_fuzznet.c`), so `ncfg ... --at` needs no change. **The line
  is 512 bytes**, fuzznet's `FZN_REQUEST_MAX`, and not the 1024 of a reply
  that 10.694 sized by. The live test found that: its first 600-byte piece
  came back `malformed a request is at most 512 bytes`. `ncfg_fuzznet_ask` now
  refuses a longer line itself, naming the bound, and
  `NCFG_FUZZNET_REQUEST_MAX` says where the number comes from.

`ask_test` stages a 2 KB `config_put` and checks that:

- it runs once by digest and pages from its kept answer;
- once run it is staged no longer;
- a piece out of order is refused;
- pieces that are not their digest are refused.

`node_fleet.sh` restarts A with its remote `admin` tier open and puts a
drop-in of about 2 KB through B. It lands in A's `conf.d` whole, and the
empty local configuration directory stays empty.

## 10.694 `ncfg --at HOST`: the socket verbs asked of another node

0312's client half. `ask.c` is the transport under every `ncfg` verb whose
answer is the daemon's. With `--at`, it writes the socket's own request line
and sends it as `call ask at HOST FROM REQUEST` through this user's
fuzznetd. It then reads the joined pages as that node's socket would have
answered them. Nothing about the transport shows past that one function, so
`wifi`, `modem`, `reload`, `confirm`, `revert`, `apply`, `config`, `secret`
and `profile` all ask that node, and `status --at` keeps its own path
(10.691).

- **Every other command is refused with `--at`, by name.** It compiles,
  observes or writes on this machine. Doing that while the operator believes
  it reached another node is the worst thing `--at` could do, worse than
  refusing.
- **Nothing under `--at` may fall back to this machine**, and four commands
  would have. Each was found by reading every subcommand of a command
  before carrying it:
  - `config put` and `rm`, `secret set`, `profile save` and `set`, and
    `wifi add` and `forget` ask the daemon only when one is listening, and
    otherwise write locally. On a machine with no daemon, an operator's
    change for the node would have landed in this machine's `/etc`. So
    `ncfg_cli_daemon_listening` answers yes whenever another node is asked.
  - `profile list` and `get` fell back to the local profiles when the daemon
    did not answer, so a node that refused the caller would have been
    reported with this machine's profiles. Under `--at` that is now an error
    carrying the node's own sentence.
  - `secret set` checked this machine's file for `--replace` and then listed
    this machine's configuration's users of the secret. Under `--at` the node
    judges `--replace`, and the report says only that the node stored it.
  - `wifi add` and `forget` read this machine's configuration and radios to
    decide what to write, so they are refused. A `wifi` verb without an
    interface found the radio in this machine's configuration, so under
    `--at` it must name one.
- **`apply --at` needs `--confirm-within`**, refused here before anything is
  asked. The node insists on it too (0312), but an operator should hear it
  from their own command.
- **A request is one fuzznet line**, and fuzznet's local line is 512 bytes
  (`FZN_REQUEST_MAX`), not the 1024 of a reply. This entry first said about
  900 bytes, which was the reply's figure. Until 10.695, a longer request was
  refused with a sentence rather than cut, because a request half-sent would
  be a different request. That ruled out a `config put` of a real
  configuration over the estate until 10.695, which sends a longer request
  in pieces.

`node_fleet.sh` runs these against A through B:

- `ncfg modem --at A` is A's answer (`no device in the configuration has a
  modem block`);
- `reload --at A` is A's refusal, naming its closed remote `admin` tier;
- `show --at` is refused as a command that works here;
- `apply --at` without a window is refused before anything is asked;
- `config put --at A` is A's refusal and leaves an empty local
  `--config-dir` empty;
- `profile list --at A` is A's answer.

With the transport branch disabled, the first two fail, because `ncfg` then
asks this machine's daemon, which is not running. With the listening guard
removed, `config put --at` writes locally and fails its check.

## 10.693 The control vocabulary is one fuzznet procedure: `ask` ([0312](doc/decision/0312-the-control-vocabulary-is-one-fuzznet-procedure.md))

The control socket has some forty verbs. Rather than a procedure for each,
`call ask FROM REQUEST` carries the socket's own JSON line, and the daemon
answers it as the socket does (`src/main/daemon_ask.c`, from `serve_one` in
`server.c`):

1. the line is read strictly by the socket's reader;
2. it is judged by `ncfg_authz_permitted` with the caller fuzznet
   identified: a peer on this machine under the `control` tiers, an
   operator of the estate under the node's `remote` block;
3. `hello` is answered with this caller's own tiers, and `monitor` is
   refused as the stream it is;
4. everything else goes to `ncfg_main_answer`, the socket's dispatcher, on
   the loop's thread. That is where a fuzznet procedure already runs, and
   where the mailbox would have taken the request.

The desk is the daemon's own, passed to `serve_node`. Every answer is paged
in the digest pages of 10.689.

- **Every answer is made once and kept**, per caller, until it has been read
  to its end or a minute has passed. Later pages are cut from the copy, so a
  `plan` is computed once rather than once a page.
- **Only a read is made again for a page.** Where no copy stands behind a
  later page, an `observe`-tier request is answered afresh and anything else
  is refused. That is not the order class of 10.351, which this first used:
  there `apply` is idempotent, and rightly, because netcfgd is declarative.
  But running it again to make page two would open a second confirm window.
  `ask_test` showed it, because the test assumed otherwise and failed.
- **An operator's apply needs a confirm window.** Without one it is refused
  before it reaches the daemon, since across the estate a change that cuts
  the operator off has no other way back. At the console, the same request
  stays legal without one. **This answered a question `gui/project.md`
  section 9 lists to raise rather than answer alone**, so it waits on the
  holder. The refusing side is the cautious one, and either answer is one
  condition each in `daemon_ask.c` and `run.c`.

`ask_test` drives the procedure with a fake dispatcher that counts its runs,
and checks that:

- an answer is made once and paged from the copy, byte for byte;
- a change is not run again for a page;
- an operator's apply is refused without a window;
- the remote and control tiers decide;
- `hello` and `monitor` are handled;
- two callers' answers are kept apart.

Removing the read-only page rule fails it, and so does removing the window
rule. `node_fleet.sh` calls `ask` at A through B: a plan comes back
(`{"response":"plan",...}`, A having no configuration), and an apply carrying
a comma through fuzznet's grammar is refused by A's closed remote `admin`
tier.

`ncfg`'s socket verbs followed in 10.694.

## 10.692 `ncfg hosts`: the estate's members, by the key `--at` takes

10.691 asks a node by its 64-digit key, which nobody types from memory.
`ncfg hosts` lists the other members of this user's estate, one key a line
or a JSON array with `--json`. It reads them from this user's fuzznetd with
`list peer [FROM]`, every page.

- **Members only.** fuzznet lists a contact, a peer paired for a share
  (its sec 436), with `,contact` after the key, and a contact is no operator
  of anything here (10.685), so it is left out. The node is not its own peer.
- **Every member, not only netcfgd's.** Which of them answers `status` is
  each node's own business, and asking all of them would turn a listing into
  a fleet-wide wait.
- **More members than room is an error**, not a list cut short. That is the
  same refusal fuzznet's own paging makes (`list_peers` in its
  `node/admin.c`).

`node_fleet.sh` showed the open question settled: B's list holds A under
the same key `status --at` used, so a peer's key is the host a call names.
`fuzznet_line_test` covers the parts the live estate cannot, using scripted
pages: two pages joined, a contact left out, a cap exceeded, and a peer
that is not a key. Removing the contact filter fails it. Its two help lines
are in agree_gate's `C_ONLY_LINES`, as `--at`'s are.

## 10.691 An operator asks another node: `ncfg status --at HOST`

The fleet of 0311 is the estate: an authenticated operator managing every
node of it. 10.688 gave each node a `status` procedure that an estate member
may call. This is the operator's side. `ncfg status --at HOST`, with HOST the
node's key in hex, asks this user's own fuzznetd to `call status at HOST
FROM`, page by page. That is the third of fuzznet's three models: a client
and its daemon calling a remote one. The command prints the node's
observation, and `--json` writes it in `observed.json`'s shape. Nothing of
the local machine is observed or written, because that node is the subject.

- **The node decides**, by its own `remote` block (0128's tiers), as 10.685
  set out: each node is configured in detail. The operator's fuzznetd
  carries the call and judges nothing.
- **This user's fuzznetd** is found where fuzznet's clients look when told
  nowhere (its sec 663): `$XDG_RUNTIME_DIR/fuzznet/fuzznetd.sock`, else
  `/tmp/fuzznet-UID/`. The operator is a full fuzznet user, with a fuzznetd
  of their own that is a member of the estate, so the holder's rule against
  storing anything for non-fuzznet users (10.683) is not touched.
- **The key is checked before it is sent.** It must be 64 lower-case hex
  digits, so no word of the caller's reaches the line fuzznet reads.
- A call across the estate waits for fuzznet's round, three seconds, so a
  page is given eight seconds rather than the local two.

`tests/node_fleet.sh` sets the estate up as fuzznet's own `live_ext.py`
phase c does. A is netcfgd serving a store made root by `fuzznetd
--new-root`; B is a fuzznetd on this user's default socket, under a scratch
`XDG_RUNTIME_DIR`, joined by `add peer ... delegable` and `add join`. It
checks that:

- `ncfg status --at A` answers A's observation;
- a host that is no member is refused, not waited on;
- a malformed key is refused before anything is asked;
- with A restarted and its remote `observe` tier closed, A denies the call
  and names the tier. Closing the tier also fails the first check, which is
  the control.

`make test` runs it under `timeout 400`, and it has a target of its own,
`node-fleet-test`. Every wait in it is bounded, by a count of looks or a
wall-clock deadline, and a trap stops both daemons on every way out.

## 10.690 The GUI's status comes over fuzznet, from one copy in `client/`

`ncfg_client_status` is the single function every status read of the GUI
and the NM shim goes through, so changing it moved both. It now asks the
`status` procedure first and the control socket where fuzznet does not
answer. The document is `{"response":"status",...}` either way, so no
caller can tell which one answered.

- **One copy, in `client/`.** The GUI and the shim link `libncfg_client.a`
  and not `libncfg`, so 10.689's `fuzznet_line.c` and `status_page.c` moved
  to `client/ncfg_fuzznet.c`, libc only. `c/` compiles it in as it does
  `ncfg_json.c` (`SHARED_SRCS`), and `ncfg`, the seen recorder and the daemon
  all use it. The joiner now returns a malloc'd string, since `ncfg_buf` is
  `libncfg`'s.
- **The run directory is only a guess where the socket says so.** The client
  knows only its control socket's path. Its directory is taken for the run
  directory, and asked for `node` and `fuzznet.sock`, only when the socket
  is named `netcfgd.sock`, as a daemon names its own. A socket elsewhere, such
  as a test's in `/tmp`, would otherwise send the client to a stranger's
  fuzznet.
- **A fuzznet that fails is left alone for a minute.** The GUI asks for the
  status often, and a fuzznet that holds its socket without answering would
  otherwise cost every refresh the 2 s wait.
- `client_test` runs a fake control socket beside a fake fuzznet that answers
  in two escaped pages and then refuses. The first status comes from fuzznet,
  and the second from the control socket. Breaking the run-directory test
  fails the first check.

**Two build faults found on the way, both of the kind that leave a stale
artifact rather than an error:**

- **The shared-object rule compiled every object from the first source.** It
  was one rule, `$(SHARED_OBJS): $(SHARED_SRCS)`, using `$<`, which was
  correct while there was one shared source. With a second, `ncfg_fuzznet.o`
  would have been a copy of `ncfg_json.o`. It is a static pattern rule now.
- **`libncfg.a` kept the deleted objects.** `ar rcs` adds and replaces
  members and never removes one, so after the move the archive still held
  `fuzznet_line.o` and `status_page.o`. It defined their symbols a second
  time beside the shared object on the same link line. A fresh clone never
  sees this, which is why it lasts. The archive is now removed and rebuilt
  from `LIB_OBJS` each time, and `ar t` lists neither.

## 10.689 `ncfg status` asks the daemon over fuzznet, and pages carry a digest

10.688's client half. The holder's rule from 0311 is that everything internal
goes over fuzznet's protocols. So `ncfg status` takes what only the daemon
knows, the regulatory-domain setter and the stations fuzznet recorded, from
the `status` procedure first. It falls back to the control socket only where
fuzznet does not answer this caller.

**Where the socket is, without configuration.** `ncfg` tries the store's
`face` file first, with the store taken from `<run>/node`, because the face
names whatever socket fuzznet was given. Otherwise it uses
`<run>/fuzznet.sock`, the daemon's default since 10.683. That is also the
only one a user who cannot read root's store can reach. `node_serve.sh`
renames the control socket out of the way, and `ncfg status --json` still
carries the station only the daemon knows. With the fuzznet path disabled,
that check fails.

**Found while writing the client: joined pages could mix two statuses.**
Each page is cut from the status as it is when that page is asked, and a
router's status moves between asks. Joined pages of two statuses usually fail
to parse. But if the two are the same length, they can parse as a status that
never existed. So each page now ends its header with a digest of the whole
status it was cut from (FNV-1a, 64 bits, sixteen hex digits):
`ok TOTAL FROM COUNT DIGEST`. The remote type 129 answer has the same header,
since it is the same function.

- `ncfg_status_pages_join` (`status_page.h`) starts again when a page names
  another digest, at most four times, then checks the joined bytes against
  the digest. A status that moves faster than it can be read is refused.
- `status_page_test` feeds it a status that changes mid-way at the same
  length, one that never holds still, pages whose digest lies, and pages that
  make no progress. With the per-page comparison removed, two of those fail.
- The page reader is strict, because a page may be another host's bytes:
  digits where numbers are, lower-case hex, COUNT exactly the bytes after it.

**One copy of the fuzznet conversation.** The bounded one-line ask, the `%XX`
escape, and the `face` lookup moved out of `seen.c` into `fuzznet_line.c`, so
the recorder and `ncfg` cannot drift apart in how long they wait.
`fuzznet_line_test` checks them against a scripted socket: a reply in two
pieces, a socket that never answers given up on within the wait, and an
absent one reported as silence.

**The GUI followed the same day (10.690)**, and the two files named above
moved to `client/ncfg_fuzznet.c` with it.

## 10.688 `status` is a fuzznet procedure: `call status [FROM]`

fuzznet's answer to 10.685's ask (its inbox message 20261103T1938Z, its secs
852 to 855) is generic rather than netcfgd's: there is no send verb for raw
extension types, because those are bytes fuzznet cannot judge. Instead:

- **local permits** (its 852): a host setting `local/permit/SUBJECT` such as
  `group:netcfgd=r user:#1001=x`, where `x` is call. A caller the node would
  otherwise deny is served as the node's own user, and nothing is stored for it;
- **procedures** (its 853): `call NAME [at HOSTHEX] [ARGS]`. A daemon
  registers them on its extension, and a procedure is called only for an
  estate member, or for a local caller that is the node's own user or that a
  permit grants `x`. The answer is at most 4096 bytes;
- **a follower's procedures are forwarded by the face** (its 51d6c0b), through
  `procedure/NAME` sockets in the store. A forwarded local caller arrives with
  its uid and primary gid but **no group list**;
- **lists** (its 854 and 855): records under `list/NAME/`, one key per member,
  `add/remove/get/list listed`, and a records rule may keep by a list.

Types 128 and 129 are listed in fuzznet's `node/types.h` as netcfgd's, so the
remote hook of 10.685 keeps working for peers that speak it.

**netcfgd registers one procedure, `status`**, which pages the status as
`get status [FROM]` does (`ok TOTAL FROM COUNT`, a newline, the bytes). One
function in `daemon_node.c` serves both the remote type and the procedure:

- a remote caller is judged by the `remote` block;
- a local caller is judged by netcfgd's control tiers against the peer fuzznet
  read, as on the socket. A forwarded caller has no group list, which denies
  any tier opened by group (`groups_known` 0, 10.683). That is the safe
  direction, and fuzznet has already judged that caller.

**Found while testing: a full answer never reaches a local client.** fuzznet
hands a local client the answer escaped (`%XX` for a space, `%`, a comma, a
control byte or DEL), in one reply line of `FZN_REPLY_MAX`, which is 1024
bytes. A status page is JSON, full of spaces and quotes, so a 4096-byte answer
escaped is several times that, and fuzznet answered `error the answer is
longer than one reply`. So the procedure sizes each page so that, escaped,
the header and the bytes fit `FZN_REPLY_MAX - 5`. Against a 13 KB status
the first page is 906 bytes.

That bound holds for a remote call too, because host B gives its own local
client the answer the same way. The mismatch between the 4096-byte answer
fuzznet allows and the roughly 1019 bytes a local client can receive is
fuzznet's own, and has been sent to it rather than worked around further.

- `node_answer_test` pages at a small escaped bound and joins the pages back
  to the socket's status byte for byte. With the sizing disabled it fails.
- `node_serve.sh` asks `call status 0` of a live daemon (`ok ok%2013041%200%20906...`)
  and checks that a bad offset is malformed.

**fuzznet's permit follows the `observe` tier.** Without a grant, fuzznet
calls a procedure only for the node's own user, so a GUI user in netcfgd's
group could not call `status`. `status` is netcfgd's subject, so
`local/permit/status` follows netcfgd's configuration. On the loop's first
pass the daemon:

- writes `group:NAME=x` for `observe = "group:NAME"`, or `user:NAME=x` for a
  user, only where the setting differs;
- clears it where the tier is root's, since the node's own user needs none;
- leaves it alone, and says so, for `any`, which no grant can express (a
  grant names a user or a group), and for a name fuzznet's grant cannot
  carry. A setting fuzznet cannot parse would refuse every grant in it.

It is `x` alone, the call: `r` would also serve that caller fuzznet's read
verbs on the subject as the node's own user (its `permit_judge`), which is
more than the tier opens.
`node_serve.sh` reads the setting back from a live daemon, and it is cleared
again by the closed-tier phase.

**Not done yet:** moving the `seen` records onto a fuzznet list; and `any`,
which wants a grant to every local user if fuzznet offers one.

## 10.687 One radio meshes and runs an access point: the `mesh_point` device

10.588's open item, and the usual shape of a mesh router: one radio for both
the backhaul and the clients. A radio was given to a mesh and did nothing else.
Now `device mesh0 { mesh_point { parent = "wlan2" } }` is a second interface
netcfgd makes on that radio's phy, the `mesh` block names `mesh0`, and an
`access_point` stays on `wlan2`.

**What it took, layer by layer:**

- **A kind, `mesh_point`, with a `parent`** -- model, language, renderer,
  plan encoding, the socket document's kinds table (6.4, now sixteen).
  **Not the document witness, which 0020 requires**, and that was this
  session's slip: `doc/schema/document.json` claims every kind and lacked
  this one, so the round trip never read it. It is carried since
  2026-11-04, as `k-mesh` in name order, and `document_test` fails when
  `mesh_point`'s member is renamed, which it could not before. A variant
  added is a minor bump under 0020: an older reader refuses only a document
  that uses it. The retired Rust's `frozen.rs` round-trips a document it
  builds itself and never reads the file, so it neither guards this nor
  breaks on it.
- **Made over nl80211, not rtnetlink**: `NL80211_CMD_NEW_INTERFACE` with the
  parent's index standing for its phy and type mesh point, as `iw dev wlan2
  interface add mesh0 type mp` sends it; taken away with
  `NL80211_CMD_DEL_INTERFACE`, because a mac80211 interface has no rtnetlink
  delete -- a link netcfgd deletes that has a `phy80211` is one of these.
  Marked as netcfgd's by the same altname as everything it creates.
- **An address of its own**, the radio's with the locally administered bit
  set (and the last octet's low bit flipped if it was set already): mac80211
  refuses to bring up a second interface with the address of one already up,
  `ENOTUNIQ`, which was the rig's first failure.
- **Never remade by deletion**: the kernel gives a mac80211 interface no
  `IFLA_INFO_KIND` to compare, so the planner creates one only where its name
  is free and never throws an interface of that name away for it.
- **One channel**: a radio is on one at a time, so a mesh point's mesh and an
  access point on its parent must name the same channel, and an access point
  left to choose is told the mesh's -- refused at compile time otherwise.

**Three faults the rig found, each a real one**, in going from a radio that
meshed to one that meshes on `mesh0` and serves an access point on `wlan0`:

- **No supplicant was planned for a mesh point the plan was creating**: the
  radio rule asked the observation whether the interface was wireless, and a
  link that does not exist yet is not. A mesh on a `mesh_point` device is
  wanted before it exists, and waits on its creation.
- **hostapd started before the radio's old supplicant stopped**, because
  teardown runs after the device walk -- and a supplicant leaving puts the
  interface back in station mode, so `wlan0` ended `managed` under an access
  point the plan had started. The access point's pass now stops a supplicant
  still running on its radio first and waits on that stop, and teardown leaves
  it alone. This holds for a radio going from station to access point too.
- **hostapd would not beacon beside the mesh** ("Failed to set beacon
  parameters", every time and not a race -- a second apply failed the same
  way): two beaconing interfaces on one radio must share a beacon interval
  where the driver says so, and the mesh was left to wpa_supplicant's own. The
  mesh network now names `beacon_int=100`, hostapd's default; with it the
  first apply converges.

Checked: `hull-mesh` gains two phases -- one apply makes `mesh0` a mesh point,
`wlan0` an access point, the peer link established on `mesh0` and the echo
crossing it; then with the device block gone `mesh0` is taken away over
nl80211. The runs before each fix are its controls: without the beacon
interval hostapd refused; without the planner's want no supplicant started on
`mesh0`; without the early stop `wlan0` ended managed. `lower_test` gains six
checks (the kind, one channel, a missing one told the mesh's, no parent, an
unknown key); `hull-steer` still passes with the access point's new ordering.
`hull-ap-lease` did not run: its image has no hostapd and wants rebuilding,
which is the rig's state and not this change.

## 10.686 `ncfg status` says who a mesh node is meshed with

10.588's open item: netcfgd joined an 802.11s mesh and nothing it reported
named the peers, where `iw dev wlan0 station dump` does. The kernel keeps them
as stations of the mesh interface with their peer link's state, so
`ncfg_observe_mesh_from` (`c/src/observe/mesh.c`), in the same generic netlink
round as four-address mode, asks one `GET_INTERFACE` dump which interfaces
are mesh points (the interface parser now reads `NL80211_ATTR_IFTYPE`) and
one `GET_STATION` dump of each (`c/src/sys/mesh_peer.c`), and keeps the peers
whose `NL80211_STA_INFO_PLINK_STATE` is established. They land in the link's
`mesh_peers`, omitted when empty -- a field added, a minor bump of the
observation (0020) -- and `ncfg status` prints `mesh peer MAC` under the link.
Something to show, not something the planner decides from; a kernel that
will not say leaves the list empty with a note.

Checked: `hull-mesh`, two hwsim radios, netcfgd's node against a bare
wpa_supplicant -- `ncfg status` names the peer `iw` shows established, once.
With the observation's call removed, the same rig is bad. `kernel_bytes` now
drives the interface and station parsers: 5.7 million runs in three minutes,
nothing found.

## 10.685 An estate operator asks a node over fuzznet: `get status`, paged

**Built** (the holder: "you are getting bogged down in details pretending they
are blockers" -- so the open details are decided here and marked as guesses).
`ncfg_main_node_remote` (`c/src/main/daemon_node.c`) answers fuzznet's remote
hop through `ext->remote`, for netcfgd's own extension types:

- **128, a request; 129, its answer** -- from fuzznet's extensions' range
  (`node/types.h`, 128 to 191), told to fuzznet so its list can carry them
  (its inbox `20261103T2000Z`). A request is a line in the local vocabulary.
- **`get status [FROM]`** answers `ok TOTAL FROM COUNT`, a newline and COUNT
  bytes of the same JSON the control socket's `status` gives, from offset
  FROM: paged, so it never depends on the remote reply cap. *Guess:* paging
  rather than relying on fuzznet's multi-frame replies, because the cap is
  fuzznet's and status grows with the machine.
- **Who:** a contact is refused -- someone the estate shares with, not
  someone it is run by. A member is judged by this node's `remote` block,
  the per-tier booleans 0128 gave a remote caller, all off by default: the
  holder's "each node can be granularly configured as to what permissions it
  has". *Guess:* any member fuzznet authenticates is an operator, and the
  node's tiers bound what it may do; if fuzznet's admin capability should
  narrow that, it narrows here.

Checked: `node_answer_test`, 11 checks -- denied with `observe` closed;
a contact refused; the status in one page byte for byte against the socket's,
and in many pages at a 40-byte reply, put back exactly; an offset past the end
an empty page; a signed offset malformed; other verbs left to fuzznet; no
observation an error. Skipping the tier check turns the first red. **Not
tested end to end:** nothing in fuzznet sends an extension's request to a
peer from a test, asked of it in the same message.

## 10.684 fuzznet is not optional: serving in the default build, and the estate is the fleet

**The holder, 2026-11-03:** "Fleet management is settled within the simple
case = every node belonging to the same estate should work with an operator
authenticated. Fuzznet is to be our distributed store by default, it is not
optional. Everything internal goes via its protocols, netcfgd is precisely
why it has those 3 different models of communication." Recorded as
[0311](doc/decision/0311-fuzznet-is-the-store-and-the-estate-is-the-fleet.md),
which also names the three models (fuzznet's section 2): netcfgd is the root
daemon judged by group, and the remote daemon an estate operator reaches.

**Built:** fuzznet's loop is linked in every build, and a daemon with a node
serves its store inside it (10.676 to 10.683): `NODE_SERVE=1`, its stub and
the separate build are gone, `--fuzznet-serve` is accepted and does nothing,
and `tests/node_serve.sh` runs in `make test`. A daemon with no node keeps its
own loop. **The size decision is the holder's answer**: `size-budget.txt` is
raised by 928,184 bytes to 2,447,392, with the reason; most of it is
fuzznet's consumer services, which come down when fuzznet makes them build
options (its sec 842). **And fuzznet is built without its log packing**
(`FZN_LOG_PACK=0`): with the loop linked, the program linked `libzstd.so.1`,
which `make linkage` refused under constraint 3 -- packing closed log segments
is fuzznet's convenience, not something the network daemon needs, and leaving
it out took the program from 2,499,208 to 2,447,392 bytes. Two gates were
red on the way and are fixed in their own commits: `agree`, since 3813fcf3
added `--fuzznet-arg` to the help; and `form_coverage`, since 10.670's
`translated` was never read by the GUI's firewall dialog, whose Save would
have deleted it. `make check` passes whole. Memory stays inside its gate: a serving daemon is
about 1.3 MB more resident than one that does not serve, since 10.679, and
the RSS gate measures one with no node.

**What an operator may do on a node is the node's own** (the holder, the
same day): "Each node can be granularly configured as to what permissions it
has." So the fleet's simple case is not one estate-wide grant: an operator is
authenticated by the estate, and what that operator may do on a machine is
set in that machine's configuration, in detail. netcfgd's tiers (observe,
wifi, admin; 0013, 0128) are the existing granularity, and the `remote` block
is where a node already says which of them reach it from off the machine.
**Next, not started:** answering estate operators through fuzznet's remote
hook (`ext->remote`) under those tiers. It waits on two things fuzznet's
framing decides -- what identifies an operator to a node (its admin
capability, or another), and how a large answer such as status travels back
to a remote caller, since `get status PATH` writes on the daemon's own
machine.

**What it changes for a machine**: a netcfgd on the default run directory
has a node (10.669) and so now serves it -- `/run/netcfgd/fuzznet.sock`
(10.683), the store's face unless a fuzznetd holds it, and the records read
in-process (10.676). The hull rigs that start one on the default run
directory pass under it: `hull-openwrt` -- which now also asserts the daemon
under procd serves its store, the socket in `/run/netcfgd` and `face` naming
it -- `hull-openrc`, `hull-sandbox` and `hull-upnp`.

## 10.683 Local callers are judged by netcfgd's group; nothing is kept for them

**The holder, 2026-11-03, on fuzznet's sec 849 `judges_local`:** "Yes,
netcfgd and raidcfgd local auth is gated by their resp. groups. External auth
is a different story and not completely fleshed out other than the simple
case. We should avoid storing anything on users that aren't full fuzznet
users. They only see what the root daemon tells them, and have no config of
their own. (if they connect to external hosts, they may need to store those
adresses/auth)"

So three things are settled for 0309:

- **A local caller of netcfgd's verbs is judged by netcfgd's tiers**, which
  name its groups (`observe = "group:netcfgd"`), not by fuzznet's own local
  rule -- the `judges_local` shape fuzznet proposed: a caller fuzznet would
  deny reaches only the extension's verbs, never fuzznet's. Told to fuzznet
  as information (its inbox `20261103T1745Z`); the flag is fuzznet's to
  build, and the holder's word to fuzznet is the holder's to give.
- **A local client keeps nothing.** `ncfg` and the GUI on the machine are
  not fuzznet users: no identity, no store, no configuration of their own --
  they ask the root daemon and show what it answers. fuzznet's local
  protocol needs none of those (a line per request on a unix socket, the
  caller judged by its credentials), so a 0309 client is a socket client and
  nothing more. **Audited 2026-11-03:** nothing netcfgd ships writes into a
  user's home today -- no `QSettings`, no XDG config, no file written by the
  GUI, `client/` or `ncfg` except where a directory is named to it. The
  exception the holder names, an external host's address and credentials,
  is the remote-access client, not yet built; it is where storage on a user
  is allowed, and only for that.
- **The socket therefore sits where those clients can find it without
  knowing anything: `/run/netcfgd`**, beside the control socket it replaces,
  with the mode and group `apply_policy_permissions` already sets from the
  control policy. fuzznet's default is per user (`$XDG_RUNTIME_DIR`), so a
  non-root client looking there would find its own runtime directory and
  never root's daemon; decided from the rule above rather than asked, since
  the alternative is a client that has to be told where the daemon is -- a
  configuration of its own. **Built in the serve build**: unless a
  `--fuzznet-arg --socket=...` names one, the daemon gives fuzznet
  `<run>/fuzznet.sock`. It does not make a following netcfgd's verbs
  reachable: measured, the follower passes a connection at its own socket
  through to the face, which answers `unsupported` -- so that stays asked of
  fuzznet (10.682's second finding). **The holder's direction, the same
  hour:** "We need to have a method for fuzznetd to forward extensions
  without fully understanding them" -- the face hands an extension's verbs
  on to the process serving them. Passed to fuzznet as information, in the
  same message.

**External callers are not decided** beyond the simple case (0128's tiers by
origin); the holder says so, and nothing here assumes more.

**What would change "nothing kept on a user"** (the holder, the same day): a
feature that needs every user authenticated toward root, for something that
is about the user rather than the machine. The holder's example is NuFW, the
authenticating firewall, now abandoned: a client agent (`nutcpc`)
authenticated each user to an authentication server (`nuauth`, over LDAP,
PAM or a file), and a daemon on the firewall held each new connection in
netfilter's queue until `nuauth` said whether that user's connection was
accepted -- rules written by who opened a connection, not by its address,
which is what made properly managed multi-user systems over a network
possible, and which today's tooling makes too hard. A netcfgd feature of
that kind would give each user an identity and something stored, and the
rule above would be revisited with it rather than worked around.
(NuFW: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NuFW)

## 10.682 0309's first verb: `get status PATH`, judged by netcfgd's tiers

**Built, in the serve build**, on fuzznet's framing (its sec 843) and its
`local_from` (`5e3b41a`, sec 849, the half of request 10 it built): a
request fuzznet's handlers decline reaches `ncfg_node_loop_t.local` with
the caller as the socket read it, converted to `ncfg_peer_t`. `get status
PATH` is judged by `ncfg_authz_permitted` -- the control socket's own check,
`observe` as for its `status` -- encoded by `ncfg_daemon_status_encode` as
the socket encodes it, written by `ncfg_caller_file_create` (10.680) and
answered `ok LENGTH`; `denied ...` and `error ...` with netcfgd's sentences
otherwise. It runs on the loop's thread between fuzznet's steps, so the
state it reads is whole. A remote origin is not answered by this hook.

Checked in `node_serve.sh`, three checks: the observation written into a
directory of the caller's and its length answered (13 KB of JSON, which
parses); refused into `/tmp`; denied, with nothing written, by a daemon whose
`observe` tier is root's. Skipping the tier check turns the last red, with
the status written for a caller who may not observe.

**Three things found on the way, for 0309's design:**

- **The control policy is read once, at start** (`ncfg_main_policy_copy`,
  `daemon_main.c`), and the socket's servers hold the same copy: an edit to
  `control` takes effect at the next start. The verb agrees with the socket
  in that; the denial check runs a daemon of its own because of it.
- **fuzznet routes no request to an extension without a service and
  product** (`--fuzznet-service`, `--fuzznet-product`): measured, the same
  request is answered with fuzznet's status line. Every phase of the test
  names `1` for both; what netcfgd should name is an estate choice, asked of
  fuzznet (its inbox `20261103T1700Z`).
- **A follower on the default socket has no socket of its own** (sec 841),
  so a client there reaches the face -- a fuzznetd, which does not know
  netcfgd's verbs. While netcfgd follows, its verbs are unreachable; told to
  fuzznet in the same message. **Not withdrawn by a socket of its own**,
  measured (10.683): a follower passes every connection to the face (sec
  666), so `get status` at a following netcfgd's own socket answers
  `unsupported`. Asked of fuzznet: a follower answering its extension's own
  verbs itself.

~~Still the holder's, through fuzznet (sec 849): whether an extension may judge
local users fuzznet would deny (`judges_local`)~~ -- **answered yes, 10.683.**

## 10.681 The seen listing is fuzzed, and `make fuzz` builds again

**A target for the listing** (`c/fuzz/seen_listing.c`): fuzznet's `list
record` page is text the estate's hosts chose -- a record is a setting its
own host signs, carried to every other by the rounds -- and what
`ncfg_seen_parse_listing` returns becomes a MAC in an access point's allow
list (10.674). The target asserts what the header promises: -1 or the count;
no more stations than room; sorted and unique; each a MAC as the kernel
spells one.

**It failed within seconds:** `ok 8 -3 1 ...` returned -3. `%lu` takes a
leading minus and wraps it, so SHOWN read as a huge count that came back
negative. The caller treats any negative as a failed listing, and SHOWN is the
local node's count rather than a peer's, so this was the contract broken
rather than an opening; but a count past `LONG_MAX` was taken into the
listing's cursor the same way. The header is now digits only and at most
`LONG_MAX`, and the input is in the corpus as `crash-negative-shown.txt`;
without the fix its replay aborts. Five minutes of the fixed target, 8.46
million runs, found nothing more. The same shape -- an unsigned parse taking a
minus -- was looked for across `c/src`: the sixteen other `strtoul`,
`strtoull` and `%lu` sites each bound their value, so a wrapped negative is
refused.

**And the exploring half had not built for a day.** fuzznet was linked into
the plain build on 2026-11-02 (10.669), and the fuzz tree's objects never got
the node module's include paths: `make fuzz` failed on `src/node/node.c` for
every target, and the `*_fuzz` programs on disk were the build before. The
replays kept passing, because they link the plain archive, and no gate runs
the exploring half -- so nothing said so until a new target needed building.
The fuzz tree now compiles `src/node/` with `NODE_CFLAGS` and links fuzznet's
archive, and all ten programs build. A shadowed `count` in `backend_ipc.c`
that clang's `-Wshadow` found on the way is renamed.

**The next lens, a parser of text somebody outside chose with no target:**
miniupnpd's lease file, whose descriptions are what any LAN device asked its
mapping to be called (10.675). It is driven by `backend_ipc` now, beside the
DHCP leases, asserting its bound, its port ranges and that no description
carries a line break into `ncfg status`: 1.36 million runs in three minutes,
nothing found. Its `%u` ports take a minus too and the range refuses the
wrap; its `%llu` expiry has no bound, so `-1` would read as a far-future
expiry, which is cosmetic and left.

## 10.680 A document for a caller goes only where the caller could have put it

**Decided from 0309 and the tiers, and built ahead of the verb that uses it.**
fuzznet's framing answers a document by writing it to a path the client names
(sec 843), and netcfgd runs as root for callers who may hold only `observe`.
Writing wherever they ask would let any of them make root create or overwrite
any file -- a symlink left in `/tmp` is enough. So
`ncfg_caller_file_create` (`c/src/sys/caller_file.c`) holds the path to one
rule: absolute; its directory owned by the caller and writable by nobody
else, so the caller could have made the file itself and nobody else can swap
