the name between check and open; the file new, created `O_EXCL | O_NOFOLLOW`
relative to the directory's own descriptor, so what was checked is what is
written into; 0600 and given to the caller. Root as the caller is held to it
too. A write that fails part way removes what it made.

**Rejected:** writing into a directory netcfgd owns and answering with the
path -- fuzznet's verbs name the path the client chose, and a second
convention for one daemon is the divergence 0309 exists to remove; and
opening as the caller with `setfsuid` around the open -- it is per thread
and would make the kernel check the caller may create the file, but alone it
still writes into a directory others may write, where a name can be swapped
under the open; the directory's ownership and mode are the rule either way,
and with them the credential switch adds nothing.

Not called yet: the verb waits on the caller's uid, fuzznet's request 10.
Checked: `caller_file_test`, 12 checks -- written in the caller's directory,
0600 and theirs; an existing file, a symlink in the file's place, a relative
path, a directory, a trailing slash, a directory not the caller's, one others
may write, and one not there are each refused with nothing written. Dropping
`O_EXCL | O_NOFOLLOW`, the owner check or the mode check turns 3, 2 and 2 red.

## 10.679 Serving's memory was mostly huge pages: refused at the top of `main`

**fuzznet's answer to the memory half of request 8** (its `e49d6fb`, sec
842): of fuzznetd's 18,720 kB resident on its machine, 14,336 kB were
transparent huge pages. With THP set to `always`, a 2 MB-aligned stretch of
anonymous memory is backed by a huge page on its first write, and the node's
roughly 32 MB of static storage is mostly cold, so it was resident 2 MB at a
time. fuzznet now refuses them in `fzn_daemon_main`, and suggested netcfgd do
it first in its own `main`, before anything is faulted.

**Measured here, THP `always`, the serve build on an empty scratch store
three seconds after start:** 16,760 kB resident before fuzznet's change
(10.676), 6,848 kB with it, and **4,664 and 4,924 kB** in two runs with
`prctl(PR_SET_THP_DISABLE)` as the first statement of `main` in
`c/src/main/main.c`. The daemon not serving is about 3.5 MB either way, and
the RSS gate is green on the default build. So 10.676's figure was this,
mostly; what serving costs in memory is about 1.3 MB, not 13.

**Every program in the multi-call binary refuses them**, `ncfg` included,
because the call is first in `main` and costs nothing where the kernel has
no such setting. Whether a router's kernel has THP at `always` is per build and
unmeasured here, which is the other reason not to scope it.

**What is not answered:** the program's size, 1,518,800 bytes default against
2,494,336 serving, and fuzznet's consumer services as build options, which
fuzznet records in sec 842 and has not started. The holder's size decision
waits on that half.

## 10.678 The backstop was switched off by anything asked more often than it

**Found** (2026-11-03) while writing 10.676's follower phase: a daemon asked
`ncfg status` every half second re-observed nothing at all -- measured, no
`look` in fourteen seconds, **in netcfgd's own loop as well as in fuzznet's**.
Every round that an event or a request ended began a fresh five seconds, so
anything arriving more often than the tick postponed it for ever. That is
exactly what `loop_internal.h` said the tick was measured to survive -- "the
backstop is switched off by exactly the chattiness it is meant to survive",
of the Rust's `recv_timeout` -- and the C had kept the same fault one level
up: the deadline was per round, not per loop.

**What it cost while it lasted:** the periodic re-observation is how netcfgd
notices drift the kernel does not announce, and how the stations seen are
read back (10.674); a status-bar script polling `ncfg status`, or a kernel
chattier than one event in five seconds, stopped both. The GUI does not poll
-- it follows `monitor` -- so a desktop with only the GUI open was not
affected. A confirm window's deadline has its own timer and was not affected
either.

**Fixed in both loops.** The own loop keeps its deadline in
`ncfg_main_run_t::next_tick`, set by the daemon: a round that ends for an
event after the deadline has passed ticks as well, and a round that ticked
sets the next one. The outside loop keeps its deadline across rounds and
moves it only on a tick. A run with no `next_tick` measures per round as
before, which is what the existing checks of the round still describe.

Checked: `loop_test`, three new checks -- an event before the deadline does
not tick, one after it does, and without `next_tick` the same one does not;
the outside loop's readiness at 3 s and at 6 s ticks on the second. Removing
the late tick, or restarting the outside deadline every round, each turns
one red. End to end, `status` every half second for fourteen seconds: three
looks in the own loop and two in fuzznet's, where there had been none.
`node_serve.sh`'s follower phase no longer makes a configuration edit to get
a pass.

## 10.677 procd names the fuzznet store: root's, where a shell's fuzznetd looks

**The holder, 2026-11-03, on 10.672's open point:** the init script passes
`--fuzznet-dir` under procd. procd starts a service with `HOME=/`, so
netcfgd's default store was `//.local/share/fuzznet` -- a node of its own,
apart from the one a fuzznetd started from root's shell keeps in
`/root/.local/share/fuzznet`, where 10.669's requirement is that the two meet
without being told.

**Which directory, decided from that requirement:** root's home from
`/etc/passwd` plus `.local/share/fuzznet`, the path a root shell's fuzznetd
takes from `$HOME`. Read with `awk` in the script rather than asked of the
daemon, because the static glibc binary OpenWrt runs answers no account
lookup without its NSS modules (10.672), so netcfgd itself cannot find root's
home there. `/root` if the line is missing. **The script makes it, 0700**,
because netcfgd never makes a store it is named: a mistyped one is refused
rather than becoming a second node (10.669). A fuzznetd packaged for OpenWrt
under procd would want the same `--fuzznet-dir`; that is fuzznet's packaging.

**The same shape under sysvinit, measured, and not under OpenRC.** The
kernel starts init with `HOME=/`, and a script run at boot inherits it:
`start-stop-daemon` passes it on, and the LSB script's daemon opened
`//.local/share/fuzznet` (`hull-openrc`, the script started with `HOME=/` as
at boot). So `packaging/sysvinit/netcfgd` names the store the same way.
`openrc-run` clears the environment, and the OpenRC script's daemon found
root's home by its own default with `HOME=/` set, so it is left as it is.
systemd gives a root system service an empty `HOME`, measured in
`hull-sandbox` (`tests/live/sandbox_writes.sh` asks `systemd-run`), and
fuzznet's default passes an empty one over to the password database as it
does an unset one -- so the unit needs nothing.
**The rig had been unable to see this**: its payload starts the scripts from
a shell holding root's `HOME`, so the first version of the check passed with
the old script. It now starts both with `HOME=/`, and the old LSB script
fails it.

Once in five `hull-openrc` runs today the OpenRC half did not run at all --
"cannot start netcfgd as localmount would not start", the rig's inert
stand-in -- and the next run passed; recorded, not explained.

Checked: `make hull-openwrt` asserts `<run>/node` names
`/root/.local/share/fuzznet`, the directory is `drwx------`, and the node's
key is the same after procd respawns the daemon -- the identity kept, not
made twice. With the script as it was, the same run reads
`//.local/share/fuzznet` and is bad. OpenWrt's BusyBox has no `stat`, which
is why the payload reads the mode with `ls`.

## 10.676 netcfgd runs in fuzznet's loop: the round split, and five asks

**The holder, 2026-11-03, on 10.669's open question** (in-loop or a thread):
"in-loop, ask fuzznet to poll extension fds during waits." So netcfgd becomes
its store's face by running inside `fzn_daemon_main`, its descriptors given
to the node's loop through `fzn_daemon_ext_t`'s `fds`/`ready`/`tick` (fuzznet
`f12ee4b`, its sec 831), and the 3 s per step in which that loop polls no
extension descriptor (10.669's last paragraph) is fuzznet's to close rather
than netcfgd's to work around. A thread was the alternative and is the one
not taken: two threads would be two writers of one store (fuzznet sec 827).

**Built: the round split, so both loops drive one round.**
`c/src/main/daemon_loop.c` ends every round in one function, `round_end`
(requests, the stream sweep, the regulatory note, the pass, the answers),
and the per-descriptor patience is one function, `look_at`.
`ncfg_main_round` -- this daemon's own `poll` -- uses both, unchanged in what
it does, and so does a loop the daemon does not own: `ncfg_main_outside_fds`
names the descriptors for the outside loop's pass, `_ready` takes one that
is readable (asking the descriptor itself for the hang-up fuzznet does not
pass on), and `_tick`, after the pass, ends a round when anything was taken
or the five-second backstop is up. Everything readable in one outside pass
is one round, which is the burst collapse. Its own loop stays for a daemon
with no store, which is every test and any machine without a node.

Checked: `loop_test`'s `an_outside_loop_drives_the_same_round`, seven
checks -- the asked source is not named, a quiet pass ends no round before
the backstop and a tick after it, fifty events in one pass are one wake, a
readiness already consumed is nothing, and a hung-up descriptor is dropped
and stops being named. Sabotaged: not marking a readiness taken fails one,
not dropping the hung-up source fails another. The other 194 checks of the
round are unchanged.

**What the move waits on: asked of fuzznet in its inbox, `20261103T1211Z`**
(6 and 7 added to the same message, after reading the follower).

1. **Poll the extension's descriptors during a wait in turn** -- the
   holder's ask. A confirm window is a deadline the operator is racing, and
   an `ncfg` request held 6 s reads as a hung daemon.
2. **What `ready` and `tick` may call, and whether either runs mid-step.**
   netcfgd's `ready` only reads its own descriptor; its pass runs in `tick`.
3. **A local request in-process.** `node_records` is static in fuzznet's
   `daemon.c`, and once netcfgd is the face, `c/src/host/seen.c` writing to
   the `face` socket is the loop's thread writing to a socket only it
   serves: a deadlock to the client's timeout, every pass. **This is the
   one that would break something if the move went first**, so the move
   does not go first.
4. **A clean stop.** `fzn_daemon_main` serves until the process is
   signalled; netcfgd stops on a byte and does its own shutdown, and wants
   fuzznet's socket closed and `face` removed rather than left as a SIGTERM
   leaves fuzznetd's.
5. **A restart after a join re-executes the argv fuzznet parsed**, which
   for netcfgd is only the fuzznet options it passes on.
6. **A follower's loop polls no extension descriptor and never ticks**
   (`follower_main`): a netcfgd started beside a running fuzznetd would watch
   nothing until that fuzznetd went.
7. **Whose is the default socket** when a face and a follower both take it.
8. **What linking the loop costs** (below): fuzznet's consumer services
   optional in its daemon build, as its spool and log files already are.
9. **For 0309, how an extension's answer outgrows one line**: `ext->local`
   writes at most 1024 bytes, `ncfg status --json` is 19,866 here, and
   `monitor` is a stream. 0309 left the carrying to be worked out with
   fuzznet when the transport is built; this is that question, with sizes.

And one to confirm: `ext_tick()` runs after every pass of the node's loop,
not once a second, which the round collapse above relies on.

**The pin is past `f12ee4b`** (at fuzznet `49b2312`, nine commits on; the
installed program 1,514,376 bytes, inside `size-budget.txt`'s tolerance).

**Built, as a build option: the daemon serving its store, in fuzznet's
loop.** `make NODE_SERVE=1` and `netcfgd --fuzznet-serve` (with
`--fuzznet-arg` for fuzznet's own node options, passed as given) run
`fzn_daemon_main` with the three calls above as its extension
(`ncfg_node_serve` in `c/src/node/node.c`, the adapters in `daemon_main.c`).
**fuzznet answered asks 1 to 5 the same hour** (its `08c9aa2`, sec 835;
netcfgd's inbox `20261103T1239Z`), and the pin is at `08c9aa2`:

- **Its waits poll the extension's descriptors** and call `ready` (ask 1).
- **`ready` may run mid-step** and may call nothing of fuzznet's but
  `fzn_daemon_stop`; **`tick` never runs mid-step, follows every pass** --
  a contract now -- and may call `fzn_daemon_local`,
  `fzn_daemon_journal_append` and `fzn_daemon_stop` (asks 2 and the
  confirmation). netcfgd's `ready` only reads its descriptor into memory,
  and its pass runs in `tick`, so both were already where they belong.
- **Seen hosts go in-process**: `ncfg_seen_in_process` hands the recorder
  `ncfg_node_local` (fuzznet's `fzn_daemon_local`, ask 3) when serving
  begins, and both the record and the listing are asked through it -- from
  the pass, so from `tick`, where fuzznet allows it.
- **The stop is `fzn_daemon_stop`** (ask 4), replacing the `longjmp`: after
  that pass fuzznet closes and removes its socket, removes `face`, releases
  the claim and returns, and the daemon's own shutdown runs after it.
- **A restart executes the daemon's own command line**
  (`fzn_daemon_ext_t.restart_argv`, ask 5), not the fuzznet options.

**And ask 6 the same afternoon** (fuzznet `7d85b54`, sec 838; netcfgd's
inbox `20261103T1338Z`): a follower polls the extension's descriptors and
ticks after every pass, `fzn_daemon_stop` ends it, and `fzn_daemon_local`
in it is asked of the face over its socket within 5 s. So the daemon no
longer tries the claim first: started beside a running fuzznetd it follows
it and goes on watching the network, and when that fuzznetd goes it takes
the claim and restarts itself as the face, through `restart_argv`. The pin
is at `7d85b54`.

**Why a build option, measured:** linking `fzn_daemon_main` grows the
installed program from 1,518,760 bytes to 2,494,056, 65 per cent. Most of it
is the chat services `node/daemon.c` calls and no feature flag leaves out --
`notes.o`, `files.o`, `stickers.o`, `groups.o`, `shelf.o` among the largest
after `daemon.o`'s own 197 KB -- and `daemon.o` declares 19 MB of static
storage. **Most of it is touched**: the same binary, three seconds after
starting on an empty scratch store, is 3,512 kB resident without serving
and 16,760 kB serving with no peers, against the RSS budget's 4,608 kB. **The holder, 2026-11-03: wait for fuzznet's answer to
request 8** -- its consumer services made optional in a daemon build --
before deciding whether netcfgd pays that. Until then the default build
carries a stub that says so, and `size-budget.txt` is not raised.

Checked: `make node-serve-test` (`c/tests/node_serve.sh`, eight checks, no
privilege): fuzznet's socket served and named in `face`; a fuzznet client's
`add record` and `list record` answered; `ncfg reload` through the daemon in
8 ms; a configuration edit compiled; **a station a real fuzznetd recorded in
the store before netcfgd started is read back in-process and shown by
`ncfg status`**; SIGTERM ends it with 0 and `face`, fuzznet's socket and
`<run>/node` all gone. Sending the recorder back to the socket while serving
turns the read-back red. (A reset of the recorder's back-off on switching to
in-process was tried and made no difference -- the startup pass never lists
-- so it is not there.) The read-back check needs the `observe` tier opened in
the test's configuration: `ncfg status` takes the seen set from the daemon
and, refused, quietly goes without, which first read as the read failing. Sabotaged -- `ready` doing nothing -- the reload took
4826 ms (the backstop's tick), the edit was never compiled and SIGTERM was
not heard (status 137, under the script's `timeout -k`): three red. Not in
`make test` or `check` while it is a build option, since it rebuilds the
node module under other flags.

**Checked beside a fuzznetd too:** `node_serve.sh` gains a second phase,
16 checks in all -- netcfgd started while a fuzznetd is the face follows it,
answers `ncfg reload` in 5 ms and reads the station back through the face;
the fuzznetd stopped, netcfgd is the face (`face` names its socket) and
answers again after restarting itself; SIGTERM ends it with 0. Clean under
`SANITIZE=1` as well. ~~A reload is not a pass that lists records~~ -- that
was this phase's first explanation for a failure, and it was wrong: the
cause was the backstop being switched off by the test's own `status`
polling, a fault in both loops (10.678). The phase now relies on the
backstop for the read-back, which checks that fix on the follower path.

**Ask 7, measured from here** (2026-11-03, fuzznet `7d85b54`; sent to
its inbox as `20261103T1430Z`): with a fuzznetd the face on the default
socket, a netcfgd on the same store given no `--socket` cannot listen there,
`fzn_daemon_main` returns 1, and netcfgd runs its own loop -- the network
configured and `ncfg` answered, but outside fuzznet's loop and never taking
the face. The face's socket is untouched. Distinct sockets work. That is the
router case, both under procd and neither told a socket. **Answered within
the hour** (fuzznet `16830dc`, sec 841; netcfgd's inbox `20261103T1441Z`): a
daemon with an extension whose path is the face's now follows with no socket
of its own, clients at the default reach the face, and it binds the path when
it takes the face. The holder had said to pass `--socket` in the init scripts
until fuzznet answered; it had, so they pass none. `node_serve.sh`'s follower
phase now runs both on one default socket.

**Ask 9 answered in the same message (fuzznet `49c8f7b`, sec 843): no new
framing.** The local protocol stays one line per request; a long listing
pages, as `list record` does; a document is written to a path the client
names and answered `ok` with its length -- so netcfgd's status would be
`get status PATH`; and a stream is events: `fzn_daemon_publish(subject,
name)`, from `tick`, reaches every `get events` subscriber, which is what
`monitor` becomes. That is 0309's carrying, settled by fuzznet's framing as
0309 said it would be; the vocabulary that rides on it is netcfgd's.

**Ask 8's memory half answered too (fuzznet `e49d6fb`, sec 842)** -- 10.679;
the program's size and the consumer services as build options are recorded
there and not started.

**0309's first verb waits on two things** (found 2026-11-03, starting it):

- **The caller's credentials** -- fuzznet's to give, asked as request 10
  (its inbox `20261103T1510Z`). 0309 keeps the control tiers (0013, 0092,
  0128), which name users and groups, and `ext->local` is handed only an
  `fzn_origin_t`; and `fzn_daemon_main` admits same-user callers alone by
  default, so a desktop's GUI user, let in today by `observe =
  "group:netcfgd"`, would not reach netcfgd over fuzznet at all.
- ~~How a root daemon writes a document to a path the client names~~ --
  **decided and built, 10.680**, given the caller's uid however it arrives.

**Next:** serving by default, once the size is decided (the holder's, after
fuzznet's request 8); 0309's verbs on 10.682's first one, once fuzznet's
`judges_local` is decided by the holder.

## 10.675 The ports UPnP opened are in the observation, and on the global tab

10.671 listed the mappings miniupnpd holds in `ncfg status` by reading its
lease file there, so a GUI user who turned UPnP on (10.673) could not see
what their devices had opened -- the objection 10.667 step 4 answered for
the command line only. The observer now reads that file for a running
miniupnpd into the upnp backend's `mappings`, as it reads a DHCP server's
leases (0303): protocol, both ports, the LAN host, the expiry and the
client's description. `ncfg status` prints from the observation, so the
file has one parser, and the global tab adds a row per mapped port while
UPnP is on.

Shown and never planned against, which is 0310's line: `hull-upnp` still
finds a second plan with nothing to do while a mapping is held, and now
also asserts the mapping is in `ncfg status --json`, which is what the GUI
reads -- against a real miniupnpd and a real `upnpc`. `upnp_test` reads the
file's lines, the malformed and out-of-range ones skipped; `client_test`
reads a status answer's mappings and leaves another kind's alone.

## 10.674 An allow list's prefix: the stations ever seen with it

10.667's third step, **reading seen back**: `allow = ["aa:bb:cc:*"]`
compiles now, and lets in the stations fuzznet's records say were ever seen
with that prefix -- by this host or by any host whose records the store
holds, so a device met at one access point of an estate is let in at the
others. A deny list's prefix expands as it did, with the records as a third
source.

- **Not blocked on the face question** (10.669), which the first reading of
  this step assumed: fuzznet's record store lets any process read and only
  writing needs the claim, and the read goes where the writes already go --
  `list record` on the socket the store's `face` names. It moves in-process
  with the writes when netcfgd runs the node loop.
- **Bounded per pass, and never a partial set** (`ncfg_seen_read`). A reply
  holds about eight records, so a pass asks at most 32 pages and the next
  carries on; the stations replace the previous set only when a listing
  ends, a new listing starts a minute after one ended, and a listing that
  stops (no face, a refusal) leaves the last whole set standing and says so
  once.
- **Stamped on every observation the daemon takes**, as `seen_stations`,
  the way the regdom setter is: the pass, an apply, the drift checks and
  the `ncfg plan` answer all expand against one set. An in-process `ncfg
  plan` takes it from the daemon's status with the regdom setter, which is
  now asked for whenever a daemon is there rather than only with a country
  observed.
- **A list only grows from what hostapd holds.** An entry hostapd already
  accepts that a prefix covers stays, so a failed reading, or a record
  fuzznet's retention lets go, never shuts out a station already allowed. A
  hostapd restart starts again from the written list and what is seen.
- **What it does not do**: admit a device never seen anywhere. That is what
  an allow list is for -- a new device with the prefix is refused until
  some host of the estate has recorded it, which is a deny-by-default
  reading of "every station of this make". An operator who wants every
  device of a manufacturer, seen or not, has no form for it, because
  hostapd holds exact addresses.

Tested in `seen_test` against a stand-in that answers page by page (two
pages joined into one set, the bound, the last set standing with no face),
in `plan_access_point_test` (seen and covered is added, seen and not covered
is not, held and covered stays, and with no records nothing moves either
way), and end to end against a real fuzznetd: records added through its own
socket appear as `seen_stations` in the observation netcfgd publishes.

**What the first run against a real fuzznetd found, in the recorder of
10.666**, which had never met one. A fuzznetd that does not serve records
answers every `add record` with its status line, `ok served granted ...`,
and the recorder took any reply beginning `ok` as a record kept -- so a
store-less fuzznetd was reported as recording everything while nothing was
kept. A kept record is answered `ok` alone, and that is what is taken now;
`seen_test` has the status line as a case, and with the old test put back
it fails. The listing already refused it. What makes a fuzznetd serve
records is a capability (`--fuzznet-service` and `--fuzznet-product`, as
fuzznet's `tool/live_trim.py` starts one); a bare `--socket` fuzznetd
answers with the status line, which is how this was met.

## 10.672 procd runs netcfgd, and an edit during a start was lost

**`packaging/procd/netcfgd` has run for the first time** (2026-11-03), 10.183
having said procd "needs OpenWrt and stays out of reach". It no longer does:
hull boots an image's own init as PID 1 (its `(init ...)`), so `make
hull-openwrt` boots the stock OpenWrt 24.10.4 root filesystem under procd,
on this host's kernel, and installs netcfgd as a package would. The routers
expected next run OpenWrt, so this is the path that meets them first.

- **What passed**: procd starts it from the shipped script and lists it
  running, and the address the document asks for appears on a device netcfgd
  made; killed with `-9`, procd starts another (`respawn`, the script's whole
  supervision policy); an edit to the file alone is applied by the inotify
  watch; `/etc/init.d/netcfgd reload` applies one through `ncfg reload`; and
  `stop` takes the process away and leaves the address, as a stop holds
  (0134). Its stdout and stderr reach `logread`, as `procd_set_param stdout`
  asks.
- **netcfgd is linked statically for it** (`make -C c netcfgd-static`, not
  in `all`): OpenWrt's libc is musl. glibc's account and address lookups
  need its NSS modules at run time and answer nothing without them, which
  every caller here already takes as "none" -- the DHCP server's `nobody`,
  the node's home directory. ~~The node's store lands at `//.local/share/
  fuzznet`~~ under procd, whose services run with `HOME=/` -- **settled in
  10.677**: the init script names the store, root's home from `/etc/passwd`.
- **The guest has none of the kernel's modules**, so the rig hands it the
  host's own dummy module; nf_tables is absent too, and the observation's
  note that no netfilter socket opens **repeated on every pass** -- a line
  every few seconds in `logread`. On a real OpenWrt build nf_tables is in,
  but a kernel without it would fill a router's log, so the note is now said
  once, and again only after a socket has opened in between. The rig asserts
  no process says it twice; with the fix reverted it failed, nine lines in
  one short run.

**The fault it found: an edit made while the daemon starts was lost.** The
daemon compiled its configuration long before it opened the watch that
catches every later edit, and an edit landing between the two raised no
event, so it was applied by nobody until the next one. Under procd that
window is every respawn. **Measured with the build from before the fix as
the control**, three trials of killing the daemon and editing the file the
instant procd's new pid appears: before, every edit was lost -- the address
each time one edit behind -- and the daemon never said a word; after, each
was applied within one to three seconds and the daemon said three times
that the configuration had changed while it was starting.

**The fix** takes the polling watcher's fingerprint of the configuration
directories (`ncfg_watch_fingerprint_of`, the mtimes of everything in them)
just before the first compile and again once the watch is open, and compiles
again where they differ. The writability probe, which creates and unlinks a
file in the configuration directory, moved to before the first fingerprint:
between the two it would have made every start look like an edit, which is
the comment's own warning about writing after the watch, met from the other
side. `watch_test` checks the fingerprint is stable over an unchanged tree
and differs once a file is written.

## 10.671 UPnP and NAT-PMP: miniupnpd, in a table netcfgd makes (0310)

**Built** (2026-11-03): 10.667's UPnP plan, all five steps.
[0310](doc/decision/0310-upnp-is-miniupnpd-in-a-table-netcfgd-makes.md) is
the design and the measurements behind it, each taken in a vm with the image
`tests/hull/upnp/` builds: miniupnpd makes no nftables structure of its own
(its first mapping failed with UPnP error 501), a mapping cannot pass
netcfgd's own drop-policy forward chain without an accept for translated
connections (10.670), miniupnpd leaves its mappings behind when it stops, and
it adds its rules straight into three hooked chains when it is told their
names -- so the table netcfgd makes is a table and three empty accepting
chains, and nothing else.

- **The language**: `global { upnp { lan = ["lan0"]; uplink = "wan0" } }`.
  Refused at compile time, each naming the line to change: an uplink without
  `nat = true`, a LAN interface with no block, the uplink named as a LAN
  (anybody on the internet could map ports), and a block missing either key.
  `secure_mode` is always on, and NAT-PMP/PCP is on the same switch.
- **The plan** says the holder's warning on every plan while UPnP is on --
  any device on the LAN may open a port without asking -- and names the
  `translated = true` rule where the forward chain drops without one, and an
  SSDP accept where the input chain drops. miniupnpd is a backend keyed by
  its uplink, started after every action on its uplink and LAN interfaces,
  and restarted when the `upnp` block's summary differs from the first line
  of the running daemon's configuration.
- **The executor** makes `inet netcfgd_upnp` before starting miniupnpd and
  deletes it after stopping it, deleting first on a start so a mapping a dead
  daemon left cannot survive. The table has an audit of its own: its name,
  its three chains, and no rule -- netcfgd cannot write a mapping. It is not
  replaced on each apply as `netcfgd` is, or every apply would drop every
  mapping.
- **The observation** finds miniupnpd by its `-f <config>` marker, as dnsmasq
  is found, and skips `netcfgd_upnp` outright: it is neither a stranger's NAT
  nor a filter neighbour -- and not netcfgd's firewall either, though its
  chain is called `forward`. **That last was a fault the rig found**: the
  first version only kept it out of the neighbours, its `forward` chain's
  `accept` was read as the firewall's `drop`, and every plan replaced a
  firewall that had not changed.
- **`ncfg status`** lists every mapping from miniupnpd's lease file, with the
  host and what asked for it: openings in the firewall no document wrote.

**Checked:** lowering refusals and a round trip; a plan test for the two
warnings and the start's dependencies; and `make hull-upnp` -- netcfgd's
router with a forward chain that drops, a LAN host and a host on the uplink
side in namespaces of one vm. Before the apply `upnpc` finds no router (the
control); after it the LAN host maps 18080 to its own 8080, a mapping to
another host is refused (UPnP error 606, secure mode), a connection from the
uplink side through 18080 reaches the LAN host, `ncfg status` lists the
mapping, a second plan has nothing to do and carries the warning once, and
with `upnp` removed miniupnpd is gone and so is the table. **Sabotaged**:
without the translated accept, the mapping is made and nothing crosses it,
and the rig says so. A first sabotage that swapped it for `state = ["new"]`
proved nothing -- that accepts every new connection from the uplink, mapped
or not -- which is worth knowing about the rule as well as the rig.

**Measured as well:** the installed program grew 17,376 bytes, and `make rss`
read 3,236 KB of its 3,328 limit where it read 3,132 before -- inside it,
and the closest this tree has come, which the next resident feature should
know before it starts.

**Not built:** IPv6 pinholes (PCP can ask for them; miniupnpd's IPv6 side
wants `ip6tables` hooks of its own and is a separate measurement), and
reading the mappings into the observation for the TUI and the GUI rather
than only `ncfg status`.

## 10.670 A firewall rule may match a translated connection

**Built** (2026-11-03): `translated = true` on a firewall rule matches a
connection whose destination this router rewrote -- nftables' `ct status
dnat`. It is the rule a forward chain that drops by policy needs for UPnP's
mappings, which no address rule can name because nobody wrote them down
(0310, 10.671), and it covers every port forward of 0298 at once, so that
forward's warning no longer asks for an address rule where a translated
accept is already there.

Explicit rather than added unseen, which is 0298's rule held to: an implicit
`ct status dnat accept` would accept what any table translated, docker's
included, in a chain the operator did not write it in.

Written as the status register masked with IPS_DST_NAT and compared against
zero, as nft 1.1.3 writes `ct status dnat`; read back as the same flag, any
other status test refused; and part of the rule's digest only where set, so
no rule digested before it changes. An undo rebuilds a rule with its
translation, or undoing a change would widen it to every connection.
**Checked:** written and read back, the digest differing, a render round
trip, and the forward warning quieted -- sabotaged by dropping the helper
from `nat.c`, which turns that check red.

## 10.669 The daemon is a fuzznet node: one store, the claim, its identity

**Built** (2026-11-02): fuzznet's objects are linked into `c/`, and the
daemon opens a fuzznet store at start, takes its claim, and loads or makes
the node's identity -- 10.668's first step, and the identity half of its
second. `c/src/node/` is the seam; nothing else in the tree includes a
fuzznet header, and `ncfg/node.h` names no fuzznet type.

**The shared store is answered, and it settles 0308's "own identity".**
fuzznet's sec 827, replying to inbox `20261102T2330Z`: a store has one
identity and one writer. The first process to take the store's `claim` (an
exclusive flock) is its **face** and alone writes; any other is a
**follower**, which reads the store and forwards writes over the socket the
face names in the store's `face` file, and takes the claim when the face
goes. So the holder's "fuzznetd and netcfgd ... lock-writing the same files"
makes them one node in two processes, and 0308's "its own identity" is the
case of netcfgd running alone -- the default, needing no fuzznetd. A follower
here loads the identity, writes nothing, and makes none if the store has none.

**netcfgd holds the claim only while it boots, and that was a fault found
before committing.** The first version kept it, as fuzznetd does. But a face
serves the store -- its socket, the rounds that carry records to the estate
-- and that loop is fuzznetd's; netcfgd does not run it yet. So a netcfgd
that started first and kept the claim made any fuzznetd started after it a
follower, forwarding every client to a face socket nobody served: fuzznetd
broken by an ordering. Now the claim is taken to load or make the identity
(only a face may make one) and given back at once; fuzznetd's follower
retries it every second and becomes the face. When netcfgd runs the node
loop itself it keeps the claim it takes -- the point at which "no fuzznetd
should be necessary" is fully true rather than true of the identity.

**Where the store is, decided from the aims:**

- **fuzznet's own default for the user** (`fzn_cli_default_dir`:
  `$XDG_DATA_HOME/fuzznet`, else `~/.local/share/fuzznet`), so fuzznetd and
  netcfgd started as root on a router meet in one store without being told
  -- the holder's requirement, met by default rather than by configuration.
- **The account's home from the password database where neither variable is
  set**, which is how a service is usually started; it is where a fuzznetd
  run from that account's shell would look.
- **`--fuzznet-dir` / `NCFG_FUZZNET_DIR`** name another, spelled as fuzznetd
  spells it. A named store is never made, fuzznet's rule: a mistyped path is
  refused rather than becoming a second node. An empty one asks for none.
- **No default store for a daemon on a non-default `--run-dir`.** That daemon
  is a test or a second instance, and the default would hand it the
  operator's own identity, or take the claim on a running fuzznetd's store.
  Every test in the tree runs on its own run directory, so none of them
  touches a home directory unless it names a store.

**A node that will not open is logged and changes nothing else**: the
network is configured as before. The daemon writes `<run>/node` -- `key=`
and `store=`, and no role, since which process serves the store can change
after netcfgd opens it -- and removes it when it stops; `ncfg status` prints it
as a section of its own, read from that file rather than the observation,
because a node is not network state and the observed model is frozen (0020).

**Measured, and what it cost:** the installed program grew 78,016 bytes over
the tree just before (1,409,376 to 1,487,392), nearly all of it Monocypher
and the identity it signs with; `size-budget.txt` carries it. Linked from an
archive of fuzznet's objects, so a link takes only what is called -- a test
that never opens a node takes nothing of fuzznet. **The first link grew it
366 KB**: fuzznet builds `-Os -g` by default and its debug sections came
along, so `c/` builds it with `-Os` through the environment, where fuzznet's
`CFLAGS ?=` takes it and its own `-std=c11` and warnings still append.
fuzznet is built into `c/fuzznet-build/`, not the bridge's `fuzznet/build/`:
two builds into one directory from a parallel `make` are two writers.

**Checked:** `tests/node_test.c`, 21 checks against a real file store and a
real flock -- where the store is in each case, the identity made once and
loaded after, **the claim free while the node is open**, the identity loaded
and nothing made with another process holding the claim, a named store that
is not there refused, and a store missing its anchor refused by name and
left unwritten. Sabotaged: keeping the claim turns three checks red. And
the real programs on scratch directories, both orders: netcfgd first, then
the fuzznetd built beside it on the same store -- fuzznetd booted as the
face with netcfgd's key and wrote `face`; fuzznetd first, then netcfgd --
which loaded the same key "beside the process serving it". `ncfg status`
showed the node, `<run>/node` went at SIGTERM, and nothing was left running.

**The recorder now goes through the store's face** (2026-11-03): with a
node, `c/src/host/seen.c` reads the socket from the store's `face` file
before each write, as a fuzznet follower does, rather than guessing
fuzznetd's default -- which a service started with no `$XDG_RUNTIME_DIR`
would look for in `/tmp/fuzznet-UID/` while a fuzznetd started in a shell
serves under `/run/user/UID/`. A store nobody serves writes nothing and says
so once; `NCFG_FUZZNET_SOCKET` still overrides it. `seen_test` puts a face
file in a store after the recorder was made and the records arrive there;
skipping the lookup turns that red.

**The scope table keeps its copy, now held in the daemon's build**
(2026-11-03), which is a different answer from 10.668's "retype it", and the
reason is worth keeping. 0308 removed the copy's first reason, fuzznet kept off
the daemon. But retyping `ncfg_scope_t` onto `fzn_scope_t` puts fuzznet's
include paths -- and through `state/scope.h` its record and commitment
headers -- on the compiler and on everything that includes `ncfg/scope.h`,
where today only `c/src/node/` sees a fuzznet header and its flags. Four enum
values do not buy that. So `c/src/node/node.c` asserts at compile time that
every value agrees, in the program that ships, beside the bridge's existing
assertion; swapping one value stops the build with the assertion's sentence.
If the language ever needs fuzznet's scope *functions* (`fzn_scope_widens`),
that is the time to retype, and the node module is where the seam would grow.

**Next, from 10.668's list:** netcfgd running fuzznet's loop as the face
(below, and 10.676 for the decision and what it waits on).

**And how netcfgd becomes a face that serves, answered by fuzznet** (inbox
`20261102T2329Z`, its sec 831, built in its `f12ee4b`). Writing records
in-process and 0309's local socket both need it. The node loop is already
one call, `fzn_daemon_main(argc, argv, &ext)` in `node/daemon.h` --
options, store, claim, face or follower, both hops, the rounds; fuzznetd's
own `main` is that call with no extension. An extension (`fzn_daemon_ext_t`)
adds options, local verbs, remote request types, journal kinds and settings
(`node/test/ext_daemon.c` is the worked example), and since `f12ee4b` it
takes the caller's own descriptors (`fds`, up to 16, asked each pass),
`ready` for each that is readable, and a `tick` about once a second. So
**netcfgd's poll loop would move inside the node's**: one loop owns the
process's descriptors, because two threads would be two writers of one
store (sec 827).

**The cost weighed, and decided by the holder in 10.676** -- in the loop,
with fuzznet asked to poll the extension's descriptors during waits. It was:
fuzznet's caution that while a round waits in turn on a peer the loop polls
neither its own descriptors nor the caller's, for up to a few seconds. For
this daemon that is a few seconds in which an `ncfg` request, a netlink
event and a confirm window's deadline all wait. Measuring how long a round
holds the loop on a real estate, and whether fuzznet can bound it, comes
before moving the reconcile loop into it.

**fuzznet's own figures, sent 2026-11-03 so they need not be measured
again**: a single wait in turn is capped at 3 s (`recv_answering` in
`node/daemon.c`, resends included), and steps follow one another, so two
back to back reached about 6.3 s with a lossy peer (its sec 747). Its local
socket and UDP are still answered during those waits (secs 748 and after);
an extension's descriptors and tick are not, for up to about 3 s per step.
So for netcfgd the figure to design against is several seconds, not one.

## 10.668 fuzznet is linked into netcfgd: 0269 is superseded

The holder, 2026-11-02, on being asked what 0269 was: fuzznet "should be
linked in directly. Separation of process concerns for separations sake rarely
adds much security but makes the code substantially harder to reason about.
All peer networking and IPC should be coming from fuzznet, and no fuzznetd
should be necessary for netcfgd."
[0308](doc/decision/0308-fuzznet-is-linked-into-netcfgd.md) records it and
supersedes [0269](doc/decision/0269-the-remote-half-is-a-separate-program.md).

**This session had built on the superseded premise**, and says so where it
did:

- **10.666's recorder talks to a fuzznetd over its socket.** That transport is
  wrong under 0308: netcfgd is its own node and writes its own store. The
  recorder's policy -- the key, the value, when to write, the bound -- is
  what carries over; the transport is replaced by fuzznet's records API
  called in-process. Until then it writes nothing on a machine with no
  fuzznetd, which is every machine, so it does no harm standing.
- **10.664 item 1 and 10.666 said the daemon "never links fuzznet"**, citing
  0269. Read them as history.
- **10.667's remote-access plan had an agent relay to `remote.sock`.** Under
  0308 the daemon speaks fuzznet to a client itself; the plan's steps 2 and 4
  are replaced by that, and 0128's tiers still decide what a remote caller may
  do.
- **The scope `_Static_assert` in `bridge/` (aa0ef36c)** was chosen to keep
  fuzznet off the daemon's build. With fuzznet linked, the original plan in
  `scope.h` -- retype the table onto `fzn_scope_t` and delete the copy --
  becomes the right one.

**Answered: the local socket too** -- "We need only one protocol, the fuzznet
protocol + extensions needed for netcfgd."
[0309](doc/decision/0309-one-protocol-the-local-socket-is-fuzznets-too.md):
`ncfg` and the GUI speak fuzznet to the daemon, local or remote alike, and
newline-delimited JSON goes (`doc/socket-protocol.md` 3.1 superseded). The
vocabulary and the tiers carry over; the framing does not. raidcfgd, which
adopted netcfgd's JSON socket, is told through its inbox, `20261102T2345Z`.

**fuzznetd and netcfgd run side by side, sharing a store** (the holder, the
same evening): "fuzznetd and netcfgd need to be able to run simultaneously but
they will be delegating and lock-writing the same files." So linking fuzznet
does not mean netcfgd owns a store alone: on a machine where fuzznetd also
runs as the same user, both open the same files and write them under locks.
Whether fuzznet's store is safe for two processes today is fuzznet's to say.
Measured here only as far as `claim/claim_file.c`, an exclusive `flock`;
nothing found says a node re-reads its in-memory state when the other writes.
Signalled to fuzznet's inbox, `20261102T2330Z`, with the recorder as the
caller -- **and answered** by fuzznet's sec 827: one store is one identity,
and the claim's face is its only writer. 10.669 has what that settles.

**The first steps, in order**: link fuzznet into `c/` (its objects, as
`bridge/Makefile` already does, minus the program's `main`); give the daemon a
node identity and a store under its state directory; move the recorder onto
the records API; retype the scope table.

## 10.667 Next, planned rather than started: remote access, UPnP, reading seen back

Three things the holder's answers (10.664) opened, each larger than the end of
the week that produced them. Written down as steps so the next session starts
building rather than deciding. Each step lands on its own and is useful alone.

**Remote access -- one client, aimed at a host** (10.664, item 3). What
exists: the daemon's `remote.sock`, whose tiers come from `global.remote` and
whose origin is the socket (0128); `tests/live/remote_tiers.sh` drives it;
`bridge/netcfgd-remote` links fuzznet and reads a frame. What is missing is
everything between a phone and that socket.

1. The client's target: `client/` and the GUI take a *target* -- the local
   socket by default, or a host -- and say which in the window's title.
   Today it is `--socket PATH` only. The connection type is the seam the
   Android build needs anyway.
2. The agent: `bridge/netcfgd-remote` grows from reading a frame to
   terminating fuzznet's session (its contact and pairing, sections 11.x
   there) and relaying lines to `remote.sock`. fuzznet's protocol is
   settled (10.567); netcfgd adds no transport of its own.
3. Pairing: the operator is root on the host, so the first pairing can be a
   command there that prints what the client scans or types -- the simpler
   path gui/project.md section 9 noted.
4. Packaging: the agent ships in its own package, installed disabled, since
   it is a network service this project never had (the open half of 6171).

**UPnP and NAT-PMP, with the warning** (10.664, item 5). miniupnpd is the
daemon (Debian 2.3.9, nftables build), run as a backend the way dnsmasq and
hostapd are: a generated configuration under `/run`, started, watched,
stopped by its own pid.

1. Language: `global { upnp { lan = ["lan0"]; uplink = "wan0" } }`, with
   `secure_mode` always on (a client maps only to itself) and NAT-PMP/PCP on
   the same switch. Refused without a NAT uplink.
2. The plan says it every time it is on, as a warning: *any device on these
   networks may open a port on this router, without asking; a compromised
   one can expose itself or anything behind it.* That is the holder's
   condition, and it is the plan's job because the plan is what is read
   before applying.
3. Coexistence: miniupnpd writes its own nftables table (`miniupnpd`); it is
   named as a known neighbour rather than reported as a stranger (the
   carve-out 10.539 asks to be named, not inferred).
4. `ncfg status` lists the mappings miniupnpd holds, so the firewall state
   outside the document is at least visible -- the objection the old parked
   question raised.
5. A rig: two machines in hull, a client asking for a mapping with `upnpc`,
   the mapping reaching the kernel and leaving it.

**Reading seen back** (10.666's half). The resolver that expands a deny
list's prefix against stations associated now (10.591) gains fuzznet's
`list record` as a second source, so an allow list may name a prefix: its
stations are the ones ever seen with it. Paged reads, bounded per pass.

## 10.666 The hosts this machine sees are written into fuzznet's records

10.591's second half, unblocked by fuzznet's records (10.662) and placed by the
holder (10.664, item 1): the daemon, which is root and observes the stations
and leases, writes them down itself, into the fuzznetd of the user it runs
as. **A socket client, not fuzznet linked**: `add record KEY VALUE` over
fuzznetd's local stream socket, the way netcfgd already talks to
wpa_supplicant and hostapd, so 0269 holds.

- **KEY** is `seen/<interface>/<mac>`, dashes for the colons fuzznet's key
  grammar does not take, which is what fuzznet's retention selects by
  (`text=seen/wlan0/`, `text=aa-bb-cc`). An interface name outside that
  grammar is not written rather than mangled.
- **VALUE** is `station` for one associated to netcfgd's access point, or
  `lease ADDRESS [NAME]` for one holding a lease from its DHCP server, escaped
  with fuzznet's `%XX`.
- **When**: first seen, changed, or a day since it was last written while it
  stays -- fuzznet keeps every record, so writing every pass would fill a
  month's bucket with one station. At most 4096 remembered between passes.
- **Where**: fuzznetd's own default for the daemon's user
  (`$XDG_RUNTIME_DIR/fuzznet/fuzznetd.sock`, else `/tmp/fuzznet-UID/`),
  written again here rather than asked of fuzznet, or `NCFG_FUZZNET_SOCKET`.
  `netcfgd.service` has no private `/tmp`, so root's is reachable.
- **Nobody listening is ordinary**: nothing is written, one note says so, and
  it is not asked again for a minute. Each wait is bounded at a second, so a
  wedged fuzznetd cannot stall a pass.

`c/src/host/seen.c`, called from the loop after each observation. Checked:
`seen_test` against a forked stand-in fuzznetd -- the key, the three records
and their exact lines, nothing rewritten a minute on, one rewritten when a
lease's name changes, two rewritten a day on, nothing and no failure with no
fuzznetd and no retry within the minute, a refusal kept for the next pass.
**Not run against a real fuzznetd**, which would need one running as root.

**Read back since 10.674**: the daemon lists the records from the same face
and an allow list's prefix expands against them.

## 10.665 A confirm window pauses while the machine sleeps

The holder's "do what makes sense for each confirm window" (10.664, item 4).
There is one kind, commit-confirm, and what made no sense was its suspend: the
deadline was wall-clock, so a window armed before the lid closed was long
past when it opened, and the first pass reverted a change the operator had
lived with all night -- at the one moment they were back to confirm it.
Nobody can confirm a sleeping machine, so the time it slept is given back.

**`CLOCK_BOOTTIME` less `CLOCK_MONOTONIC` is exactly the time spent
suspended**, and nothing else: no polling, and immune to a wall-clock step. A
window records it when armed (`asleep_seconds` in `confirm.json`), and its
deadline moves later by however much more has been slept since. A step of
the wall clock still moves an open window, as `confirm_test` already pinned;
a window written before this keeps the old reading, and the reader takes the
new member where it is.

Checked: `confirm_test` -- a window armed before a night's sleep is open when
the lid opens with the forty seconds it had left, closes once those run
awake, closes on time for a machine that stayed awake, and keeps its sleep
count through the file; the old reading still holds for a window with none.
Sabotaged (the sleep ignored), two checks fail. `reconcile_test` and
`daemon_test` pass. Never run across a real suspend: `tests/live/` cannot
suspend a machine, and this one is the holder's desktop.

## 10.664 Five answers from the holder, 2026-11-02

Asked at the end of the /go runs of 2026-11-02, answered the same evening.
Each closes a question this document holds open somewhere; the entries that
held them now point here.

1. **Seen hosts: the daemon writes them itself.** "As it is the root user that
   runs netcfgd and scans them it also is the one to write down what it sees
   into the fuzznet data store." So the recorder is the daemon, not the
   bridge, and it talks to the fuzznetd of the user it runs as -- root's. That
   is a local socket and a line protocol, not fuzznet linked into the process:
   0269 keeps fuzznet's *code* out of the process holding CAP_NET_ADMIN, and a
   socket client of a local daemon is what netcfgd already is to
   wpa_supplicant and hostapd. Closes 10.662's seam and 10.591's second half.
2. **The scope enum: the holder did not know what it was**, so it is decided
   here from the aims rather than asked again. It is the four-word list of how
   far a setting travels -- host-private, host, group, estate -- which fuzznet
   owns as `fzn_scope_t` and netcfgd kept a copy of so the daemon builds
   without fuzznet. **The copy stays and is held to fuzznet's** by a
   `_Static_assert` in `bridge/record_encode.c`, the third answer 10.567
   named: no new dependency for the daemon, and a drift stops the bridge
   building. Sabotaged: a misstated pair fails the build naming the drift.
3. **Remote access is the same client.** "A client should connect to a local
   netcfgd by default or be configurable to connect to a different host." So
   `agent/` (or whatever terminates fuzznet's protocol on the host) is wanted,
   and the GUI and the Android build are one client with a target -- local
   socket by default, another host when told. Closes "whether agent/ exists".
4. **Confirm windows: "do what makes sense for each".** For commit-confirm
   across a suspend, what makes sense is that a window does not run out while
   nobody can be at the machine to confirm: it pauses while the machine
   sleeps. Built, 10.665.
5. **UPnP / NAT-PMP: yes, with a warning that it is a security risk.** Any
   device on the LAN may then open a port on the router; the plan says so
   whenever it is on.

## 10.663 A firewall rule may keep hours: parental controls, held by the kernel

Found walking the router aim: every consumer router can keep a child's
devices offline after ten on school nights, and netcfgd's firewall could not
say it, so the answer was a hand-written nftables table beside netcfgd's.
[0307](doc/decision/0307-a-firewall-rule-may-keep-hours.md) has the decision
and what was rejected.

    drop "bedtime" {
    	mac   = ["@host_list:kids"]
    	hours = "21:00-07:00"
    	days  = ["sun", "mon", "tue", "wed", "thu"]
    }

- **In local time, held in UTC.** `meta hour` and `meta day` read the kernel's
  clock, which is UTC; nft converts the hour and not the day, so its own rules
  match the wrong day near midnight. `c/src/model/schedule.c` expands a
  schedule into UTC pieces -- moved and split wherever local or UTC midnight
  falls -- at the offset in force when the rules are built, and each piece is
  one kernel rule: `meta hour`, `byteorder hton`, `range eq`, then `meta day`
  and `cmp`, as nft 1.1.3 encodes `meta hour "08:00"-"09:30" meta day 1`
  (measured with `nft --debug=netlink`). Pieces are one more axis of 10.592's
  expansion and count against its 256.
- **The pieces are in the digest**, so a summer-time change is a firewall that
  is not the document's, and **the loop puts it back by itself**: a firewall
  replace is otherwise an apply's to make, and this one is the clock's,
  recognised exactly by `ncfg_nft_firewall_only_schedule_moved` -- the
  document's firewall given the kernel's pieces matches what is installed.
- **The undo copy carries `utc_pieces`**, since the local schedule cannot be
  recovered from them; the builder takes them as they are and they digest as
  the rules they were read from. A compiled document never has them, and
  `tool/form-unread-keys.txt` waives the field for the GUI with that reason.
- The observation's rule gains `time` (the piece, `"1 25200 30599"`), the
  comparison compares it, `ncfg status` says it for a person
  (`time mon 07:00-08:29:59 UTC`), the renderer writes `hours` and `days`
  back, and the GUI's firewall dialog edits them.

Checked: `schedule_test` (the parse, the days, fourteen expansions written out
by hand across offsets east and west, the piece text); `nft_test` (a Monday
night an hour east is two rules on two UTC days, read back to its pieces; the
digest moves with the offset; an undo copy digests as its source; the clock
alone moving is recognised, and not when anything else differs too);
`lower_test`, `render_test`; `firewall_load` with a schedule in the fixture.
**In a real kernel**, `tests/live/firewall.sh` under `unshare -rn`: Monday
08:00-09:30 an hour east is listed by nft as `meta hour "07:00"-"08:29:59"
meta day "Monday" drop`, a window past midnight is two rules with one digest,
the probe reads a piece back with its digest recomputing, `ncfg apply` then
`ncfg plan` says nothing to do, and the same document planned five hours west
is a table to replace.

## 10.661 Five stops waited on a file the daemon removes before it exits

**Found by `make check` at f353458d**, under a machine at load 65:
`supplicant_launch_test` failed "the supplicant it was told to stop has gone
by the time the stop returns" -- 10.650's own check, which had passed every
run before. Not a flake: 10.649 and 10.650 made both stops wait, and both
waits re-read the pid file. **wpa_supplicant and hostapd remove their own pid
file on the way out, before they have exited**, so the wait said "gone" for
as long as deinitialising took after the unlink -- the same gap 10.649 exists
to close, reopened by the instrument. The fake supplicant does it too, from
an `atexit` hook, and Python's finalisation after it is the window load
widened.

**`ncfg_process_still(pid, marker)`**: whether that pid is still a process
carrying netcfgd's marker. Both stops take the pid before `TERMINATE` and
wait on it; a zombie, or a pid reused by something without the marker, reads
as gone. dnsmasq's stop is untouched: it does not remove its pid file on
exit, so re-reading the file was sound there.

**The same shape, searched for: three more stops.** openvpn, radvd and pppd
each remove their own pid file as they exit, and each stop waited by
re-reading it -- openvpn's comment even said so, as the reason the wait
usually returned at once. Each now follows the pid it signalled, by the
marker its `running_pid` already used: the management socket path, the
generated radvd configuration, the pppd options file. `ra_test`'s slow
stand-in now removes its pid file before its half-second exit, as radvd does;
the old wait fails "a start that follows cannot meet the daemon it replaced"
and the new one passes. openvpn and pppoe have no stand-in that exits slowly,
so for them the change is the same code as the two proved, not a third proof.

Proved both ways, deterministically. The fake supplicant gained
`FAKE_SUPPLICANT_EXIT_DELAY_MS`, which the launch test sets to 300 and
nothing else does, so the live scripts are no slower; with it the old wait
fails that check and the new one passes. `service_test` gained an access
point whose stand-in removes its pid file 0.2 s in and runs 0.6 s more: the
old wait fails "the stop waited for the process, not the file", the new one
passes.

`; delegated <prefix>`, kept apart from the link's own addresses because a

## 10.655 An OWE network can be added, from the desktop and from `ncfg`

0227 left it open and
[0306](doc/decision/0306-an-owe-network-can-be-added.md) closes it:
`wifi_add` carries `owe`, so "Enhanced Open" -- encrypted, no passphrase --
can be added at the `wifi` tier. Before, the wifi tab refused and printed the
block to write by hand, which needs `admin`, and the tray's new networks left
OWE out.

- **The daemon** writes `wifi { owe = true }` and stores nothing, and refuses

  compares the kind as well.

- **The GUI**: an OWE scan row opens the add dialog saying "encrypted, with no
  passphrase (OWE)"; the hidden-network prompt (10.653) offers OWE as a fourth
  kind; the tray offers OWE networks among the new ones, marked `encrypted`.

Checked: `daemon_wifi_test`, `wifi_profile_test` (installs and compiles back
to OWE, not open), `cli_wifi_test` (no prompt reached, block says `owe`),
`proto_test` (the member round-trips), `client_test` (the request carries
