CLI has refused by name since 0154.

## 10.652 The tray offers the networks it heard that nothing names yet

**Found by walking the desktop aim** (10.590's brief: for a laptop's owner,
joining a network is the whole interaction). The tray's `Connect to` listed
the saved networks the last scan heard, and every other one -- the cafe, a
friend's flat -- meant `Another network...`, the window, the wifi tab, finding
the row and `Add`. 10.590 kept it that way because "a new network is a block
written", and that reason had gone: `wifi_add` has been the `wifi` tier since
0124 and carries typed fields, never config text (0117), so the tray may ask
for it exactly as it asks for `wifi_connect`.

**Below the saved networks, `New networks`**: the first eight SSIDs the last
scan heard that no access point in it is configured for, strongest first,
each saying whether it wants a passphrase, an 802.1X login or nothing.
Choosing one opens the window's own add dialog on that access point -- the
same fields and refusals as the wifi tab, and the review a plan would
otherwise be -- and joins the network once the daemon has loaded it.

- **The rule is the client library's, `ncfg_new_choices`**, beside
  `ncfg_join_choices` and for its reason: the TDE tray will offer the same
  list. It leaves out an SSID some network already names (that one is offered
  above, by id, and a second block for it would be wrong), a hidden or
  non-text name (nothing to recognise in a menu), and OWE (0227: `wifi_add`
  cannot say it yet). Those stay reachable through `Another network...`.
- **Joining waits for the load, by SSID.** `wifi_add` is answered when the
  block is written, before the watcher has re-read the configuration, and
  `wifi_connect` joins only what the loaded document names. The id may be the
  daemon's choice, too, since the dialog leaves it optional. So the tray asks
  `saved_networks` for the SSID every half second, up to ten seconds, and
  joins by the id it finds; past that it says the network was added and where
  to choose it.
- **Still no scan of its own.** The list is the last scan the operator asked
  for, as before.

Checked: `client_test` holds the rule to each exclusion beside a case it
keeps; `gui/tests/tray_choices` holds the tray's conversion, every field the
rule reads included. The menu and the dialog it opens still want a
notification host (10.590), so the click path is compiled and not driven.
The TDE tray does not have this either, for 10.590's reason.

## 10.650 The supplicant's stop had 10.649's shape too, and the class is closed

Derived from 10.649 rather than found: that fault's shape -- a stop that
returns while the process it stopped is still exiting -- was looked for in
every backend stop. dnsmasq, openvpn, the DHCP clients, radvd, autoip and
pppoe all wait; **wpa_supplicant's did not**, being the other stop that speaks
a control socket. It sent `TERMINATE`, took `OK`, and removed the pid file at
once, so the next observation read a supplicant still exiting as absent, and
a start that followed -- the next apply, or a revert -- began a second one
whose control socket the first removed on its way out. A plan's own restart
of a supplicant is the wedged case only, where the stop fails first, so the
exposure is across applies rather than within one; it is radvd's ending in
10.566.

The fix is 10.649's: wait at most 3 s for `ncfg_supplicant_running_pid` to
answer 0, and keep the pid file of one that will not go. **The test had
been hiding it**: `supplicant_launch_test` waited up to three seconds for the
fake to go after the stop returned, which is the window the stop left open.
It now asks `/proc/<pid>/cmdline` the moment the stop returns -- not
`running_pid`, which reads the file the stop removes -- and with the wait
taken out fails three runs of three.

So the 10.566 table is complete: every backend netcfgd stops waits for the
process to go before its record does. **And dnsmasq's wait had no test at
all**, so it is pinned the same way now: a stand-in naming the generated
configuration, which is the ownership marker, takes 0.4 s over SIGTERM and
must have gone when the stop returns, and one that ignores it must leave the
stop failed with its pid file kept. With the wait removed all three fail.

## 10.649 An access point restarted for any changed field could be left dead

Found by 10.648's rig, and not specific to its key. Restarting an access
point -- a changed `ssid`, `channel`, `security`, `width` or any other field
hostapd reads once -- is a `backend.stop` and a `backend.start`, and the stop
returned as soon as hostapd answered `TERMINATE` with `OK`. hostapd answers
before it has deinitialised, so the start began beside the old process, and
the old one, finishing its exit, removed the pid file and control socket the
new one had just made and took the interface down. **Measured in
`make hull-ap-lease`, three runs of three**: after the restart no hostapd was
running, `run/hostapd/` held only the log, `wlan0` was down, the station was
scanning -- and the apply had printed `ok` for both halves.

It is 10.566's class, the fifth instance and the one its table left out,
because this stop speaks a control socket rather than sending a signal. The
fix is that class's: the stop waits, at most 3 s, until
`ncfg_hostapd_running_pid` answers 0, and one that will not go is a failure
that keeps its pid file so the start that follows sees it rather than
beginning a second access point on the radio. The config file still goes
either way, since it holds the passphrase.

`service_test` drives it with a stand-in recognised as the access point's
hostapd -- `-P <pid file>` in its command line, which is the ownership marker
-- that takes half a second to go. The check asks the process itself whether
it has exited, not `running_pid`: the stop removes the pid file, so a check
of the file passed with the wait removed, which is how the first draft of the
test was found vacuous. With the wait removed the three checks fail; with it,
the rig passes.

## 10.648 Guest wifi: an access point that keeps its stations apart

`isolate_stations = true` on an `access_point` is hostapd's `ap_isolate`: a
frame from one station to another on that access point is not relayed. It is
the half of a guest network a firewall cannot give, because such a frame
never leaves the radio; keeping guests off the rest of the network is the
firewall's half, and the example says so. Estate-scoped, as `hidden` is,
since whether a network's stations may reach each other is the network's
property. Off unless asked for and omitted when off, so earlier documents are
unchanged; read once by hostapd, so changing it restarts the access point,
and the running value is read back out of the generated file as the other
read-once keys are. Named for what it does rather than OpenWrt's `isolate`,
which does not say what is kept from what.

Carried through the lowering, the document and observation models, the
hostapd render, the restart comparison, the profile renderer, the client
library and the GUI's access point dialog -- the form gate named the client
as the one reader missing, and the dialog would have deleted the key on Save.

**Measured live** in `make hull-ap-lease`, which gained a second station on
a third hwsim radio: with nothing isolated one station pings the other
through the access point (the control); the edit plans a restart naming
`access_point.isolate_stations`; once both rejoin, the first still reaches
the router and no longer reaches the other station. **Sabotage**: with the
`ap_isolate` line not rendered the stations reach each other again, with
the access point up and both associated, so it is that line that keeps them
apart. Unit tests: lowering (and a non-boolean refused), the hostapd line
only when asked, the round trip, and the restart with a started-with control;
the render and plan sabotages each turn their test red.

## 10.647 `make hull` on 2026-10-31: 17 of 18, and a steer plan that missed once

All eighteen rigs with `make -k hull` against hull b01be07: seventeen pass,
the lossy delegation rig among them. `hull-steer`'s band machine failed once:
the plan taken a minute after the join carried no steer, and the apply a
moment later steered the station to 5 GHz all the same. Three reruns pass.

**Two explanations measured and set aside.** A steer waits for
`connected_time` 60 and skips a station silent past `inactive_msec` 30000
(`plan/wifi.c`). The payload now prints both from hostapd as the plan is
taken, and across the three reruns it read 65 s connected and 1.4 to 6.4 s
silent, nowhere near either bound. The observation is taken fresh for each
plan (`observe/current.c`), so it is not a stale one either.

**One left standing, unproven.** `ncfg_observe_hostapd_stations` stops its
STA-FIRST/STA-NEXT walk at the first request that fails and returns what it
has, so a request that timed out on a loaded host reads as nobody
associated, with no warning -- which fits a plan that was simply empty. The
failed run left no trace that would confirm it.

**So the walk now says when it was cut short**, at the holder's word. It asks
with `ncfg_supplicant_request` rather than `ask`, which folded hostapd's
`FAIL` -- the end of the list -- into the same 0 as no reply at all; a
request with no reply sets `associated_unread` on the observation, and the
planner warns, on any access point that steers, that hostapd *stopped
answering partway through its stations* and how many it did list. The steers
for those are still planned: a short list is not a reason to move nobody.
`ncfg ap stations` refuses a short list rather than printing it, as it
already did for one that would not fit in memory. The fake hostapd in
`c/tests/hostapdfake.h` learned a station walk that can go silent after N,
which is the only way to produce the state; sabotaging either the flag or the
warning turns its check red.

A red `hull-steer` with an empty plan now carries the warning if this was the
cause, and the hostapd line beside it says which bound held the steer if not.

**Found 2026-11-06, and it was the silent bound after all.** `make -k hull` failed
`hull-steer` again, and in five more runs three failed, on either machine. Printing
hostapd's line on the weak machine too read `inactive_msec=30916` at a failed plan and 264
and 312 at passing ones: an idle station says nothing for long stretches, and the three
reruns of 2026-10-31 happened to fall short of 30 s. The rule was right and the rigs had an
idle station, so they now take the plan once hostapd has heard it, waiting up to 45 s; the
image has no ping, which a first fix used and which logged 127 on every call while the
runs it was credited with passed for the wait. The walk's warning stays.

## 10.645 A rig's verdict directory is replaced when another account made it

Both accounts run these rigs, and each `tests/hull/*/verdict` is made by
whichever ran first: on 2026-10-31 `regdom` and `mesh` were the other
account's, 2775 group `users`. The host honours the group bit and a vm's
shared folder does not -- it writes as the running account without its
supplementary groups -- so from the second account every payload failed at its
first write (10.644).

`hull_verdict` in the Makefile now makes each of the fourteen directories:
one this user does not own is removed with `rmdir` and made again. `rmdir`
because it removes only an empty directory, and each target has already
removed its own verdicts by name just before -- so anything still there is
another rig's or another account's, and the target refuses with the owner's
name rather than sweeping it. The parent being group writable is what lets
either account remove the other's empty directory; a sticky bit there would
stop it, and the refusal would say so.

Re-owning the two directories once was the alternative, and it fixes today
and not the next time the other account runs a rig first.

**Measured**: `make hull-regdom` from this account replaced the other's
directory and every machine wrote its verdict, where before none could. Nine
of ten passed; the roam station could not make its first join in 15 s, which
the directory has no part in.

## 10.640 Block lists: the router refuses ad names

Decision 0305, which 0303 had deferred and the holder asked for: a
`block_list` block holds names, from `domain`, from `file`s a list is
published in, with `allow` taking names out; a forwarding `dhcp_server` applies
the lists it names in `block`, which is UniFi's per-network switch with the
list written once. Each blocked name answers NXDOMAIN with everything under
it (`address=/name/`), an allowed one goes back upstream (`server=/name/#`),
and a blocking server answers `use-application-dns.net` NXDOMAIN, which turns
off Firefox's own DNS over HTTPS. All measured against dnsmasq 2.91 on the
host before it was written.

**netcfgd reads the lists; dnsmasq never does.** A list is somebody else's
file, and given to dnsmasq as configuration one `dhcp-script=` line in it runs
as root. `ncfg_block_list_name_of_line` reduces each line -- hosts, bare name,
plain adblock rule, dnsmasq `address=`/`local=`/`server=` -- to one lowercase
name of `[a-z0-9_-]` labels or nothing, and the server's
`<run>/dhcp-server/<iface>.block` is written from those, sorted and once each.
**The schedule is the file's**: the summary digests each file's bytes, so a
refreshed list restarts the server on the next plan and a refresh that
fetched the same bytes does not. A file not there, or past 64 MiB, is left out
with a plan warning, because a LAN with no DNS is worse than one not filtered
yet; a server blocks at most 1,048,576 names (300,000 measured at 0.56 s to
start and about 26 MB in dnsmasq).

**A transparent proxy was asked about and rejected** (0305): HTTPS is
filtered by URL only by decrypting it, a CA on every client; undecrypted, it
sees the server name DNS already blocks. Pi-hole's old block page existed
because its IP-answer mode sent browsers to the router; NXDOMAIN needs none.

**Measured in `make hull-dhcp-server`**: with the file not fetched the plan
warns and restarts the server naming `blocking 1 list`; the client cannot
resolve `ads.example.test` or a name under it, resolves the allowed
`ok.ads.example.test` and an unlisted name through the upstream; the file's
arrival is a planned restart, its hosts and adblock names stop resolving, and
its `dhcp-script=` line is nowhere in what dnsmasq reads. The GUI gains a
block lists tab and a `block` field in the interface dialog, held by
`block_list_load` and `interface_load`. The example gate names the example's
blocking interface as known-incomplete, for `access_point "Family"`'s reason,
and `file` left the renderer's waivers now that a block list writes it.

## 10.636 DHCPv6, and a static prefix nothing can advertise

0303's fourth slice: `dhcp_server { range6 = "::100-::1ff" }`, suffixes that
dnsmasq puts in whatever prefix the interface holds when it starts
(`constructor:`), so the range follows a delegated prefix as it moves. No
`enable-ra`: router advertisements stay radvd's (0009). Refused on an interface
with no IPv6 prefix of its own -- a static global or ULA address, or a
delegated one. The summary names the range, so turning it on is a restart. Two
plan warnings: a range no managed advertisement tells hosts about, and an input
chain dropping UDP 547.

**Measured in `make hull-dhcp-server`.** The image has no radvd, so the client
is told not to wait for an advertisement (`noipv6rs`, `ia_na`,
`tests/hull/dhcp-server/dhcpcd-v6.conf`); it is leased `fd00:7::188` from the
range and offered the router, `fd00:7::1`, as its DNS server, since the
forwarder is on. The rig's lease check, which read `lan0.conf` at the end of
the run, now records its answer at its own stage: later stages rewrite the
file, and this one dropped the lease it looked for.

**Found on the way: `advertise` took delegated prefixes only**, refusing a
ULA or a static global prefix as "never a prefix itself, which no config file
can know". **Closed by 10.637** (decision 0304): `advertise` takes a static /64
now. The warning still says, for a static prefix with no `advertise` block,
that one is what tells the hosts to ask. +40 bytes, as measured.

## 10.632 Every whole-block dialog is checked against what netcfgd compiles

10.631's check, carried to the other dialogs that save a block whole.
`interface_load` and `device_load` now compare `ncfg show`'s entry before and
after each save, refusing a lookup that finds nothing so two absences cannot
pass as equal; `device_load` gains a WireGuard device whose private key is in
the keyring and whose peer's preshared key is in `pass`. A new
`network_load` saves a passphrase network using every network key
(`proto = "wpa3"`, BSSIDs, roam, addressing, routes, dns), a TLS network
whose three certificates sit in three stores, and a PEAP network. All came
back the same: the fault 10.631 found was the access point's alone. Making
the network dialog skip `proto` fails the new probe.

One thing it showed that is not a fault: a network whose `ca_cert` is a
*path* cannot be saved by a client that is not root -- the daemon refuses,
since a path is a file root opens -- and nothing is changed. The probe uses a
stored certificate for that reason.

## 10.631 Saving a WPA3-only access point let WPA2 back in

Derived from 10.628's shape -- a reader that reduces a value the dialog then
rebuilds with a default -- and found by comparing what netcfgd *compiles*
rather than what the reader reports, since a reader cannot report a key it
drops. `access_point_load` now writes an access point using every key the
language has and compares `ncfg show`'s `access_points` before and after a
save through the dialog. One key changed: `proto = "wpa3"` came back
`wpa2_wpa3`. The reader never read `security.proto` and the dialog had no
field for it, so pressing Save on a WPA3-only access point made it accept
WPA2 clients again -- the fault the network dialog had and fixed (its
comment says so), on the access point side never wired.

`form_coverage_gate.py` could not see it and cannot: `security` is a custom
member, so the gate checks the word `security` and nothing inside it. The
compiled comparison is the check that reaches it. The reader takes `proto`
now, the dialog offers it as "generation" and restores it, and the probe
passes; every other key already came back the same.

## 10.628 Saving an access point moved its passphrase to a file

Found while reading the access point reader for the mesh tab. It took the
secret's *name* out of the security block, and the dialog put `@secret:` in
front of it -- which is the file provider. So an access point with
`psk = "@secret:keyring:ap"` (or `pass:`, `exec:`) was rewritten as
`@secret:ap` the first time anybody pressed Save, and then asked for
`/etc/netcfgd/secrets/ap`, which does not exist. Wrong since the dialog was
written (56b37cf9). The reader now returns the reference as the language
spells it, with `reference_text`, which the network and interface dialogs
already used for the same reason (10.611); the dialog shows it as it is.

`gui/tests/access_point_load.cpp` saves a keyring-backed access point
unchanged through a real daemon. With the fix reverted it fails both checks,
reading back `ap`.

## 10.625 A tool in sbin is not missing because a PATH lacks sbin

The shape of 10.624's correction, searched for: a live script asking `command
-v` for a tool that lives in `/sbin` without putting `/sbin` on its PATH. `make
live` adds it, so the suite was never affected; run by hand from an ordinary
user's PATH -- which sessions here do constantly -- such a script reports a
tool missing that is installed. Of four found by a grep, two already searched
`/sbin` themselves (`ap.sh`, `qdisc.sh`) and were left alone; `dhcp.sh`
(dnsmasq) and `switch_network.sh` (dhcpcd, whose metric section was skipped
with a note) now add it, as `port_forward.sh` does. Both run whole by hand from
a PATH with no `/sbin`, the metric section included.

## 10.624 SLAAC on a forwarding interface, against hull's advertiser

**Asked for by the holder 2026-10-30** ("go ahead with the slaac.sh hull
advertiser"), on hull's session's suggestion. `tests/live/slaac.sh` needs
dnsmasq to advertise and skips on a machine without it.

**Corrected the same day: it was never skipping here.** This entry and its
commit (8df73d60) said dnsmasq was absent on this machine and the test had
never run. Both were wrong: dnsmasq is at `/sbin/dnsmasq`, and `which dnsmasq`
had been asked from a PATH without `/sbin` -- an empty search read as an
absence, the trap `slaac.sh`'s own `find_in_sbin` exists to avoid. Run as the
Makefile runs it, `slaac.sh` passes every check here. What the rig below adds
is what remains true: a second advertiser, independent of dnsmasq, that
answers only when solicited -- so the sysctl's place before `link.up` decides
whether an address comes at all -- and netcfgd's first rig on hull's chroot
engine.

`make hull-slaac` (`tests/hull/slaac`) is its twin and **the first netcfgd rig
on hull's chroot engine**: one machine of `(network none)` on a segment of
`(subnet6 "fd42:84::/64") (advertise true)`, its `eth0` the segment's, the
host's build of netcfgd run from the repository mounted read-only. **hull
advertises only when solicited, and a kernel solicits only when it would act on
the answer**, so the wire is proved first at `accept_ra` 2 before anything is
concluded from an address that does not arrive at 1; and the ordering
assertion matters more here than under dnsmasq, since with no unsolicited
advertisement a sysctl written after `link.up` would leave the interface with
none at all rather than a late one. Eleven checks, all passing on the first
run: the wire, the counter-proof, the plan's sysctl with its reason and its
place before `link.up`, the address from the prefix after the apply, a second
plan with nothing to do, the handback to 1, and a value netcfgd never wrote left
alone. `slaac.sh` stays: the two advertisers disagree about unsolicited
advertisements, and each test covers the case the other cannot.

## 10.623 A forward rule may match where a packet leaves

**Asked for by the holder 2026-10-30** ("go ahead with the forward chain
out-interface match"), after the last `/go` run named it as 0294's to widen.
Decided in [0302](doc/decision/0302-a-forward-rule-may-match-where-a-packet-leaves.md):
`out_interface` in the forward chain, encoded as `oifname`, refused in `input`
and `output`. It runs through every layer a firewall rule has -- the model, the
lowering, the digest text (only where set, so no installed rule changes
identity), the encoder, the decoder (`oifname` in `forward` is
`out_interface`, in `output` still `interface`), the kernel rule and the
observation, the comparison and the planner's undo copy, `ncfg status` and the
profile renderer.

`tests/live/firewall.sh` installs `drop "guest-lan" { interface = "guest0";
out_interface = "lan0" }` in a real kernel: nft lists it as `iifname "guest0"
oifname "lan0" drop`, and the probe reads both interfaces back into their own
fields with the digest recomputing. `lower_test` has the refusals in `input` and
`output`; `render_test` the round trip. The example configuration shows a
guest network in its forward chain.

## 10.621 The compiler's fuzzer, seeded with a router, found two leaks

A `/go` run 2026-10-30. `c/fuzz/corpus/config_parse` held five seeds, none of
them a router: no DHCP server, forward, firewall, advertisement or delegation,
so the code this week added was fuzzed only as far as mutation could stumble
into it from a laptop's configuration. `seed-router.conf` now carries all of
it, and five minutes of `make fuzz FUZZ_TARGET=config_parse` found:

- **A second `probe` block leaked the first's command and arguments**: the
  replacement freed the struct and not what it owned. Once per compile, and the
  daemon compiles on every edit to its directory.
- **A route naming `via` (or `src`) twice leaked the first address**, the second
  replacing it unfreed. Refused now rather than only freed -- a route with two
  gateways is a mistake to say, not a choice to make by taking the last -- and
  a repeated `metric` or `table` with it, which overwrote silently the same way.

Both inputs are in the corpus as `regress-*.conf`, replay clean under
LeakSanitizer, and `lower_test` has the refusals and the second probe winning.
Ten more minutes across `config_parse` and `document_json` (1.2 and 0.7 million
runs) found nothing further.
`document_json` had the same gap -- four seeds, none a router -- and has
`seed-router.json` now, the router seed compiled; five minutes from it (4.2
million runs) found nothing.

**10.622, the other three targets, asked for by the holder the same day.**
`observed_json` has a real router observation -- forward, reflection and
hairpin rules, the masquerade and the firewall's chains, read back from a
namespace after `ncfg apply` -- and `socket_message` a `config_put` of a
forward by reservation name, `show`, and the router document as a reply.
**`backend_ipc` gains dnsmasq's lease file**, which no target reached: it is
the most hostile text netcfgd reads on the router side, since the name in each
line is whatever a LAN client sent. The parser is split from its file read
(`ncfg_dhcp_server_lease_in_text`) so the fuzzer can drive it; the seed carries
a client that called itself `$(reboot);evil`, which the plain-name filter must
drop. Four minutes each -- 0.8, 0.4 and 1.7 million runs -- found nothing.

**And an intermittent in `make check`, found while verifying it**: the Rust
`netcfgd-sys` log tests share one process-wide level, and
`every_level_is_reachable_by_name` sets it to each severity in turn while
`the_default_level_...` asserts the default on another thread. It failed once
reading `Warning` -- the third value the other test's loop stores, which is
the trace of the interleaving and nothing else sets it. Both take one lock now.
Thirty runs of the unlocked pair did not reproduce it, which is what an
intermittent does, so the evidence is the value it failed on, not the reruns.

## 10.620 What netcfgd runs, against what its own firewall drops

A `/go` run 2026-10-30, from the lens of the last fix: 10.619 found that a
firewall whose `input` chain drops by default silently starved the DHCP
server, because netcfgd adds no rule of its own (0294) and nothing said so.
The same shape, searched for: every service netcfgd runs that listens for
traffic arriving at the router.

**Four more, now plan warnings naming the rule to write** (`c/src/plan/
firewall_warn.c`), warned and never opened, as 0298 does for a forward:

- **No rule accepting replies at all**: the router's own DNS, DHCP renewals and
  every connection it opens are answered and the answers dropped. Said once.
- **A DHCPv6 client** (UDP 546): the reply comes from the server's link-local
  address to a request sent to a multicast group, so conntrack does not call
  it established, and the lease and any delegated prefix never arrive even
  with replies accepted. OpenWrt carries a rule for exactly this.
- **IPv6 on an interface that uses it** (ICMPv6): neighbour discovery and
  router advertisements are never established, so SLAAC, an RA server's
  solicitations and the link's IPv6 itself stop.
- **A WireGuard device with a `listen_port`** (that UDP port, on any
  interface): a peer that starts the handshake is never answered.
- **And one chain over, a masquerade whose `forward` chain drops replies**:
  every connection the LAN opens is answered and the answer dropped, which
  reads as a dead uplink. Warned where an interface has `nat` and nothing in
  `forward` accepts established traffic.

**And a fault in 10.619's own test of the same thing**, found writing these: it
counted any accept rule with no protocol and no port, so `accept "established"
{ state = ["established"] }` -- the most common rule there is -- silenced the
DHCP server's warning while letting no request in. A rule limited to states
now counts only for the states it names. `plan_input_test` covers each warning,
that the rule it names silences it, and that regression; with the state check
taken out, 4 of its 10 checks fail.

## 10.619 The LAN is answered by a DNS forwarder

**Asked for by the holder 2026-10-30** ("go ahead with the LAN DNS
forwarder"), the question two `/go` runs had parked. Decided in
[0301](doc/decision/0301-the-lan-is-answered-by-a-dns-forwarder.md), which
adds a row to 0009's table: `dhcp_server { dns_forward = true }` makes the
interface's dnsmasq answer DNS there too, forwarding to `/etc/resolv.conf` --
the router's own resolution, so there is no second upstream list to drift --
and, with no `dns`, offering the router to the hosts. A host's lease name
resolves on the LAN.

**Measured before it was written, in the rig's image (dnsmasq 2.91)**:
`interface=lan0` alone also binds `127.0.0.1:53` and `[::1]:53`, and failed
outright beside a resolver already on loopback; `listen-address` does not stop
it; `except-interface=lo` does, and two LAN instances ran beside a loopback
resolver with it. So the forwarder writes `port=53`, `except-interface=lo`,
`domain-needed` and `bogus-priv` where the DHCP-only server writes `port=0`.
The summary line says `dns this router, forwarding dns`, so turning it on is a
restart and a server without it keeps the line it had.

**And a gap 0297 left, closed with it**: a firewall whose `input` chain drops
by default, with no rule accepting UDP 67 on the interface, silently starved
the DHCP server. Both that and the forwarder's UDP 53 are now plan warnings
naming the rule to write, as 0298 does for a forward. A rule narrowed by
source still counts; one on another interface does not.

`make hull-dhcp-server` carries it end to end: an upstream dnsmasq on
`127.0.0.2` answering `example.test`, the router's resolv.conf naming it,
`dns_forward` turned on (planned as a restart), port 53 bound on
`192.168.7.1` and lan0's link-local address and not on loopback, the client
offered `dns=192.168.7.1`, and through it resolving `example.test` to
10.9.9.9 and the reservation `desk` to 192.168.7.50. Units: the dnsmasq lines
and summary, the plan's silence on DNS when forwarding and its two firewall
warnings with their rules, the lowering, and a profile round trip. The GUI's
interface dialog has an "answer DNS for this network" box, which the form gate
required before the client read it.

## 10.618 A forward may name a reservation

**Asked for by the holder 2026-10-30** ("go ahead with the port forward
reservation names"), the item 0298 deferred as wanted. Decided in
[0300](doc/decision/0300-a-forward-may-name-a-reservation.md): `to` is an IPv4
address or the name of a `dhcp_server` reservation on any interface, resolved
by the compiler after every interface is read; none or two matches are
refused. The document keeps the address in `to` and the name in `to_host`, so
every rule is unchanged and the renderer, the client and the interface dialog
write the name back.

**A fault of this change's own, caught by trying it before testing it**: the
pass that remembers an interface with a named forward reused `i`, the index of
the loop over blocks it sits in, so `ncfg show` spun at full CPU forever on any
configuration with one. The first compile by hand hung and `timeout` killed it;
the loop has its own index now. Worth knowing as a shape: `lower.c`'s loop
body is long enough that its index is out of sight.

Tests: `lower_test` resolves a name across interfaces and refuses an unknown
one, one reserved twice, and an address-shaped one; `render_test` round-trips a
forward by name and checks the name, not the address, is written;
`interface_load`'s forward names its reservation and Save writes `to = "tv"`.
The form gate caught `to_host` before the client read it.

## 10.617 The form gate reads every sub-block, and found the probe's counts

A `/go` run 2026-10-30, from the lens of 10.613 and 10.615: each silent drop
on Save had been a member the reader never mentioned, inside a sub-block the
gate did not read. **`tool/form_coverage_gate.py` now holds every sub-block
the four dialogs read field by field** -- routes, DNS, 802.1X, `advertise`,
the DHCP server and its reservations, port forwards, guard, probe, roam,
access control, neighbours and steering: 155 members of 4 blocks and 18
sub-blocks. It reads every model file, since some tables live beside their
types, and its function finder now skips a prototype, which would otherwise
have checked a helper with a forward declaration against whatever function
followed it. A copy of the client with route `src` removed fails it by name.

**It found one more, in the probe**: `down_after`, `up_after`, `hold_down` and
`require_lease`, which the language has had all along, were dropped by an
interface's Save -- a probe tuned not to flap went back to the defaults. The
client reads them (the parser's 3, 2, 0 and on where none is stated), the
dialog has a field for each and writes only what differs, and
`live_interface_dialog` sets all four and finds them in the file and in the
daemon's reading. In the live test rather than `interface_load`: a probe is a
program netcfgd runs as root, and the daemon takes one only from root.

**The same lens on the other writers found nothing.** `ncfg wifi add` refuses
to overwrite a network or a credential, the radio switch replaces only its own
drop-in, and the TUI writes no configuration. The profile renderer mentions
every member added since its audit (port forwards, hairpin, reservations,
`wds`, the probe's counts).

## 10.616 A network's hooks are edited, as an interface's are

The last refusal a configuration file could reach, and it rested on a claim
that had stopped being true: that the GUI had no way to read a network's
hooks. `hook_scripts` has named the network a hook belongs to since 10.34;
the Qt row simply dropped the field, so nothing could match on it.

- **One hooks editor**, `ncfg_hooks_editor` in `hook_dialog.h`, moved out of
  the interface dialog and used by the network dialog too -- the same move
  10.615 made for addressing and routes. It loads one block's hooks, the
  interface's or the network's, refuses where a body was withheld or the
  count disagrees, and writes each back verbatim.
- **The client counts a network's hooks** (`hook_count`) rather than naming
  them; the scripts are checked against that count, as an interface's are.
- `live_network_dialog` writes a network with a `post_up` hook, opens it, saves
  it with a changed metric, and reads the script back byte for byte.

**After 10.615 and this, nothing a configuration file can say is refused by a
dialog.** What is still named -- a device's `match`, an `advertise` exec
backend, a DNS server's port, a route's scope and the rest 10.615 lists -- has
no spelling in the language, so it can only arrive in a document netcfgd did
not compile, and the refusal is there for that.

## 10.615 Addressing and routes carry everything the language writes

**Asked for by the holder 2026-10-30** ("go ahead with the remaining dialog
refusals"). Measured first: which refusals a configuration file can reach at
all, by compiling each key the reader named. That found worse than refusals.

**Three silent drops on an interface's Save**, the class `wds` was in 10.613.
The client read each addressing entry's head and nothing after it, and the
dialog wrote the head back, so a static address's `preferred_lft` and
`valid_lft`, a `dhcp6` prefix delegation request (`pd`, `pd_hint`,
`pd_length` -- what a router's uplink asks for) and SLAAC's `privacy` were
deleted by pressing Save. **And the delegated-address refusal never fired**:
it looked for a member called `from`, and the document's delegated entry has
`prefix` and `suffix`.

- **Each entry carries its options**, the language's own words after the head
  (`peer 10.0.0.2 preferred_lft 600`, `pd pd_length 56`, `privacy
  prefer_temporary`), and a delegated entry its `@pd:wan0/1=::1/64`. A
  `dhcp6` mode, rapid commit, any `dhcp4` option and a delegation's index have
  no spelling in the language, so they are named rather than written.
- **One addressing list and one route table**, `gui/src/address_editors.h`,
  used by the interface and network dialogs. The network dialog had one
  addressing choice and refused a network addressed twice; it has the list
  now, and the two cannot drift because there is one copy.
- **A route's `src`, `table` and `onlink` are columns** in both. `scope` and
  `proto` have no word in a route line and stay named.
- **An exclusive routing domain reads back as `~suffix`**, the language's
  spelling, rather than being refused.

**What is still named, and why nothing compiled can reach it**: an `advertise`
exec backend and a prefix's delegation index, a DNS server's port or SNI,
resolver options, DNSSEC and transport, a route's scope or protocol, and a
neighbour's `signal` or `band` (a `neighbour` takes `channel` alone; the
`signal` and `band` keys are `steering`'s, which 10.607 carries). Each refusal
guards a document from elsewhere, as `match` does on a device. A network's
`hooks` were the one a configuration could still reach, and 10.616 took them.

`interface_load`'s refusal case is now this round trip: an interface carrying
each of the above is opened, saved, and found in the file and in the daemon's
reading. It found its own fault on the first run -- its "it is saved" check
matched the note's wording, so a permission refusal read as a save; it asks the
dialog's outcome now. `live_interface_dialog`'s layout check walks up through
the shared editor, requiring each step to be in its parent's layout, so an
orphan inside it still fails.

## 10.614 The `live_wifi` intermittent was the fake supplicant's `-B`

**Asked for by the holder 2026-10-30** ("go ahead with the live_wifi flake").
Recorded three times and never explained (10.604, and two entries under
10.6x): `live_wifi` failing *"activating scans straight away, so the table is
already filled"* and *"and pressing scan again refills it"*, with 0 rows and
then 6, during sabotage runs and other loaded moments, and passing otherwise.

**The cause is in the harness, and netcfgd's assumption is right.** A real
`wpa_supplicant -B` forks only once its control interface is up, and netcfgd
relies on it: `start_supplicant` gives the new supplicant its networks over
the socket the moment the start returns. `tests/live/fake_supplicant.py`
returned from the parent straight after the fork -- under a comment saying it
must not -- and bound its socket in the child a moment later. On a loaded
machine the child lost that race, the start failed at the socket,
`set_radio` answered with the failure, and the view's `activate()` showed it
and never scanned: 0 rows. The supplicant came up anyway, so the next scan
found all six.

**Measured, both ways.** The child delayed by a second before binding: those
two checks fail with those two numbers. The parent made to wait for the
child's word that it has bound, with the same one-second delay: `gui_wifi.sh`
14 of 14. The wait is a pipe the child writes after `bind`, bounded at ten
seconds, so a child that dies before binding fails the start rather than
hanging it. Every live script that starts the fake was rerun against it.

**Two lenses were wrong, and are worth naming.** 10.6x's negative sweep looked
for a scan that does not fill the table, and the fault was the activation
before it; and "nothing in `secrets_view` can reach the wifi scan" was true and
beside the point, because what the sabotage run supplied was load.

## 10.613 The device dialog carries a bridge port, and stops dropping wds

**Asked for by the holder 2026-10-30** ("go ahead with the device dialog"),
the dialog 10.612 left: it refused `master`, `access_control`, `match`,
`bridge_vlans`, an `ifb` and a rate finer than a kbit.

- **A port of a bridge or bond** is a group of its own: what it joins
  (`master`) and a VLAN table -- an id or a range, pvid, untagged -- written
  as the language writes `vlans`. The document holds one entry per id, so the
  connection joins consecutive ids with the same flags back into the range
  that was written. A cell is checked before Save as an id or a range, and a
  range is refused as a pvid, as the compiler refuses it.
- **A port its bridge lists could not be edited at all.** The compiler turns a
  bridge's `members` into `master` on each member (lower.c), so a cable in a
  bridge read back with a `master` nobody wrote in its block, and the refusal
  fired on it: its MTU could not be changed from the window. The client now
  says whether the master's own `members` names the device
  (`master_by_members`); the dialog shows it read-only and does not write it,
  so the membership is not stated twice.
- **`wds` was dropped by Save, silently.** Nothing read a device's
  `wifi { wds }`, and `tool/form_coverage_gate.py` checked a block's own
  members, not a sub-block's -- the blind spot it named. It reads now and has a
  checkbox, and the gate holds the device's `wifi`, `modem`, `ethtool`,
  `qdisc` and port VLAN tables to the same rule (`NESTED`). Two qdisc members
  are waived: the arriving rate is moved onto the synthesised `ifb` and
  cleared from the device, and `ingress` is set only on that `ifb`. A copy of
  the client with `"wds"` removed fails the gate, naming it.
- **Rates are carried exactly**, in bits, rather than in kbit with a finer
  rate refused. The field still shows kbit (the nearest, and at least 1);
  while it shows what was loaded, Save writes the loaded rate back exactly,
  as `1234567bit` where it is not a whole kbit.
- `access_control` was never a device member -- it is an access point's -- so
  naming it guarded nothing and it is gone. **What is still refused**: a
  `match` block, which the language cannot write either, and the `ifb`, which
  netcfgd synthesises. The form scrolls, as the other three do.

`gui/tests/device_load.cpp` is new, an `interface_load` for devices: a daemon
over hand-written drop-ins for a port with VLANs, a port by its bridge's list,
a radio with `wds` and a rate in bits; each is opened, saved and read back
through the daemon, and the files are checked for what the dialog wrote.

## 10.612 The dialogs carry what they used to refuse

**Asked for by the holder 2026-10-30** ("go ahead with the other dialogs"),
after 10.611: each dialog still refused to save a block carrying a key it had
no field for (10.606). Taken one dialog at a time.

**The interface dialog** gained, beside forwarding and NAT and the DHCP
server: a reservations table (name, MAC, address) inside the server, a port
forwards table (name, protocol, port, host, host port, hairpin), an
`advertise` group (prefixes as written, `@pd:wan0/1`; backend; managed;
other config; DNS; lifetime), an IPv6 token and a guard's reason. Each left
the client's unmodelled list; what of `advertise` has no field -- an `exec`
backend, a prefix naming which of several delegations it is -- is still
named and refused. A table cell is text written into the block, so each is
checked as the word or number it must be before Save (a name, MAC or host has
no quote, brace, semicolon, `=` or space; a port is 1 to 65535; hairpin is
blank, `yes` or `no`) and the compiler checks the rest. **The form now
scrolls**: it had grown taller than a laptop's screen, and the probe
detection's row hiding, which found the form as the dialog's first layout
item, holds it as a member instead -- the scroll area is that item now.

`interface_load` saves an interface carrying all of it and finds each in the
file the dialog wrote. `gui_wifi.sh` 14 of 14.

**Then wired 802.1X**, the last interface key the client refused: an
"authenticate this port" group with the same keys a network's `wifi` block
takes (10.611) and the password as its reference -- blank writes
`@secret:dot1x-<interface>` -- with a field to store a new one under that
name, refused for the keyring as in the network dialog. The interface
reader's unmodelled list of keys is empty now; what it still names is the
inside of a key -- an `advertise` with an `exec` backend, a route with a
`src`, a peer or delegated addressing source. `interface_load`'s refusal case
is a route with a `src` now, after `ipv6_token`, a reservation and `dot1x`.

**Then the network dialog**: pinned access points (`bssid`, space-separated),
roaming (on, the threshold and the two intervals, written inside `wifi` where
the language reads it), a routes table, and a resolver scope (mode, servers,
search, routing domains). Routes and DNS were already read and simply had no
field; they read with the unmodelled sink now, as an interface's do, so a
route with a `src` is still named. **Two things stay refused**: addressing
beyond the dialog's one DHCP choice, and a network's `hooks`, which have no
read path in the GUI -- the hook requests serve an interface's. The form
scrolls, as the interface dialog's does, and holds its form as a member for
the same reason. `gui_wifi.sh`: a network pinned to two access points,
roaming, with a route and a DNS scope opens on them and keeps every value
through a Save; one addressed twice is refused with its file as it was.

**Then the access point dialog**: fast roaming with its mobility domain and
the key's reference as written, and a neighbours table (BSSID, channel). With
10.607's width, reports, steering and wds that is every member of an access
point; the only refusal left is inside a neighbour -- a `signal` or `band`
the language's `neighbour` block has no key for. The form scrolls. A
neighbour's cells are checked before Save. `gui_wifi.sh`: an access point
with fast roaming, a domain, a key and a neighbour opens on them and keeps
them through a Save that changed its channel.

**What is still refused, after all three**: on an interface, an `advertise`
with an `exec` backend or a prefix naming its delegation, a route with a
`src`, and a peer or delegated addressing source; on a network, addressing
beyond one DHCP source, and its `hooks`, which the GUI has no way to read;
and the device dialog's own list, which 10.613 took up.

## 10.611 The network dialog edits enterprise networks

**Asked for by the holder 2026-10-30** ("go ahead with the enterprise network
dialog"), the first of the items the holder ranked under "making everything
work": since 10.606 the GUI refused to save any 802.1X network -- eduroam
included -- because the client did not carry its identity or certificates,
and before 10.606 it saved them away.

- **The client carries the 802.1X block**: method, identity, anonymous
  identity, phase 2, `domain_suffix_match`, and `ca_cert`, `client_cert` and
  `private_key` as the language writes them -- a path, or an `@secret:`
  reference for a stored one. `eap` left the unmodelled list.
- **And the credential's reference as written**, `credential_reference`:
  `@secret:NAME`, or `@secret:keyring:NAME` and the other providers, the
  renderer's spelling. **This was a second fault, in PSK networks too**: the
  dialog wrote `psk = "@secret:<id>"` whatever the document said, so Save
  repointed a passphrase kept under another name or in the keyring, and the
  network stopped joining at the next apply. The bare `credential` name could
  not have said which store it was in.
- **The dialog** opens on every one of those, gains a server-name field
  (0206's reason: `ca_cert` alone accepts any certificate a public CA signed)
  and a private-key field for TLS, and writes each reference back as it was
  while the network keeps the same kind of credential; a new network, or one
  changing kind, gets `@secret:<id>` as before. **A new passphrase goes into
  the store the reference names, under its name**; for one in the keyring or
  `pass`, which netcfgd reads and does not write, Save refuses and says to
  change it there.
- `client_test` reads an enterprise network with a CA path, a stored client
  certificate and key and a password named apart from the network, and a
  keyring passphrase, each as written. `gui_wifi.sh`, all 14 probes: a PEAP
  network written by hand opens on its identity, CA and server name, and a
  changed metric saves with all of it and the password still `@secret:
  uni-login`; a keyring network keeps its reference through Save, and a new
  passphrase for it is refused.

## 10.610 Hairpin: a forward reachable from inside

**Asked for by the holder 2026-10-30** ("go ahead with hairpin NAT"). Decision
[0299](doc/decision/0299-a-forward-is-reachable-from-inside-by-default.md):
every forward is reflected unless it says `hairpin = false`, OpenWrt's
default.

- **Reflection**, in `prerouting`, `name=IF/NAME@reflect`: nft's `iifname !=
  "wan0" ip daddr U tcp dport 443 dnat ip to A:Q`, measured. One per IPv4
  address the uplink has -- the document's static ones and the observed ones,
  deduplicated -- so a DHCP uplink is reflected at its lease and the table is
  replaced when the lease's address moves. `fib daddr type local` was
  rejected: it would capture the router's own LAN address too.
- **Return path**, in `postrouting`, `name=IF/NAME@hairpin`: `oifname "lan0"
  ip saddr NET ip daddr A tcp dport Q masquerade`, from the interface whose
  static IPv4 network holds the host. None, and a plan warning, where no
  interface holds it. Addresses are matched as the firewall matches them --
  four bytes, masked where the prefix is short -- not nft's three-byte load
  for a /24; the kernel takes both. `postrouting` now exists where an uplink
  is masqueraded or a return path written.
- **One decoder for the three roles**: it walks the expressions recording
  what each comparison matched and then holds the result to the shape its
  role is written with. The return path carries only the host's port, so its
  `port` is the host's on both sides. The planner compares the rule sets
  sorted, since the kernel's order is per chain. A forward's own digest has no
  role line, so a forward installed by 10.609 reads back as itself.
- A forward's label is letters, digits, `-`, `_` and `.`, so `/` and `@`
  cannot be in the identity. Scope number `port_forward.hairpin` 0x0002002c.
- **Live, `tests/live/port_forward.sh`**: the lan side is a bridge with the
  server and a second host on it. The rule set lists as nft writes it; a
  second plan is empty; the lan host dialling 203.0.113.1:443 is answered
  "through, from 192.168.1.1" -- the router, as the return path costs -- and
  with `hairpin = false` the same connection is refused, the control. The
  wan-side cases from 10.609 pass beside it.
- `make check` green; `nat.sh` and `firewall.sh` pass under `NCFG_LIVE=1`.
  ~~The size gate has about 4 KB left~~ -- **re-derived on the holder's
  instruction 2026-10-30** to 1,339,300, each commit since the wireless day
  built from `git archive` and attributed in `size-budget.txt` (the DHCP
  server +13,216, port forwards +13,072, hairpin +4,296, reservations
  +4,264, the rest under 200). The ceiling is 1,379,479 with the 3%
  tolerance. Stripped, the binary is 1,203,632 bytes, so 0024's 1 MB verdict
  stands for the C too, by about 200 KB.
- **The holder's direction on size, 2026-10-30**: "We will have build options
  to remove unnecessary parts and we can optimize later by removing
  superfluous parts." So the ratchet is what keeps growth visible and
  attributed, not a reason to hold back a feature: when a feature crosses the
  ceiling, re-derive the budget as above and say what bought it. Fitting a
  small box is the build options' job (compiling out what that box does not
  use), and trimming is later work -- neither is a cost to charge each feature
  as it lands.
- **And the holder's priority, the same day**, on asking for build options
  and then stopping them before any code: "let's work on making everything
  work before lower priority work like this". Build options and size work
  wait; what comes first is that every feature netcfgd has works end to end.
  The measurement taken for the options is kept here so it is not retaken:
  by object file, wifi is the largest separable part but reaches every layer;
  the nftables half (NAT, firewall, forwards) is about 60 KB in five files
  behind one op and one planner call; the TUI is about 20 KB behind
  `ncfg_tui_run`. An optioned build would run the suite minus the test files
  whose subject is the feature, plus a test of the refusals.

## 10.609 Port forwards

**Asked for by the holder 2026-10-30** ("go ahead with port forwards"). Decision
[0298](doc/decision/0298-a-port-forward-is-translation-on-the-uplink.md)
amends 0294, which had left nat redirection out of layer one.

```
interface wan0 {
	nat = true
	forwarding = true
	port_forward "web" { protocol = "tcp"; port = 443; to = "192.168.1.10"; to_port = 8443 }
}
```

- **On the interface, not in `firewall`**: translation is addressing (0022's
  own test), and a forward is the inverse of the masquerade the uplink
  already carries. Labelled; `protocol` tcp or udp; one `port`; `to` one
  IPv4 host; `to_port` defaults to `port`. Two of one name, or one protocol
  and port, on an interface are refused. Scope numbers 0x00020028-2b.
- **A fourth chain in netcfgd's table, `prerouting`**, type `nat` at
  `dstnat`, written only where a forward exists. Each forward is the
  expressions nft 1.1.3 writes for `iifname "wan0" tcp dport 443 dnat ip to
  192.168.1.10:8443`, measured with `--debug=netlink` -- no `nfproto` guard,
  the port always loaded into register 2 and `flags 0x2` -- with 0295's
  comment, `name=wan0/web sha256=...`. Same transaction as NAT and the
  firewall (`ncfg_nft_build_replace_all`); the audit admits the one new chain
  name.
- **Read back** by `ncfg_nft_forward_read`, which takes only the shape the
  builder writes and accepts the range maximum the kernel echoes; the
  observation gains `port_forwards` and `port_forwards_unread`, both omitted
  when empty. The planner compares them in order and plans `nftables.replace`
  under `port_forwards` where they differ, with a reason in words (`wan0/web
  tcp 443 -> 192.168.1.10:8443`) and the installed forwards as the inverse.
- **Two warnings, no hidden rules**: a forward on an interface without
  `forwarding = true` (IPv4 forwards by the arriving interface's setting),
  and a `forward { policy = "drop" }` with no accept rule naming the host --
  the warning writes out the rule. OpenWrt's implicit `ct status dnat accept`
  was rejected, 0298 says why.
- `ncfg status` lists each forward under its link; the GUI's interface dialog
  refuses to save over forwards (the client names them unmodelled), which
  `form_coverage_gate.py` caught before the client did -- its first catch.
- **Live, `tests/live/port_forward.sh` under `unshare -rn`, in `make live`**:
  wan and lan namespaces on veth pairs; `ncfg apply`; `nft list ruleset`
  shows the chain and the rule as nft writes it; a second plan is empty; a
  connection from 203.0.113.2 to the router's 443 reaches the lan server
  ("through, from 203.0.113.2"); a hand-added prerouting rule is replaced;
  no forward leaves no chain; and the control -- the same connection with
  the forward gone -- is refused.

`make check` green, and `nat.sh`, `firewall.sh` and `port_forward.sh` pass under
`NCFG_LIVE=1`. The installed binary read 1,335,000 bytes against 1,304,300,
inside the 3% tolerance -- since re-derived, 10.610.

Not done, and in 0298: `to` naming a reservation, a port range, and a
forward table in the GUI. ~~Hairpin NAT~~ -- 10.610.

## 10.608 The interface dialog serves DHCP

A `/go` run 2026-10-30. 10.606 put `dhcp_server` on the interface dialog's
refusal list, which was correct and left a router's LAN interface
uneditable in the GUI at all. It is a field now, beside forwarding and NAT:
a box to serve DHCP, the range (empty for the 100th to the 249th host), the
lease (0 for 12 hours) and the DNS servers to offer (empty offers none, as
0297 says). Reservations have no table here, and an interface whose server
reserves hosts is still refused, naming `dhcp_server (its reservations)`.

The client reads the range back as the language writes it, `A-B`, from the
document's `range_start` and `range_end`, so the field round-trips.

**And `interface_load`'s "saveable" check never saved.** Its fixture opened
`admin` to `root` only, so Save was refused for permission and the check --
that the note did not say "would delete" -- passed on the refusal. With
`admin` open it then failed for a second reason: the fixture declared `eth0`
in `netcfgd.conf`, and the dialog's `interface-eth0` drop-in is a duplicate
the loader refuses. The fixture's interface lives in that drop-in now, which
is where an interface the dialog edits lives, and the probe checks the file
it wrote -- by its header, since the hand-written file already said all
three DHCP values -- and that the daemon reads the server back.

- `interface_load`: the server, range, lease and DNS are loaded; Save writes
  the dialog's own file with all three and the daemon compiles it; a server
  with a reservation is refused naming the reservations.
- `gui_wifi.sh`: all 14 probes pass.

## 10.607 The access point dialog carries width, reports, steering and wds

A `/go` run 2026-10-30, the end state 10.606 named: refusing made the
dialog safe, and carrying what it can is what makes it useful. The four
members 10.593-10.600 added that are a word or a number are fields now -- a
width list (the channel's own, 20, 40, 80 and 160 MHz, the last two marked
5 GHz), a neighbour reports box, a steering signal in dBm with "not by
signal" at 0 and a 2.4-to-5 GHz box, and wds. Steering's two controls are
disabled while neighbour reports are off, because the compiler refuses
steering without them and a disabled control writes nothing.

The client reads `width`, `neighbour_reports`, `wds` and `steering` into
fields on `ncfg_access_point_config_t`, and they left its `unmodelled` list;
fast roaming with its domain and key, and `neighbour` blocks, stay on it --
the key is a secret, and a neighbour list is a table this dialog does not
have.

- `access_point_block`: each is written only where it says something, and
  steering as `steering { signal = -75; band = true }`.
- `gui_wifi.sh`, 14 probes: an access point written by hand with `width =
  20`, reports and `steering { signal = -75 }` opens on both and keeps both
  through Save; one with a `neighbour` block is refused, naming it, and keeps

## 10.606 The wifi dialogs deleted what they could not show

Found by a `/go` run 2026-10-29, deriving the lens from 10.605 -- a feature
added to the model that a consumer had to be told about -- and asking which
consumers of an interface, a network and an access point list the members
they handle. **Two GUI dialogs saved a whole block with `replace` from the
fields they have**, and nothing stopped them:

- **The network dialog** wrote id, security, ssid, hidden, metric,
  autoconnect, metered and one `config` word. It did not *load* addressing or
  metered at all, so opening any network and pressing Save reset both; and it
  had no field for a pinned `bssid`, `roam`, `hooks`, routes, DNS, addressing
  beyond one DHCP source, or an enterprise network's identity and
  certificates, which the client does not even carry. Each of those was
  deleted by Save. The client's own comment said whatever read a saved
  network "composes a whole block or refuses to"; the GUI did neither.
- **The access point dialog** had no field for anything 10.593-10.600 added:
  `fast_roaming`, `mobility_domain`, `wds`, `roaming_key`,
  `neighbour_reports`, `neighbour` blocks, `steering`, `width`.
- **The interface dialog** already refused through `unmodelled` (since
  `1c78ae98`, which measured the same deletion on an interface), but its list had not gained `dhcp_server`, so it would
  have deleted a DHCP server the same way. Checked by comparing every
  interface member the document declares against what the client reads:
  `dhcp_server` was the only one missing.

**Fixed by the interface dialog's rule, extended**: the client names what
each dialog cannot carry in an `unmodelled` sentence on `ncfg_saved_network_t`
and `ncfg_access_point_config_t`; both dialogs refuse Save while editing one
that has any, naming them and pointing at `ncfg config edit`; the network
dialog now opens on its addressing and metered; `dhcp_server` joined the
interface list. Carrying the fields rather than refusing is the better end
state: 10.607 did it for the access point's simple fields, 10.608 for the
interface's DHCP server and 10.611 for an enterprise network; the rest is
still refused.

- `client_test`: a network with a pinned BSSID and a route names `bssid,
  routes`, one with a single DHCPv6 source names nothing; an access point
  with steering and width names `steering, width`.
- `gui_wifi.sh` (all 14 probes pass, under `unshare -rn`): an access point
  written by hand with `width = 20` is named, Save is refused saying `width`,
  and the width is still there; a metered DHCP network opens on both and
  keeps both through Save; a network pinned to a BSSID is named, Save is
  refused, and its file is byte for byte as it was.
- **Three GUI probes ran the Rust daemon.** `interface_load`, `access_policy`
  and `reconnect` start a real daemon by a compiled-in path, and it was
  `target/debug/netcfgd` -- built only because `make check`'s cargo step
  builds it, and not what ships (0266). Found when `interface_load` failed on
  a `dhcp_server` the Rust compiler has never heard of. They name `c/netcfgd`
  now, and `make gui` builds the C first.
- **And qmake does not rebuild on a changed `DEFINES`.** After the path
  changed, the probes' existing objects still carried the old one -- `strings`
  on the binaries showed `target/debug/netcfgd` -- and `interface_load` kept
  failing for a reason no longer in the tree until its `.cpp` was edited. The
  two others were rebuilt by removing their objects. A tree with an older
  build of `access_policy` or `reconnect` will run them against whatever is
  at the old path until those objects are rebuilt; a fresh build is right.
- **`tool/form_coverage_gate.py`, in `make check`, so the next member is not
  missed.** It holds each saved block's members -- device, interface, network,
  access point, from their `ncfg_field_t` tables -- to a string literal in
  the client reader its dialog loads through, or a reason in
  `tool/form-unread-keys.txt` (`declared`, provenance; an interface's `hooks`,
  which its dialog carries itself). Run against the client from before this
  fix it reports all twelve deletions above; with `width` taken out of the
  access point list it goes red. It sees top-level members only, and a
  member read is not a member written back -- the network's routes and DNS
  were read and still dropped by a dialog with no field for them.
- **The first run had two failures in `live_wifi`** (the table empty right
  after activation, six rows after a second scan). The two networks this
  test wrote are removed at the end of their cases now, but they were not the
  cause: the fake supplicant's `-B` returned before its socket was bound
  (10.614).

## 10.605 Reservations: a fixed address for a named host

A `/go` run 2026-10-29: after the range itself, the setting a router is most
often asked for -- the printer, the NAS, the host a port would be forwarded
to -- and an additive key under 0297's policy block, with no new daemon and
no new grammar shape.

```
dhcp_server {
	dns = ["192.168.1.1"]
	host "printer" { mac = "AA:BB:CC:DD:EE:01"; address = "192.168.1.10" }
}
```

- **Labelled, as an access point or a firewall rule is**: the label is the
  reservation's identity and the name dnsmasq gives the host. A set, sorted
  by name; the MAC uppercased as every hardware address in the document is,
  so two spellings of one MAC are one reservation.
- **Checked where the range is**, in `ncfg_dhcp_server_range`, so the
  compiler, the profile renderer, dnsmasq's file and the planner refuse a bad
  one alike: not a plain host name (10.602's rule, now the model's
  `ncfg_dhcp_server_plain_name`, shared with the lease reader), not a MAC,
  outside the network, the router's own address, or two sharing a name, MAC
  or address. **An address inside the range is allowed**: dnsmasq never
  gives it to anybody else.
- **dnsmasq gets `dhcp-host=MAC,address,name`.** The `# serves:` line gains
  `, N host(s) <digest>` -- a count for the operator reading the plan and an
  FNV-1a digest of every reservation so that any edit is a difference, since
  the line is bounded and a long list could not fit in it. Absent with no
  reservations, so a running server with none is not restarted by the
  upgrade. A changed reservation is a restart, as every other change is.
- **Scope numbers** `dhcp_server.host.mac` 0x00020026 and
  `dhcp_server.host.address` 0x00020027, the interface's as the range is.
- **Live, `make hull-dhcp-server`**: a client holding .201 from the range is
  given a reservation at .50; the plan reads `... dns 192.168.7.53, 1 host
  9860f143 (was ... dns 192.168.7.53)`, the file carries
  `dhcp-host=86:15:93:2A:9B:62,192.168.7.50,desk`, and the client asking
  again is moved to .50.

`make check` green; the installed binary read 1,321,928 bytes against the
1,304,300 budget, inside its 3% tolerance, so the budget was left alone. The
registry gate's control had used `address` as "another block's key", and an
interface has one now; it moved to `lookup`, a routing rule's, and the gate's
comment says why.

Not done: a reservation by client identifier rather than MAC, and a reload
by `SIGHUP` through `dhcp-hostsfile` instead of a restart -- leases survive a
restart, so the gain is a second's outage, not worth a second mechanism yet.

## 10.604 Associated, leased and named, over the air

A `/go` run 2026-10-29. 10.601 served a veth and the access-point rigs
associated stations that asked for no address, so the path a router exists
for -- a phone joins, is given an address, and is listed by name -- had been
run only in halves. **No image held hostapd and dnsmasq together**; the hwsim
image does now (`hostapd` added to its build step and its tool check), and
`make hull-ap-lease` runs it.

- **One vm, two hwsim radios.** netcfgd runs the access point and a
  `dhcp_server` on wlan0; wlan1's phy is moved into a namespace (`iw phy ...
  set netns`), so the station's address is not also an address of the access
  point's stack, where the server's replies would be delivered locally and
  prove nothing about the air.
- **Measured, VERDICT ok**: the first plan starts the access point, adds the
  address, starts the DHCP server; the station joins in 3 s; dhcpcd is given
  192.168.4.211 (inside the default .100--.249), router 192.168.4.1, the DNS
  server named and the 12 h lease; `ncfg wifi clients wlan0` lists
  `02:00:00:00:01:00  phone  192.168.4.211` through the daemon's socket, and
  `--json` carries `"hostname":"phone"` and the address; a second plan has
  nothing to do.
- **The first run's red was the payload's own** -- a backend called
  `hostapd` where the plan says `access_point`, a hook copied without its
  execute bit, a JSON match with a space the compact form does not have --
  and netcfgd's output in that run already showed the station named. Each
  assertion was therefore seen red before it was seen green.
- `hull-hwsim` and `hull-dhcp-server` pass on the rebuilt image. **An image
  built before this has no hostapd**; the payload says so in its verdict,
  and `make hull-image` rebuilds it.

## 10.603 A stations tab in the GUI

**Asked for by the holder 2026-10-29** ("go ahead with a station view in the
GUI"): the CLI (`ncfg wifi clients`) and the TUI could say who was on an
access point netcfgd runs, and the GUI, which can configure one, could not.

- **The client library gains `ncfg_client_ap_stations`** and
  `ncfg_stations_t`/`ncfg_station_t`, decoding every field the socket's
  `ap_stations` reply carries; a number hostapd did not report is a `has_`
  flag cleared, never a zero. Tested against the socket witness's own
  `ap_stations` line, and driven by the reply fuzzer as reader 21.
- **One `stations` tab, straight after `wifi`**, listing every running
  access point's stations in one table with the access point as the first
  column -- a router runs one or two, and "is my phone on the 5 GHz one" is a
  column read rather than a chooser. Columns: access point, device, station,
  name, ipv4, signal, connected, idle, state. An access point whose stations
  cannot be read is named under the table without hiding the others.
- **`state` uses the CLI's words**, from `ncfg_station_row::state()`, so the
  two clients agree: `listed` is the anomaly under `deny` and the normal case
  under `allow`, which `gui/tests/station_states` holds.
- **Idle is in seconds** because steering's 30 s silence rule (10.597) is
  read against it; connected is minutes, as the TUI rounds.
- **Read-only.** Removing a station is a change to the access point's
  `access_control` list, which the access point dialog writes; a kick button
  here would be a second, unrecorded way to say it, undone by the next apply.
- **The note says where a name comes from**: only from netcfgd's own leases,
  and as the device chose to call itself, so it identifies nothing.

Not live-tested: the view against a daemon running a real access point needs
hostapd, which the GUI's live harness does not start.

## 10.602 Hostnames from the leases

**Asked for by the holder 2026-10-29** ("go ahead with hostnames from the
leases"), the first open item 10.601 named: a station list has shown a MAC
since 0040, because netcfgd ran no DHCP server to learn names from.

- **The source is netcfgd's own lease files**, every
  `<run>/dhcp-server/*.leases`, by the station's MAC
  (`ncfg_dhcp_server_lease_of`). A MAC is one host, so this answers for a
  radio that is the served interface and for one bridged into it alike,
  without working out which. Only an unexpired lease counts; an expiry of 0
  never expires. Nothing outside netcfgd's own directory is read, and only
  files named `.leases` in it.
- **The name is the client's, and untrusted**: it is carried only where it is
  a plain host name -- letters, digits, hyphens and dots, starting with a
  letter or digit, at most 63 characters. Otherwise the address is still
  carried and the name left out. The socket witness holds one of each: a
  `laptop`, and a `<script>` that comes out as its address alone.
- **`ap_stations` gains `hostname` and `ipv4`**, after `address`, both
  optional, decoded by the client library and re-emitted by `--json` in the
  daemon's order (the JSON form is held to the socket witness byte for byte,
  which is what caught the first placement).
- **`ncfg wifi clients` gains NAME and IPV4 columns only where some station
  holds a lease**, so a table for an access point netcfgd serves no DHCP on
  is the one it always was -- `cli_test`'s existing table is the control. A
  name longer than its column is cut there.
- **The TUI shows the name in place of the MAC** where there is one.
- **The GUI showed no associated stations at all** when this landed -- its
  `ap_stations` was the access-control editor's field. It has a stations tab
  since 10.603, which shows the name.
- **What the observe tier exposes grew**, and `doc/socket-protocol.md` says
  so beside its existing warning: a device's name is very often its owner's.
- 0040 carries an amendment: the "no hostname" it recorded has a source now,
  and its "nothing invented" half stands.

## 10.601 A DHCP server, policy handed to dnsmasq

**Asked for by the holder 2026-10-29** ("go ahead with amending 0009 for a
DHCP server"), after the previous run parked it: 0009's table said **DHCPv4
server: no**, and a station joining a netcfgd access point was given no
address. [0297](doc/decision/0297-a-dhcp-server-is-policy-served-by-dnsmasq.md)
amends that row to the shape the RA row already had -- policy yes,
implementation dnsmasq -- and says why each choice below was made.

### What 10.601 measured, dnsmasq 2.91 on the hwsim image

- `port=0` turns dnsmasq's DNS side off, and **it then offers no DNS server
  unless `dhcp-option=6` names one**; it offers its own address as the
  router by default.
- Two instances, two interfaces, `bind-interfaces`: both serve.
- `dhcp-authoritative` NAKs a client asking for an address from another
  network, so it gets a new one at once.
- The lease file is plain text: expiry, MAC, address, name, client id.

### What 10.601 built

- `dhcp_server { range, lease, dns }` in an `interface` block. The range,
  default and refusals are one model function, `ncfg_dhcp_server_range`, the
  compiler, the renderer and the planner all call: the network is the
  interface's first static IPv4 address; the default is its 100th host to
  its 249th (OpenWrt's), cut at the last host; refused with no static IPv4
  address, too small a network, a range outside it, backwards, or taking in
  the router. `lease` from 120 s, default 12 h. `dns` never guessed: none is
  a plan warning.
- **An eleventh backend kind, `dhcp_server`**: start, stop, adoption, liveness,
  teardown when the block goes, the ledger's row and the observation
  witness. Files under `<run>/dhcp-server/<interface>.*`.
- **The restart identity is a sentence.** The generated file's second line
  is `# serves: <range>, <lease> s, dns <servers>`; the observer reads it
  into the backend's `served`, the planner computes the same line from the
  document, and a difference is a stop and a start whose reason shows both
  -- dnsmasq does not re-read its range on `SIGHUP`. The lease file is kept.
- The access point's no-address warning no longer says "netcfgd serves no
  DHCP"; it names `dhcp_server`.

### What the live run found, twice, in netcfgd's own code

`make hull-dhcp-server` served correctly from the first run -- the client
was given an address in the range, the router, the DNS server and the
lease -- and failed because **every plan after the first planned the start
again**: netcfgd did not recognise its own running server. Two causes, each
a whole-argument or ownership rule `ncfg_process_pid_of` is right to keep:

- The configuration path was passed fused, `--conf-file=<path>`, and the
  marker must be **a whole argument** of `/proc/<pid>/cmdline`. Now `-C
  <path>`, as radvd's `--config <path>`.
- dnsmasq **drops to `nobody`** once it holds its sockets, and the owner rule
  takes root or the asker. The file now says `user=nobody` rather than
  leaving it to the build, and the check also accepts that uid -- no wider a
  door, since the pid file is dnsmasq's, written as root into netcfgd's own
  directory, and the marker is netcfgd's own path. Keeping dnsmasq root was
  the alternative, and is a DHCP parser facing the network with root.

Neither could have been caught by a unit test that reads its own rendering;
both were the vm's. The second plan is now empty, a changed lease is a
restart (dnsmasq's pid moved, the lease file kept), and every check passes.

**And one mis-edit caught by reading back**: the `served` field was first
inserted into `applied_dns_fields` rather than the backend's table -- a
search for the next `},` -- which compiled and would have read a backend's
offset into a DNS record. Found by grepping where it landed.

### Open

- ~~**Hostnames from the leases**~~ -- done: 10.602 for the CLI and TUI,
  10.603 for the GUI, and 10.604 ran the whole path over the air.
- **DHCPv6** stays out (0297): RA and SLAAC address the hosts.
- **Another `backend`**: udhcpd, odhcpd, Kea -- a key as `advertise.backend`
  has, once one is measured.

## 10.600 802.11ax

The next step 10.599 named, taken by a `/go` run 2026-10-29.

### What 10.600 measured, hostapd 2.10 on hwsim

| configuration | result |
|---|---|
| 2.4 GHz channel 1, `ieee80211ax=1` | `wifi_generation=6`, 20 MHz |
| 5 GHz 36, 802.11ac at 80 MHz, `ieee80211ax=1`, `he_oper_*` at 80 | Wi-Fi 6, 80 MHz |
| the same without the `he_oper_*` lines | also Wi-Fi 6, 80 MHz |
| 5 GHz 36, `ieee80211ax=1` with no 802.11ac | **Wi-Fi 4**, 40 MHz |
| 5 GHz 149, 802.11ac and ax at 40 | Wi-Fi 6, 40 MHz |

hwsim lists HE per interface type -- "HE Iftypes: managed, P2P-client" and
"HE Iftypes: AP, P2P-GO" -- so it is read for access points, from the
band's `IFTYPE_DATA`.

### The risk the vm cannot show, and what answers it

**A hostapd built without `CONFIG_IEEE80211AX` refuses `ieee80211ax=1`** as
an unknown configuration item and does not start: the item is parsed under
that option and nowhere else. Debian's has it; whether every OpenWrt or
Alpine variant does is not something to assume for every access point on
an upgrade. So the hostapd that will run is asked:
`ncfg_hostapd_program_has_he` reads the binary for `he_oper_chwidth`, a
keyword that exists only where that parser was compiled in, cached by size
and modification time. The daemon and `ncfg` name the program their exec
would find, through `ncfg_process_find` into `roots.hostapd`, and the
observation carries the answer as `hostapd_has_he`; **empty asks nothing**,
as `roots.resolv_conf` does, so a test answers for the machine under test
rather than whatever hostapd the build machine has. The planner and the
executor both read it, so a hostapd without 802.11ax is never planned a
line it cannot take -- which would otherwise be a restart every pass.

### What 10.600 built

- `IFTYPE_DATA` entries naming `NL80211_IFTYPE_AP` with `HE_CAP_PHY`, per
  band, into the link's `high_efficiency: ["2.4", "5"]`.
- The channel plan's `he`: on 2.4 GHz where the radio has it, on 5 GHz only
  beside 802.11ac. Written as `ieee80211ax=1` and, at 80 and 160 MHz,
  `he_oper_chwidth` and `he_oper_centr_freq_seg0_idx` with 802.11ac's values
  -- as hostapd's documentation asks, since hwsim could not tell.
- `ieee80211ax` read back into the restart identity. An access point on an
  HE radio with an HE hostapd restarts once on upgrade.

### The same risk in what was already written

The lens from the probe, taken across every keyword the renderer writes:
**a keyword missing from the binary is certain** -- hostapd matches keys as
strings, so one whose string is not in the program cannot be accepted,
whatever its build options -- and several of netcfgd's are behind options.
`vht_oper_chwidth` is `CONFIG_IEEE80211AC`'s, and 10.598 wrote 802.11ac by
default; `sae_password` is `CONFIG_SAE`'s, and the default `wpa2+wpa3`
writes it; `mobility_domain` (802.11r), `bss_transition` (802.11v),
`rrm_neighbor_report` and `wds_sta` back opt-in features. So the probe reads
the binary once for all seven (`ncfg_hostapd_optional_keys`), the
observation carries the ones it lacks as `hostapd_lacks`, and:

- **802.11ac is withheld where its keyword is missing**, as 802.11ax is.
  Unlike 802.11ax, an unasked hostapd still gets it: 10.598 gave it without
  asking and nearly every build has it, so the asymmetry keeps that.
- **A feature the document asks for that needs a missing keyword is a plan
  warning**, naming the keyword, the feature and the way out -- `proto =
  "wpa2"` for SAE, removing the feature or installing a hostapd with it --
  before a restart would stop the access point and leave it down. The plan
  goes on: whether to change the document or the hostapd is the operator's.

`plan_access_point_test` asserts both, and `hostapd_test` that a minimal
binary is read for exactly the keywords it carries.

### What 10.600 showed live

`hull-roam`'s station joins as Wi-Fi 6 on 2.4 GHz, `hull-steer`'s band
machine moves it to Wi-Fi 6 at 80 MHz with the HE lines written, and
`hull-width`'s joins as Wi-Fi 6 at 160 MHz. **The advisory machine's
stand-in neighbour had to move to 5 GHz**: with netcfgd's 2.4 GHz access
