point now HE at 20 MHz (wpa_supplicant's estimate 286802 kbit/s), an HE
neighbour at 40 MHz on 2.4 GHz did not beat it and the station rightly
stayed -- the advisory request working as designed, a fourth time.

## 10.599 160 MHz

**Asked for by the holder 2026-10-29** ("go ahead with 160 MHz").

**Never the default, decided from the band plan before the measurement.**
Both of 5 GHz's 160 MHz blocks, 36-64 and 100-128, take in channels shared
with radar, so a 160 MHz access point listens before it may beacon at every
start and radar can move it off the channel. That is a cost worth paying on
purpose and not one to hand everyone on upgrade, so `width = 160` asks for
it and the default stays 80, whose blocks 36-48 and 149-161 need no wait.

### What 10.599 measured, hostapd 2.10 on hwsim, US domain, DFS on

| configuration | result |
|---|---|
| 36 `[HT40+]`, `vht_oper_chwidth=2`, centre 50, `vht_capab=[VHT160]` | 62 s of listening, then 160 MHz |
| the same without `[VHT160]` | 61 s, then **80 MHz, said nowhere** |
| 100 `[HT40+]`, centre 114, `[VHT160]` | 62 s, then 160 MHz |
| 64 `[HT40-]`, centre 50, `[VHT160]` | 61 s, then 160 MHz |

So `[VHT160]` is written with the width, and only where the radio says it
can: bits 2-3 of `VHT_CAPA`, the supported channel width set, read into the
link's `hundred_sixty_mhz` (hwsim's `0x038004fa` has them). The listening is
real even with 36 as the primary, so a plan for 160 MHz on 36 to 48 says so
in a warning of its own; a primary that is itself a radar channel already
had one. Automatic selection at 160 was not measured, so 160 asks for a
`channel` and is 80 without one.

### What 10.599 built

- `width = 160`, refused on 2.4 GHz with 80. In the channel plan: 160 MHz
  centred on 50 or 114, for a channel in the block, on a radio with the
  bits; otherwise one step down to 80, with the first reason kept.
- The file: `vht_capab=[VHT160]`, `vht_oper_chwidth=2` and the centre.
  `vht_oper_chwidth=2` is read back as `started_with.hundred_sixty_mhz`, so
  160 is part of the restart identity with the other widths.
- **And a gap in 10.595 it exposed**: see the correction there -- neighbour
  lists are now sent by the daemon under `report`, and `hull-steer`'s band
  machine applies until a plan has no neighbour left to add, bounded.
- `make hull-width`: netcfgd's access point on 100 with `width = 160`; the
  plan warns, the file holds all five lines, a station associates at
  `WIDTH=160 MHz` as Wi-Fi 5 once the listening is over, and a second plan
  has nothing to do.

## 10.598 802.11ac and 80 MHz

**Asked for by the holder 2026-10-29** ("go ahead with 802.11ac").

### What 10.598 measured, hostapd 2.10 on hwsim, US domain

| configuration | result |
|---|---|
| 36 `[HT40+]`, `ieee80211ac=1`, `vht_oper_chwidth=1`, centre 42 | 80 MHz, `wifi_generation=5` |
| 48 `[HT40-]`, centre 42; 149 `[HT40+]`, centre 155 | 80 MHz, generation 5 |
| automatic channel, `vht_oper_chwidth=1`, no centre | ACS chose 36; 80 MHz |
| `vht_oper_chwidth=0` with `[HT40+]`; no `ht_capab` | 40 and 20 MHz, generation 5 |
| centre 58 written for channel 36 | **ran at 80 MHz** |

hwsim's 5 GHz band carries `VHT_CAPA` `0x038004fa`, which includes 160 MHz.

**The last row is the reason the centres are a unit test.** hwsim accepted
a centre that is wrong for the channel, so the vm cannot catch one; a real
radio's firmware may not be so forgiving. `hostapd_test` pins all five
blocks channel by channel. 132 was also tried and refused -- but as a radar
channel the measurement had not enabled DFS for, so it decided nothing.

### What 10.598 built

- **Read**: `NL80211_BAND_ATTR_VHT_CAPA` in the 5 GHz band, into the link's
  `very_high_throughput`, answered with `high_throughput`. 80 MHz is
  mandatory for VHT, so this is also "can do 80"; 160 is a further bit, not
  read.
- **The rule grew into a plan**: `ncfg_access_point_secondary` became
  `ncfg_access_point_channel_plan`, which answers width, secondary, centre
  and whether 802.11ac runs, from `ncfg_radio_widths_t` -- the three things
  the radio is read for. Default on 5 GHz is the widest the radio can do; a
  wider width that cannot be given falls back one step and says why. The
  80 MHz blocks are 36-48, 52-64, 100-112, 116-128 and 149-161, centred on
  42, 58, 106, 122 and 155; 132-144 is left out with 144, so 132-140 is 40.
- **`width = 80`**, refused at compile time on 2.4 GHz, where it does not
  exist; and by the renderer, for a document the reader accepted.
- **`ieee80211ac` and `vht_oper_chwidth` are part of what hostapd was
  started as**, compared beside 10.597's width where the radio was read.
  A 5 GHz access point on a VHT radio restarts once on upgrade.

### Live

`make hull-steer`'s band machine: `wlan1.conf` holds `[HT40+]`,
`ieee80211ac=1`, `vht_oper_chwidth=1` and centre 42, and the steered station
reads `WIDTH=80 MHz` and `wifi_generation=5`. The other wifi rigs pass over
the change.

**And the first run found band steering broken by it.** The band machine
planned no steer at all: an access point at 80 MHz reports itself in its
80 MHz operating class -- 128 by Annex E, inferred rather than read: what
the run showed is that widening the test past 125 made it pass -- and the
planner's test for "a 5 GHz element" took only
the 20 MHz classes, 115 to 125 -- so the moment the 5 GHz access point got
wider it stopped being a 5 GHz target. The tests now take Annex E's whole
ranges, 81-84 for 2.4 GHz (83 and 84 are its 40 MHz classes) and 115-130
for 5, and `plan_access_point_test` has a sibling reporting class 128. The
unit tests could not have caught it: they wrote the element by hand in the
20 MHz class, which is the fixture-built-from-the-code shape 10.116 names.

**Next**: 160 MHz, from `VHT_CAPA`'s supported-width bits, where a domain
allows a whole 160 MHz block (36-64, 100-128) -- done since, in 10.599;
then 802.11ax, done in 10.600.

## 10.597 40 MHz

**Asked for by the holder 2026-10-29** ("go ahead with 40 MHz"), the next
step 10.596 named.

### Measured first, hostapd 2.10 on hwsim, US domain

| `channel`, `ht_capab` | result |
|---|---|
| 36 `[HT40+]`, 40 `[HT40-]` | runs; station `WIDTH=40 MHz` |
| 1 `[HT40+]`, 11 `[HT40-]` on 2.4 GHz | runs; 40 MHz |
| 0 (automatic) `[HT40+]` on 5 GHz | ACS chose 36; 40 MHz |
| 36 `[HT40-]`, the wrong way | **refuses to start** |
| 165 `[HT40+]`, no partner | **refuses to start**: "Frequency 5845 (secondary) not allowed" |

**So a wrong secondary is not a slower access point, it is none.** hostapd
does not fall back to 20 MHz. That decides the shape: netcfgd writes a
direction only where it is certain of the pair.

### What 10.597 built

- **Read per band**: bit 1 of `HT_CAPA`, "supported channel width set", in
  each band of the `GET_WIPHY` dump, so the observed link carries
  `forty_mhz: ["2.4", "5"]` -- per band because a radio may differ, and a
  `[HT40+]` the band cannot do refuses the start. hwsim reports `0x107e`.
- **The rule, in the model** (`ncfg_access_point_secondary`, beside the band
  helpers, as the mobility domain's is), so the file and the planner's
  comparison agree: `width` decides, or by default 40 on 5 GHz and 20 on 2.4;
  then the radio in that band; then the channel. The pairs are the ones
  inside one block of the band -- 36-64, 100-136, 149-161 -- so no domain
  allows one channel of a pair and forbids the other; 140/144, which several
  domains lack 144 for, and 165 upwards stay at 20. Automatic selection on 5
  GHz is told `[HT40+]`, measured to pair; on 2.4 GHz with no channel the
  direction cannot be known, so it stays at 20 and says so.
- **`width = 20 | 40`** on an access point, estate scope like the channel
  plan; a `width = 40` that cannot be given is a plan warning naming why.
- **Part of what hostapd was started as**: `ht_capab` naming HT40 is read
  back as `started_with.forty_mhz` and compared only where the radio's answer
  was read, for 10.596's reason. A 5 GHz access point on an HT40 radio
  restarts once on upgrade.

### What the live run taught

- `make hull-steer`'s band machine: the station steered to the 5 GHz access
  point reads `WIDTH=40 MHz` on 5180 and `wlan1.conf` holds `[HT40+]`;
  `make hull-roam` asserts its 2.4 GHz station reads `20 MHz`.
- **A false pass, caught, and a gap in steering behind it.** The first run
  had the band machine fail its request-mode check: the station had been
  sent nothing. With 5 GHz now 40 MHz, the payload's scan after unpinning
  the station handed wpa_supplicant a candidate so much better that it
  roamed there by itself -- and the 2.4 GHz hostapd kept listing the station
  until its inactivity timeout, so netcfgd planned a steer, sent it to
  nobody, and recorded it. The payload no longer scans and now has the weak
  machine's stay-put control. **And steering skips a station hostapd has not
  heard from in 30 s** (`inactive_msec`, now in `steerable`): a ghost of one
  that left, or one asleep, is not a station to move.

## 10.596 802.11n where the radio has it

**Asked for by the holder 2026-10-29** ("go ahead with ieee80211n"). Until
now nothing wrote `ieee80211n` (10.116), so every netcfgd access point ran at
802.11a/g rates, 54 Mbit/s at best, on hardware that has had HT since 2009.

**No setting.** Whether a radio has HT is a fact about the radio, so it is
read rather than written down: a split nl80211 `GET_WIPHY` dump, HT being
any band's `NL80211_BAND_ATTR_HT_CAPA`, joined to interfaces by the wiphy
index `GET_INTERFACE` carries (`src/observe/wiphy.c`). The observed link
carries `high_throughput`; the executor is handed the HT radios by name, as
it is the route metrics (`ncfg_service_t.high_throughput`), and writes
`ieee80211n=1`.

**HT20 and nothing more**: no `ht_capab`. Every HT radio can do it, and the
optional features -- 40 MHz, short guard interval, the rest -- are bits of
`HT_CAPA` this build does not read yet; asking hostapd for one the radio
lacks fails the start. WMM, which HT requires, follows by hostapd's own
default, and the live reading below is the evidence: wpa_supplicant will
not associate as HT without it.

**An unanswered read is not "no".** `high_throughput` is optional on the
link, absent where the kernel did not say. The planner compares it with what
hostapd was started with (`ieee80211n` in the file, read back as
`started_with.high_throughput`) only where it was answered: otherwise one
failed read would restart an access point to take HT away and the next to
give it back. An access point started before this build, on an HT radio,
restarts once to take it -- the cost of the change, paid once, on upgrade.

**Live.** `make hull-roam`: both access points rendered with
`ieee80211n=1`, and the station joined as `wifi_generation=4`, where earlier
runs the same day showed `WIDTH=20 MHz (no HT)`. `make hull-steer`'s advisory
machine needed its stand-in neighbour moved from HT20 to HT40: with netcfgd's
access point now HT20 too, the two tied on wpa_supplicant's throughput
estimate and the station rightly stayed. Both steering machines pass, and
`make hull-wds` and `make hull-roam-sae` were run again over the change.

**Next, in order**: 40 MHz from the `HT_CAPA` bits the radio reports, then
802.11ac on 5 GHz from `VHT_CAPA` -- both done since, in 10.597 and 10.598.

## 10.595 Neighbour reports and steering: measured, and the design

**Asked for by the holder 2026-10-29** ("go ahead with neighbour reports and
steering"), 10.587 items 2 and 5.

### Measured first, in a vm on hwsim with hostapd 2.10

Two access points of one network on two radios (channels 1 and 11), a
WPA2 station in a namespace:

- `rrm_neighbor_report=1` makes each hostapd hold its **own** entry:
  `SHOW_NEIGHBOR` answers `02:00:00:00:01:00 ssid=72726d
  nr=0200000001008f000000510b060603000000` -- the BSSID, the SSID in hex,
  and the report element (BSSID, BSSID info `0x8f`, operating class 81,
  channel 11, PHY type 6).
- `SET_NEIGHBOR <bssid> ssid=<hex> nr=<hex>` with the other's entry answers
  `OK`, and `SHOW_NEIGHBOR` then lists both.
- The station's `NEIGHBOR_REP_REQUEST` came back as two
  `RRM-NEIGHBOR-REP-RECEIVED` events, one per access point.
- `BSS_TM_REQ <sta> neighbor=<bssid>,0x8f,81,11,6 pref=1 abridged=1` is
  **accepted and advisory**: status 0, target the current access point, the
  station stayed. With `disassoc_imminent=1 disassoc_timer=100` the station
  **moved** to the named access point. A first attempt passing a sixth field
  failed `FAIL`: that field is an optional-subelement hexdump.
- A station that can be steered says so in `STA`'s `ext_capab` (bit 19,
  BSS transition): `04004a02...` has it.

### The design

1. **Neighbour reports, `neighbour_reports = true` on an `access_point`**:
   `rrm_neighbor_report=1` (and `rrm_beacon_report=1`). Opt-in, because
   changing every access point's file restarts every access point on
   upgrade. **Neighbours on one machine are automatic** -- every other access
   point this document runs with the same SSID gives its own entry, read
   from its hostapd -- which is the 2.4 GHz-and-5 GHz router, the commonest
   case, and needs nothing from anyone. **Neighbours on other machines are
   declared** -- `neighbour "aa:bb:cc:dd:ee:01" { channel = 36 }` inside the
   access point -- until fuzznet can carry each host's own entries (10.594).
   hostapd holds the list in memory, so it is observed (`SHOW_NEIGHBOR`, on
   the connection the station lists already use) and converged by plan ops,
   as the station lists are: visible in `ncfg plan`, no restart.
2. **Steering, opt-in per access point**, by `BSS_TM_REQ` to stations whose
   `ext_capab` says they can be steered. Opt-in, because moving people's
   devices is a choice to make, not a default. **Rewritten before it was
   built**: the first version had both cases send disassociation imminent,
   and the measurement above says what that costs. wpa_supplicant ignores
   an advisory request while its own signal is good (the station stayed),
   and a request with disassociation imminent disassociates it whether or
   not it moved -- so a weak station with nowhere better to go would have
   been cut off every round. So the two cases differ:
   - **Weak signal (`signal = -75`): advisory**, naming every neighbour.
     The station is weak, which is exactly when wpa_supplicant weighs the
     candidates, and it decides; nobody is disconnected. Not disruptive.
   - **Band (`band = true`): disassociation imminent**, towards this
     machine's own 5 GHz access point of the network, for a station on
     2.4 GHz heard at -60 dBm or better -- the one case where an advisory
     request is ignored by design and where the target is known to be
     near, being on the same box. Disruptive, so the control-path guard
     refuses it on an operator's interface. **Once per station per hour**,
     recorded in `/run` as it is sent, so a station whose 5 GHz is poor and
     that comes back is not moved and cut again every round.
   Both want a station connected a minute or more, so one that has just
   arrived -- including from a steer -- is left to settle. Steering needs
   `neighbour_reports`, which is where the targets come from, and that now
   also writes `bss_transition=1`, so steering itself is the daemon's
   behaviour and turning it on or off restarts nothing.

### Item 1 built

- **The language**: `neighbour_reports = true`, and `neighbour "BSSID" {
  channel = N }` blocks inside the access point. Refused: a neighbour with
  reports off (it would tell nobody), one without a channel, one on a
  channel no operating class covers (`ncfg_neighbour_class`: 81, 82, 115,
  118, 121, 124, 125), one declared twice, and a label that is not a BSSID.
  BSSIDs are kept in hostapd's lowercase spelling.
- **The element of a declared neighbour is this access point's own with the
  BSSID, the class and the channel replaced**, BSSID info and PHY type kept
  and the optional subelements dropped. That assumes the neighbour is of the
  same kind, which a network of access points netcfgd runs is; a mixed
  network reports a slightly wrong PHY type, which a station only uses as a
  hint. Stated in the example file.
- **The ops**: `neighbour.add` (`SET_NEIGHBOR`, which replaces an entry of
  that BSSID) and `neighbour.del` (`REMOVE_NEIGHBOR`), neither disruptive,
  each the other's inverse and an add's inverse carrying the element it
  replaced. The access point's own entry is never planned. Nothing is
  planned against a hostapd not yet running with reports on: the restart
  that turns them on comes first, and the list converges on the next pass.
  **Corrected in 10.599: under the default `on_drift = "report"` there was
  no next pass**, so a fresh access point's reports stayed empty until
  somebody ran `ncfg apply` again -- found when the 5 GHz hostapd, slower
  to come up at 80 MHz, missed the rig's second apply and band steering,
  which finds its target in the list, moved nobody. The daemon now always
  sends `neighbour.add` and `neighbour.del`, beside `station.steer`, for
  steering's reason: the document asks for the lists and filling them
  undoes nothing anyone did.
- **Live, `make hull-roam`**: both access points report, roam-b declares
  `02:00:00:00:09:00` on 36. The second apply planned three adds, a third
  plan had nothing to do, and after its FT roam the station's own report
  request to roam-b listed roam-a on channel 1, roam-b on 6 and the declared
  one as class 115 channel 36. Neither sibling nor declared entry is
  anything hostapd learns alone, so the reading cannot come from elsewhere.
- **A rig's `verdict/` made by the other account is not writable from the
  guest**, though it is `2775` group `users` and both accounts are in the
  group: the guest's write came back `Permission denied`, so the vm's share
  evidently does not carry the host user's supplementary groups. Removing
  the empty directory and letting the target recreate it fixed it. Whoever
  meets "the payload left no verdict" should look at the owner first.
- **The document reader takes any neighbour, so the renderer refuses by name**
  what the language would: a BSSID not in hostapd's spelling, one declared
  twice, a channel no class covers, neighbours with reports off. Found by
  `lower_test`'s extreme sweep (`"a:b"`, channel 0), which is that sweep
  doing its job.
- **~~`supplicant_launch_test` fails under a long `TMPDIR`~~, closed
  2026-10-30, and it was a fault users could meet.** The refusal for a radio
  another manager holds was 437 bytes of prose with the `-P` path in the
  middle, so the 512-byte `err` had room for about forty characters of run
  directory: `/run/netcfgd` fits, but any longer `NCFG_RUN_DIR` cut the
  message off before what to do -- this test under `/tmp/claude-1000` was
  enough. Tightened to 384 bytes and reordered so the advice comes first and
  the path last, where a path too long even for that loses its tail and not
  the instructions. The test now builds a run directory 300 bytes longer
  itself, rather than depending on the run's `TMPDIR`; with the old message
  back it fails. The 108-byte socket path limit was the first guess and was
  not the cause.

### Item 2 built

- **The language**: `steering { signal = -75  band = true }` in an
  access point, refused without `neighbour_reports`, empty, twice, or with
  a signal that is not one. `neighbour_reports` now also writes
  `bss_transition=1`, so steering is wholly the daemon's and its block
  restarts nothing.
- **Observed**: each associated station whose `ext_capab` has bit 19, with
  its signal and connected time (`steerable`), and the steers of the last
  hour (`steered`), from `<run>/hostapd/<radio>.steered` -- one line per
  station, its last steer, rewritten with nothing older than the hour, so
  the file is bounded by the window.
- **`station.steer`**: `BSS_TM_REQ` with every neighbour but the access
  point itself as a candidate, or the one target, `pref=1 abridged=1`, and
  `disassoc_imminent=1 disassoc_timer=100` for a band steer. Disruptive
  only when imminent, so the guard refuses a band steer on an operator's
  interface and never an advisory one. No inverse, and the plan's
  "cannot be undone" warning says so.
- **Planned** for stations connected 60 s or more: band first, for a
  station on 2.4 GHz at -60 dBm or better when this machine's 5 GHz access
  point of the network is already on this one's neighbour list; otherwise
  advisory below `signal`, when there is a neighbour at all. Held for the
  hour after an imminent steer and five minutes after an advisory one. A
  warning where `band = true` and the document runs no 5 GHz access point of
  the network.
- **The daemon sends steers under `on_drift = "report"`**, a third exception
  beside `preference` and a pending SIM, in `ncfg_reconcile_restrict`: the
  block is the configuration asking for continuous behaviour, it undoes
  nothing anyone did, and otherwise steering would need a second setting
  nobody would think of. The neighbour lists are still ordinary drift.
- **Live, `make hull-steer`**: 2.4 GHz channel 1 and 5 GHz channel 36 on
  one machine, a station joined on 2.4. A plan in its first seconds steered
  nobody (the control); after 62 s the plan carried one imminent steer to
  the 5 GHz BSSID, the apply moved the station to 5180 MHz, the record held
  it, and the plan after steered nobody.
- **The advisory case, live: `make hull-steer`'s second machine,
  `weak.conf`.** netcfgd's access point on channel 1 with `steering { signal
  = -45 }` and a declared neighbour -- a plain hostapd with 802.11n on
  channel 6, standing in for another machine's. The station and netcfgd's
  radio drop to 0 dBm. A plan in the first seconds steered nobody, the
  station stayed put for the minute with the better access point in its scan
  results, and the plan after carried one steer. The station received it as
  `request_mode=0x3`, no disassociation bit (the band machine's is `0x7`),
  moved to the neighbour, the record marked it `0`, and the next plan was
  empty. Four things the run taught, each now in the code or the payload:
  - **hostapd's default validity is one beacon interval, about 100 ms**, and
    wpa_supplicant scans for the candidate before acting, so it found the
    list expired. The executor sends `valid_int=255` (about 26 s);
    `service_test` pins the exact command and a sabotage removing it goes
    red there. Found only by the vm.
  - **hwsim reports signal as transmit power minus 50, and `iw` takes no
    negative power**, so -50 dBm is the weakest a station can be made, which
    is why the threshold is -45 rather than a real-world -75.
  - **wpa_supplicant 2.10 chooses by estimated throughput**: at -50 and
    -30 dBm two 802.11g access points both estimate 54 Mbit/s, the tie keeps
    the current one, and the station stayed. That is the advisory request
    working as designed -- the station decides -- and why the neighbour here
    runs 802.11n. A real weak station estimates less and moves.
  - **The control caught a false pass.** A scan the payload asked for after
    weakening the station gave wpa_supplicant the stronger neighbour, and it
    roamed on its own inside the minute; the reading that "the steer moved
    it" would have been wrong. Without bgscan an associated wpa_supplicant
    reconsiders only on new scan results, so the payload no longer scans.

## 10.594 How the hosts reach each other, and what fuzznet and WireGuard are for

Asked by the holder 2026-10-29: how the hosts reach each other for mesh,
roaming and repeaters, and whether to link them over fuzznet or WireGuard.
Answered from the renderer and the rigs rather than from memory.

**No netcfgd talks to another for any of these.** A mesh is over the air:
nodes peer by SAE on the shared channel and mesh ID, and the kernel forwards.
A repeater is over the air: a station in four-address mode, given its own
interface in the access point's bridge. FT-PSK needs **no path between the
access points at all**: `ft_psk_generate_local` has each derive the roaming
keys from the passphrase, and the station roams over the air. Only FT-SAE
moves anything between access points -- hostapd's own key exchange, as
Ethernet frames of ethertype 0x890d broadcast on the access points' bridge
(`r0kh=ff:ff:ff:ff:ff:ff`, `r1kh` answering any), so the access points must
share one Ethernet segment. `make hull-roam-sae` proves it as two netcfgds
whose bridges are joined by a veth.

**What crosses machines is agreement, not traffic**: the same mesh ID,
passwords and roaming key everywhere, put on each machine by hand today.
**Keeping that agreement is fuzznet's, as already decided** (10.567, 10.542):
the estate-scope keys carry wire numbers for it and wait on fuzznet's record
half. The open part is the secrets -- 0029 keeps them out of the document, so
a roaming key or a mesh password reaching a new access point wants a path of
its own, which is a question for fuzznet's design rather than this tree's.

**WireGuard is not needed for these, and is not to be created implicitly.** A
station roams only between access points in radio range of each other, which
share a segment in practice; mesh and repeater links are their own transport,
encrypted per hop by SAE. The one case it serves is FT-SAE access points on
different segments: the key exchange is Ethernet-only, so it would need an
Ethernet tunnel -- VXLAN or GRETAP over WireGuard -- bridged into the access
points' bridge, which the language already expresses as the operator's
choice. netcfgd making such a tunnel on its own would be configuration no
file holds (constraint 1). Whether fuzznet itself wants WireGuard beneath it,
for NAT or reachability, is fuzznet's; its messages are authenticated already.

**What is checked, and what cannot be from one machine.** An FT-SAE access
point whose radio is in no bridge is warned about (since `d3a6dd2c`), and the
control half -- a bridged radio is not warned -- is tested now too. Access
points in bridges on *different* segments are not detectable from one host:
that needs the network-wide observation fuzznet is for.

### How FT-PSK decides which access point a station uses

**It does not; the station does.** Fast roaming makes a move between access
points cheap -- the keys are ready at the target without a full handshake --
but which access point a station is on is the station's choice, by signal.
There is no controller, and nothing in netcfgd assigns stations. What exists
to steer them is the access point's station list: deny a station on every
access point but one and it can only associate there (0039, the
"single-host half" of the Ubiquiti-style roaming 0036 named), and with estate
host lists (10.591) that list is written once. `bss_transition=1` is set, so
802.11v transition requests are accepted by stations that support them, but
netcfgd sends none: band and signal steering are 10.587 item 5, parked
behind neighbour reports (item 2).

### Whether FT-SAE's Ethernet exchange is secure

**Encrypted and authenticated, with replay protection, by the shared key** --
hostapd's FT messages between access points (RRB-OUI) are sealed with the
roaming key; the 2.10 binary's own strings name the encryption ("Failed to
encrypt RRB-OUI message") and the sequence numbers that refuse a replay
("Invalid sequence number", a sequence-number nonce). The key is SHA-256 of
the `roaming_key` secret, 256 bits, which is what that scheme takes. Not
measured on the wire here; the source of that claim is the binary.

What it rests on, and what follows:

- **The whole exchange is as strong as the secret.** The key is a hash of it,
  so a low-entropy `roaming_key` can be guessed offline from captured frames.
  It should be a random value of its own, not a word.
- **It is one network-wide credential.** The wildcards mean any device on the
  segment holding the key can ask for a station's keys, and one access point
  compromised is all of them compromised. Per-pair keys (listing each
  `r0kh`/`r1kh`) would narrow that, at the cost of every access point naming
  every other -- a list fuzznet could keep, and nothing here can.
- **It is broadcast on the LAN**, so a segment the access points share with
  untrusted hosts carries it to them: sealed, but present. A management VLAN
  for the access points' bridge keeps it off the user LAN.

## 10.593 An apply through the daemon reported as a local one does

**Found by `make hull-natcap`**, run to check the op's rename against a real
kernel: nine checks failed, every one an apply that the kernel refused and
`ncfg` reported as exit 0. Since 7e13290e a plain `ncfg apply` goes through
the daemon wherever one runs, and the client's printer for the daemon's journal
(`say_journal`) was a second answer to "how did the apply go" that 0293 had
not reached: it had no word for `unmet`, printed it raw and did not count it,
so an apply with something red exited 0 -- against 0293's "unmet is a failure".
It also spoke another vocabulary (`Done`, `Failed`) from the local journal's
marks, and **printed nothing at all under `--json`**, which a script parsing
the output reads as an empty document.

Now the daemon path uses the local marks (`ok  `, `FAIL`, `red `, `skip`,
`back`) with the op and interface, counts `unmet` as a failure with the
local summary, and under `--json` copies the daemon's records into the local
document's shape -- the daemon writes them with the same journal writer, so
the two are byte-identical, measured by applying one config through each.
`cli_test` holds the marks, the exit and the JSON; `hull-natcap` passes all
its checks again.

**Its `Fixes:` trailer names the wrong commit**, as 10.589's did: 7d10ed66
says `7e13290e6ef8`; the commit is `7e13290e2bdb`. Pushed, so left, and
recorded here where the next reader of either will look.

**A firewall change with no confirm window now says so in the plan**, the
same day: an `input` that drops the operator's ssh would leave the machine
out of reach with nothing to put it back, and 10.546 is the holder's word that
the control path is part of what is configured. The warning names
`--confirm-within` and `global { confirm }`; a document whose `confirm`
arms a window plans without it (`plan_setting_test`).

## 10.592 The firewall, enforced: host lists in its rules, and the slices to get there

**Asked for by the holder 2026-10-29: host lists on the firewall side.** That
meant finding out the firewall is not enforced at all -- 10.564: it compiles,
round-trips and reaches the document, and nothing turns it into ops -- because
the planner waited on 0295's product half. **The holder answered it the same
day: `ncfg status` must show the installed firewall as rules**, so 0295 is
accepted as decoder (A) with identity (B), built together. The example file
now says in capitals that a `firewall` block is not yet enforced, which it had
not said.

**Measured before building, in an unprivileged `unshare -rn` namespace with
the host's `nft`:** a user namespace can hold an nftables table, so the whole
firewall can be exercised against the real kernel with no root; and
`ether saddr & ff:ff:ff:00:00:00 == aa:bb:cc:00:00:00 drop comment
"name=x"` is accepted and listed back as written -- **nftables masks
natively**, so a prefix needs no expansion here, unlike hostapd (10.591), and
works on an accept as well as a drop.

### The slices, in order

1. **Done: `mac` in a rule.** `drop "strangers" { mac = ["@host_list:banned",
   "aa:bb:cc:*", "00:11:22:33:44:55"] }` -- nftables' `ether saddr`, which
   0294's closed vocabulary gains on the holder's request. Resolved from the
   host lists as an access point's are, the names and what was written kept
   for the renderer, sorted as a set. **Refused in `output`**, where a packet
   this host sends has no sending station yet, so the rule would never match.
   It means nothing on an interface with no Ethernet header (WireGuard, PPP),
   where it simply never matches; that is not refused, since `interface` is
   optional and a rule may span both kinds.
2. **The `sys/nft` layer.** *2a done*: `ncfg_nft_build_replace` writes the
   table with the NAT chain, the three filter chains and their policies, and
   each rule as nftables' own expressions -- family, protocol, destination
   port, address with its prefix mask, arriving or leaving interface, state
   as a conntrack bitmask, station with its mask, verdict -- carrying
   `name=NAME sha256=DIGEST` in the comment TLV. `tests/live/firewall.sh`
   sends it in an `unshare -rn` namespace and reads it back with `nft list
   ruleset`: every rule lists as the document wrote it, a replacement leaves
   nothing behind, and a rule matching both families is refused with the
   table untouched; giving an IPv4 source the destination's offset fails it.
   The audit now allows the three filter chains and still refuses a fifth.
   *2b done*: a rule with several values -- ports, addresses, stations, or
   both families -- is **one kernel rule per combination**, each carrying
   the written rule's name and digest, so a decoder groups them by name; a
   combination of an IPv4 source and an IPv6 destination is skipped, a rule
   with no other is refused, and one that would become more than 256 kernel
   rules is refused with the count. Chosen over nftables' anonymous sets,
   which are compact and native but need interval sets -- its most intricate
   encoding -- for every CIDR and mask, and a decoder for them; the language
   and the identity would not change if sets replaced it. *2c done*:
   `ncfg_nft_firewall_rule_read` decodes one kernel rule -- every
   expression layer one writes, its comment's name and digest -- and refuses
   anything else by name: a rule with no identity, or one wearing an
   identity with an expression netcfgd never writes (`limit`, measured with
   a hand-added rule). The digest's text normalises addresses as the decoder
   prints them, because the kernel holds `192.168.7.9/16` as
   `192.168.0.0/16`; with that, the digest recomputed from every
   single-valued rule read back equals the one written. Regrouping a written
   rule's several kernel rules by name is the observer's, in slice 3. The original plan, for the record:
   the three filter chains and every rule
   expression layer one writes -- protocol, ports, addresses, interface,
   state, `ether saddr` with its mask, the verdict -- each rule carrying B's
   name and digest in nft's comment TLV; and A, the decoder of those back
   into `ncfg_firewall_rule_t`. Checked against the kernel in a namespace,
   with `nft list ruleset` as the independent reader.
3. **Done, 2026-10-29: plan, apply, observe.** The observation carries
   each filter chain's policy and every kernel rule as decoded, with the
   reasons for any it could not read, and `ncfg status` lists them. The op
   is renamed `nftables.replace` and carries the uplinks *and* the firewall,
   because the table is replaced whole; its inverse carries the installed
   firewall regrouped from the observation, so a rollback does not leave the
   host open. **Convergence is decided by decoding the document's own
   transaction** and matching it in order against the installed rules, field
   by field -- so a hand edit that kept a rule's comment is still a
   difference. Another table's filter chain at the same hooks is named in
   the plan (0294) and left alone. `tests/live/firewall.sh` drives `ncfg
   plan`, `apply` and `status` against the kernel: installed, converged, a
   hand-added rule named and removed, a host list edit alone planned, a
   neighbour reported and untouched, the firewall taken out with the
   document. Reducing the comparison to the policies fails four of its
   checks; `plan_setting_test` holds the five planner cases without a
   kernel.

   The original plan for this slice, for the record: the table holds NAT and the firewall, and 0294
   replaces the whole table in one transaction -- so one op must carry both
   rather than `nat.replace` beside a firewall op, each of which would drop
   the other's chains. An observer reading the chains back through A, the
   `(name, digest)` comparison, and `ncfg status` showing the rules.

Slice 1 checked by `lower_test` (resolution across declaration order, a
prefix on an accept, the output refusal, an undeclared list, a malformed
address) and `render_test` (round trips with and without a list) -- the
round trip found an order dependence on the first run: the rule's set was
resolved in the list's written order and the list renders sorted, so a saved
profile compiled to a different document. It is sorted canonically now.

## 10.591 A host list manager: wanted, and how it stores what it sees

**Asked for by the copyright holder 2026-10-29**: "a host list manager, so we
can have seen devices, whitelists, blacklists of different sorts, preferably
intermixable with a limited set of wildcard rules". The "later" in that request
was about **the wildcards, not the manager**, and the holder added that the
wildcards may land with it. Nothing is built yet.

**What it is**: named lists of hosts that other blocks refer to, of three
kinds -- hosts *seen* (observed, not written), and allow and deny lists an
operator writes -- that can be combined, with a small set of wildcard forms
rather than a pattern language.

### Decided by the holder, 2026-10-29

- **Wildcards are expanded where a consumer needs it.** hostapd takes exact
  MACs, so a wildcard is resolved against what has been seen into the
  concrete list that consumer can hold.
- **Seen hosts, leases and the like are stored persistently, per host.** Not
  disposable `/run` state, and not config under `/etc` either: they are
  observations, kept keyed by the host that made them.
- **That data is distributed the normal way, because this is a fuzznet-based
  project.** Storage and every operation across the network goes through
  fuzznet's generic calls, not a protocol of netcfgd's own -- the scope
  decision 10.567 already records ("every project using fuzznet uses
  fuzznet's high-level abstractions").
- **Retention is a built-in rule engine that netcfgd uses**, rather than one
  netcfgd writes. How long a host keeps what it saw is a rule set, not code
  here.

### What the tree already has

- `access_point { access_control { allow | deny = [...] } }` -- exact MAC
  addresses, inline, one access point at a time
  ([0039](doc/decision/0039-a-station-list-is-one-list.md)).
- `ap_stations` on the socket -- the stations an access point holds now, one
  source of *seen*; the leases netcfgd's DHCP server hands out are another.
- The firewall model (10.563, [0283](doc/decision/0283-firewall-and-queuing-are-in-scope.md))
  -- address-keyed rules, the other likely consumer.

None of these is a list another block can name.

**0039 constrains the output, not the feature.** It refuses `allow` and `deny`
on one access point together, because hostapd holds one list and a precedence
rule would let a deny list silently do nothing. Combinable lists are therefore
resolved at compile time into the one list each consumer holds, and `ncfg
plan` shows the resolved list, so the precedence is visible.

### What it needs from fuzznet, measured 2026-10-29 at fuzznet `0f33b17`

**fuzznet's retention engine is for logs today.** `log/retain.h` is the rule
engine -- prune and keep rules by `age`, `size` or `count`, selecting by
program, host, machine, level, subsystem and text, set per host and
estate-wide by a root (its sections 475 and 476). Holdings retention (its
section 152) is a different thing: a per-host tri-state saying whether a host
keeps a catalogue item. **Neither covers records such as seen hosts or
leases.** Whether the log engine generalises to records, or records get an
engine of their own shape, is fuzznet's design; netcfgd brings the caller.
Signalled to fuzznet in its inbox, `20261029T1119Z`.

### When: fuzznet's record half comes after its messaging core

**The holder, 2026-10-29: fuzznet is the retention engine, and it is in a core
refinement phase** -- fully functional over a limited subset, focused on
messaging and the ecosystem that needs, with most of what this feature asks
of it deferred until after. So persistence, distribution and retention of
*seen* wait for fuzznet, and are not worked around here.

**The feature splits at that seam, and the first half needs nothing from
fuzznet:**

1. **Now-able:** the lists as configuration, combining them, and wildcards
   expanded against what is observed *at the time* -- the stations an access
   point holds, the leases the DHCP server has out -- resolved into hostapd's
   exact list and into firewall rules, and shown in `ncfg plan`. *Seen*
   means "observed now" in this half.
2. **After fuzznet's record half:** *seen* that persists per host, is shared
   across machines, and is pruned by fuzznet's rules. The first half's
   resolver takes this as a second source and does not change shape.

**What is deliberately not built is a stopgap store**: a local file of seen
hosts with its own pruning would be a second retention engine to retire, and
a format other code would grow to depend on -- the placeholder 10.567 found
this tree still holding for coordination.

### Built: exact addresses, 2026-10-29

    host_list "family" { mac = ["00:11:22:33:44:01", "00:11:22:33:44:02"] }
    access_point "Family" {
    	...
    	access_control { allow = ["@host_list:family", "00:11:22:33:44:03"] }
    }

- **A `host_list` block** holds exact MAC addresses, normalised and sorted
  as a station list is. **An access point names one** inside its `allow` or
  `deny` as `"@host_list:NAME"`, beside literal addresses; several lists and
  addresses on one side are joined. 0039 still holds: one side per access
  point.
- **Resolved at compile time into `stations`**, after every block is read,
  so a list may be declared later or in another drop-in. The planner,
  hostapd's list file and `ap_stations` read `stations` and do not know
  lists exist. **A name no `host_list` declares is refused**, not read as
  empty: empty is "nobody" on an allow list and "everybody" on a deny list.
- **The document keeps what was written** -- `lists`, and `written` for the
  literal addresses beside them, both omitted when no list is named, so
  every earlier document is byte for byte what it was -- because two
  writers put an access point back into configuration and each would
  otherwise save the addresses and drop the list. `ncfg profile save`
  renders the reference; the client library gives the GUI's access point
  dialog `@host_list:NAME` plus the written addresses instead of the
  resolved set (`ncfg_client_access_points`), which the dialog was filling
  from and writing back.
- **Scope: estate-wide**, decided by the holder 2026-10-29. It is also what
  the reference needs: an access point's `access_control` travels, so a list
  it names has to travel with it or arrive as a reference to nothing. `mac`
  is kind `0x00080001`.

Checked: `lower_test` (resolution across declaration order, repeats
dropped, the missing and malformed refusals, two lists and an empty one, a
block naming none unchanged), `render_test` (round trip by production's
equality; the saved access point names the list), `client_test` (the
editor's form, plain and sanitised), `scope_test`, the witness, `make
example` with the new block as a named exception, `registry`, `agree`.
Sabotage: not resolving fails two `lower_test` checks; rendering the
stations instead of the reference fails both `render_test` checks.

### Built: OUI prefixes on a deny list, 2026-10-29

Asked for by the holder: `"aa:bb:cc:*"`, the manufacturer's three octets and a
star, in an `access_control` or a `host_list`, beside addresses and lists.

**hostapd cannot hold one, and says nothing about it.** Measured in a vm
with two hwsim radios and hostapd 2.10, the AP at `02:00:00:00:00:00` and a
station at `02:00:00:00:01:00`:

| accept list holds | `ACCEPT_ACL SHOW` | the station |
|---|---|---|
| the station's address | that address | associates |
| `02:00:00:00:00:00/ff:ff:ff:00:00:00` in the file | `02:00:00:00:00:00` | refused |
| a mask for another OUI | `aa:bb:cc:00:00:00` | refused |
| that mask by `ADD_MAC`, which answers `OK` | `02:00:00:00:00:00` | refused |

So a mask is read as one exact address, from the file and over the socket,
and `aa:bb:cc:*` is refused outright. **A prefix is therefore expanded into
the addresses it matches, and only on a deny list.** The planner denies every
station it sees associated with the prefix -- the observation reads them by
`STA-FIRST` and `STA-NEXT` on the connection it already makes for the lists,
the walk `ap_stations` used and now shares -- and keeps every entry hostapd
already holds that a prefix covers. The second half is what stops it
oscillating: a denied station is disassociated, is not associated on the next
pass, and a set drawn from the associated alone would release it to come
straight back.

**On an allow list a prefix expands against the stations ever seen**
(10.674), since *seen* now persists in fuzznet's records: a station an allow
list refuses never associates, so the associated stations are no source for
it. Until 2026-11-03 it was refused at compile time for that reason.

**What a deny prefix costs**: a matching station associates and is denied
within a pass of the reconcile loop, and after a hostapd restart the window
opens once more, because hostapd starts with the written addresses only.
**Corrected 2026-10-29: under the default `on_drift = "report"` the loop
did not send it**, since `ncfg_reconcile_restrict` dropped the
`access_control.add` as drift -- so a station of a denied manufacturer
stayed connected until somebody ran `ncfg apply`. Found by the lens from
10.599's neighbour-list gap, the same shape: an op planned only from what
was observed after a start. A station put on a deny list is now always
sent; taking one off, and the allow list, stay drift (`reconcile_test`).
`ncfg_access_control_names` is the one answer to "does this list name that
station", read by the planner and by `ap_stations`' `listed`, so `ncfg wifi
clients` should flag a prefix-denied station still connected as it does a
listed one -- by construction, since no test drives that request with a
prefix.

Checked: `lower_test` (normalised, kept apart from the stations, written and
through a list, the allow refusals, short, long and non-hex prefixes),
`render_test` (round trips with and without a list), `plan_access_point_test`
(associated and covered is denied, associated and not is left, held and
covered stays, held and not is removed), `client_test` (the editor's form),
`tests/live/acl.sh` against the fake (the address goes out and the prefix
never does, then it converges), the witness and `make example`. Sabotage:
dropping the held half fails two planner checks; not reading the associated
stations fails two live checks.

**What it does not do yet**: a list on the firewall's side.
**A changed list reaches a running access point**, through the planner's
existing `access_control.add` and `del`: `tests/live/acl.sh` edits only the
`host_list` block, the access point's block unchanged, and the joiner's
`ADD_MAC` and the leaver's `DEL_MAC` arrive with no restart, then nothing is
left to plan. A station the list shares with what hostapd already holds is
kept. That is against `fake_hostapd.py`, which implements the lists as
`hostapd/ctrl_iface.c` does; not resolving lists fails six of its checks. No
real hostapd has held a list from one.
`ncfg_document_validate` does not check that a document read from JSON names
only lists it carries; one compiled here always does.

### Still open

- Wildcard forms beyond the OUI prefix -- a mask, a name pattern -- are not
  asked for. A mask meets the same hostapd limit and would expand the same
  way.

## 10.590 The tray joins a saved network, which is the whole interaction it was for

**Found by walking the aims rather than by a defect.** The brief's second
group "should never meet a permission wall, a tier, or a config file. Joining a
network is the whole interaction" -- and the tray, which is where that person
lives, could show state, disconnect and switch profiles, and could not join
anything. Changing network meant opening the window and finding the wifi tab.

**`Connect to`, a submenu**: the saved networks the last scan heard, strongest
first, the one the radio is on ticked, then `Scan for networks` and `Another
network...`. Two things the tray's header had ruled out stay ruled out:

- **It does not scan on its own.** The list is the last scan *the operator
  chose* from that submenu, with the time it was taken and the daemon's reason
  where the results are the previous scan's. Nothing scans on a timer or on the
  menu opening. Because the menu has closed by the time a scan returns, the
  result is said in a balloon rather than left for a reopening to discover.
- **Nothing needs a plan.** A join is `wifi_connect` by the network's id,
  exactly the wifi tab's, so it is the `wifi` tier and writes nothing; an
  access point no block names has no id and is not offered. `Another
  network...` opens the window on the wifi tab, since a new network is a
  block written. **Superseded in part by 10.652**: writing that block is the
  `wifi` tier too, so the tray now offers the unsaved networks it heard and
  adds one through the add dialog.

Two choices in it worth knowing. **Access points carrying one network are one
entry** at the strongest signal heard, since the supplicant picks the BSS; two
*blocks* naming one SSID -- a passphrase and an enterprise login -- are two
entries labelled with their ids. And **the ticked entry does nothing when
clicked**: selecting the network a station is on can reassociate, a dropped
connection for a click meaning "yes, this one".

**The rule is the client library's, `ncfg_join_choices`**, because the TDE
tray offers the same list and a rule written in each tray is how three
clients came to spell one access point three ways. It was first written in
the Qt tray and moved down within the hour; the Qt side is a conversion.

**The TDE tray does not have it yet**, and that is the open half. It cannot
be built on this machine: `/opt/trinity/include` holds five headers and no
`ksystemtray.h`, so a change there would be code nobody compiled. With the rule
in the client it is a submenu and four wrappers in `ncfg_tde_connection`, for
whoever has the TDE development headers.

Checked: `client_test` holds `ncfg_join_choices` to all of that, plainly and
under ASan and UBSan, and `gui/tests/tray_choices` holds the Qt tray's
conversion to it. The menu and the clicks still want
a notification host, which no machine here has (the measurement is under M8's
entry in section 10's item 5), so they are compiled and not driven.

## 10.588 A mesh (802.11s): the block, and joining it

**What a `mesh` is here**: an 802.11s mesh one radio joins, the third thing a
radio can be after a station and an access point. Every node of a mesh names
the same mesh ID (the block's label), the same channel and the same security,
and peers with any other that does -- no controller, no master. It is the
wireless backhaul of 10.587's list, item 3.

**Decided from the aims, the shape:**

- **Bound to a device, like `access_point`**, because a mesh is something one
  radio does rather than a network any radio may try. The radio does nothing
  else: a second mesh or an access point on it is refused, whichever block is
  written first -- one radio in two modes would have the planner pick one and
  the other plan nothing in silence.
- **`channel` is required.** Mesh points do not search for each other; they
  meet on the channel they were given, so a mesh with no channel may never
  form.
- **SAE or nothing.** 802.11s authenticates peers with SAE alone, so `psk` is
  a SAE password, the document records `proto = "wpa3"` rather than the
  station default it is not, and WPA2, OWE and EAP are refused by name.
- **Its keys travel; its `device` does not**, as an access point's: kind
  numbers `0x0007xxxx`, and the block's default scope is the estate's.

**Built, step 1 (2026-10-29): the block compiles, renders back and plans a
warning.** Grammar, model (`meshes`, appended after `firewall` and left out
when empty, so earlier documents are unchanged), sorting, `ncfg profile save`,
the secret walk, and the scope tables. `ncfg plan` says a mesh is accepted and
not yet joined, which stands until step 2: **the radio's supplicant is not
told about it**. Tests in `lower_test` (each refusal, both orders of the radio
conflict), `render_test` (SAE and open round trips) and `scope_test`; the
witness carries one.

**Built, step 2 (2026-10-29): joining.** A radio given to a mesh wants a
supplicant whether or not a `device` block gives it a `wifi` one, and the
supplicant driver is a radio's for it. The supplicant is given the mesh as its
one network -- `mode 5`, the mesh ID as `ssid`, the channel as a `frequency`,
SAE with `ieee80211w 2` (or `key_mgmt NONE` open) -- cleared first and
selected, the way a wired 802.1X port is given its one network. **What a radio
is handed is digested by one function** (`ncfg_service_radio_fingerprint`):
the executor's record and the observation's comparison both ask it, because
two answers would repopulate the supplicant on every reconcile. The bridging
warning for a three-address station does not fire for a mesh point, which
carries a bridged frame's own addresses.

**Measured before it was written**, in a hull vm over the control socket: each
`SET_NETWORK` answered OK, the interface became a mesh point by itself, and two
nodes peered (`mesh plink: ESTAB`). **Verified by `make hull-mesh`**: netcfgd's
node on wlan0, joined by `ncfg apply` from a `mesh` block and an `interface`
block, and a bare `wpa_supplicant` node from a file on wlan1 in another
network namespace. The peer link is established, a UDP echo crosses (and the
same echo before the apply does not -- the control), and **a second `ncfg plan`
has nothing to do**, which is the record and the observation agreeing. With
the reference node given another password the link stays `LISTEN` and nothing
crosses, so the node is authenticating with its secret. The first run of the
rig found the supplicant driver refused for a radio no `device` block named,
which is how the driver came to ask about meshes. Unit tests in
`supplicant_test` (settings, digest moved by channel and by password) and
`plan_radio_test` (a supplicant with no `wifi` block, none when unmanaged;
sabotaged red once).

**Not built**: ~~a mesh and a station or access point on one radio at once~~
-- **a mesh and an access point, built in 10.687** (a station beside a mesh
is not); and mesh gating to a wired LAN beyond bridging the mesh interface. ~~`ncfg status` saying who the
peers are~~ -- **built, 10.686.**

**Found on the way: the example gate could not see two of the language's ten
blocks.** It read the block heads out of the Rust's lowering, which has eight;
the C's has `firewall` (0294) and `mesh` too, and `firewall` had never been
written in `netcfgd.conf.example`. The gate reads the C's dispatch now and the
example documents both; the NAT section's "NAT in it and nothing else" was
0294's to correct and had not been.

## 10.587 Fast roaming between access points, and the access point modes still missing

**Where the access point stood** (2026-10-29, asked by the holder: "are all
the AP modes implemented? normal, mesh, repeater, ubiquiti style roaming"):
one mode, a plain access point -- SSID, `psk`/`owe`/open security, channel,
band, hidden, regdom, an allow or deny list. Roaming existed only on the
station side (`roam { }` and `bssid` lists, 0089/0090). No mesh, no repeater,
and nothing on the access point side for a station moving between two of them.

**Built: `fast_roaming = true` on an `access_point`**, which is what
"Ubiquiti-style roaming" mostly is -- UniFi's "Fast Roaming" is 802.11r and its
"BSS Transition" is 802.11v.

- **802.11r by FT-PSK with locally derived keys** (hostapd's
  `ft_psk_generate_local`). Each access point derives the roaming keys from
  the passphrase itself, so two machines running one network share nothing but
  the configuration -- which is what makes it fit netcfgd, one machine at a
  time, before fleet management (M9) exists. `ft_over_ds=0`: over the air,
  since over the distribution system is a key exchange through the LAN.
- **The mobility domain is derived** from the SSID: the first two octets of
  SHA-256 over its bytes. Every access point of a network must advertise the
  same one, and deriving it is how independently configured machines agree.
  `mobility_domain = "4f2a"` states one, to join another vendor's access
  points. **The derivation is a wire fact now**: changing it splits every
  network between versions.
- **`nas_identifier` is derived too** (`netcfgd-<domain>`), because hostapd
  refuses FT without one -- measured, "FT (IEEE 802.11r) requires
  nas_identifier to be configured as a 1..48 octet string" -- and the same name
  on every access point works with local derivation, which a two-access-point
  experiment showed before anything was written.
- **`bss_transition=1`** advertises 802.11v transition management. Nothing
  sends a transition request yet; that is steering, below.
- **Key management is stated once** (`ncfg_access_point_key_mgmt`):
  `WPA-PSK FT-PSK` for `wpa2`, `WPA-PSK FT-PSK SAE` for `wpa2+wpa3`. The
  renderer writes it and the planner compares a running access point against
  it, so turning fast roaming on or off restarts the access point naming the
  key management it will run; a moved domain restarts it by its own arm,
  since the key management does not change.
- **Refused by name**: on `wpa3` alone (SAE's keys come out of each
  association, so they would have to travel between access points), on a
  network with no passphrase, and a `mobility_domain` without `fast_roaming`
  (a number copied to make roaming work, silently doing nothing being the worst
  answer).

**Verified** by `make hull-roam`: one vm, three hwsim radios, netcfgd running
two `access_point` blocks offering one SSID, and a bare `wpa_supplicant` that
joins one and roams to the other. Both rendered `mobility_domain=01ff` (computed
off the machine); the first association authenticated as open system (the
control) and the roam as fast transition, `auth_type=2`, in about 220 ms.
With `fast_roaming` taken out the rig fails on exactly those lines. Unit tests
in `hostapd_test`, `lower_test`, `plan_access_point_test` (a sabotage of the
key management comparison turned all three red) and `render_test`; both
witnesses carry the fields.

**What it does not show, said because the number invites it**: the roam
without fast transition took 199 ms in the same rig. hwsim has no radio, so the
4-way handshake FT-PSK saves costs almost nothing there; the rig proves the
mechanism, not a speed-up. On a real radio FT-PSK saves that one handshake --
real but modest. The large saving is on networks whose handshake is expensive,
SAE and 802.1X: SAE is built now (item 1 below), 802.1X is not.

**The example gate compiles against the C now**: it read the Rust's debug
build, which refused `fast_roaming` -- `linkage`'s reason for moving (0266),
met by this gate later.

### What is still missing, in the order worth building

1. **WPA3 fast roaming (FT-SAE) -- built** (2026-10-29). `roaming_key =
   "@secret:NAME"` on an `access_point` with `fast_roaming = true` and a
   `proto` with WPA3 in it adds FT-SAE beside SAE; WPA3 alone with fast
   roaming and no key stays refused, and a key that nothing would use
   (no fast roaming, or WPA2 alone) is refused rather than ignored.
   **Measured in a vm first**, two bare hostapds on two bridges joined by a
   veth: the keys travel over RRB with `r0kh=ff:ff:ff:ff:ff:ff * <key>` and
   `r1kh=00:00:00:00:00:00 00:00:00:00:00:00 <key>`, so nothing lists the
   other access points; **with one `nas_identifier` on both the roam is not
   a fast one** (the target takes itself for the key holder), so an access
   point with a key is named `netcfgd-<domain>-<its radio's address>`; with
   mismatched keys the roam is not a fast one; and FT-PSK still roams fast
   under distinct names with keys mismatched, so transition mode carries both
   in one hostapd and FT-PSK without a key renders exactly as before.
   **The key is its own secret and not derived from the passphrase**:
   whoever holds it can pull any station's PMK-R1 off the LAN, and SAE's
   property is that the passphrase does not get you that. It goes to hostapd
   as SHA-256 of the secret, so the secret is any text and another vendor's
   access point is given `printf %s <secret> | sha256sum`. RRB rides the
   radio's bridge, so a radio in none is warned about. A rotated key is a
   restart, compared as the digest in `r1kh` and folded into
   `secret_matches`. **Found on the way**: the passphrase comparison read
   only `wpa_passphrase`, which a WPA3-only access point does not write, so
   its passphrase was never compared and a rotation never restarted it; it
   reads `sae_password` where there is no `wpa_passphrase` now. `make
   hull-roam-sae` runs two netcfgds, one per namespace and bridge, sharing
   only the configuration and the secrets: a station joins A by SAE (the
   control) and roams to B by FT, both second plans empty; with the two
   stores holding different keys the roam is not a fast one and the rig
   says so.
2. **Neighbour reports (802.11k)** -- `rrm_neighbor_report`, filled by
   `SET_NEIGHBOR`. An access point cannot learn its neighbours; they would be
   declared in the configuration until fleet management can say them.
3. **Mesh (802.11s)**: a `mesh` block joined through `wpa_supplicant`
   (`mode=5`, SAE), as wireless backhaul -- built and joined (10.588).
4. **Repeater.** Four-address (WDS) mode at both ends, `wds = true` (OpenWrt's
   spelling for both). **Measured in a vm first**: without four-address mode
   the kernel will not put a station in a bridge at all and nothing crosses;
   with `4addr on` on the station and hostapd's `wds_sta=1` and `wds_bridge`,
   hostapd makes an interface per station (`wlan0.sta1`) in the bridge and an
   echo crosses -- and **without `wds_bridge` that interface joins no bridge
   and nothing crosses**, so the renderer is told the radio's bridge (its
   device's `master`). **The access point side is built** (2026-10-29):
   `wds = true` on an `access_point` renders both lines, a change restarts it,
   and a radio in no bridge is warned about. **The station side is built
   too** (2026-10-29): `device { wifi { wds = true } }` is a
   `link.set_wds` op -- nl80211 `SET_INTERFACE` with `4ADDR`, planned
   before the radio's `set_master` because a three-address station cannot be
   enslaved -- the supplicant is started with `-b <bridge>`, `plan/radio.c`'s
   bridging warning is lifted for it, and the observation reads each
   interface's `4addr` back (`wds` on a link), so a second plan is empty.
   **And the access point's own radio is not enslaved by netcfgd**: the
   kernel refuses `EOPNOTSUPP` for an AP-type interface before hostapd has
   it, so `ncfg_plan_master` skips an access point's radio and hostapd is
   given `bridge=` and does it. That was a fault in the AP side as first
   committed, found by the rig. `make hull-wds` checks both ends, each
   against a reference end (a bare four-address `wpa_supplicant`; a bare
   hostapd with `wds_sta`): a UDP echo from a host behind the repeater to
   one on the LAN, silent before the apply and crossing after it, both
   halves. Multi-AP backhaul (`multi_ap`) and a routed relay are the
   alternatives beside it, not built.
5. **Steering**: band steering and a minimum-signal kick are policy loops over
   802.11v transition requests, and want the neighbour reports first.

All five can be checked in hull on hwsim, as this was.

## 10.586 A card's port type: reported, and who should set it

**What it is about.** A VPI card -- the ConnectX family -- runs each port as
Ethernet or as InfiniBand, and a port in InfiniBand mode has no Ethernet
interface at all: a configuration naming one meets an interface that is not
there, and nothing in rtnetlink says why. The holder's cards: QLogic IBA7322
QDR HCAs (`ib_qib`, InfiniBand only) are being replaced by ConnectX VPI cards
run as Ethernet for file sharing, where InfiniBand buys nothing -- RDMA still
works as RoCE (NFS over RDMA, SMB Direct), and Ethernet needs no subnet
manager. So InfiniBand interfaces themselves (IPoIB, pkeys, connected mode)
are not being built.

**Built: the port type, read only** (2026-10-29). The observation carries
`ports` -- every physical port devlink describes, from one `PORT_GET` dump per
observation: device (`pci/0000:05:00.0`), number, type (`eth`, `ib`, `auto`,
`notset`), and the interface or RDMA device it became. devlink is the
kernel's vendor-neutral description of a card's ports, and the dump needs no
privilege. CPU ports, a switch's internal ones and representors are devlink
ports too and are left out; a port that will not read is left out with a
note. `ncfg status` prints a *card ports* section; a port running as
InfiniBand says there is no Ethernet interface because of it, names its RDMA
device, and gives `devlink port set <device>/<n> type eth`. Checked on this
machine's real ConnectX-3 Pro (ml350g6-01, `05:00.0`): both ports `eth`, as
eth2 and eth3, as `devlink port show` says. `devlink_test`, a replay through
the observation in `current_test` (an Ethernet port, an InfiniBand one, a
CPU port and an unnumbered one), the witness, and `kernel_bytes` fuzzing.

**Not built: setting it, and the two ways differ in whose job they are.**

- **The firmware default is openmlx4's, by hand, once.** `LINK_TYPE_P1/P2` is
  NV configuration read at the next boot; openmlx4 `config set` writes it for
  the ConnectX-3 generation, `mstconfig` for ConnectX-4 and later. A reconcile
  loop must not drive it: it cannot converge without a reboot, so a plan would
  carry the change until one happened; and writing a card's firmware from a
  configuration daemon is the kind of act openmlx4's safety model exists to
  keep deliberate. netcfgd depending on a firmware tool would also be its first
  mandatory external tool for a card setting. Choosing a card's mode once, for
  good, is exactly what the holder's cards need -- **with the holder's caution
  (2026-10-29): openmlx4 has been tested thoroughly against every known source
  but little on real cards**, so a firmware write with it is the least proven
  step on offer. Its own `dump` first, which is the card's identity and what
  makes a rescue avoidable.
- **Which is a point for the runtime half below**: it writes no firmware, and
  a driver reload puts the firmware's default back.
- **The runtime type is netcfgd-shaped, and is the open half.**
  `DEVLINK_CMD_PORT_SET` with a type is generic, takes effect at once, and a
  daemon re-applying it at start makes it as lasting as the configuration --
  which is netcfgd's whole model. In mainline only mlx4 implements it (mlx5's
  type is firmware only), it needs `CAP_NET_ADMIN`, and it destroys the
  interface it replaces. Building it means: a card-keyed block, since the
  setting belongs to a PCI device's port and not to a netdev that may not
  exist yet; a plan that sets types before anything is planned for the
  interfaces they create; and renaming (`eth2` becomes `ib0` and back).
  **Not built because it cannot be checked here**: this kernel ships no
  `netdevsim`, no VM can have an mlx4, and hull does not pass a PCI device
  into a vm (its draft did; it no longer declares it). **Passing the real
  card through is not a rig either**: the holder, 2026-11-13, "testing like
  this will still brick hardware" -- a guest driving the card's real
  firmware is the card at risk, whoever's kernel it runs in. So this waits
  for something that can be checked without a real card, and is not to be
  proposed as a hull request.

## 10.585 What the kernel lets a moving machine do with its regulatory domain

**Measured 2026-10-27 for [0296](doc/decision/0296-the-regulatory-domain-follows-the-machine.md),
by `make hull-regdom`** (`tests/hull/regdom/`): three `mac80211_hwsim` radios
in a vm on the host's kernel (6.12, cfg80211 a module, signed regdb
required), cfg80211 reloaded between experiments for a fresh domain, and the
global country read from `iw reg get` after each step. Four runs; the
readings were the same in every run that took them.

**The kernel already follows a moving machine, one association at a time,
provided the machine goes idle between countries.**

    associated to DE's access point             00 -> DE at once        E4
    disconnected, nothing else running          DE -> 00 at once        E16
    associated to US's access point             00 -> US at once        E17
    SE set by hand, then associated to DE       SE -> DE at once        E10, E20
    the same through the supplicant's country=  SE -> DE at once        E13
    SE by hand, DE heard, then idle             DE -> SE at once        E21
    a scan that hears DE, never associating     stays 00                E3

So a country heard from the associated access point wins over one set by
hand or by `wpa_supplicant`'s `country=` -- which is what `wifi.set_regdom`
sends -- and on idle the domain returns to the hand-set country, or to the
world domain where there is none. A scan alone moves nothing.

**And it sticks while anything else on the machine is not idle.** With an
access point running in the same kernel, a disconnect left DE in place for
the full ten seconds, and associating to US afterwards still read DE:

    disconnected from DE, an access point up    stays DE                E5, E7, E11, E14
    then associated to US                       stays DE                E8

E7 and E8 read at first as "the first country heard sticks", which is the
holder's complaint exactly. **They were the rig**: its own access points kept
the machine from being idle. E15 to E17 are the same move with the access
point stopped after the disconnect, and the domain follows. Kept because a
real machine can be in the same state -- a laptop sharing its connection as
a hotspot will not follow, by the same mechanism.

**hostapd's `country_code` sets the whole machine's domain** (E1, at once),
and **hostapd will not run if it cannot**: in a user namespace of its own it
waits for the change it asked for and disables the interface
(`COUNTRY_UPDATE->DISABLED`). For netcfgd that means an `access_point` with
a `regdom` is a machine-wide setting today, which the example file does not
say. For the rig it meant no access point configured with `country_code` can
be a clean instrument; the access points advertise the Country element as
raw bytes through `vendor_elements` instead, with `country_code` unset, and
E2 checks the domain stays at 00 while the station hears DE.

**Channels 12 and 13, measured the same day: US disables them, the world
domain allows them only passively, and joining any ordinary network opens
them.** On a radio following the global domain, with channel 14 as the
control (Japan's alone), the rig's table reads:

    00 (world)   12 noIR   13 noIR   14 noIR
    US           12 off    13 off    14 off
    DE, GB       12 ok     13 ok     14 off
    JP           12 ok     13 ok     14 ok

Of twelve countries checked by the probe, US was the only one without 12 and
13. So a laptop set to US and carried to Europe cannot see a network on 13 at
all -- and the moment it joins any network on 1 to 11 there, association
adopts that access point's country (E4, E10, E17) and 12 and 13 open. That is
a conclusion composed from two measurements, not one run: a plain radio's
channels were the global domain's in every reading, which is what lets them
compose. **So the stuck case is narrower than first written**: a machine in
the wrong domain somewhere every network it could join is on a channel that
domain forbids -- and, measured below, only when that domain was set by hand.

**Measured across two kernels the same day, and the stuck case is a country
set by hand, never an unset one.** One kernel could not hold an access point
on a channel its station is forbidden: hwsim's `regtest=7` gives radio 0 a
driver hint of its own, and a country set by hand still reached it (13 `off`
under US, `noIR` under the world), and hwsim's custom domains stop at
channel 11. So `wire.conf` runs two vms on a segment -- the access point's in
DE with a real hostapd, `country_code` and all, on channel 13 -- and
`relay.py` in each registers with hwsim over generic netlink and carries
every frame across over UDP, which is what `wmediumd` does within one kernel.
Two runs, identical:

    station's domain      ch 13 before   hears it   ch 13 after scan   joins   domain after
    DE (the control)      ok             DE         ok                 yes     DE
    nothing set (00)      noIR           DE         ok                 yes     DE, at once
    US, set by hand       off            nothing    off                no      US

**The world domain heals itself**: the beacon is heard passively, cfg80211's
beacon hint lifts `noIR` on that channel, the station joins and adopts the
country. **A country set by hand that forbids the channel is stuck**: the
access point is invisible, nothing is joined, nothing tells the kernel where
it is -- and E21 says idle returns to that country rather than to the world.

**That is the design constraint 0296's mechanism has to meet.** Setting a
country by hand is the one act that can strand a machine, and it outlives
every move until it is set again. So a location source that sets the domain
must be right or stay silent: a stale fix carried across a border is exactly
how a laptop gets US in Europe. Leaving the domain unset and letting
association and beacon hints work is safe everywhere this rig has looked; a
country set from location is an improvement only where the source is
current.

The relay is an instrument and is checked as one: the control has to join
through it or the run fails, and every transmitter address it sees must be
one it computed (`42:00:00:00:<idx>:00`, hwsim's permanent address with the
0x40 bit), or a relay injecting to the wrong radio would drop everything
silently. "Refused" in its counts is the kernel declining frames for a
channel the radio was not on -- some during any scan, all of them under US.
Not built: channel widths beyond 20 MHz, and scanning 6 GHz while associated on another band, which this rig cannot do.

**5 GHz and radar channels, the same relay, the same answer** (`wire5.conf`,
two runs). Four access points in a US kernel -- 36, radar channels 52 and
100, and 149 -- and the station in each domain in turn, a fresh kernel per
access point since joining one adopts a country:

    station's domain   36       52 (radar)   100 (radar)   149
    US (control)       joins    joins        joins         joins
    nothing set (00)   joins    joins        joins         joins
    JP, set by hand    joins    joins        joins         invisible, stays JP
    CN, set by hand    joins    joins        invisible     joins

Every join adopted US at once. **The world domain joins radar channels too**,
and there the beacon does not lift `noIR` -- the flag reads the same after
the scan -- yet association works; on 36 and 149 it is lifted as at 2.4 GHz.
**A country set by hand strands the machine exactly in that country's
gaps**: JP has no band at 149, CN none at 100 to 140, and an access point
there is invisible to it.

**And no gap between Europe and the US on these channels**, which was the
case this half was first written to find. The table:

    00        36 noIR   52 noIR,radar   100 noIR,radar   149 noIR   165 noIR
    US, DE, GB 36 ok    52 radar        100 radar        149 ok     165 ok
    JP        36 ok     52 radar        100 radar        149 off    165 off
    CN        36 ok     52 radar        100 off          149 ok     165 ok

The first run's control assumed channel 165 is unusable in Europe and failed
on DE; the parser was right and the premise was not -- this regulatory
database allows 5725-5875 MHz in DE and GB. The control is CN's channel 100
now, which China has no band for.

**One thing unexplained.** hostapd logged a completed radar check on its own
interface for all four access points, 36 and 149 included, which the US
table does not mark radar, and all four came up together after about 60
seconds. It changes nothing the station reads, and the logs went with the
vm; recorded rather than guessed at.

**6 GHz breaks the pattern: there, an unset machine does not heal**
(`wire6.conf`). The world domain has no 6 GHz at all, so a machine with no
country set cannot see a 6 GHz access point, cannot join one, and nothing
on that band will ever tell it where it is:

    station's domain   ca5 (5975 MHz)              ca101 (6455 MHz)
    CA (control)       joins                       joins
    nothing set (00)   invisible, stays 00         invisible, stays 00
    US                 joins, adopts CA            joins, adopts CA
    DE                 joins, adopts CA            invisible, stays DE
    CN                 invisible                   invisible

    00         5975 off   6135 off   6455 off   6615 off   6875 off
    US         all five noIR (the database says PASSIVE-SCAN)
    CA         all five ok
    DE, GB, JP 5975 ok    6135 ok    6455 off   6615 off   6875 off
    CN         all five off

So the conclusion drawn from 2.4 and 5 GHz -- leaving the domain unset is
safe everywhere -- **does not hold at 6 GHz**: unset means no 6 GHz until
something else sets a country, which in practice is joining a 2.4 or 5 GHz
network first. A 6 GHz-only network is unreachable to it. That is the one
place measured where a location source does not merely avoid harm but
supplies something nothing else can, and it is worth weighing in 0296's
mechanism: the cost of a wrong country (stranded in its gaps) against the
cost of none (no 6 GHz at all).

**And US cannot run a 6 GHz access point from Linux with this database.** It
marks US 5925-7125 MHz `PASSIVE-SCAN`, every channel is `NO_IR`, and hostapd
refuses: "Frequency 5975 (primary) not allowed for AP mode". The first 6 GHz
run put the access points in US and both refused to start; a probe read the
rule for twelve countries, and CA, BR and SA allow the whole band without
it, so the access points are in CA. A US station still joins them -- like the
world domain on 5 GHz radar channels, `noIR` stays set and association works
anyway. For netcfgd that means an `access_point` on 6 GHz in a US-domain
machine cannot work, which `ncfg plan` should be able to say before hostapd
does.

6 GHz admits no open network, so these access points are WPA3 -- SAE with
hash-to-element and protected management frames -- and the station joins
through `wpa_supplicant`, not `iw connect`.

**RNR, measured: the report does not make 6 GHz visible to an unset machine,
and whether it can move there afterwards is not something this rig can
answer** (`wire_rnr.conf`). One hostapd process runs `home` twice in a CA
kernel -- 5 GHz channel 36 with `rnr=1`, and 6 GHz at 5975 MHz, both WPA3 --
and the 5 GHz beacon carries element 201 naming the other (`83 05`: operating
class 131, channel 5). The station joins through wpa_supplicant:

    station's domain   plain scan sees       joins first   domain after
    CA (control)       5 GHz, 6 GHz, report  5975 MHz      CA
    nothing set (00)   5 GHz, report         5180 MHz      CA
    DE, US             5 GHz, 6 GHz, report  5975 MHz      CA
    CN                 5 GHz, report         5180 MHz      CA

The unset machine hears the report naming the 6 GHz BSS and cannot list the
