BSS itself -- its 6 GHz is off -- so it joins 5 GHz and adopts CA, after
which 5975 reads `ok`. **It then never reaches 6 GHz, and that reading is the
rig's, not the regulation's**: with CA set by hand and the join pinned to
5 GHz, a scan of 5975 while associated finds nothing either. Scanning 6 GHz
while associated on 5 GHz does not work here, for reasons in hwsim or the
relay that were not chased.

**What follows by deduction, not measurement**: an unset machine can reach
6 GHz only by a move that never goes idle, since idle returns it to the world
domain (E16), where 6 GHz is off again. A supplicant that disconnects to
change band undoes the country that made the band reachable.

**Two instrument faults, both caught by the run's own check.** The first
three runs read "no report" because `iw scan` prints no element it does not
parse unless given `-u`; the element was in the beacon throughout, and was
misattributed first to hostapd building the beacon too early -- the
`update_beacon` added for that stays, harmless. And hull refuses a machine
name with an underscore (`ap_rnr`), which is a DNS label rule; the machines
are `ap-rnr` and `station-rnr`, the files keep theirs.

**A roam keeps the country, and takes up the next one; only a disconnect
passes through the world domain** (`wire_roam.conf`). Four open access points
on 2.4 GHz channel 1 -- one network advertising DE twice, one spanning a
border, DE and US -- and a station with no country set that joins the first
by BSSID, scans while connected (same channel, which this rig can do) and
roams with `wpa_cli roam`, the domain sampled every 50 ms throughout:

    within a country, DE to DE          DE, throughout
    across a border, DE to US (roam)    DE, then US -- no world domain between
    the same move by disconnecting      DE, 00, then US

So the move that never goes idle is a roam, and it is enough: cfg80211 takes
the new access point's country on the reassociation. The trap the RNR half
deduced is real in the third row -- a supplicant that changes access point
by disconnecting spends a moment in the world domain, which at 6 GHz is the
band switched off. **Not measured is whether a 5-to-6 GHz move is a roam**,
since this rig cannot scan 6 GHz while associated.

**And a sampler fault, caught by its own check.** The first cross-border run
read "US" alone: the sampler started in the background and the roam
finished before its first reading, so anything before US was invisible. It
now waits for two readings before the roam, and a sequence that does not
begin with the country before the move is "not measured".

**The first piece of 0296 is built: the observation carries the domain**
(2026-10-27, moved into the observation 2026-10-28). Where the observation
has a radio, a round beside the offloads and WireGuard asks nl80211 `GET_REG`
over the same generic netlink seam and stores the country in
`observed.regdom` -- so the daemon has it on every tick, a client reads it in
the `status` answer, `observed.json` carries it, and `ncfg status` prints it
under the listing (for `00`, that no country is set and 6 GHz is off). It was
first a note only the command line printed, on the reasoning that the
observed witness is shared with the Rust; it is not -- the C writes the
witnesses since 0279 -- and a fact clients need belongs where the daemon
answers from. What it cannot say is *who* set the domain: `GET_REG` does not
carry the initiator, only the `REG_CHANGE` notification does, so "and from
what" waits for a daemon that listens. The family lookup the offloads and
WireGuard rounds each carried is one `observe_genl_family` now, and
`family_open` moved out of `kernel_genl.c` unchanged into `genl_socket.c`.

**The override is built: `global { regdom = "XX" }`** (2026-10-28). It is
`global` because the kernel keeps one domain; a radio's own key stays inert and
its warning now points here. The planner sets it through a radio's supplicant
(`wifi.set_regdom`, whose executor already existed) **only when the domain
differs and no radio is associated**, which is what the measurements above
decide: associated, the kernel follows the access point and should; idle, it
returns to a country set by hand by itself, so once set it stays set without
netcfgd fighting anybody. With no supplicant of netcfgd's on a radio, the plan
says it is not set yet. Verified end to end in a vm: the built daemon with
`regdom = "DE"` took a fresh kernel from `00` to `DE` in about a second,
`ncfg status` read `DE`.

**Who set the domain is built** (2026-10-28, asked for by the holder). A
`GET_REG` reply carries the country and its rules and no initiator
(attributes 33 and 34, read off a real kernel), so the daemon subscribes to
nl80211's `regulatory` group -- a sixth watch, its own generic netlink socket,
joined by group number since nl80211's are above the 32 a bind mask reaches --
and keeps the last `REG_CHANGE` it heard on its state. Every observation it
takes passes through `ncfg_daemon_state_reobserve`, which stamps
`observed.regdom_set_by` (`kernel`, `user`, `driver`, `access_point`) **only
where the country heard is the country observed**: the notification and the
question are two messages, and a setter put on a country it was not heard
setting is a wrong answer where none is the honest one. A lost notification
(`ENOBUFS`, a cut datagram, one that will not read) forgets what was heard. A
change made before the daemon started has no setter, which is the boot case
and is said by saying nothing rather than by guessing. The kernel sends no
country for the world domain, a custom world or an intersection, only the
type; those are `00`, `99` and `98`, the names `GET_REG` uses. `user` is all
of user space: `iw reg set`, netcfgd's own `global { regdom }` and hostapd's
`country_code` are one request to the kernel.

**`ncfg status` observes for itself and asks a running daemon for the setter
alone**, under the stamp's rule: only where the daemon's domain is the one it
just observed. Its own observation never could carry this, since only a
process subscribed at the time heard it. **Taking the daemon's whole
observation was built first and rejected the same day**: `tests/live/qdisc.sh`
sets a qdisc with `tc` and asks 0.3 s later, and the daemon watches no `tc`
group, so its observation was a pass old -- as it is for any sysctl, ethtool
setting or resolver file -- and two checks failed. Having a status request
cost the daemon a fresh observation would give both, and is the route the
loop declines on purpose: a polling client would hold it at an observation a
second (`ncfg_main_woke_for`). Whether the daemon's `status` answer should be
fresher is a question about every client, not about this field, and is not
decided here. `ncfg_observed_from_status` reads the answer (the type reader's
`tag` slot sets the envelope's `response` aside); a daemon absent, refusing
the caller's tier, or answering something unreadable costs the listing that
one fact and nothing else.

Verified by `make hull-regdom-heard`: the access point of the two-kernel rig,
and a station running the host's build with an empty configuration. Before
anything moves the daemon names nobody (the control: `00` set before it
started); joining `de13` from the world domain, `DE access_point` within 0.1 s
and `ncfg status` printing "set by the access point this machine is
associated to"; leaving, `00 kernel`; `iw reg set SE`, `SE user`. Unit-level,
`regdom_test` (the notification's three shapes, a radio's own change and
another family's message passed over, four refusals), `daemon_test` (the
stamp, its mismatch, a reload keeping it, a loss forgetting it) and
`cli_test` (the status answer read, the setter taken only for the same
domain), each with a sabotage that turned it red; `kernel_bytes` fuzzes the
notification parser, seeded with one. **What it does not survive: cfg80211 unloaded and reloaded under a
running daemon.** The family is re-registered with a new id and the old
subscription is gone without a word, and a radio attaching retries only
where nothing is subscribed. Rare outside a rig; noticing it would mean
watching the genl controller's own notifications, and it has not earned that.
**One test-harness fault found on the way, and fixed after it**: a
`cli_test` fake daemon that was never connected to waited for ever, so
sabotaging a route to the daemon hung the suite rather than failing it. The
fake now gives up after ten seconds by `alarm`, and `answered` reports a fake
nobody asked as a failure naming the verb -- a route reporting nobody there
fails 24 checks in under two minutes instead of hanging.

**And one instrument fault, caught by the control.** The first table read
channel 14 as usable under US, which it is not anywhere but Japan: `iw`
prints a disabled channel as `(disabled)` and the parser matched
`Disabled`, so every disabled channel read as usable, and a `grep -A3`
window read some channels' flags off their neighbours. Channel 14 is in the
table so that fault cannot recur unseen.

**Also not measured**: two access points disagreeing (the kernel takes the
associated one's country, so 0296's "agreement across several" is netcfgd's
to do from scans, not the kernel's); a roam between countries without a
disconnect (`iw connect` over a live association was refused, E19); drivers
that manage their own domain in firmware, which hwsim cannot stand in for.

**The holder's direction, given while this ran: fuzznet's location subsystem
should be the main source.** It is the source that knows the country *before*
association, which is what the gap above needs, and on a laptop with no GPS
it can carry a fix from another of the owner's machines. Two things stand
between it and a regulatory domain, and neither is designed:

- **fuzznet has no country.** Its `location/` holds fixes -- latitude,
  longitude, accuracy, from gpsd -- and nothing in its code or `project.md`
  maps one to a country or names ISO 3166. **The holder placed the lookup in
  fuzznet, 2026-10-27, possibly using an online service.** That is fuzznet's
  to design; netcfgd left the need in its inbox (20261027T1557Z): an ISO
  3166-1 alpha-2 code with its age and provenance, and an explicit unknown --
  and, since an online lookup sends the machine's position to a third party,
  a pointer to fuzznet's open per-recipient precision question.
- **netcfgd's fuzznet edge is design, not build** (decision 0133), so reading
  a fix means netcfgd talking to a fuzznet node, which nothing does today.

This amends 0296's first bullet -- the country inferred from what the radio
hears -- to a second source behind a primary one; it is recorded here rather
than in 0296, which is accepted, and wants a record of its own once the
mechanism is designed.

## 10.578 The refusal arm, made cheap by one knob the other path already had

10.574 named this arm unexercised and priced it at the full 3000 ms. The price
was wrong, and the reason it was wrong is the finding: **`confirm_stopped`
already took `machine->patience_ms` and the waiter added to `stop_recorded` did
not.** One question -- how long to wait for a client to go -- had a knob on one
path and a constant on the other.

Threaded through, so both paths read the same figure. The field's own comment
said *"How long a stop waits for `dhcpcd -k`"*, which was true when only the
dhcpcd branch consulted it; it says both paths now, because a machine wanting a
different patience wants it for whichever client it runs rather than for one of
three.

### The test the knob paid for

A client that **ignores `TERM` outright** -- `trap '' TERM`, not merely slow,
since anything slow races a process that was going to exit anyway -- with
`patience_ms` at 100. The stop must refuse, and the refusal must name the
client and the interface and say the pid file was kept.

**The pid file surviving is the point rather than a detail.** It is what lets
the next pass find the client at all, so a stop that forgot an unkillable one
would make it permanently unidentifiable -- which is `pppoe`'s measured
incident (10.476) arriving in another backend, and the thing 10.571's four
fixes were all about.

### The control hung rather than failing, which is a better answer

With the refusal arm disabled the test did not fail -- **it hung**, and the
runner killed it at 120 seconds. Of course it did: the client ignores the
signal, so without a patience the loop has no exit at all. So the arm is not
merely a better error message, it is **the bound on an unbounded wait**, and a
daemon without it would spin in a reconcile pass forever on one stubborn
client.

`running-code.md` asks what makes a loop stop before it is run. This is that
question answered from the other end: the thing that makes it stop is the
thing a test had never exercised.

### What it broke, and why that was the useful part

Threading the figure through turned an older test's success into a refusal:
`a_recorded_client_slow_to_exit_is_waited_for` drives a stand-in that takes
about 500 ms, and `a_machine` sets 200 ms because two other tests drive clients
that never stop. The fixture had been **passing on a default it did not
mention**, and only became a race when that default started reaching it.

Both figures are stated together now -- the slow test sets 1500 ms for itself
and says why, and `a_machine`'s comment says its 200 reaches both paths. A
fixture whose correctness depends on a number declared in another function is
one nobody can read.

## 10.577 The lens from today's bugs found one more, and taught what a SIGPIPE guard can be tested for

Four defects in one day shared a shape: **a guard applied in one place and
absent in a sibling doing the same thing** -- `pppoe`'s stop wait missing from
four backends, `answer.c`'s `MSG_NOSIGNAL` missing from `management.c`,
`c_nm_signals.sh`'s kill-by-pid missing from two live scripts.
`working-practice.md` says to derive the next lens from the last bug, so the
sweep asked the question that shape implies: **which other socket writes lack
`MSG_NOSIGNAL`?**

### One real instance

**`apply/dhcpcd_control.c` wrote to dhcpcd's control socket with a plain
`write`**, in a loop, over `AF_UNIX`/`SOCK_STREAM`. In production that code
runs inside the daemon holding `CAP_NET_ADMIN`.

**And the peer is one netcfgd may have just asked to die**, which is what puts
it in the same class rather than merely near it: `confirm_stopped` reads this
socket in a loop *after* the stop has sent `-k`, so the window where dhcpcd is
closing is a window netcfgd deliberately stands in. `send(..., MSG_NOSIGNAL)`
now, as `answer.c` and `management.c` do.

### Two candidates cleared, and the reasons are worth keeping

So the next sweep does not re-examine them:

- **`backend/supplicant/client.c` is `SOCK_DGRAM`.** A datagram socket whose
  peer is gone gives `ECONNREFUSED`, not `SIGPIPE`. Exempt by protocol rather
  than by care.
- **`host/portal.c`'s HTTP write runs in a privilege-shed child with a death
  timer.** `ncfg_portal_fetch` is called after `ncfg_privilege_shed` and
  `ncfg_privilege_die_after`, so a `SIGPIPE` there kills a process designed to
  be disposable and the parent reads a failed probe. Worth a better message
  some day; not a daemon death.
- The remaining `write` calls are to pipes in forked children whose reader is
  the parent that forked them, so the peer is alive by construction.

### What the control taught, which is more useful than the fix

A fixture was written, and **it passed with the guard removed** -- so it never
reached the write at all. Which is the trap this tree had just written up about
openvpn (10.573), walked into again within the hour.

The diagnosis is the finding: **whether a SIGPIPE guard is testable from
outside depends on whether the protocol reads before it writes.**

- openvpn's management client connects, **reads the greeting**, then writes.
  That read is a window a stand-in can close in, and a marker file makes the
  ordering deterministic.
- `dhcpcd_control.c` connects and writes immediately. There is no window, so
  nothing outside the process can place a close between the two. A stand-in
  that closes early is simply not listening when netcfgd connects, and the
  connect fails before any write.

**So the fixture was removed rather than kept.** It asserted that the call
returned, which it does either way: a check that cannot fail reads as
coverage, which is the thing this tree says is worse than an absent check --
and keeping it would have been that sentence written one hour earlier and
ignored one hour later.

**The guard therefore rests on inspection and on the two siblings that are
tested.** Stated plainly rather than implied: `management.c`'s equivalent has a
deterministic control that exits 141 without it, `answer.c` carries the rule
with its own incident, and this third site is the same call on the same kind of
socket for the same reason. Reaching it under test would need a delay injected
into netcfgd between connect and write, which is a production seam added for a
test and not worth it for a one-word change.

## 10.574 A daemon that left under the command is a stop that took

10.573 recorded this as deliberately unfixed and said it wanted its own commit
and test. Done here, and the change is to stop semantics rather than to a
signal disposition, which is why it is separate.

**`Broken pipe` from `signal SIGTERM` is the ordinary way openvpn says it is
going**: the socket closes under netcfgd's write. The stop reported that as a
failure, which asks an operator to fix a tunnel that is gone -- and this file
already held the rule in its own words a few lines above, *stopping one that
is already stopped is not an error*.

**It asks by waiting rather than by reading the errno.** `EPIPE` is the shape
that was measured; a daemon can also close before the write and give `no answer
to \`signal SIGTERM\`` from the read, which is what the new fixture actually
produces. Keying on an errno would have covered the instance and missed the
class, so the arm calls the same `wait_for_exit` the rest of the stop uses: if
the daemon has gone, the stop took.

**The refusal arm is unchanged, and that was the thing to be careful about.** A
daemon genuinely alive and refusing still costs the patience and still gets the
named refusal 10.571 describes -- the sentence exists because a complaint about
neither of two tunnels is useless to an operator, and nothing here weakens it.

### A tidy-up that now has two callers, so it has one place

Arriving at "the tunnel is gone" by two routes meant two tidy-ups, and a
tidy-up that differs between them is how one of them leaves a management
socket that takes the bind on the next start. `forget_tunnel` is that one
place: pid file, socket, credentials.

### The fixture, and what it is not

A listener that greets and hangs up, and **no pid file at all** -- which is the
state a daemon that has finished leaving is in, and is what makes netcfgd take
the management path rather than the pid one. The assertions are that the stop
succeeds and that the socket is gone afterwards, the second being the one that
matters for the next start. Sabotaged by removing the arm: both fail.

**~~The refusal arm is not exercised~~ -- both are now.** dhcp's is 10.578,
and the cost quoted here was wrong: `machine->patience_ms` makes it a tenth of
a second, and `confirm_stopped` had that knob all along while the waiter here
used a constant. With it disabled that test hangs rather than failing, a
client ignoring `TERM` giving the loop no other exit.

**openvpn's is bought at the full 3000 ms**, its patience being a `#define`
rather than a field, and adding a parameter to a public stop for a test is the
production seam 10.578 declined. It asserts the keeping rather than the
sentence: the pid file must survive, because removing it while the daemon
lives is the socket collision proved earlier in that file. Sabotaged, four
checks fail and the pid file is deleted.

## 10.573 Telling openvpn to stop could kill netcfgd, found by a test failing under load

`make check` went red after the management-path fixture landed, with
`c: some checks failed` and **no failing check named anywhere in ten thousand
lines of log**. The same target had passed standalone minutes earlier. What it
turned out to be is a real defect in netcfgd, and the way it hid is worth as
much as the defect.

### The defect

`management.c` sent a command as two plain `write()` calls -- the command, then
its newline -- to a unix socket whose peer is openvpn. **The command netcfgd
most often sends is `signal SIGTERM`**, so netcfgd was writing to a process it
was in the act of telling to die. A peer that closes between the two writes
makes the second raise `SIGPIPE`, whose default action ends the process -- and
that process is the daemon holding `CAP_NET_ADMIN`.

**The rule was already written down in this tree, for the other direction.**
`answer.c` uses `send` with `MSG_NOSIGNAL` and says why: *"a client that hung
up between the accept and the answer would otherwise raise `SIGPIPE` and end
the daemon. That is not hypothetical... A daemon holding `CAP_NET_ADMIN` must
not be killable by a client disconnecting."* `deliver.c` guards the same hazard
with `sigaction` around a write. The management client was written with `write`
anyway.

So this is not a hazard nobody had considered. It is **a rule learned on one
socket and not carried to the socket where the peer's death is intended rather
than merely possible** -- the same shape as 10.571's four-of-five stop bugs,
where `pppoe`'s lesson had not reached its siblings.

Both writes use `send(..., MSG_NOSIGNAL)` now. `EPIPE` comes back as an error
with a sentence, which is what a refusal has to be here.

### How it hid, which is the transferable half

Three things stacked, and each alone would have been survivable:

1. **A process killed by `SIGPIPE` prints nothing and fails no check.** It
   stops. There is no `FAILED` line to grep for, because nothing got as far as
   deciding anything was wrong.
2. **Its buffered stdout dies with it.** Measured in the control below: the
   output ends mid-sentence at `rather than the tail, whi`, several tests
   *before* the one that died, because everything after the last flush was in
   a buffer nobody wrote. So the log points at the wrong place, which is worse
   than pointing nowhere.
3. **The suite redirects its own stderr** for a later test, and the redirect
   spans the calls that died. Anything the kernel or the shell might have said
   went into a file the suite then deleted.

The visible result was a gate that said `c: some checks failed` and an
openvpn suite whose early checks appeared and whose summary never did. **Seven
of its check texts were in the log and none of the new ones**, which is what
located it: not a failure message, but the absence of output after a known
point.

### Why it was intermittent, and why that was the clue rather than the excuse

The peer has to close before netcfgd writes, which needs an interleaving.
Standalone the test won the race every time; under `make check` -- with three
other sessions' builds running, and `Resource temporarily unavailable` from a
thread spawn elsewhere in the same log -- it lost it.

**The comfortable explanation was available and wrong**: the machine was
loaded, the new fixture is timing-dependent, re-run it. `running-code.md` names
that trap -- *a comfortable explanation that ends an investigation is more
expensive than no explanation at all* -- and the fixture really was
timing-dependent, so the comfortable story was even true as far as it went. It
was not the whole of it: load did not cause the bug, it only made the window
wide enough to fall into.

### What the fixture needed to become a test, in three wrong versions

The first draft read one byte then closed, and reported `no answer to
\`signal SIGTERM\``: both writes had succeeded and the READ had failed, so it
was exercising the reply path while claiming the write path. The second closed
without reading and reported the same thing, netcfgd being quicker than the
child. The third waited on a marker the child never wrote -- an edit that had
aborted before saving -- so a two-second timeout did the synchronising, the
marker check failed, and **the test passed for the wrong reason**.

What works is a handshake: the child closes, writes a marker, and the parent
waits for the marker before sending. Now the message is
`could not send \`signal SIGTERM\`: Broken pipe` every time, which is the write
path and nothing else.

**And a check of mine was vacuous on the way through** -- `message[0] != '\0'
|| 1`, which cannot fail -- replaced with `!sent && message[0] != '\0'`. A
check that cannot fail reads as coverage, which is worse than an absent one.

### The control

With `MSG_NOSIGNAL` removed, `./c/tests/openvpn_test` exits **141** -- 128 plus
`SIGPIPE` -- with its output truncated mid-line. With it, the command returns
an error carrying a sentence and the suite passes. So the fix is proved against
the failure it prevents, and the test is proved against the fix.

### What is not fixed, and is a question rather than an oversight

**An `EPIPE` mid-command now reports a failed stop for a tunnel that may be
gone.** If openvpn closed the management socket because it was already exiting,
netcfgd says `could not stop the openvpn tunnel`, where the honest answer is
that the tunnel is stopping. The existing code falls back to the pid path only
when the *connect* fails, not when a command does.

The fix would be to ask `ncfg_openvpn_running_pid` after a command failure and
treat "nothing running" as the stop having taken -- which is what the file
already says in its own words, *stopping one that is already stopped is not an
error*. That changes stop semantics, where this entry changes a signal
disposition, so it wants its own commit and its own test rather than riding
along. **Done, as 10.574**, and by waiting rather than by reading the errno:
`EPIPE` was the measured shape and a read that meets a closed peer is the same
condition, so keying on the errno would have covered the instance and missed
the class.

## 10.571 openvpn's stop, the third of the class, and the one with a worse ending

Named at the end of 10.566 as the remaining candidate and measured rather than
patched on suspicion. It is the same defect as `autoip`'s (10.565) and the RA
daemon's (10.566): the stop signalled and then removed the record immediately,
so a daemon still exiting read as absent and a restart's start met the daemon
it was replacing.

**`ncfg_process_terminate` is a bare `kill` and nothing above it waited**, so
both of openvpn's stop paths carried it:

- **The pid path**, `stop_by_pid`, signals and unlinks the pid file.
- **The management path**, which sends `signal SIGTERM` over the management
  socket. That call returns as soon as openvpn has read the line, not when it
  has gone.

### The management path's extra hazard, which the file already knew about

That path also unlinks the **management socket**, and the comment directly
below the unlink says why that is dangerous without noticing that it was:
*"The daemon removes its own socket on the way out."*

So the sequence was: netcfgd removes the socket path, a restart's openvpn binds
a new socket at the same path, and the daemon that was still leaving unlinks
that path as it exits -- **deleting the live tunnel's socket.** After which
`ncfg_openvpn_connect` fails for a tunnel that is running perfectly well, every
later stop falls back to the pid path, and nothing in the symptom points at a
stop that happened minutes earlier.

**The knowledge was in the file and the conclusion was not drawn.** A comment
explaining that something else owns a path is an argument for not racing it,
and it sat one line below the race.

### The fix, and the patience

The same shape as the other two: wait for the process to go, then remove the
record, and fail with a sentence naming the interface when it will not. The
waiter asks `ncfg_openvpn_running_pid`'s own question -- which matches the pid
file against this tunnel's socket path -- rather than repeating its care about
a recycled pid.

**3000 ms, which is dhcp's `NCFG_DHCP_STOP_PATIENCE_MS` rather than autoip's
1000**, and the difference is not arbitrary: openvpn runs its `--down` script,
drops routes and takes the tun device away on the way out, where an autoip
client only has to let go of an address. A patience that is too short turns a
working stop into a refusal.

### The fixture, and what it asserts

A stand-in that **recites the socket path**, because `running_pid` deliberately
will not match on the interface name alone -- `vpn0` is a short string an
unrelated command line could contain. It writes its pid where openvpn writes
its own, traps `TERM` and takes half a second over it, which is the window the
old code returned inside.

**The assertion is the relationship rather than a duration**: *after the stop
returns, the daemon is gone*. A timing check would pass or fail with the
machine; this is false exactly when the wait is missing. It reads
`/proc/<pid>/cmdline` rather than calling `kill(pid, 0)`, a process nothing has
reaped being a zombie that `kill -0` reports as alive.

It also waits for the stand-in to have written its pid before stopping, and
asserts `running_pid` finds it. **Without that the test could pass by the stop
finding nothing at all**, which is the vacuous version of the thing being
checked.

Sabotaged both ways: with the wait removed from the pid path the check fails,
restored the suite is green.

### The management path is covered too, and the hazard is reproduced

This section first said the management path was *not* exercised -- a listener
answering `SUCCESS` and a holder keeping the pid alive being what it would take
-- and named it rather than assuming the shared waiter was enough. **It is
written now**, and it turned out to be the better of the two tests, because the
socket hazard can be reproduced rather than merely argued.

The stand-in does what openvpn does: it answers the management command, lives
on, and **unlinks the socket path as it exits**. After the stop returns the
test writes a file where the next start's socket would be, waits past the
stand-in's remaining life, and asserts the file is still there. Nothing may
delete it but a daemon that has already gone.

**Sabotaged, both assertions fail** -- the liveness one and, the one that
matters, *"and it survives, so the stop did not leave the old daemon to delete
the new tunnel's socket"*. So the race is not a reading of the code: with the
wait removed, the departing daemon really does delete the live tunnel's
management socket, and the test says so in the words an operator would need.

What is still not exercised is narrower and worth keeping honest: a daemon that
**refuses** to go, which is the arm that returns the refusal sentence. Both
paths' waiters share that arm and neither test drives it, since a stand-in that
never exits would cost the suite the full patience of 3000 ms twice over. Named
rather than claimed.

### The class is not closed at three, and the sweep that said so was wrong

This entry first ended *"the class is closed at three -- `pppoe` already
waited, `dhcp` has `confirm_stopped`"*. **`dhcp` has a fourth instance**, found
by checking the claim instead of asserting it, which is the only reason it was
found at all: the sentence was about to be committed as a closing statement.

Every signalling site in `c/src/backend/` is one of five --
`dhcp.c:1307`, `pppoe.c:542`, `openvpn.c:637`, `ra.c:356`, `autoip.c:241` --
and reading each one's next lines rather than trusting the module's reputation:

- `pppoe`, `ra` and `autoip` wait. `openvpn` does now.
- **`dhcp`'s `stop_recorded` signals and unlinks the pid file**, with no wait.

**So the tally is four of five**, and it is worth stating because it says what
kind of defect this is. Five sites signal a process in `c/src/backend/`; one
was right and four were not. `pppoe` is the one that was already fixed, and
its comment carries the incident that paid for it -- measured in the guest
tier, netcfgd printed `ok backend.stop ppp0` while pppd was still holding
`ppp0` ten seconds later, with its options file already removed, so
`ncfg_pppoe_running_pid` answered 0 from then on and **every later stop
reported success**. One surviving signal made the session permanently
unidentifiable and the failure permanently silent.

That is the shape in all five: the fix is three lines and the symptom appears
somewhere else entirely, hours later, as a start that will not take or a
backend that cannot be identified. A rule learned once in `pppoe` was not
carried to the four siblings doing the same thing, which is what makes
"derive the next lens from the last bug" worth more than a checklist --
`autoip` was found by looking for the shape rather than by anything failing.

**`confirm_stopped` is not the cover it looks like.** It reads dhcpcd's control
socket, and `ncfg_dhcp_stop` calls it only in the dhcpcd branch;
`stop_recorded` then runs unconditionally for **udhcpc and odhcp6c**, which
have no control socket -- and `confirm_stopped`'s own comment says that a
machine with no dhcpcd socket must not be read as a client that would not die.
So the two clients with nothing to confirm them are exactly the two that go
through the unconfirmed path. A module having a confirmer says nothing about
whether a given path calls it.

**The odhcp6c case is the one with teeth**, and `stop_recorded`'s own comment
supplies the reason: odhcp6c answers `SIGTERM` by sending a RELEASE and calling
its script one last time with no prefixes, *which is what empties the report*.
Stop it, forget it immediately, and that emptying lands after netcfgd has
recorded the stop as done -- so the report can be rewritten under a plan that
has moved on, and a restart can meet a client still mid-release while an ISP
still believes the prefix is ours.

Fixed in its own commit rather than folded into this one, so each change is
reviewable on its own.

### A note about the size, and a number this entry first got wrong

The two waiters cost 40 bytes between them, and `make size` read **1194240 of
1194300**. `size-budget.txt` is left alone: its rule is to record at the
measured size rather than let a real feature ride the 3% tolerance, and 40
bytes is noise beside a figure the recorded number already covers.

**This section first said the margin was 60 bytes and that the next change of
any substance would fail the gate. That is wrong.** The figure `make size`
prints after "of" is the recorded limit, and the gate fails at
`limit + limit * tol / 100` -- 3% on top -- so the ceiling is about 1230129 and
the headroom is some 35,800 bytes rather than 60.

The mistake is worth keeping because of its shape: **the printed number was
read as the threshold without reading the recipe that enforces it.** A gate
that reports `X of Y` invites exactly that, and `evidence.md`'s rule about a
number justifying the work applies to a number justifying a *warning* just as
much -- this one would have sent the next person to make a deliberate,
reviewable edit to a limit that had plenty of room, which is work created out
of a misread.

## 10.570 The delegation rig is not waiting on hull any more, and the handles are measured

10.527 parked `several machines on one wire` on hull's segments work, and
10.524 said it waited on it. **Both are stale, and the second was stale in a
way that would have kept the item parked indefinitely**: a reader meeting
"waits on another project" does not go and check, which is how a deferral
outlives its reason. Corrected in place rather than appended to, because an
entry recording a non-decision decays like one recording a fix and more
quietly.

Measured in the hull binary this workspace has, 2026-10-25, rather than taken
from the message that prompted the look:

    hull exec [-t] ID [--] CMD [ARG...]
    hull segment NAME [impair MACHINE|all in|out|both [KEY=VALUE|down]...]
    hull segment NAME tamper MACHINE|all in|out|both [KEY=VALUE]...
    hull segment NAME inject MACHINE|all frame=HEX|size=N [count=N] [every=MS]

So two things netcfgd had no handle for now have one. **`hull exec` returns a
status per named machine**, which is the verdict collector a multi-machine rig
needs; and **segments carry impairment, tampering and frame injection**, which
is more than "several machines on a wire" and reaches tests this tree has
never been able to write -- delegation under loss, an RA or an autoip exchange
against a tampered or injected frame.

**What remains is netcfgd's own work, and the hard part is not the wiring.**
A single-machine rig reads `VERDICT ok` out of one payload's stdout and that
works because there is one stream and one exit. A delegation test's
assertions are **relational** -- this host handed out a prefix, that host
configured from it -- so a collector has to gather a verdict per machine and
**fail the run when a machine never produced one.** A machine that never
reached its payload must not read as a machine that passed, which is the
vacuity trap the kernel tier already guards on one machine (`run.sh`: a boot
that never reached the payload leaves no line, and an absent line must fail
rather than be silence). On several machines there are as many ways to be
vacuous as there are machines.

**Not started, and deliberately not designed from here.** Which handle serves
the collector -- `hull exec` per machine, or each machine writing a verdict to
a shared volume the host reads after -- is a choice to make while writing it,
with hull's own view in hand: reading a consumer's convenience as a library's
design is the error fuzznet's section 2 names about this tree's brief
(10.567), and it applies to hull equally. The want is recorded, the blocker
is gone, and the next session to pick up the live tier should start here.

## 10.568 The fuzznet pin moved 403 commits, and what it cost to absorb

10.567's finding was that this tree's vendored fuzznet was pinned at
`97719d9`, 2026-09-28, five days before `state/scope.h` landed -- so the
scope vocabulary the holder settled as fuzznet's was not in this tree's build
and nothing said so. The holder's word, 2026-10-25, was to do it. Bumped to
`0f33b17`, 2026-10-25: **403 commits**.

**The bump and its absorption are one commit and have to be**, because the
pin alone does not build. `build-and-commit.md`'s rule that a build never
moves a pin is unaffected -- it forbids a *build* advancing it, which is why
`bridge/Makefile` fetches the gitlink and nothing else, and this is the
reviewed commit that rule exists to require.

### What moved, and what the bridge had to learn

**Only two things, which is the headline.** `record_encode.c`,
`record_emit.c` and `netcfgd-remote.c` compiled unchanged through 403
commits, and the three suites' 92 checks pass. For a seam this tree does not
exercise daily, that is a better result than expected.

**One: fuzznet grew a system dependency, and the bridge links objects rather
than a library.** fuzznet gained log packing (its section 459), probes for
libzstd, and links `-lzstd` itself. `FUZZNET_OBJS` takes every fuzznet object
without a `main`, so it took `log/pack.o` and `log/gather.o` with it and the
link failed on eight `ZSTD_*` symbols.

**The fix asks `nm`, and the reason it is not `-lzstd`.** Whether those
objects reference zstd is a property of the machine fuzznet was built on,
because its probe decides. Naming the library unconditionally fails to link
where the probe said no; omitting it fails where it said yes. **Both are the
same error -- a claim about another tree's configuration** -- so
`FUZZNET_LIBS` asks the objects the link is about to take, exactly as the
list above it asks which object holds `main`, and for the reason that
comment already gives: the objects know what they need and nothing else has
to. A dependency fuzznet adds later arrives as an undefined reference naming
its symbol, which beats a stale list.

**Both arms measured**, since a detector that always says the same thing is
not one: over the 200 linked objects it yields `-lzstd`, and over the same
list with `log/` removed it yields nothing.

**Two: `fzn_record_sign` gained a parameter** -- `prev`, the id of the
previous record in an (issuer, stream), fuzznet's section 500. **One call
site in this tree, and it is in a test**: `record_encode.c` fills the fields
and does not sign. netcfgd does not chain -- nothing here keeps a stream's
tail -- so it passes a zeroed `prev`, which fuzznet's contract makes the
honest value at seq 1 rather than a placeholder.

### A control that failed in the wrong place, and what it taught

Sabotaging the new round-trip check -- a `prev` of `{1}` -- did not fail the
comparison. **It failed the sign**, two checks earlier. fuzznet refuses a
non-zero `prev` at seq 1 outright: `FZN_RECORD_ERR_MALFORMED` from
`fzn_record_sign`, `FZN_RECORD_ERR_SHAPE` from `fzn_record_open`, both
deliberate in its `record.c`.

So the control tested fuzznet's validation rather than netcfgd's assertion,
which is `evidence.md`'s trap about a sabotage moving something other than
the thing under test. What came out of it is better than the check it failed
to control: **that refusal is the property that makes "netcfgd does not
chain" safe to express as a zeroed field**, so it is now asserted here
rather than relied on silently. If fuzznet ever relaxes it, this tree finds
out.

### A fault in fuzznet, signalled rather than worked around

**`FZN_LOG_PACK=0` does not build fuzznet.** It was the first route tried --
the bridge has no business packing logs, and a program the Makefile says must
stay small should not carry the code -- and fuzznet's own `node/daemon.c`
includes `node/heard.h` inside `#ifdef FZN_LOG_PACK_ON` while calling
`fzn_heard_when` outside it, at three sites. So the daemon does not compile
with packing off:

    node/daemon.c:5596: error: 'FZN_HEARD_OK' undeclared

A dependency's fault is signalled and not fixed from the consumer
(`harmonization.md`), so it went to fuzznet with the reproduction and this
tree took the other route. It is also why `FUZZNET_LIBS` is the better fix
on its own merits: it needs nothing of fuzznet to change.

### What was checked and found sound, so nobody re-checks it

**`FUZZNET_DEFS` is a hand-maintained list of fuzznet's feature flags**, and
its comment says why -- a header compiled under different flags from the
object it calls is the quietest kind of wrong. A 403-commit bump is exactly
where such a list goes stale, so it was checked rather than assumed: no
fuzznet *header* gates its contents on `FZN_LOG_PACK_ON`, only that one `.c`,
and the four headers the bridge includes are `wire/seal.h` and its own. The
list survived intact.

### What the bump buys, and the fork it exposes

`fzn_scope_t` is now in this tree's build, so the placeholder enum
`c/include/ncfg/scope.h` has promised to delete since 2026-09-29 can go. **And
the obvious way to do it contradicts a decision this tree holds**, which is a
contradiction to flag rather than resolve in passing:

- `scope.h`'s own plan is that "this enum goes and the table in
  `compile/scope.c` is retyped onto it".
- `compile/scope.c` is in `c/`, whose `SRCS` wildcards every `src/*/*.c` into
  the daemon's library. Retyping it onto `fzn_scope_t` puts fuzznet's headers
  on the daemon's include path and makes `make -C c` require the submodule.
- **0269 and the brief's section 3 keep fuzznet away from the process holding
  `CAP_NET_ADMIN`**, and `bridge/Makefile` states the same argument in both
  directions: it compiles one source out of `c/` rather than linking
  `libncfg.a` precisely so the small program stays small.

**The reach, measured rather than estimated: 109 mentions of `ncfg_scope_t`
or `NCFG_SCOPE_*` across nine files** -- four in `c/` (the header, the table,
`compile/walk.c`'s one call at line 181, `walk.h`) with two of its tests, and
three in `bridge/`. Structurally it is one enum, one table and one call site;
textually it is a rename touching both sides of the seam, which is why the
branch chosen decides whether the daemon's build gains a dependency or the
bridge gains a check. The third answer neither branch states may be the right
one: the vocabulary is
fuzznet's and the **agreement** between the two spellings is checkable at the
one place both are visible, which is the bridge. A `_Static_assert` there
costs nothing, fails the build the day they diverge, and leaves the daemon's
build as 0269 wants it. **Taken, 2026-11-02** (10.664): the holder, asked,
did not know the enum, so it was decided from the aims.

## 10.567 The coordination half is fuzznet's, decided a month ago, and this tree is still holding the placeholder

The copyright holder, 2026-10-25: *"should parts of the network planning and
running of deployment tasks become a generic part of fuzznet? As other projects
may need to distribute and propagate internal/external settings and commands in
very much the same way?"* -- and then, having been told it was signalled for a
cross-project pass: *"do the cross project pass?"*

**The pass's answer is not the one this entry first carried**, and the first
version is not kept, because an open question that has been answered reads as
diligence and is the error that is caught by nothing. What it said: that the
question names a third column neither netcfgd nor fuzznet holds, that four
pieces of it exist here and are candidates for extraction, and that nothing
should move until a second consumer speaks. Three of those four claims are
wrong, and the measurement that shows it took one afternoon of reading a
sibling tree.

### What the pass measured

fuzznet's own tree at `87df072`, its `project.md` sections 420, 540, 615, 700,
724 and 728, `state/scope.h` as committed, and its reply in this tree's inbox
(`20261025T1455Z`, recorded below). fuzznet had already written the answer as
its own section 729 before the pass asked.

**The third column is not unheld. It is fuzznet's, by the holder's own scope
decision**, which fuzznet's section 2 states in the holder's words: *"every
project using fuzznet uses fuzznet's high-level abstractions rather than
extending the protocol with its own concepts, so that network code and
dependencies leave the consuming project"*, superseded further by its section
298 -- *fuzznet is to contain what its consumers need in order to use its
features*. The brief's two columns were netcfgd's reading of a seam, and
`evidence.md`'s rule applies to the reading: a claim about another tree is a
measurement nobody took. fuzznet's section 2 says so itself about this very
tree -- *"reading a consumer's constraint as the library's boundary is the
specific error"*.

### The four pieces, measured rather than proposed

1. **The scope vocabulary is fuzznet's and already built.** `state/scope.h`,
   fuzznet's `d2f5de3`, 2026-10-03: the same four names, `HOST_PRIVATE = 0`,
   an unknown byte read as host-private, and host-private refused a subject by
   a code of its own. Its header names this tree: *"netcfgd's holder set the
   scopes as a general feature of this library rather than of any consumer,
   and netcfgd holds a placeholder enum to be deleted when this lands."*
   **This was never an open question** -- `c/include/ncfg/scope.h` has said
   since 2026-09-29 that the holder settled it and that the enum exists only
   until fuzznet carries it, and `08f8cbe8` recorded fuzznet's signal on the
   day the file landed. What stays netcfgd's is the table: which key has which
   scope, and the registry gate that fails on an unclassified one.
2. ~~**Commit-confirm with a revert window is genuinely absent from fuzznet**,
   measured as zero occurrences of the concept in its headers and confirmed by
   its own reply.~~ **Built in fuzznet since, on the holder's word** (its
   `5ac9528`, sec 873; 10.707): `set staged SECONDS SCOPE KEY VALUE`, then `add
   confirm TOKEN`, with a revert every host holds and applies itself. The text
   below is what was true before it. This tree's `confirm.c` is the only implementation in the
   workspace, and fuzznet's reply accepts that it would fall on its side of
   the line if the holder wants a staged-commit token.
3. **Standing splits, and the split is the useful part.** fuzznet computes
   standing for its own settings at read -- who set a value, at what rank, and
   whether that act still counts under a revocation's or removal's cut
   (`fzn_node_apply_act_stands`, its sections 540, 700, 728). That is the "may
   this setter set this, and does it still stand" half. **"Applied here, unmet
   there, and why" is about what a consumer did with a value, and is
   netcfgd's.** 0287 and 0293 keep it.
4. **"Settled" is defined for messages and costed for settings.** A message
   line is settled once every device of the user holds it (its section 615).
   For settings it is its section 724, `list setting-holders`, asked the same
   day by fuzzypickles, costed and not built behind its section 689 freeze. So
   netcfgd is the **second** asker rather than the originator, and the answer
   is to wait for 724 rather than to build a second one. The hard half --
   which nodes need a value -- is answered in fuzznet by the scope itself,
   and the place it meets netcfgd's "every node whose rules reference it" is
   group membership, which fuzznet has no settings for yet. **Built since**
   (fuzznet `f1fdea6`, its sec 868, told here 2026-11-03): `FZN_SCOPE_GROUP`
   cells, set as `group=NAME`, a host's membership as its `group/member`
   setting, and the value in force resolved own cell, then first group, then
   estate (`get setting here KEY`). **What it does not do yet** is keep a
   group's value from the estate's other hosts. Every host holds the bytes
   and only members resolve them, so a zone's mesh password or roaming key
   would reach non-members. ~~Sealing values to a group's members is recorded
   in fuzznet as the holder's question.~~ **Built since, on the holder's word**
   (fuzznet secs 874 and 875; 10.707): `set sealed group=NAME KEY VALUE` seals
   to each member's prekey, and a later member receives it within a minute.

~~The fifth, command propagation, neither tree has.~~ **fuzznet has it now**
(its `e904cf9`, sec 872; 10.707): `call NAME at estate` and `at group=NAME`.

### The finding that is actually netcfgd's, and it is a stale pin

**The placeholder is in use at the one seam where the real type is
available.** `bridge/` links fuzznet, is fetched by `bridge/Makefile` and
reached by `make check` through `bridge-test`, and
`ncfg_record_stream_of(ncfg_scope_t)` maps a scope to a journal stream right
beside the `fzn_record_*` calls it was written for.

**Why it has not retired: the submodule is pinned at `97719d9`, 2026-09-28,
five days before `state/scope.h` landed.** So the real enum is not in this
tree's build, and nothing said so -- the placeholder compiles, the gate is
green, and the only visible symptom is a header promising a deletion that
cannot happen. A pin that is five days stale is indistinguishable from a
current one until somebody asks what is on the other side of it.

**The remedy is a reviewable pin bump and then the retyping**, in that order
and not as a side effect of anything: advancing a submodule is a change to
what this tree builds against, and 22 days of fuzznet history includes its
section 728 -- a **breaking** wire change to the setting object, landed
2026-10-25, which situ classes breaking and which a node built before it
refuses. So the bump has to be measured against the bridge rather than
assumed, and it is its own piece of work. What it buys is one vocabulary
instead of two for the concept both trees agree is one.

### What is left for the holder, and it is two things rather than a column

**Whether fuzznet grows a staged-commit token and command propagation.**
Those are the two pieces of the coordination layer nobody has built, the line
fuzznet accepts covers both, and netcfgd holds a working implementation of the
first that it did not write for export. Everything else in this entry is
either already decided, already built, or already costed somewhere else.

**And the pass's own lesson, which cost more than the answer.** This tree
deferred a question its own header had recorded as settled a month earlier,
and wrote the deferral up carefully enough to look like care. `harmonization.md`
is right that an extraction is not made from inside one project -- and it does
not follow that the *question* is open, because the holder may have answered it
somewhere a session in this tree never reads. The cheaper instrument was the
sibling's code: `state/scope.h` explains itself in its own header, and reading
it would have replaced the whole deliberation.

## 10.566 radvd had the same stop bug with a worse ending, and openvpn is next

Named as a candidate at the end of 10.565 and measured rather than patched on
suspicion: `ncfg_ra_stop` signalled, unlinked the pid file and returned, and
`ncfg_ra_running_pid` reads **only** that file -- so a radvd still exiting read
as *absent*.

**Which is worse than autoip's ending.** There, a dying client was adopted and
nothing happened; here a restart is a stop and then a start, so the start met
an interface the old daemon still held. Two radvds sending conflicting router
advertisements on one link, from a stop that reported success -- and nobody
would trace that back to a stop.

The fix is the same as autoip's and `pppoe`'s: wait for the process to go,
then remove the record, and fail with a sentence if it will not. The waiter
asks `ncfg_ra_running_pid`'s own question rather than repeating its care about
recycled pids, and the common case returns on the first look because radvd
removes its own pid file on the way out.

### The fixture, and what it has to carry

A fake radvd that leaves a holder reciting the config path -- which is what
`running_pid` matches on -- writing that holder's pid where radvd writes its
own, and trapping `TERM` to take half a second over it. The check is "a start
that follows cannot meet the daemon it replaced", and it reads
`/proc/<pid>/cmdline` rather than `kill(pid, 0)`, for `running-code.md`'s
reason: a process nothing has reaped is a zombie and `kill -0` calls it alive.

Sabotaged both ways: with the wait removed the check fails every run, with it
in the suite is green.

### The class, counted

Four backends signal a process and then forget it, and they are not all the
same:

| backend | waits? | what the early return costs |
|---|---|---|
| `pppoe` | **yes**, and its comment says so | -- |
| `autoip` | now | the dying client is adopted (10.565) |
| `ra` | now | a restart starts a second radvd |
| `openvpn` | **no** | unmeasured; its `running_pid` is pid-file-only |

**openvpn is the one left**, and it is named rather than fixed because the
measurement has not been taken: its `running_pid` reads the pid file plus the
tunnel's own socket path, so the shape matches `ra`'s and the expected ending
is a second openvpn on one interface -- but "expected" is the word this week
has been about. Its test has a fake-daemon harness already, so the fixture is
the same half-hour as this one was.

## 10.565 The autoip stop adopted the client it had just killed

"continue with outstanding features or bugfixes", the copyright holder,
2026-10-25. The outstanding bug worth taking first was the one making the gate
lie: `autoip_test`'s "after which netcfgd has no client on that interface" had
failed in two of the day's `make check` runs and passed on every direct re-run.

### The defect, which is production's and not the test's

`ncfg_autoip_stop` sent `SIGTERM`, removed the pid record, and returned.
`ncfg_autoip_running_pid` then found no record, **fell through to its adoption
path** -- which exists because `KillMode=process` leaves a client across a
netcfgd stop (0134, 0142) -- scanned `/proc` by command-line marker, and found
the process that had the signal but had not yet exited.

So a stop reported success while the next look said a client was running. A
reconcile reading that does nothing, which means **link-local addressing
silently absent after a restart**: netcfgd thinks the client it just stopped is
one it should keep.

`kill()` returning says the signal was queued, not that the target has run.
That is the whole race, and on a machine busy with kernel builds and vms it
opened about one run in five.

### The fix is the sibling backend's, and the order is the fix

`dhcp.c`'s `confirm_stopped` is the same shape pointed the other way -- look,
sleep a named step, give up at a named patience -- so `autoip` gets
`wait_for_exit` beside its existing `wait_for_client`, and **the record is
removed only once the process is gone**. Removing it first is what opened the
adoption window. If the client is still there at the end of the patience the
stop fails and says so, leaving the record in place so the next pass sees the
same pid rather than adopting it.

It asks `/proc` for the pid's arguments rather than `kill -0`, which
`running-code.md` records as a false pass: a reparented process nothing reaps
is a zombie, and `kill -0` calls one alive.

### Made deterministic, because six green runs prove nothing

Non-reproduction is what "intermittent" means. So the suite gained a client
that is slow to exit: a holder trapping `TERM` and taking half a second over
it, which holds the window open on every run rather than on one in five. With
the fix reverted that check fails every time; with it, the suite is green.

**The fixture was wrong twice before it was right**, and the first mistake is
worth keeping: a holder that slept sixty seconds never ran its handler at all,
because **a trap does not interrupt a foreground child**. The fix under test
then waited its full patience and reported honestly that the client would not
go -- correct behaviour for a client that will not go, and the wrong fixture
for one that is merely slow. It is a loop of short sleeps now.

### What the flake was hiding, which is worth more than the fix

`make check` stops at the first failing target, so a failure in `c-test` meant
**two later gates never ran at all** -- and the firewall commit before this one
went out with both of them red:

- `registry-gate`: `lower_firewall.c` had no block attribution. A new
  top-level block has to be registered in `scope.h` with a replication scope,
  which is a decision rather than a formality: layer one's firewall is
  `HOST_PRIVATE`, the narrowest, because that header's own rule says widening
  a scope publishes what the author never offered and narrowing one only fails
  to share. An operator's rules for the host in front of them are not estate
  business until a layer exists that says they are.
- `scope_test`: the block went into the enum between `RULE` and `LINKSET`
  while its name was appended to a **positional** initialiser, so
  `NCFG_BLOCK_FIREWALL` read as "linkset". The test caught it as "linkset:
  default is not what the rule gives it" -- a misordered enum wearing a wrong
  scope's clothes. It is last in the enum now, with a comment saying why.

So the intermittent cost more than its own red: it was a lens cap over
everything behind it. `make check` is clean end to end now, which it had not
been all day.

## 10.564 The firewall's lowerer and renderer, and three checks that paid

0294's grammar is a configuration surface now: `lower_firewall.c` reads it and
`render.c` writes it back. The two landed together on purpose -- a writer with
no parser emits a config netcfgd cannot read, and a parser with no writer drops
the block the first time anything rewrites the file -- and the refusal from
10.563 is what made the gap between them safe to stand in meanwhile.

`render_test` holds the round trip: every match, all three actions, two chains
with policies and one with rules, text in and text out through the parser.
That form rather than a string check, for the module's own stated reason: it
proves the renderer against **what the parser actually accepts**, so a block
written in a shape the language does not have fails there instead of at
somebody's next apply.

### What the grammar refuses, and why each one is a refusal

Thirteen diagnostics, each naming what to write instead. The ones that are
judgements rather than typos:

- **`policy = "reject"`** -- nftables has no such policy, and rendering it as
  `drop` would be the compiler choosing somebody's security posture. The
  sentence says to write a `reject` rule at the end of the chain.
- **A chain with no `policy`** -- the two answers are opposite for every packet
  no rule matched, and a firewall whose author did not say which is not one.
  Refused rather than defaulted either way.
- **A port on a protocol that has none** -- the kernel would refuse the
  transaction and name a netlink message, which reads as netcfgd's fault. A
  rule with ports and no protocol is refused for the same reason: its author
  has not decided between tcp and udp.
- **Two rules with one name in a chain** -- the name is the rule's identity
  (0287), so the second would take the first's standing and a red row would
  name a rule nobody can find.

### Three checks that found defects in the hour they were written

**A state list is validated whole before any of it is kept.** Written the
other way first: a list with one typo in it left the rule matching the words
before the typo, which is a rule nobody asked for.

**"A second chain" was keyed on `rule_count`.** A second
`input { policy = "accept" }` with no rules walked straight past the check and
silently replaced the first chain's policy. `lower_test` caught it. A chain
that was written is a chain that was written, rules or not -- it tracks three
flags now.

**And the lowerer's own duplicate-`firewall` check was dead.** The merge pass
already refuses a second top-level block of one head, with a better sentence
than mine: it names the first block's line and offers `override firewall`. The
test asserts the merge pass's wording now, and what is left in the lowerer is
an assertion that says so -- reaching it would mean the merge pass had changed
underneath, and silently overwriting the first ruleset is the one outcome worth
refusing outright.

### The size, which is the other half of 10.563's measurement

+4,376 bytes, of which text is **+6,450** against the model's +1,778 (the file
shrank elsewhere). A table-driven model charges once for four operations; a
grammar charges for every refusal it can name. The refusals are the larger
half, and that is the trade this tree makes on purpose: those bytes buy a
config file somebody can fix without reading the source.

### What is still not built

The planner, the transaction and the observer. A `firewall` block compiles,
round-trips and reaches the document today, and `ncfg plan` says "nothing to
do" about it -- correctly, since nothing yet turns chains into ops. That is
the next slice, and 0294's all-or-nothing transaction and per-rule naming are
what it has to deliver.

**And the three are not independent: the planner cannot be written until the
observer's identity question is answered.** Found on starting it -- see 10.572
and 0295, which is `proposed` rather than accepted because half of it is the
holder's.

## 10.563 The firewall model, and a gate that would not let it be half a slice

0294's implementation order was "the model and the round-trip first". The
model is in: `ncfg_firewall_t` with three chains, each a policy and an ordered
list of `ncfg_firewall_rule_t`, declared in three field tables so the freeing,
copying, comparison and JSON come from the declaration rather than from code.
`document_test` reads a document carrying one, checks the rules are in the
document's order rather than sorted, and writes it twice to compare the bytes.

### Two things the tree refused to let me do

**An `OMIT_EMPTY` struct is still written.** The field went in as
`NCFG_F_STRUCT` with that flag, on the theory that a zeroed firewall would
vanish the way an empty list does. The frozen witness caught it immediately --
it is compared byte for byte with what the Rust writes, and it parted from
itself at byte 118,077 with `"firewall":{"input":{"policy":"accept"},...}`
written into every document that has no firewall at all. It is
`NCFG_F_OPT_STRUCT` now, a pointer, so absent is NULL and **absent is
structurally not the same as empty** -- which the model wanted anyway: a
document with `firewall { input { policy = "accept" } }` writes a chain that
accepts everything, and one with no block writes no chains.

**And a model field may not exist without the renderer answering for it.**
`tool/field_coverage_gate.py` holds every document field to being either
written or refused by the config renderer, and named six of mine. That is the
gate telling me "model only" is not a state this tree allows, and it is right:
the renderer's output is a config file netcfgd reads back, so a field the
writer ignores is a field `ncfg wifi add` would silently drop from somebody's
configuration.

So `render.c` **refuses** a document carrying a firewall, with a sentence
saying the syntax is not implemented yet. Writing the block would be worse
than refusing: the parser does not know `firewall { ... }`, so netcfgd would
produce a file it could not read -- and the choice between losing the block
and emitting an unreadable file is exactly the one the gate exists to force
somebody to make out loud. The six fields are waived in
`tool/renderer-unread-fields.txt` with that reason, and **the waivers retire
themselves**: the gate faults on a waiver the renderer has started reading, so
landing the writer will name them.

### What the size says, which is the useful thing about this slice

+4,616 bytes to 1,189,824, of which text is +1,778 and `data` +1,664: **the
tables are const data rather than code**, and that is the whole of what four
operations cost for eleven fields across three types. No more code will be
written for freeing, copying, comparing or serialising this model however the
feature grows; what grows is the lowerer, the renderer, the planner and the
transaction, which are code.

### What comes next, and why it is one commit rather than two

The lowerer and the renderer land together. Separately, either one is a trap:
a renderer without a parser writes files netcfgd cannot read, and a parser
without a renderer silently drops the block on the first rewrite. The refusal
above is what makes the gap safe to stand in meanwhile.

## 10.561 The rest of the capability layer, and two sentences the states found

"do the remaining ruleset kinds then", the copyright holder, 2026-10-25. The
enumeration first, because "remaining" needed defining: of the forty-odd op
kinds, the ones that reach the kernel and can fail for a capability reason are
the link kinds and their settings, the queuing family, NAT, the bridge vlans,
offloads, the IPv6 token, the policy rules and the sysctls. Seven had
sentences. **Netfilter rules beyond NAT do not exist as ops at all** -- 0283's
five layers are not built -- so the remaining work was the kinds that do
exist, and two of them turned out to matter.

### WireGuard needs no sentence, measured rather than assumed

It looked like the obvious gap: `wg.set_device` and `wg.set_peers` have no
capability arm, and WireGuard is a module (`CONFIG_WIREGUARD=m`) on exactly
the machines netcfgd targets. Measured in `tests/hull/natcap/` with the module
unreachable:

    FAIL link.create wg0  kind: wireguard
         could not create wg0: RTM_NEWLINK failed: EOPNOTSUPP ... a link kind
         this kernel does not know is refused like this ...
    skip link.up wg0,  skip addr.add wg0

**The device never exists, so the setter never runs.** The sentence an
operator gets is the link-kind one written yesterday, and a `wg.set_device`
arm would be an arm for a state that cannot occur -- which is the mistake the
NAT hint made with `EOPNOTSUPP` and this is the same mistake declined.

What the state did earn is a sharper link-kind sentence. It gave the rule
"a module of its own" and no mapping, so a reader would look for `vlan.ko`.
Measured on this kernel: `dummy`, `veth`, `vxlan`, `macvlan`, `wireguard`,
`ifb`, `tun` and `bridge` each have `CONFIG_<KIND>` and a module of that name,
while a **`vlan` is `8021q` (CONFIG_VLAN_8021Q)**, a **`bond` is `bonding`
(CONFIG_BONDING)**, and a tunnel's module depends on its type. The sentence
says the rule and the three exceptions.

### A bridge that cannot filter: the suspect sentence was innocent

The other candidate was a sentence that looked *wrong*: a refused per-port
vlan is explained as "the bridge does not have `vlan_filtering = true`", a
configuration cause, and a kernel built without `CONFIG_BRIDGE_VLAN_FILTERING`
cannot filter whatever the config says. So the kernel tier gained a fourth
state, k3: `CONFIG_BRIDGE=y` with filtering off.

**The hypothesis was wrong and the state found something better.** The vlan
sentence never appears:

    FAIL link.create br0  kind: bridge
         could not set the settings of br0: RTM_NEWLINK failed: EOPNOTSUPP --
         this kernel does not have what the request needs; a module may not be
         loaded
    skip bridge.vlan.del br0,  skip bridge.vlan.add br0,  skip link.up br0,
    skip addr.add br0

The vlans are skipped behind an earlier refusal -- and **that refusal had no
sentence at all**, only the generic errno text, which on this kernel is wrong
in the one way that matters: the module is loaded and the option was never
built. So the sentence that needed writing was the missing one rather than the
suspect one.

**Two things about that line are worth knowing.** The action reads
`link.create br0` while the failure is the settings step, because
`finish_create` carries the settings out under a synthetic `link.set_bridge`
op and the journal names the action that asked for the device; the `doing`
text is what tells them apart. And the arm now covers all five kind setters,
since a kind's settings go to the kernel as one request that is refused whole.

### Why these stay required, which is 0293's line being held rather than moved

A bridge whose `vlan_filtering` could not be set still carries traffic, so
0293's test -- is the interface usable without this action's work -- would
make it optional. It is not, and the reason is that the test is about
reachability and this is about **isolation**: a bridge that forwards between
vlans because the kernel cannot separate them is not a slower bridge, it is a
different one. Applying the address and the routes on top of that would be
netcfgd completing a configuration whose security property is absent. 0293
says widening the optional list is a decision rather than a tidy-up; this is
that decision, declined, with its reason.

## 10.558 The rigs run from built images, and hwsim lost two checks

"do the migration then", the copyright holder, 2026-10-25, after 10.557
measured both of the blockers gone. All four rigs now take their userland from
a `hull build` image instead of a `docker export` directory.

### What each rig takes its userland from now

Each rig's `hull.conf` carries a `(build ...)` form beside its machine, so one
file holds both the image and the guest, and the source is a stored ref --
`netcfgd/hwsim`, `netcfgd/sandbox`, `netcfgd/openrc`, `netcfgd/natcap`. The
four `bake-rootfs.sh` scripts are gone, `hull-image` builds the four refs,
`hull-clean` untags them, and `$(DIST)/hull` is not produced at all any more:
docker is out of the test tier. `tests/kernel/` materializes the natcap image
when it needs a directory to pack into its initramfs.

Three things the bakes did that the store does for free: the setuid and setgid
bits (restored by `chmod` from the image's own listing before, carried now),
the non-root owners (impossible before, carried now), and the "once, and after
a package change" rule -- a step's cache key is the hash of its own form, so
asking again when nothing changed costs a lookup.

**Two things had to be carried forward by hand.** The openrc rig's `localmount`
stand-in is a file now, `tests/hull/openrc/localmount`, copied in by the step
and keyed into the cache by `inputs` -- a service script is easier to read as a
file than as a heredoc inside an s-expression. And each build step opens by
refusing a hull that leaves a materialized tree root 0700, which is the
property 10.557 needed `b7126fe` for; it checks the property rather than the
version, because that is what the step actually needs.

### The module share, which is hull's to decide

**A stored-source machine does not get hull's implicit module share.** Measured
on `b7126fe`: `/usr/lib/modules` empty, no mount for the release, the only 9p
mount the root -- so `modprobe dummy` failed and natcap lost 19 checks on its
first run from a built image. hull's own account, same day: the agent makes
that place only when it lays the overlay itself, which a `dir:` source above an
overlay does and a stored source does not, reaching the engine's host-side
overlay instead. Recorded there as a finding; whether the implicit share should
extend to stored sources is their holder's call.

Every rig names the mount itself now, which is better regardless:

    (volume (host "/lib/modules") (guest "/usr/lib/modules") (mode ro))

The whole tree rather than one release, so nothing here pins a kernel version,
and the dependency is visible in the spec rather than implicit in the runtime.

### Where it stands, including the part that is worse

| rig | from a built image |
|---|---|
| natcap | 37 of 37 |
| sandbox | 31 of 31, **systemd as pid 1** |
| openrc | 13 of 13, `openrc-init` as pid 1, service started and stopped |
| hwsim | 25 of 27, and **27 of 27** once the payload mounts its own tmpfs |

The two init rigs are the half 10.557 listed as untested, and they pass: a
built image boots its own init. natcap passes once the modules volume is named.

**hwsim lost its two roam checks on the first attempt**, which is the half of
this entry worth reading. Both failures were the `on roam` hook not firing
after the station moved -- `and that is a roam`, `named by the access point it
moved to` -- against a last recorded run of 27 of 27 (10.529, hull `4161c8a`,
2026-10-22). Three things had changed since: this image, a fortnight of
netcfgd's own commits, and hull from `4161c8a` to `b7126fe`.

The package versions are not it: `wpasupplicant 2:2.10-24`, `iw 6.9-1` and
`dnsmasq-base 2.91-1+deb13u2` are what the old exported tree carried and what
the step installed.

### It was the write path, and `(mutable overlay)` is not one thing

**The control ran once hull's session was clear: the same rig against the old
`dir:` source, with today's netcfgd and today's hull, passes 27 of 27.** So the
image source is the variable -- not a fortnight of commits and not hull's
version.

What differs is where a guest's writes go. Timed in a 4G guest, 200 MB:

| source, both `(mutable overlay)` | the root | 200 MB to root | to `/tmp` |
|---|---|---|---|
| `dir:` | overlay, tmpfs upper | 234 ms | 155 ms |
| stored ref | **plain 9p to the host** | 3165 ms | 3263 ms |

`/tmp` goes with it, being on the root. So a stored-source machine writes 14
times slower, and **this payload is the write-heavy one**: it untars the tree
and builds netcfgd in the guest, which is hundreds of small files. The run took
27 minutes against the control's 5.

**The failure was not the slowness, it was what the slowness did.** The daemon
log the rig prints on a failed roam says it:

    [drift] Warning: wlan2: backend.restart refused: the backend is running
    and silent, and netcfgd will not kill a daemon that may only be busy

netcfgd read its own supplicant as wedged, so no roam event arrived and the
hook never fired. Nothing about netcfgd changed; the guest got slow enough that
a liveness judgement went the other way.

**The fix is netcfgd's rather than hull's**, because a rig should not depend on
where a runtime puts its writes: the hwsim payload mounts its own tmpfs on
`/tmp` and `/work` before it builds, and says loudly when it cannot -- a silent
fall back to 9p is a slow run that looks like a fault in netcfgd, which is
exactly what this was. Reported to hull as well, since the capability line for
the stored case reads "an overlayfs in the guest; writes are held in the
machine's memory and go with it" and for a stored source neither half holds.

With that, **hwsim is 27 of 27 from its built image** and the run is back to
about seven minutes. The other three rigs write little and passed as they
were; they are left alone rather than given a tmpfs they have not been
measured to need.

**The shape, because it is not about wireless.** A test that passes on one
runtime and fails on another, with identical packages and identical code, was
measuring the runtime's write path through a liveness timeout. Nothing in the
rig said it depended on write speed -- and the failure surfaced three layers
away, as netcfgd apparently mishandling a roam. The lesson for the next rig is
the one the payload now carries in a comment: own the filesystem you write to,
or inherit whatever the machine runtime decided this week.

## 10.557 Both bake blockers are gone, on a hull built for the purpose

hull fixed the root mode at their `b7126fe` -- `materialize_locked` sets the
tree root 0755 last, where `hull_store_checkout` already did for a run and
materialize did not -- and said plainly that the measurement that matters is
netcfgd's: whether apt's sandbox then engages, and whether `systemd-sysv`
installs where the 0700 root stopped it. Both now measured here.

### How, which is two deliberate choices

**hull was built in a scratch clone, not in its own tree.** `git clone` of
their checkout into the session's scratch, `git checkout b7126fe`, the `situ`
submodule initialised, `make -j12` -- so nothing was written into a tree
whose session is live, and a concurrent `make` could not delete a binary
under their test run. The binary reports `commit b7126feb21ef` rather than
`-dirty`, which is the point of doing it this way rather than rebuilding
theirs.

**Both step forms were changed on purpose.** A step whose key the store holds
is not run, and the key is the parent manifest plus the step's form -- so
re-running yesterday's line would have replayed yesterday's result and
reported a pass without executing anything. Each new step opens by printing
`stat -c '%04a %u:%g' /`, which both defeats the cache and makes the fix
visible from inside.

### What the two steps said

    the tree root: 0755 0:0                 (it was 0700)
    su -s /bin/sh _apt -c 'id -u; cat'     42, and the file read
    apt-get update, unsandboxed warnings:   0
    the hwsim set, unsandboxed warnings:    0
    partial afterwards: 0700 42:0 archives/partial, 0700 42:0 lists/partial

So **apt's sandbox fully engages** -- it drops to `_apt`, which now owns and
writes its own partial directories -- and the root mode was the whole of it,
as suspected.

**And the sandbox rig's own blocker is gone with it.** Its header's reason for
baking with docker was that "a build step maps one uid, so a maintainer script
that gives a file to its own system user cannot, and `systemd-sysv` has
several". That set -- `systemd systemd-sysv udev dbus util-linux iproute2` --
installs in a step with exit 0, every binary the bake checks present,
`/sbin/init` in place, `systemd-network:998` and `messagebus:997` created, and
files actually owned by them:

    systemd-network  /var/lib/systemd/network, /run/systemd/netif/*

The stored manifest keeps them, four entries at `(owner (gid 998) (uid 998))`
beside `_apt`'s three and eleven setuid or setgid files -- which is the whole
of what a `docker export` through `tar -x` as a user drops.
