### What is still untested, and it is not small

**That a built image boots systemd as pid 1 in a vm.** Installing the packages
is not the sandbox rig's subject; running 31 checks under real systemd is.
Likewise the openrc image's `/sbin/openrc-init` path. Both should be *more*
faithful from a stored image than from an export -- owners and setuid bits
carried rather than reconstructed -- but "should" is the word this week has
been about, and neither has been run.

So the position is: **nothing technical requires docker for these images any
more**, two blockers measured gone on a named hull commit, and what remains is
a tier-wide pass plus the two boot tests that would prove it. Still the
holder's call, now with the risk named rather than guessed.

**Where the report landed, named so the claim is checkable**: hull carries both
measurements in its own section 7 at `1d2da2e`, with the boot half recorded as
untested and netcfgd's. "Reported to hull" asserts an act and leaves no
artifact; a commit in their tree is one, and `harmonization.md` asks for the
second rather than the first.

## 10.554 The queuing half, and a send that could not explain

"continue", the copyright holder, 2026-10-25. 0283 puts firewall **and
queuing** in scope, and the capability work so far was all NAT. The three
queuing sentences netcfgd already shipped were written the same way the NAT one
was -- from reasoning, against a host that has everything -- so the rig now
measures them.

### Two guesses right, and neither sentence usable

| op, in the state it was measured | measured | the sentence it had |
|---|---|---|
| `qdisc.set`, no `sch_cake` | `RTM_NEWQDISC`, ENOENT | "could not be loaded" |
| `ingress.redirect`, no filter | `RTM_NEWTFILTER`, ENOENT | two module names |
| `link.create`, kind absent | `RTM_NEWLINK`, **EOPNOTSUPP** | nothing at all |

**The errnos were right this time**, which is worth saying plainly after
10.552: a guess is not wrong because it is a guess, it is unknown. What the
first two lacked is the half an operator acts on. `qdisc.set` named neither the
module nor the option and asserted a cause the errno cannot carry -- a kernel
built without `cake` never had a module to fail to load -- so it now gives the
rule, `sch_<kind>` and `CONFIG_NET_SCH_<KIND>`, with `cake` spelled out as the
instance. `ingress.redirect` gains `CONFIG_NET_CLS_MATCHALL` and
`CONFIG_NET_ACT_MIRRED`, for the reason `nft_chain_nat` taught: a module name
is not an option name, and neither of these two is spelled after its module
either.

### The third had no sentence because the mechanism was not wired to it

A config asking for `ingress_bandwidth` on a kernel with no `ifb` does not
reach the mirror at all. It dies at **action 0**, creating `ifb-wan0`, and the
sentence an operator got was the generic errno text: "this kernel does not have
what the request needs; a module may not be loaded".

**`send_built` was a second send path.** `c/src/apply/kernel.c` had its own
send-and-report helper, used by six ops -- link create, the link setters, the
master, addresses and routes -- that never called `ncfg_kernel_hint`. So
however much netcfgd knew about those failures, it could not say it. The helper
takes the op kind now and delegates to `ncfg_kernel_send_bytes`, which reports,
tolerates and explains; the tolerate table was checked first and has no arm for
any of the six, so this is a sentence gained and no behaviour changed.

**The order the two faults were found in is the lesson.** The `link.create` arm
was written, unit-tested and passing while the daemon still printed the bare
errno -- `evidence.md`'s correct function that is not a working feature, and
`an interface is only as wired as its least-used method`. The unit test could
not see it because it calls the hint directly. The rig saw it because it reads
what the daemon printed.

### What a capability gap costs, which is a question rather than a finding

In that state the plan stops at action 0 and **seven actions are skipped,
including `addr.add wan0`** -- so asking for ingress shaping on a kernel that
cannot do it leaves the interface with no address. That is apply's documented
first-failure behaviour meeting an optional feature, not a bug, and the rig
asserts it so it cannot drift quietly.

It is also exactly what 0287's per-rule standing is for: a construct the kernel
cannot provide should be able to be red while everything around it applies.
Whether that generalises from rules to ops -- an optional op failing without
taking the basic configuration with it, and which ops are optional -- is a
design question and the holder's, not one to settle while wiring a sentence.
Raised rather than recorded as settled.

## 10.553 The kernel built without it, the experiment 10.552 only argued

"do the custom kernel then" -- the copyright holder, 2026-10-24. 10.552
measured the errno by blocking module autoload and **argued** that this is the
same state as a kernel compiled without the construct. `running-code.md` is
exact about that gap: name the experiment that would confirm the comfortable
story and run it, because a refusal leaves the question open and a disproof
removes a branch. Decision 0292 has the result; `make kernel-natcap
KERNEL_SRC=<tree>` is the tier.

### Three kernels, two options, no module support at all

Debian's `linux-source-6.12` (6.12.113) with `CONFIG_MODULES` **off**, so
there is no loader to blame and absent means compiled out:

| kernel | config | the apply |
|---|---|---|
| k0 | `NFT_NAT=y`, `NFT_MASQ=y` | **applies NAT**, `ok nat.replace` |
| k1 | neither | `NFT_MSG_NEWCHAIN` refused, **ENOENT** |
| k2 | `NFT_NAT=y`, no `NFT_MASQ` | `NFT_MSG_NEWRULE` refused, **ENOENT** |

**Identical to the blocked-autoload rig, state for state and message for
message**, and `EOPNOTSUPP` nowhere again. So the argument holds and the
cheap rig is evidence rather than an approximation of it.

**k0 is why the other two mean anything.** A kernel this small refusing NAT is
consistent with any of the things `x86_64_defconfig` minus modules leaves out;
the same kernel with the two constructs restored applying NAT is what narrows
it to the constructs. And the guest derives its own expectation from
`/proc/config.gz` -- `CONFIG_IKCONFIG_PROC` is in the config for that reason
alone -- so a run against the wrong bzImage fails instead of passing quietly.

### `CONFIG_NFT_CHAIN_NAT` does not exist

`net/netfilter/Makefile` has `obj-$(CONFIG_NFT_NAT) += nft_chain_nat.o`. The
module an operator loads and the option a kernel builder selects **are spelled
differently**, and netcfgd's sentence named only the module -- so anyone taking
it to a kernel config searches for a symbol that is not there.

Found by making that exact mistake: `config-kernel.sh` was written with
`-e NFT_CHAIN_NAT`, and its own readback check refused the build, which is the
one way this could have been caught cheaply. The sentence carries both
spellings for both constructs now, and `apply_kernel_test` and the rig both
hold it to that. It matters for netcfgd's actual audience: on an embedded
router a kernel is built rather than modprobed, so the config symbol is the
half that can be acted on.

### What the tier is, and why it is not under hull

`tests/kernel/` drives qemu directly: `config-kernel.sh` (configure and read
the config back), `make-initramfs.py` (a `gen_init_cpio` spec from the natcap
rootfs), `kinit.sh` (PID 1, the measurement, a sysrq power-off), and `run.sh`
tying them together. **hull cannot boot a kernel it is given** --
`engine/qemu.c:1029` is `/boot/vmlinuz-<release>` and the spec's
`vm.kernel` `path:` form is declared but unbuilt (hull's section 1188) -- so
this tier exists outside the hull family and collapses into another rig the
day that key lands. Signalled to hull's inbox as `20261024T2008Z`, with the
two things an unprivileged runner needs: `/dev/console` declared in the
initramfs spec (a user cannot `mknod` one, and without it PID 1 is silent and
looks hung) and `CONFIG_IKCONFIG_PROC` so a guest can say which kernel it is.

### The division of labour between the two tiers

`make hull-natcap` is the standing test: minutes, no source tree, 23 checks,
and it guards the sentences. `make kernel-natcap` is the occasional control:
a 1.6 GB tree, three builds, and it answers the one question the rig cannot
ask about itself. 0292 settles that both stay, and closes 10.552's open
question about pinning a kernel -- not because pinning is unwanted but
because hull cannot express it yet.

## 10.552 The errno was measurable after all, in a vm, and it was the wrong one

"If you need to thoroughly test this kind of stuff you can use a hull VM with a
custom kernel" -- the copyright holder, 2026-10-24, on 10.551's claim that the
kernel's answer could not be measured here. **No kernel had to be built, and
the claim was wrong within the day.** Decision 0291 has the measurement; this
is what it cost and what it changed.

### What made the state reachable

A hull `(backend vm)` guest boots the host's kernel with an **empty module
table** and its own `/proc/sys/kernel/modprobe`. Blocking autoload there leaves
a construct unreachable by the same lookup that fails when it was never
compiled: `nf_tables` asks for the chain type, asks the module loader, asks
again, and returns its own error without regard for why the module never
appeared. So "the modules may be absent, unbuildable or blocked" -- the
sentence 10.551 shipped -- names three states that are one state to the kernel,
and the cheapest of them is a one-line write in a guest.

Neither of the other tiers can do it, which is why this was never measured:
`make live-container` and `make live` share the host's kernel, where both
modules are loaded and a chain type is registered globally.

### What the kernel says, 22 checks in `tests/hull/natcap/`

| state | the answer |
|---|---|
| `nf_tables`, no `nft_chain_nat` | `NFT_MSG_NEWCHAIN` refused, **ENOENT** |
| plus `nft_chain_nat`, no `nft_masq` | `NFT_MSG_NEWRULE` refused, **ENOENT** |
| no nftables module at all | the socket will not open, EPROTONOSUPPORT (93) |

**`EOPNOTSUPP` arrived in no state**, and it is what 0283 and 0287 both
reasoned about and what 10.551's arm hedged on. It is gone from the hint, and
`apply_kernel_test` now asserts it gets nothing: an arm for a code nothing
produces is an untested arm, and its presence is what made the sentence hedge.

Two controls, because three refusals prove nothing on their own: a guest with
the modules loadable applies NAT with all four actions `ok`, and with autoload
blocked a module nothing loaded cannot arrive (`ip link add type dummy` is
refused). Each failing state also asserts its plan held the `nat.replace`,
since a converged machine plans nothing and reports an empty success -- which
is exactly how the first draft of this measured nothing four times over.

### The finding the measurement produced, which is bigger than the errno

**ENOENT cannot carry the diagnosis.** `kernel_nat.c` has always said that
deleting a table which is not there is ENOENT, and that delete is in the
transaction whenever the dump saw the table -- so a table that vanished in the
gap lands on the identical code as a missing module. One errno, three faults,
three different remedies.

The discriminator was arriving with every error and being discarded: an
`NLMSG_ERROR` carries the header of the message that caused it, and
`socket.c:382` already decoded it to spell `RTM_NEWLINK`. It had no name for
anything on the netfilter protocol, so **every nftables refusal in this port's
history read "a netlink request failed"**. `ncfg_nft_message_text` names the
eleven messages netcfgd sends or reads, and the refusal now reads
`NFT_MSG_NEWCHAIN failed` -- which is the difference between "no chain type"
and "no masquerade" stated in the kernel's own vocabulary.

No protocol is threaded to do that, and that is measured rather than assumed:
an nftables message is `(NFNL_SUBSYS_NFTABLES << 8) | kind`, so 2560 or more,
against a largest `RTM_*` of 108. The one collision is `NFNL_MSG_BATCH_BEGIN`,
subsystem 0 type 16, which is `RTM_NEWLINK` exactly; a marker asks for no
acknowledgement and was refused in none of the four states, so it is written
down in `nft.c` rather than guarded.

### Three instrument faults, all of which reported success

The rig's own history is the useful part, because each fault produced a clean
run that measured nothing:

- **`modprobe -r` never unloaded**, netcfgd's table and dummy device holding
  the references, so three states ran with every module loaded. Visible only
  in a state line nobody had asked to be printed.
- **`modprobe dummy nf_tables` loads neither.** The second word is a
  *parameter* of the first module, and the complaint went to a `2>/dev/null`.
  Two states ran with no `nf_tables` while their labels said otherwise.
- **The control on the block tested `sed`'s exit status**, through a pipe, and
  announced "the block is not blocking" directly above the output proving it
  was. A pipeline's status is its last command's.

None of the three would have failed a check, because at that point the script
had no checks -- which is the argument for the rig over a session's one-off
probe, and for the vacuity assertions inside it.

### What is still open

**A probe rather than a refusal.** A hint explains a failure that has already
happened; 0287's red row *before* an apply needs netcfgd to ask what a kernel
supports, and nftables publishes no "list your expression types" request.
Asking by attempting -- a transaction into a throwaway table, rolled back --
is the obvious shape and writes to the kernel to answer a question about it,
so 0291 leaves it to the holder.

**The other ruleset op kinds.** `nat.replace` is one op with one sentence. The
rest of 0283's layers each want one, and each wants a state in the rig rather
than a guess.

**A pinned kernel.** hull declares `(kernel "path:...")` and has not built it,
so the guest runs the host's kernel: the rig can say what 6.12 answers and not
what 5.4 does. The module-blocked state is the same lookup either way, so this
would buy version evidence rather than correctness.

## 10.551 The capability hint for NAT, keyed on a guessed errno (superseded by 10.552)

"continue", the copyright holder, 2026-10-23. 0287's red row has to say
something, and 10.545 named the translation that makes it say it: a kernel
refusal is an errno, and what an operator can act on is a module name.
`ncfg_kernel_hint` already did this for four op kinds; `nat.replace` is the
first of the ruleset kinds to get one.

    this kernel has no nftables NAT: `nft_chain_nat` provides the chain type
    and `nft_masq` the masquerade, and netcfgd asks for both -- the modules
    may be absent, unbuildable or blocked

### The errno "could not be measured here", which was wrong -- see 10.552

**This section's claim did not survive a day and the entry is kept as written
so the error is legible.** It said the kernel's answer could not be measured on
this machine, keyed the arm on `ENOENT` and `EOPNOTSUPP` together for that
reason, and argued for the pair as caution. The holder's one-line reply --
use a vm -- produced the measurement in an afternoon: it is `ENOENT`, for both
the chain type and the masquerade, and `EOPNOTSUPP` in no reachable state. The
hedge was an untested arm, and the sentence quoted above has been replaced.

What the scope of the claim should have been is the transferable part: the
measurement was impossible **on this host**, and this tree has four tiers, one
of which boots a kernel whose module table it owns. A capability is absent
somewhere by arrangement, and "cannot be measured" needed the words "with the
tier I was standing in".

The rest of this section still holds, and is what the measurement agreed with:

    Error: unknown chain type
    Error: The arp family does not support this hook
    Error: Chain of type "nat" is not supported, perhaps kernel support is
    missing?

The third is the case in question, and the interesting part is its last four
words. **The tool that owns the vocabulary hedges too** -- between a wrong hook
and an absent module -- because from where it stands those are the same lookup
failing. That reading was right and is why the replacement sentence still
refuses to name one cause: the kernel's single `ENOENT` covers a missing
module, a missing expression and a table that vanished mid-apply. What was
wrong was hedging in the **errno** rather than in the sentence, where a guess
cannot be tested.

### What is still missing, named so it is not mistaken for done

This is one op kind of the ruleset family. The red row 0287 describes wants
the same treatment for the rest, and the piece that cannot be written from
here at all is the **probe**: a hint explains a refusal that has already
happened, where a red row before apply would need netcfgd to ask the kernel
what it supports. 10.541's generation read is the only nftables capability
question the daemon currently asks.

### The size, which is a page rather than a sentence

`make size` went from 1,180,976 to 1,185,072 -- +4,096, one page, for a
sentence. `size` says the code grew by 279 bytes and that `data` and `bss` are
byte-identical, so the page is section alignment being crossed rather than the
hint costing four kilobytes. Recorded in `size-budget.txt` with that
measurement, because the next reader will otherwise divide 4,096 by one
sentence; the before figure comes from building HEAD with the two files
stashed, not checked out over.

## 10.550 `global { locked = [...] }`, which refuses at plan time

"go ahead", the copyright holder, 2026-10-23. 0290's lock, built on the subject
key from 10.549: a list of subject keys netcfgd may not set, refused by the
planner, with no per-apply waiver.

    global {
        locked = ["mtu:eth0", "addr:eth0/192.0.2.5/24"]
    }

`plan_lock_test` holds it to eleven checks, and the refusal reads:

    locked:  `mtu:eth0` is locked
    lift it: remove `mtu:eth0` from `global { locked = [...] }`

**The `override_with` field names an edit rather than an invocation**, which is
0290's rule rather than a wording choice: a guard's refusal carries `ncfg apply
--allow-disruption <iface>` and a lock has no waiver at all, so naming a flag
there would be a lie in the one field an operator acts on. The test asserts the
absence of `--allow-disruption` for that reason.

### Three things the tree gave for free, and one it refused to

**The model is table-driven**, so one `ncfg_field_t` entry carried the
freeing, copying, comparison and JSON. The hand-written work was the lowering,
the rendering and the refusal.

**No scope entry was needed, and that is the right answer rather than an
omission.** `global` defaults to host-private and the scope table lists only
the keys that travel -- so a lock stays on the machine that declared it, which
is exactly 0290's point: a lock that travelled would let one node's declaration
be distributed to others.

**And the `agree` gate refused the first version.** It compiles the same
configuration with the C and the Rust and compares the documents as values, so
a key the C writes and the Rust does not know makes them differ -- four
fixtures went red. The fix is `NCFG_FF_OMIT_EMPTY`, which is also independently
right: an empty `locked` and no `locked` mean the same thing, unlike
`connectivity.ignore`, where an empty list clears a default and has to be told
apart from silence. With the flag the witnesses are byte-identical and
`answer_test`'s embedded copy of the document response needed no change either
-- both of which I had already edited before finding the flag, and both of
which were reverted.

### The report I wrote and removed

A lock that refused nothing was going to be reported, with a flag per entry
set when it refused something. **It is gone, because a plan contains only
changes**: on a converged machine no lock matches anything, so the line would
fire on every plan -- which is the noise that teaches people to skip the line
that matters.

The hazard it was aimed at is real, and **it is closed in the same session by
the check the report could not be**: a lock whose *class* does not exist can be
known useless without looking at the machine at all. `mut:eth0` and a bare
`eth0` are each warned about once, naming the entry, while `mtu:eth0` is not --
and the warning fires on an entry that can never match rather than on every
converged plan, which is the whole difference.

`ncfg_op_subject_class_known` answers it by **walking the op kinds rather than
from a second list**, so the classes it accepts are exactly the classes
`ncfg_op_subject` can produce and the two cannot drift. The scope half is
deliberately not checked: an interface that does not exist yet is a reasonable
thing to lock in advance, and a class this build does not know is either a typo
or a document written for a newer netcfgd -- which is a thing to say and not a
thing to refuse. 88 bytes, so the installed total is 1180976 of 1181000.

### Two fixture faults, because both were mine

**The MTU is a device's, not an interface's.** The first fixture put `mtu` on
an interface and the document reader refused it: "an interface carries `mtu`,
which this build does not know; a document is refused rather than half read" --
which is the reader doing its job.

**And `link.up` was not planned for that fixture at all**, with or without a
lock, so the assertion "the link still comes up, which a guard would have
stopped" proved nothing in either direction. Replaced with an address beside
the MTU: the lock refuses `mtu:eth0` and the `addr.add` on the same interface
is planned, which is what per-value means and is provable here.

### Measured

`make check` rc=0, every suite passing, the agree gate at 4 configurations
compiled by both programs to the same document, and **the installed size
unchanged at 1180888** -- the lock's code landed inside existing section
padding, which is the likely explanation rather than a measured one.

Schema: a **minor** addition. With `OMIT_EMPTY` a document that locks nothing
renders byte for byte as before, so nothing already written changes; a document
that does lock something carries a key older builds refuse, since this reader
refuses keys it does not know rather than half-reading a document.

### And the plan prints the subject, because the warning promised it

The typo warning says a subject key reads `class:scope` "as `ncfg plan --json`
writes them on each action" -- which was not true when it was written, and is
now. Each action in the plan's JSON carries its `subject`, so **an operator
locking a value copies the key rather than guessing its spelling**. On the
action rather than inside the op writer, because the inverse is written by the
same function and two subjects on one action would be two answers to one
question.

**Blessing the plan witness validated the subject design better than the unit
test did.** 45 actions over a real fixture produced 45 keys, every changed line
in the witness a `"subject"` and nothing else, and they read as intended:
`accept_ra:eth0`, `acl:wlan0/02:00:00:00:00:aa`, `addr:eth0/192.168.1.10/24`,
`backend:eth0/dhcp4`, `bond:bond0`, `dns:host`, `hook:eth0/post_up`,
`iprule:host/100`.

33 of those 45 are distinct, and **every key shared by two actions is one
object with two sides** -- `addr.add` with `addr.del`, `link.up` with
`link.down`, `qdisc.set` with `qdisc.reset`, `link.set_master` with
`link.unset_master`, `ingress.redirect` with its clear. No two different
objects share a key, which is the property the whole design rests on and which
a hand-built fixture could not have shown.

### What is still open, in the order it is cheapest

The guard keyed on subjects rather than on interface names (0289), which needs
a declaration surface for a guard on a subject -- today a guard lives in an
interface block and there is nowhere to write `route:eth0/default`; and a
rule's standing (0287), which needs the capability translation to make its red
row say anything.

## 10.549 One subject key, asked for from three directions

"go ahead", the copyright holder, 2026-10-23, on the identity work that 0287,
0289 and 0290 each named independently: a rule's standing must attach to the
same row after a re-plan, a guard needs a subject better than a string compared
against an interface name, and a lock needs to name the value it will not let
netcfgd set.

`ncfg_op_subject(op, out, size)` is that, in `plan/action.c` beside
`ncfg_op_name` and `ncfg_op_interface`, with `subject_test.c` holding it to
five properties.

### The shape, and why the class is the object rather than the action

`class:scope` or `class:scope/detail`, scope being the interface or `host`.

**Two actions against one object share a subject**: `link.up` and `link.down`
are both `link:eth0`, because a standing must survive one becoming the other
and a lock must cover both directions of a change rather than one. **A value
that can be owned separately gets its own class**: `link.set_mtu` is
`mtu:eth0`, not `link:eth0`, or locking an MTU would stop the link coming up.
**And distinct objects of one class differ**: `addr:eth0/192.0.2.10/24`, so a
list shows two rows and a lock covers one address.

Eight kinds need a detail to be unambiguous -- an address, a route by its
destination, a routing rule by the priority `document.h` already calls the
thing it is "selected by across the whole system", a backend by its kind, a
VLAN by its id, an ACL entry by its station, a hook by its phase. The rest are
named by class and interface, and where that is coarser than a lock might
eventually want, the absent detail says so rather than a number being invented.

**Truncation is a refusal**, not a short key: a key cut short can collide with
another object's and then names the wrong thing.

### The check that matters is completeness, and it caught my own count

The test walks every op kind rather than the ones somebody remembered: 45 are
classified, 3 are deliberately excluded -- the commit family, because arming
and confirming a window is how a change is made safely rather than
configuration, and a lock over them would cover the mechanism that rescues a
locked-out machine.

**The excluded count is what found the bug, and the completeness check did
not.** The loop first read `<= NCFG_OP_COMMIT_CONFIRM` and reported 45
classified with 2 excluded of 47 -- one short of `NCFG_OP_COMMIT_REVERT`, which
my earlier enum extraction had also missed. The completeness assertion passed
in that state, because a kind outside the loop is a kind not asked about. So
the pair of assertions is the point: a count that must add up catches what a
pass-or-fail cannot.

### What it cost, which is the part to argue with

**4136 bytes**: 1176752 to 1180888, recorded at 1181000 rather than left to
ride the 3 per cent tolerance, which is `size-budget.txt`'s own rule -- the
tolerance is for compiler noise, and spending it on a feature makes the next
feature fail for the wrong reason.

**And nothing calls it yet.** Four kilobytes of foundation is defensible in a
file that has carried model code for unimplemented features, and it is still
four kilobytes. The leaner form is written down beside the figure: most classes
are the op name's prefix before the dot, since 0082 gives every op one name, so
a dozen overrides for the link attributes that deserve their own class would
replace the forty-five-arm switch. Not taken, because the switch is where a new
op kind announces that nothing can lock or guard it -- which is the property
`subject_test` asserts -- but the trade is recorded rather than assumed settled.

### What it unblocks, and in which order

A guard keyed on a subject rather than an interface (0289), a lock that names
a value (0290), and a standing attached to a row that survives a re-plan
(0287). None of those is built; all three now have the key they each asked for,
and the next of them is the holder's to pick.

## 10.546 The control path is part of the configuration, and survivability is the target

The copyright holder, 2026-10-23, widening 0285 and then narrowing what can be
promised:

> note that for networking the atomicity may also need to cover interface
> configuration or any other subsystem and applied in a sensible order... It is
> very common in networking that the connection goes down until all parts of a
> configuration are in place, and for us this is bad, because control and
> decisions come over network.

> I am hoping you can prove me wrong, but I find it unlikely netcfgd will
> become smart enough to never hose its necessary connections. This will
> probably remain an operator responsibility.

`0288` is both, and the second is not a caveat on the first -- it decides what
the first is for.

### The holder is right, and the attempt to prove otherwise is the trap

Three structural reasons, not effort:

  * **The topology is outside the machine.** Whether the uplink's VLAN is
    carried by a switch two hops away, whether the operator's session comes
    through a jump host, whether a route being replaced is in somebody else's
    path -- none of it is visible from a node.
  * **A correct change can break connectivity anyway**, through a switch's MAC
    table, an upstream conntrack, an ISP's lease.
  * **Intent is not derivable.** "This cuts the path my instructions arrive on"
    and "this *moves* my instructions to a new path, which is the job" are
    identical from inside. A tool that refuses the second to prevent the first
    cannot perform a migration.

**So the target is that an operator's mistake is survivable rather than
prevented** -- and most of that is already built: detect and declare, which
needs no topology knowledge; the local revert timer, which needs netcfgd to be
able to undo rather than to be clever; make-before-break, which `plan/build.c`
already does and argues; and exactly one refusal netcfgd can justify on its own
evidence.

**That one is: a revert that would not restore what it came from.** Local
knowledge -- the pre-change state was reachable by construction -- and arming a
timer whose expiry lands somewhere unreachable turns a recoverable mistake into
two. What netcfgd cannot do is prove a change safe, and it must not imply it.

### What the tree already had, which is more than I expected

`plan/build.c` sequences its passes with a reason at each step and ends with
teardown, and its comment is this decision made once already:

> Teardown comes last, so a change to an address is make-before-break: the new
> address is in place before the old one goes. On a machine being reconfigured
> over the network that ordering is the difference between a brief overlap and
> a lockout.

So make-before-break and an argued order exist per host. What is missing is the
same discipline **across** nodes -- add the new subnet on every node before
withdrawing the old from any -- which is inherited rather than invented.

### Three things the record settles beyond that

**Atomicity is a property of a change, not of a subsystem.** 0285's two classes
were written with rules in view and are not about rules: a jointly dependent
change is usually an address, a link, a route, an MTU and a rule at once, which
is the normal shape of moving a network to a new subnet.

**Where no gap-free order exists, the gap is declared and bounded -- and the
confirm window must exceed it.** A node that applies a correct change, loses
its control path for the length of that change, and reverts because nothing
confirmed has used the safety net to undo something that was working. So the
window is derived from the declared gap, and a gap longer than the window is a
change to refuse or re-stage rather than attempt.

**A directive must be executable to completion offline.** No step may need a
round trip, because the control path is precisely what a node may lose in the
middle; a node that stalls waiting for an instruction sits in the half-applied
state the design exists to avoid. So it carries the resolved plan, its instant,
its window and its revert, and a node cut off part way **finishes, then
decides** -- locally.

### And netcfgd does not know its own control path today

`SO_PEERCRED` identifies the local peer process, a uid and a pid; the bridge
holds the network connection and reports nothing about which interface, address
or route it arrives over. So the planner cannot tell that the address it is
replacing is the one the instruction came in on -- which is the cheapest of the
three uses (order it last, say so, choose the window) and the precondition for
the other two.

## 10.541 The generation check, and a queue-shaped fixture that broke six checks

"do the generation check then, let's try to grow into this, we are never going
to get everything perfect straight away... Approximately right is better than
very detailed/specific and completely wrong." -- the copyright holder,
2026-10-23, after 0283 and 0284 named it as the first thing that does not wait
on a design answer.

**What it closes is the report, not the write.** A transaction is atomic, so
netcfgd's own table is never half-applied; but the conflict list comes from two
dumps taken one after another, and docker, podman, libvirt and `firewalld`
commit tables between them on a real machine. The dumps cannot tell -- each is
well-formed -- so the list names a table that has gone or misses one that
arrived, silently and only sometimes.

nftables offers no compare-and-swap. What it does offer is a counter the kernel
bumps on every commit, so: read it, take the dumps, read it again. Equal means
they describe one ruleset.

`ncfg_nft_build_gen_request` and `ncfg_nft_gen_read` are 40 lines in `nft.c`,
and `observe/netfilter.c` brackets its two dumps with them, **three attempts**
and then a warning. Bounded on purpose: a container host starting a compose
file is a machine whose ruleset changes faster than two dumps take, and the
honest answer there is the last reading plus a sentence saying it may be torn,
not an unbounded retry inside a pass that has a deadline.

### Three details that are the whole correctness of it

**A kernel that will not say is not a kernel that moved.** No generation -- an
older kernel, a netlink this process may not ask -- means no check, and the
observation stands exactly as it did before this existed. The alternative is
three readings and a warning on every pass on such a machine.

**Absent is not zero.** A reply with no `NFTA_GEN_ID` is refused rather than
read as a generation of 0, because a counter can hold 0 and two unrelated
replies would then compare equal -- which is the one way this check could
report a ruleset as settled when it had moved.

**No `NLM_F_DUMP`.** There is one generation, not a list of them, and asking
for a dump of it is answered differently by different kernels -- the sort of
difference that appears on one machine and not another. Asserted in
`nft_test`, flags and all.

### The test says which reading was kept, and the fixture had to change to let it

The retry case answers **different uplinks in its two rounds**: `wan0` in the
torn one, `wan1` in the settled one, plus a conflicting table that only the
second round can see. So the assertion distinguishes a retry from a reader that
noticed nothing and got lucky, which an identical second round could not.
Controlled by making the mismatch unnoticed, where both checks fail.

**And adding a third request to the fixture broke six checks that had nothing
to do with it.** `current_test`'s nftables seam is a *queue*: replies are
served in request order, so the generation request ate the answer meant for the
rule dump and everything shifted by one. The fixture now answers four requests
-- generation, rules, chains, generation -- and the comment at it says why,
because the next request added here will do the same thing again. A fake that
serves a sequence is a fake that encodes the caller's order as a fact.

### What it cost, and what is still open

**128 bytes**: the installed total went from 1176624 to 1176752 of a 1177000
ratchet, which leaves 248. Two extra netlink round trips per observation, both
tiny. 0283's size question is now a near-term one rather than a design-time
one: the next feature of any size raises the ratchet deliberately or lands
outside the default build.

**What no mechanism can close**: a change landing between the second generation
read and the transaction. The write is safe regardless -- atomic, and only
netcfgd's table -- so what remains is a report computed moments before a
change, which is a property of a ruleset with several writers rather than a
defect to fix.

## 10.539 The scope was never the holder's, and 0283 says so

"We have not chosen such a narrow scope, that is your invention. We want full
firewall and queuing support. netcfgd is a network configurator software. Those
are basic networking. And later we want distributed rules to be integrated with
higher level subsystems like guest network, auth etc." -- the copyright holder,
2026-10-23, on being told that netfilter support was complete.

**It was complete against a scope sessions wrote and the holder had not
chosen**, and the answer that said so cited the tree correctly, which is the
part worth recording: the narrow scope was load-bearing in five places and each
cited the others.

  * `0022` -- "netcfgd translates addresses because address translation is
    addressing. It does not filter packets, because filtering is security
    policy", accepted 2026-07-30.
  * `0023` -- the root qdisc and at most a rate, "no classes, filters or
    actions", quoting 0022 as precedent for refusing a general model.
  * `0009` -- the original exclusion of masquerade, which 0022 amended.
  * `c/src/plan/nat.c` -- "security policy, which this project has no model of
    and will not grow one by accident".
  * the design document's own type table -- `forwarding : bool? // sysctl
    only, never a firewall rule`.

So a session asking "is this complete?" reads five independent-looking
statements of the same invented boundary and reports a narrow thing as
finished. **That is the cost of a scope decision nobody ratified**: it does not
read as a decision any more, it reads as the shape of the problem.

`0283` supersedes 0022, amends 0023 and 0009, and states the direction
including the later half -- distributed rules integrated with guest network and
authentication, which is a constraint on the design from its first line rather
than a feature to add afterwards, because a rule whose subject is "a guest
device" cannot be a static ruleset written at apply time.

### What the old records got right, and keeps

They did not argue that filtering belongs elsewhere. They argued that a
configuration language covering it is larger than the one netcfgd has for
addressing, and that writing into a ruleset netcfgd does not own means fighting
another tool. Both are true; neither is a scope argument. **Cost is a reason to
stage work and ownership is a coexistence problem** -- and 0022's mechanism
work stands unchanged: netlink rather than shelling out to `nft`, tag what you
own, replace atomically.

### The vocabulary moves, which the holder named the same day

"The netfilter landscape keeps changing all the time, so we need to be able to
handle the syntax changing a bit while rules are being applied." Three halves,
one of which already held:

  * **Reading tolerantly holds**, because attributes are looked up by number
    and `wire.h` separates absent from malformed. It is now asserted rather
    than assumed: `nft_test` feeds a rule carrying an unknown attribute and an
    unknown expression between the two netcfgd reads, plus a chain record with
    unknown attributes inside the hook nest, and requires both to be
    recognised. **Controlled** by making the reader refuse an unfamiliar
    expression, where the case fails -- and that is the failure that matters
    most, because netcfgd's claim on a rule is what the expressions say, so an
    intolerant reader stops recognising its own rules.
  * **Noticing the ruleset moved mid-apply does not hold.** The write is safe
    -- atomic, and only netcfgd's table -- but the conflict report is computed
    from a dump taken earlier, so a table that appeared or vanished in the gap
    makes it wrong in both directions. nftables publishes a generation
    (`NFT_MSG_GETGEN`, `NFTA_GEN_ID`) for exactly this.
  * **Refusing legibly on a feature difference does not hold either**:
    `EOPNOTSUPP` from a statement is a kernel too old for that construct, and
    saying which construct is the only form an operator can act on.

### What is unresolved, and it is design rather than drift

0283 lists six questions and none is decided: ownership beside another
firewall and beside container runtimes, zones against flat rules, the default
policy a bare `firewall {}` implies, how far queuing goes and whether netcfgd
creates the `ifb` device 0255 refused, how identity enters a rule and over
which interface, and size -- the ratchet stands at 1176624 bytes of 1177000,
which is 376 bytes of headroom, so this either raises it deliberately or lands
as separately installable backends.

**None of those is answered by writing code first**, which is why this entry
ends at the record rather than at an implementation.

## 10.538 Three of the six, and the switcher swept nothing on busybox

"fix the six alpine failures then", the copyright holder, 2026-10-23, after
10.537 named them. Three are fixed and verified on both libcs; three are
intermittent and are now characterised rather than explained. `make
live-alpine` reads **68 passed, 9 skipped, 3 failed** where it read 64, 9 and 7.

### The one that is netcfgd's rather than a test's

**`packaging/netcfgd_select.sh` swept nothing on any busybox machine**, which
is a shipped script and netcfgd's own audience. `sweep_children` enumerated
with `pgrep -x "$program"` at two sites, and busybox's `-x` is not procps':
measured on Alpine with busybox 1.37, against a process whose `comm` is exactly
`wpa_supplicant`,

    pgrep -x wpa_supplicant   ->  nothing, rc=1
    pgrep    wpa_supplicant   ->  the pid

So `stand_down` found no orphaned `wpa_supplicant`, `dhclient`, `udhcpc`,
`hostapd`, `pppd` or `openvpn` and reported having looked -- the same symptom
the script's own comments quote a user reporting from a different cause: "I
STILL had to kill orphaned dhcpcd and wpa_supplicant."

It reads `/proc/<pid>/comm` now, in a `pids_by_comm` helper. That is what `-x`
was asking for, it needs no package on any machine, and the kernel's
15-character truncation applies identically -- which the `children_of` lists
already account for and say so.

### Three glibc assumptions a second libc exposed

  * **BusyBox dispatches on `argv[0]`, so a renamed copy of `sleep` or
    `/bin/sh` is not a program.** `select.sh` and `resolv_defended.sh` build
    decoys that way -- a process whose `comm` the sweep must match -- and on
    Alpine each was a busybox printing `applet not found`. The decoys are
    copies of `python3` now, which ignores its own name and still finds its
    standard library; measured on glibc and musl, `comm` reading the new name
    on both. The suite already needs python3, so nothing was added.

    **The first fix for this was wrong and measuring caught it.** Busybox falls
    back to `argv[1]` only when `argv[0]` is itself named `busybox`, so
    `wpa_supplicant sleep 120` fails exactly as before -- written, tested,
    found wrong, replaced, all before it was believed.
  * **`getent` is glibc's and musl has none.** `c_daemon_tryout.sh` probed DNS
    with it, so on Alpine every look failed and the tryout never saw the
    network return: nine of `c_daemon_watch.sh`'s checks failed about a network
    that was up. It now takes the first of `getent`, `nslookup` or `host` that
    exists and stops when none does, because an absent probe must never read as
    a resolution failure. `c_daemon_watch.sh` stubs all three -- stubbing only
    `getent` left the real busybox `nslookup` in the path and changed nothing.
  * **BusyBox `mktemp` takes no suffix.** `mktemp ...XXXXXX.log` answers
    `mktemp: : Invalid argument` where GNU coreutils places the suffix, so
    `$log` was empty, the redirect failed and the C daemon never started. The
    X's go last. One site in the tree, found by sweeping for the shape rather
    than for the file.

All three verified both ways: `select.sh` 28 of 28 on Alpine and passing here,
`resolv_defended.sh` 11 of 11, `c_daemon_watch.sh` 26 of 26 on Alpine *and* 26
of 26 here.

### The three that remain are intermittent, and that is all that is known

`displace.sh`, `revive.sh` and `link_local.sh` fail **one check each** in some
full-suite runs. What has been measured:

  * each passes run on its own, repeatedly: **15 runs, 0 failures**, five of
    each, with four spinners loading the container;
  * all 80 scripts exited 0 in one full-suite run taken immediately
    afterwards;
  * they failed one check each in two other full-suite runs.

So it is neither load nor isolation: it is something the suite leaves behind,
intermittently. **Non-reproduction is not evidence** -- `running-code.md` is
explicit, and the three runs above do not weigh against the two that failed.
No cause is claimed and no fix is guessed at.

**That experiment was run and it caught nothing**, which is worth recording as
carefully as a reproduction would have been. The suite was looped in one
container -- bounded at four attempts, a wall-clock ceiling and the usual
per-script timeout, with the attempts sharing `/run` and `/tmp` because
isolated runs had already failed to reproduce it:

    attempt 1: every script exited 0, after 986s
    attempt 2: every script exited 0, after 1727s
    attempt 3: every script exited 0, after 2475s
    attempt 4: every script exited 0, after 3209s

320 script runs in 53 minutes, no failure. Then `make live-alpine` itself ran
clean for the first time: **71 passed, 9 skipped, 0 failed**. So the count is
335 isolated runs plus 5 clean whole-suite runs against one failure that
happened -- and the three scripts stay recorded as intermittent rather than
fixed, because four clean runs do not outweigh a failure anybody saw.

**The real defect was in the tier, not in the hunt.** `live-alpine` printed
only a failing script's last line and kept nothing, so the one failure that
did occur left no evidence and no amount of looping could recover it. It keeps
every script's output while it runs now, deletes a passing or skipping one's
immediately, and prints a failure's own `FAIL` lines -- expected and actual --
under the summary, with the files left in `dist/live-alpine-log/`.
The next occurrence is readable without ceremony, which is what the looping
was a substitute for.

Two faults of mine on the way there, both the sort this file exists to
record. The logging first left **root-owned files in the host tree** that the
user could not remove, which is what `live-container`'s own comment warns
about for build output; the container hands `/dist` back to its owner now, and
the files already written were removed by another container rather than by
reaching for `sudo`. And inspecting the generated script, I started the target
and killed the make client with `kill %1`, which leaves the container running
-- the hazard this workspace has measured twice and which I had cited twice in
the same session. Killed by name, and confirmed gone.

## 10.536 The 40 test findings, and the gate now reads 324 sources

"fix the clang findings in c/tests then", the copyright holder, 2026-10-23,
closing the item 10.529 left open when the `clang` gate went in reading the
library and counting the tests.

### 36 of the 40 were the enum decision arriving at the call sites

Every sign-conversion finding was one shape: an enum passed to a function
taking `int`. That is the cost of 10.525, where the holder settled that a
`_name` takes `int` -- clang treats an enum with no negative enumerator as
unsigned, so every call converts. The library's own sites were fixed that day
with an explicit cast, `ncfg_tier_name((int)tier)`, and the tests were not.

**Two sub-shapes, one rule.** 21 sites passed a plain enum lvalue and 15 cast
*to* the enum type first -- `ncfg_proto_request_name((ncfg_proto_request_kind_t)kind)`,
which was right when the callee took the enum and is pointless now. So the rule
is the same at both: the converted expression is narrowed at the call,
replacing an enum cast where there is one. Uniformly correct, because the
underlying expression is either an enum field or a small loop index, and
`(int)` is value-preserving for every enumerator here -- where dropping the
cast instead would have left a `size_t` conversion at the loop-index sites.

**Clang gave the edit its coordinates.** This tree has already paid for a
column-based cast insertion that landed inside other expressions (10.525), so
the sites came from `-fdiagnostics-print-source-range-info`, which brackets the
converted expression, and the rewrite went bottom-up and right-to-left so no
edit moved a column still to be used.

**Three proofs, none of them the tool's own word.** Each edit asserted at the
time that the new line equalled the old but for the cast; then the diff was
re-checked independently afterwards, symmetrically -- the first version of that
check stripped `(int)` from the new line only and reported two false
differences on a line that already had one, which is a checker bug wearing a
finding's clothes. Then clang: 40 findings to 4. Then the suite: 82 suites, 0
failures, including `socket_witness_test`, which regenerates
`doc/schema/socket.json` and compares, so the witness is byte-identical.

### The other four were clang telling the truth about a real ambiguity

`-Wstring-concatenation` fired on four two-part string literals inside array
initializers -- "did you mean to separate the elements with a comma?" All four
are deliberate continuations of one long string, and a comma would have changed
what the test asserts. clang names its own remedy in the note: parenthesise the
literal. Tested on a fixture first, then applied, which is the honest fix
because it states in the source what the reader has to work out otherwise.

### Two more in the shim's tests, and they were a different thing

`client/tests` was already clean; `adapter/netcfgd-nm/c/tests` had two
`-Wmissing-field-initializers` on `nmc_device_slot_t` initializers written
before the struct gained `scan_wanted`. Zero is the right value -- no scan
pending is what the chooser should see -- but it was zero by C's rules rather
than by anyone saying so, and an initializer that stops short of a field says
nothing about which. Named, with the reason.

### So the gate holds the zero rather than counting it

`syntax-tests` was a tally: it piped clang's output through `grep -c` and could
not fail. It is a gate now, in the same shape as `syntax` -- `-Werror`,
`-fsyntax-only`, print the count on success -- and `client/` and
`adapter/netcfgd-nm/c/` have one too. The root `clang` gate runs all six, so it
reads **324 sources**: 206 library and 98 test in `c/`, 2 and 1 in `client/`,
16 and 1 in the shim.

**Seen to fail.** One cast removed from `value_test.c` and the gate stopped at
`syntax-tests` with `Error 1`, which is the defect it exists to catch.

### And the restore was the mistake, not the control

Putting that cast back, I ran `git checkout -- c/tests/value_test.c` on a file
whose 36-site sweep was **uncommitted** -- so it reverted all six of that
file's casts, not the one-line sabotage. `CLAUDE.md` singles out exactly this
command for exactly this reason: a bad commit has a reflog and discarded
uncommitted work has nothing. Nothing was lost in the end, because the sweep is
reproducible from clang's own ranges and re-running it found the same six sites
and produced an identical diff -- but that is luck in the shape of
determinism, and it would not have held for a change derived by hand.

The lesson is the one the earlier sabotage in this session already followed
and this one did not: **copy the file aside before breaking it on purpose**, the
way `autoip.c` was copied an hour earlier. The cheaper lesson is to commit the
sweep before testing the gate that guards it.

## 10.535 A gate became a build's default goal, and `make nm` built nothing

"run make live-container one more time", the copyright holder, 2026-10-23. The
first run failed where no run had failed before:

    nm.sh: skipping: netcfgd-nm is not built (make nm)
    c_nm_signals.sh: NCFG_LIVE is set but this cannot run: the C shim is not built

Reproduced with the step's output visible rather than guessed at. `make nm`
printed `syntax: cc read 16 source(s) with no warning`, exited 0, and produced
no program.

**The clang gate's own target had become the default goal.** 10.529 added
`syntax` to three builds that morning, and in two of them it went in ABOVE
`all` -- which is what a bare `make` in that directory then does. Asked of make
rather than read out of the file:

    c                        all
    client                   syntax
    adapter/netcfgd-nm/c     syntax

So `make -C client` and `make nm` had been building nothing for four hours.

### Why nothing noticed, which is the part worth keeping

`make check` reaches every artifact through an explicit target, so it was
unaffected and green the whole time -- the gate that would notice is not the
gate that runs. On this host the shim binary from 00:22 simply stayed where it
was, so a bare `make nm` was a silent no-op over a stale file: exactly the
hazard `build-and-commit.md` names, a verdict read off a binary the build step
did not rebuild. **The container is the one place it was loud**, because it
cleans first and `c_nm_signals.sh` turns its own skip into a failure under
`NCFG_LIVE` -- the suite's refusal to tolerate a skip is what made a silent
build failure visible at all.

### The fix, and the gate it earned

The `syntax` targets moved below `all`; `.DEFAULT_GOAL := all` pinned in all
four hand-written builds -- `c`, `client`, `adapter/netcfgd-nm/c`, `bridge` --
so an insertion cannot repeat it; and `default-goal` added to
`PORTABLE_GATES`, which is in `check` and `check-ci` by construction.

**The gate asks make, rather than reading the makefile.** `tool/say-goal.mk`
is loaded as a second `-f` after a directory's own makefile, so that
makefile's first target still decides `.DEFAULT_GOAL` and the extra one only
prints it; naming its target on the command line is what keeps it side-effect
free. A grep for `all:` would have agreed with both broken makefiles, which is
`evidence.md`'s rule about asking the thing itself.

**Seen to fail before it was trusted**: with the pin removed and `syntax` put
back on top, `default-goal: client builds `syntax`, not `all`` and the gate
exits 2. `gui/` is excluded because qmake writes it and `fuzznet/` because it
is a vendored submodule; both answer `all` today and neither is this tree's to
pin.

### The second run: 80 of 81, which is where a container can get to

72 scripts report `all checks passed` in that wording, four more pass in
wordings of their own -- `c_daemon_watch.sh: 26 checks, 0 failed`,
`config_arrives.sh` twice, `network_arrives.sh`, `control_helper.sh: ok` -- so
**76 invocations pass, 4 skip, and all 80 before the last one run.** The 81st
and last is `sandbox_writes.sh`, which needs systemd as pid 1: a container
cannot be talked into that, and its coverage is `make hull-sandbox` at 31 of 31
(10.530). The previous measurement was 75 of 81.

`link_local.sh: all checks passed` there, which is 10.533's fix in the tier
where its four checks failed. `nm.sh` and `c_nm_signals.sh` pass again.

### The four skips, and one of them was lying about how to fix it

  * `hwsim.sh` -- no `mac80211_hwsim`; `make hull-hwsim` runs it, 27 of 27.
  * `delegation.sh` -- no `odhcp6c`, which Debian does not package;
    `make vm-delegation` builds it.
  * `gui_wifi.sh` -- no `qmake6`, which the container's package list does not
    install.
  * `association.sh` -- the probe was not built. **Measured rather than
    assumed**, because adding `make -C c examples` to the container script
    looked like a one-line coverage gain: with the probe built the script gets
    one step further and then says "no netcfgd is running to compare against".
    So that line buys a different skip rather than a run, and is not added.

Its skip message named `cargo build -p netcfgd-host --example live_association`
-- a real target, since the Rust core is still in the tree, and the one thing
that cannot satisfy the path it checks, because `$build` is `c/`. **A skip
message that sends a reader to build the other implementation is worse than
one that says nothing**, so it names `make -C c examples` now.

## 10.531 The openrc script ran, and `need localmount` is a Gentoo name

`packaging/openrc/netcfgd` -- 28 lines of `openrc-run` -- had never been
executed anywhere, and `tool/vm/payload/init.sh` said so in its own header
along with the reason: openrc depends on `insserv`, `systemd-sysv` conflicts
with it, so the tier's Debian guest cannot install openrc at all. The header
named the remedy and called it a second image and the holder's call.

`tests/hull/openrc/` is that image: a `debian:trixie-slim` with
`sysvinit-core openrc lsb-base` and no `systemd-sysv`, exported to a rootfs
directory, booted by hull with `(init "/sbin/openrc-init")`. 114M, sysvinit
3.14-4, openrc 0.56-1, eleven setuid or setgid bits put back by the bake the
way `tests/hull/sandbox/` does it.

**Both halves of the payload now pass there, 13 checks**, and both are firsts:
the LSB script under a non-systemd init, and the `openrc-run` script anywhere.

### The first run failed three, and the reason is a real portability fact

    Service 'netcfgd' needs non existent service 'localmount'
     * ERROR: netcfgd needs service(s) localmount
    FAIL start brought the daemon up, with a pidfile pointing at it
      pidfile: absent
    FAIL and `start_pre` made the runtime directory
    FAIL status agrees it is running

`depend()` says `need localmount`. Gentoo and Alpine ship that service;
**Debian's openrc does not** -- it keeps sysvinit's `mountall.sh`, and nothing
in `/etc/init.d` provides the name, measured by reading the baked image. So
openrc refuses the service outright before `start_pre` ever runs.

It is not a defect in the script. Its second line says who it is for, and for
Gentoo and Alpine the dependency is correct -- `localmount` is where a
writable `/run` and `/var` come from, and `checkpath --directory /run/netcfgd`
has nothing to write into before it. **The guest was wrong, not the
packaging.**

So the image supplies the name: `bake-rootfs.sh` bakes an inert
`/etc/init.d/localmount` with `provide localmount` and a `start()` that
returns 0, and says in its own header why. The rejected alternative was
editing `packaging/openrc/netcfgd` to suit the one distribution it is not
written for, which is weakening a correct dependency to make a rig pass --
the rig testing itself. The stand-in is deliberately inert, because what is
under test is netcfgd's script and not whether a mount ran; anything more
would be this image pretending to be Gentoo.

**The A/B is the two runs**, one variable between them: without the stand-in,
three checks fail with the pidfile absent; with it, `* /run/netcfgd: creating
directory`, `* Starting netcfgd ... [ ok ]`, `status: started`, and 0 failed.
Which also settles the control question for this half -- these six checks have
been seen to fail, for the reason claimed, before they were seen to pass.

An earlier hand-probe in the same guest had succeeded, which is why the
failure was a surprise: the probe ran before openrc cached dependencies for a
service it had never seen. A dependency openrc has not resolved yet is not a
dependency it will accept.

### What each guest proves now, and what still nothing does

  * `make vm-init`, the Debian systemd guest: the LSB half only, through
    `systemd-sysv-generator`. Re-run after this change and still 0 failed.
    The openrc half reports itself untested there and is counted neither way,
    and its message no longer claims those 28 lines are unexecuted anywhere.
  * `tests/hull/openrc/`: both halves, pid 1 `openrc-init`, softlevel
    `sysinit` after 600 ms.
  * `tests/hull/sandbox/`: the LSB half under `/sbin/init`, and the systemd
    unit (10.530).

Still nothing proves either script integrates with a real boot -- ordering,
`provide net`, what waits on what -- because all three guests start the
service by hand. The payload has said so from the start and still does.

Alpine is the other OpenRC world and stays out of reach: it is musl, and its
init is busybox with openrc underneath rather than `openrc-init`, so it would
be a third image proving the same 28 lines. `apk-container` already builds the
C against musl, which is the half of that worth having.

## 10.530 The systemd payload on hull: 30 of 31, then 31 of 31

"do the systemd payloads then", the copyright holder, 2026-10-23, after hull
`bfeb65f` fixed the setuid bug and `0681fb3` gave a machine the image's own
init. The rig is `tests/hull/sandbox/` and it runs
`tool/vm/payload/sandbox_writes.sh` **unchanged** -- the same file
`make vm-sandbox` runs on this tree's own VM tier (0265), which is what makes
the two comparable.

**It works, and the comparison was 30 of 31 against 31 of 31 -- it is 31 of 31
now**, hull having fixed the one difference the same night; the measurement
that closed it is at the end of this entry. In the hull guest: PID 1 is systemd 257, `/run/systemd/private` appears 1.3 seconds in,
`systemctl is-system-running --wait` says `running`, and `systemd-run` imposes
the unit's properties. The native tier, run the same afternoon for the
comparison, passes all 31.

### The one that differs, and it is not the script

The failing check is one of the script's own controls: with `ExecPaths=`
dropped, executing from netcfgd's runtime directory must be **denied**, or the
check above it measured the machine rather than the unit's declaration. Under
hull it is allowed, so the control fires -- correctly, which is the whole
reason that control exists.

Measured on both guests, same systemd 257.13-1~deb13u1, same Debian 13:

    native   /run tmpfs rw,nosuid,nodev,noexec,relatime,size=99028k,mode=755
    hull     /run tmpfs rw,nosuid,nodev,size=404248k,mode=755,inode64
    native   a script in /run: Permission denied
    hull     a script in /run: RAN

So `/run` carries no `noexec` in a hull guest, and a unit property that relies
on it is silently unenforced there. **What was established** was the difference
and its consequence; what was not, at the time, was who mounts it that way --
with the init hand-over removed, `/run` is not a mount point at all, so it
looked like systemd's own mount in both cases, with the flags differing for a
reason not yet named. The ratio differed too, 10 per cent of RAM on the native
guest and 20 in the hull one, which was the hint that the mount was not made
the same way.

**hull answered it, and the answer is the initramfs.** From their `828f72d`:
on this tree's native tier `initramfs-tools` mounts `/run` before systemd
starts and systemd keeps that mount; a hull guest has no initramfs, so systemd
made `/run` itself, and its own defaults carry no `noexec`. That accounts for
all three differences measured here -- `noexec`, `relatime`, and 20 per cent
against 10 -- which is more than the finding asked for and is why it is worth
recording in their words. Under `(init ...)` a hull guest now mounts `/run` as
a distribution's initramfs leaves it: `nosuid,nodev,noexec`, mode 0755, 10 per
cent of memory.

**The finding went to hull with both lines.** It is their fifth from this tree
and the first that only a tier comparison could produce: one guest passing a
control and another failing it, with the script, the distribution and the init
identical.

### What this says about the move

For this payload hull is one mount option short of equivalent, and the gap is
visible rather than silent because the script carries a control for exactly
this. That is the argument for controls restated by somebody else's
environment: a suite without them would have reported 30 passes and no
failure, and the missing enforcement would have been invisible.

The rig stays. It was the cheapest reproduction of the difference, and it is
now the check that the move is complete -- hull asked for exactly that, and it
is what the re-run gives.

### 31 of 31, against hull 828f72d

Re-run the same night, same rig, same rootfs, only the hull binary newer:
`sandbox_writes.sh: all checks passed`, and the line that had been the one
failure reads `ok   and cannot without the unit's ExecPaths=, so that line is
load-bearing`. So the control is back to discriminating: executing from
netcfgd's runtime directory is allowed with `ExecPaths=` and denied without
it, which is the property the unit declares and the only thing that makes the
check above it mean anything.

hull reports their own suite caught two sabotages of the new mount, and that
the same fix closed a second bug of theirs -- a machine with secrets had a
1 MiB `/run`, which would have been systemd's whole `/run`. Their measurement,
in their voice; what this tree measured is the line above.

## 10.527 hull runs the test this workspace never could

"Hull doesn't need to be FULLY usable, it needs to be useful for you and not
broken. You judge.", the copyright holder, 2026-10-22, lifting the deferral in
10.524 and handing over the judgement.

**The judgement: yes, for `hwsim.sh`, and that is the whole of what was
tried.** 27 checks, no failures, exit 0, in a vm on hull `4161c8a` -- the first
time this workspace has run that script at all. `make live` skips it for want
of real root, and `make live-container` cannot answer it in principle: a
container shares the host's kernel and this host has no `mac80211_hwsim`, which
the target's own comment has said since it was written. A vm loads the module
into a kernel of its own, and `iw dev` then shows the radios.

The rig is kept, at `tests/hull/hwsim/`: a machine file, the payload, and the
script that bakes the guest image. No Makefile target yet, and that is
deliberate -- the image has to be baked by docker today (below), and hull's
spec and CLI may still change before 1.0, which hull says itself.

### What it took, which is the part worth knowing

- ~~**Build nothing in the guest.**~~ **It builds in the guest now**, since
  hull `7b47668`. The first attempts could not: gcc's driver printed a bare
  `cc1` where it prints a path, which turned out to be hull giving the workload
  no PATH at all, so the driver could not resolve its own argv[0]. With the
  PATH exported, the guest compiles the C -- `cc (Debian 14.2.0-19)`, a binary
  of 1177000 bytes against the share's 1177000 -- and `hwsim.sh` passes its 27
  checks against the guest's own build rather than the host's.

  That is the shape `build-and-commit.md` argues for and the reason the rig
  changed: a build in the runner's image catches what a developer machine
  hides, and a test running the host's binary is a test of the host's
  toolchain. The payload falls back to the share where an image has no
  compiler, and says so out loud. The bake script installs one, which costs
  about 300 MB of image.

  **The measurement is of the committed rig, not of a scratch copy**: baked by
  `tests/hull/hwsim/bake-rootfs.sh` as it stands and run by its own
  `hull.conf`, both at the commit this entry is in.

- **And the baked image is not the image it looks like**, which is this rig's
  own caveat rather than hull's. `docker export` through `tar -x` as an
  ordinary user drops every setuid bit and every owner: the
  `debian:trixie-slim` image has eight setuid-root programs and the exported
  tree has none, all of it `funk:users` 0755. `hull materialize` of the same
  image keeps all eight, so hull's path is the faithful one.

  `hwsim.sh` does not care -- it is root in the guest and calls no setuid
  program -- but a payload that calls `sudo`, or `mount` as a user, must not
  use this image. **And it masked a hull bug rather than meeting it**: 9p shows
  a guest every file as the host user's, so a setuid-root program becomes
  setuid-1000 and root running it is refused, which an image with no setuid
  bits cannot show. Two faults cancelling into an appearance of health, which
  is the reason the bake script now says so at length.
- **A root-shaped `PATH`.** The agent runs the command without `/usr/sbin`, and
  netcfgd looks for a DHCP client on `PATH` alone -- deliberately, `dhcp.c`
  saying an operator's own client in front of the packaged one is a choice it
  honours. So an installed `dhcpcd` read as "not installed" and the address
  half of the test failed. Any init gives root the sbins; the payload does it
  instead.
- **The packages come from docker, not from hull.** Three roads and each has a
  snag, measured: into a `(mutable overlay)` vm the install truncates silently
  -- it left a gcc with no `cc1`, which is worse than failing; with `(mutable
  direct)` the guest writes through 9p as the host user, so dpkg's `chown`
  fails and apt dies; and in a `hull build` step the packages install and then
  `dnsmasq-base`'s postinst fails, a build step mapping one uid so that a
  maintainer script cannot give a file to its own system user. The findings
  went to hull's session, which is where they belong.

  **And a fourth claim was wrong and was mine.** That step was first reported
  as calling four of seven packages "unable to locate" after a successful
  update -- offered as hull's snag. hull measured it and it does not
  reproduce: a build step is offline unless it says `(network true)`, mine did
  not say it, and `apt-get update` exits 0 when it cannot fetch. So the update
  "succeeded" against nothing and only cached names resolved. Re-run with the
  network declared, all seven install.

  **The shape is one this tree keeps meeting from the inside**: a command that
  exits 0 having done nothing, and a reading taken from its status rather than
  from its effect. `apt-get update` with no network joins `make` with the
  host's mtimes (10.526) and the gate over an empty file list -- and this time
  the cost was a wrong finding in somebody else's queue, which is worse than a
  wrong one in my own.

### And it found one thing in this tree

`hwsim.sh` reported "cannot reach the access point" on a guest whose image
simply had no `iputils-ping`. That is the false-negative class the file's own
preflight comments are about -- a tool that is not there is not a network that
does not work -- and it is the one check in the file that had no skip. It says
so now.

### What is not claimed

Nothing else was tried. The other 80 live invocations still run under `make
live` and `make live-container`, which reaches 75 of 81 (10.523); this is one
script that neither tier can run, not a move of the tier. The systemd and
OpenRC payloads wait on hull's init hand-over, and several machines on a wire
on segments, which landed the same day and nothing here has used.

## 10.525 Five clang warnings, and the count that overruled the convention

Noted as open earlier on 2026-10-22 and closed here: `clang
-Wsign-conversion` reported five implicit conversions in `src/plan/` that gcc
never reports, all the same shape -- a kind held as an `int` passed to a
`_name()` function that takes its enum.

**They are not cosmetic, because `make fuzz` compiles these sources with
clang.** `FUZZ_CFLAGS` carries the project's whole warning set and `FUZZ_OBJS`
covers every library source, so those five printed on every fuzz build. That
is what makes this code in the way of a tool this project runs rather than a
tidier spelling.

### The wrong turn, which the measurement caught

`value.h` states the convention plainly -- "`_name` returns NULL for a value
outside its set" -- and **an enum parameter cannot honour that**: a value
outside the set has been converted by the time the body could check it. Sixteen
of these functions take an `int` and `ncfg_outcome_name` says why in its own
comment. So the four the warnings named were changed to take an `int`, which is
what the convention argues for.

**That took the library from 5 clang warnings to 30**, which is what the entry
first concluded from: the kind is held as an enum in more places than as an
`int`, so an `int` parameter moved the conversion to other call sites.

**And that conclusion was drawn from a half-done change, which is the lesson
here.** The holder settled it on 2026-10-23 -- take `int` -- and done
completely it goes the other way: 33 casts come OUT of the tree and 16 go in,
because `(ncfg_x_t)` casts existed all over it for no reason but the old
signature, and `document.c` and `observed.c` each carried a `VALUE_SHIM` whose
naming half was a function per set doing nothing but `_name((type)value)`.
Those are gone; the sets name `_name` directly. 41 files, 89 insertions, 97
deletions, and clang reports 0 over `src/` and `client/` as it did before.

So the count I argued from was real and measured the wrong thing: warnings
under a partial conversion, where the question was casts after a complete one.
A number is only an argument about what it counted.

So the signatures are unchanged and the five int-holding call sites carry an
explicit cast. Clang over `src/` and `client/` reports **0**, a fuzz target
builds with none, gcc builds unchanged, and the C suite passes -- the casts
change no behaviour, which is what makes this a readable diff rather than a
risk.

### What is left, named rather than swept

Ten `_name` functions still take their enum and sixteen take an `int`, which is
a real inconsistency against a convention `value.h` states for every set. A
signature change across the tree is its own piece of work and the count above
says it would be the wrong direction anyway for the ten -- so what is wanted is
a decision about which form the convention means, not a sweep. Nothing in the
build currently sees it: at zero warnings both forms compile silently.

**And nothing keeps the count at zero.** There is no clang gate here; `make
fuzz` is where the warnings showed and it is not part of `check`. A gate that
compiled the library with clang for warnings alone would hold it, which is the
shape ossacli's `check-clang` has -- raised here rather than built, since a new
gate is a convention change and the one that exists is another tree's.

## 10.523 nm.sh in a container, and the two reasons it had never run in one

"run nm.sh in the live container", the copyright holder, 2026-10-22, after
10.522 recorded that this machine has no `nmcli` and that 0282's two
expectations in that file were therefore derived from the shim's source rather
than observed.

**It passes: 124 checks, nothing skipped**, with `NCFG_LIVE=1` so that a
missing tool would have been a failure rather than a pass -- which is the
setting that matters here, since the whole question was whether the script runs
at all. Both lines 0282 changed are in it: `every named access point the scan
found is listed` and `and the names came through`, and the three signal
conversions beside them (-40 to 100, -100 to 0, -53 to 79) are unmoved by the
two networks the fake gained.

### `make live-container` could not have run it, for two reasons

Neither is a defect in the script and both are the same shape as the
`dhcpcd-base` finding that target's own comment records -- a container run
covering less than the host while looking like more.

- **`nmcli` is not in `LIVE_PACKAGES`**, and only `network-manager` ships it.
  So nm.sh skipped, and its skip read exactly like the two that the comment
  above the target explains as expected.
- **The shim was never built in there.** The container script built the Rust
  workspace and the `ncfg` symlink; the live scripts drive `c/netcfgd` and
  `adapter/netcfgd-nm/c/netcfgd-nm` **by path**, and those arrived only as
  whatever binaries `cp -a /src /work` happened to copy out of the host tree.
  Where the host had not built them the script skipped; where it had, the
  container was running the host's binary rather than one built in it.

Both are fixed: the package list gains `network-manager`, `libdbus-1-dev`,
`pkg-config` and `python3-dbus`, and the container script cleans and then
builds the C and the shim before `make live`. `libdbus-1-dev` is what the
shim's build needs and is how the first attempt failed -- `#include
<dbus/dbus.h>` not found, which is a better error than a skip and is the only
reason this was found in one go.

**The clean is the half that makes the build real, and without it the fix was
hollow.** `cp -a` preserves mtimes and `c/Makefile`'s `.build-flags` stamp
records the flag string rather than the compiler, so a build in the container
inherits the verdict the host left -- nothing to be done -- and compiles not
one file. That is a build step that looks like one and is not, and it was found
by reading the mechanism rather than by watching it: the recipe sends both
builds to `/dev/null`, so there is nothing in the log either way. The whole
value of building in the image the runner uses is that its toolchain is not the
one here, which an inherited binary gives up entirely.

**The way to notice this class is to run a script in there and read its
output.** Nothing about the package list looks wrong until a script says
`skipping` in a container built to stop it skipping, and a suite that reports
every skip as expected is one where a new skip is invisible.

### And running the target found two more of the same thing, one of them loud

**`bc` is not in the image, and `apply_race.sh` pipes a count through it.** The
script exited 127, `make live` stopped there, and the 66 script invocations at
or after it -- of 81 -- never ran at all. So the target had been covering a
third of the suite while printing 362 passing checks on the way, which reads
exactly like a full run to anybody not counting. The host has `/usr/bin/bc`,
which is why nobody met it here.

**`dhcpcd_orphan.sh` then stopped it at 35 scripts, and the cause was not
namespaces.** Its guard is `unshare --map-root-user --map-auto --mount --uts
--net`, and `--map-auto` reads `/etc/subuid` and `/etc/subgid`, which an image
does not ship for root -- `no line matching user "root" in /etc/subuid`.
Probed directly in the image rather than inferred: with a `root:100000:65536`
line in both files the call succeeds, and nested inside another user namespace
it cannot, which is why the container script writes the files and the Makefile
runs that script without an outer `unshare`. A developer machine has the
equivalent line for its own user.

**Both are the same shape as `nmcli`**, and the shape is the finding: an image
is not a machine, and every tool a script reaches for is a thing the host
happens to have. The guard against it is not a longer list, it is running the
suite in there and reading where it stops.

**Where it stops now: 75 of the 81 invocations, and `nm.sh` is one of them** --
`nm.sh: all checks passed` inside `make live-container`, which is the whole
point of this entry reached through the target rather than through a one-off.
Zero failures on the way, from 15 invocations before `bc`.

It stops at `sandbox_writes.sh`, which says why: no systemd in a container, so
the unit's real sandbox cannot be checked. That is a third member of the family
the target's own comment already keeps -- `hwsim.sh` wants a module the host
does not have and `delegation.sh` wants a package Debian does not ship -- and
it is the kind of limit a container cannot be talked out of. A guest with its
own init is on hull's roadmap (10.524).
