**`docker run --group-add users` is what gets past `control_exposure.sh`, the
invocation that used to be the end, and the first version of this entry blamed
that flag for something it cannot do.** The claim was that the
flag moved the stopping point backwards, because `link_local.sh` failed four
checks about the pid of the client netcfgd started on a run with it and passed
on a run without -- "isolated with nothing else changed", which is the sentence
to distrust.

**The flag is inert inside the namespaces every other script runs in.**
Measured after the claim was committed: `unshare -rn` denies `setgroups`, so
the groups inside are `0 65534` whether the flag is passed or not -- and `0
65534` is also what they are on the host, from a user that has eighteen. The
one script the flag reaches is the one invoked WITHOUT `unshare`, which is
`control_exposure.sh`, which is what it was added for. So it is back in, and
this is what "nothing else changed" is worth without checking that the thing
changed can reach the thing measured.

**The load story is out too, which leaves the failure unexplained.** It was
the first reading -- another project was building in a second container -- and
the test is cheap: `link_local.sh` on the host at load 172 passes all 19
checks. Two explanations, both measured, both gone. One failing observation
stands with no account of it, which `running-code.md` says is the state to
leave visible rather than close: non-reproduction is not evidence against an
intermittent, and the two reproductions since (the host under load, and the
container without the flag) are not evidence either.

**The next experiment was named rather than guessed at**: run that script in
the container under quiet load with the flag, and keep `$work` -- the apply's
own failure text says neither "error" nor "failed", so the check above reports
no failure either way, which is why this presented as a missing pid file
rather than as a refused start, and `apply.txt` is the file that would say
which.

**Run on 2026-10-23, and it was the source rather than the container that
answered** (10.533). That prediction about the failure text was right and it
names the exact branch: `ncfg_autoip_start` confirmed a detached client with a
single look at `/proc`, so a client whose own process was not yet in place was
reported as a failed start while it ran on unmanaged. The start waits now. Four
environmental explanations have been disproved in all -- the flag, host load,
container load and a `noexec` `/tmp` -- and the defect that fits the evidence
is gone, which is not the same as knowing what that one run did.

### The container also found an intermittent that is not the container's

`network_arrives.sh` failed its second check -- "and told the supplicant about
it" -- on a run where every later check passed, while this machine was also
building another project in a second container. The check reads
`grep -c "ssid <hex>" daemon.log` with no wait, and **the check above it cannot
be the synchronisation point**: `associated()` reads netcfgd's view of
`STATUS`, and the fake supplicant reports the station as already on `HomeFiber`
before anybody has configured anything -- which that script states in as many
words about the `JOIN` checks forty lines further down.

The two `told_about` checks below it have always been wrapped in `awaits`; this
one was not. It is now. **Non-reproduction is not what justifies the fix** --
the script passes here either way, and it passed in the container run before
this one -- the mechanism is: an unsynchronised read of a log another process
writes, on the one check in the file that lacked the wait its siblings have.

## 10.514 The schema already had every event kind; my filter did not

"add a line per event kind to the schema", the copyright holder, 2026-10-21 --
asked for on the strength of 10.513, which was **wrong**. The lines were
already there.

    doc/schema/socket.json:53   {"response":"event","event":"confirm_armed",...}
    doc/schema/socket.json:63   {"event":"observed",...}
    doc/schema/socket.json:64   {"event":"reloaded",...}
    doc/schema/socket.json:65   {"event":"drift",...}
    doc/schema/socket.json:66   {"event":"confirm_armed",...}
    doc/schema/socket.json:67   {"event":"confirm_resolved",...}

Five kinds, in the shape a monitor stream actually delivers -- a bare
`{"event": ...}` line -- plus one wrapped in a response. The C enumerates
exactly those five (`NCFG_PROTO_EVENT_OBSERVED` through
`..._CONFIRM_RESOLVED`, with `_COUNT`), and the Rust witness generator
enumerates them through an exhaustive match that refuses to compile if a
variant appears. Nothing was missing from anything.

**What was missing was in my seed generator**, which filtered the schema for
`"response":"event"` and found one line. So the monitor target was seeded with
one kind out of five, and the sentence I wrote -- "the schema carries exactly
one event line" -- was true about the string I searched for and false about
the question I was answering.

### The error is the same one this week has been about

A corpus that does not reach the reader reports success as loudly as one that
does (10.511), and this is the next layer down: **a generator that does not
find the seeds reports a corpus as loudly as one that does.** Both were caught
by asking what an input reaches rather than whether it parses -- and this one
only after it had been written into an entry, a commit message and a reply to
the holder, which is why the instruction came back as "add the lines".

So the honest fix is three things and none of them is a schema edit:

* the filter takes both shapes, and the generator fails rather than writing
  nothing if it finds no events. The corpus is five kinds now, and a probe
  says so: `confirm_armed`, `observed`, `reloaded`, `drift`,
  `confirm_resolved`, then the stream ends;
* **the claim is now a gate**, in `tool/ledger_gate.py`, which already reads
  this witness for requests. Every kind `event_names[]` holds must have a line
  and every line must name a kind this build can emit -- so the next reader
  does not have to grep for the right string, and `make check` says
  "5 event kind(s), each with a line" on every run;
* 10.513's section is struck through rather than quietly amended, because a
  wrong measurement that produced an instruction is worth leaving visible.

### Both arms of the gate, and the arm that matters most

    a kind with no witness line   remove `{"event":"drift"...}`: "socket.json
                                  has no line for the `drift` event, which
                                  this build emits"
    a line nothing can emit       add `{"event":"invented"}`: "socket.json
                                  carries an `invented` event and this build
                                  cannot emit one"
    the table gone missing        rename `event_names`: "has no event_names
                                  table, so this would check the witness
                                  against nothing"

The third is the one worth having. `word_table_gate.py` already holds that
table to one word per enum value, so the two gates between them say: the table
is complete, and the witness carries all of it. Neither sentence is believed
any more.

## 10.511 A corpus is part of the detector, measured twice over

"fuzz the client library's readers too", the copyright holder, 2026-10-21.
`libncfg_client.a` is linked by `ncfg`, by the Qt client and by the
NetworkManager shim, and every one of them learns what the machine is doing
through a reader in it. There are twenty-one that take one request and build
C structures from the reply -- framing, then JSON, then a typed walk -- and
only the JSON layer had ever been fuzzed, from the daemon's side.

3.9 million executions, 2,932 new coverage units, no crash and no leak. The
corpus is clean under ASan and UBSan as well as at `-Os`.

### A reply, without a daemon and without forking

One listening unix socket, made once for the process. Per input: connect a
client to it, accept the other end, **write the reply before calling the
reader**, then shut the writing half down so the reader sees an end of stream
rather than waiting for one.

The order is the whole trick, and it is what makes this single-threaded. A
reader writes its request and then blocks reading the answer, so a target that
called it first would have nobody to answer. Queued first, the bytes are
already in the socket when the reader looks, and the request it writes lands
in a buffer nobody drains -- which is fine, because it is one short line.

**Is netcfgd not trusted?** The socket is `root:netcfgd` and netcfgd is what
answers on it, so this is not netlink and it is not a D-Bus client. It is a
boundary all the same, for two reasons worth stating rather than assuming: the
path is settable, so a client can be pointed at a socket somebody else owns;
and a daemon one version ahead of the library answers with fields this build
has never seen, which is the ordinary case on a machine mid-upgrade and is
exactly what a typed walk gets wrong.

### The finding is about the corpus, and it is the sharpest of the week

The sabotage was an off-by-one: `*into_count = count + 1` in `read_routes`,
which makes the free walk one entry past the array.

    with the schema-derived seeds   971,215 executions, nothing
    with one seed added             caught in seconds, as a
                                    heap-buffer-overflow in
                                    `ncfg_saved_networks_free`, with the line

Nothing about the fuzzer changed between those two lines. **The corpus never
reached the function.** `ncfg_client_saved_networks` sends `{"request":"show"}`
and walks `networks[]` out of the document it gets back, and
`doc/schema/socket.json` -- which is where the seeds come from, being the
protocol's own record and what `tests/client_test` validates against -- has no
document line with a network carrying routes. So the reader was being called
and the function under it never ran.

That is the lesson to keep from all of this week's fuzzing: **a corpus is part
of the detector, and a target with the wrong corpus reports success exactly as
loudly as one with the right one.** It is the vacuous pass this tree keeps
finding, wearing a fuzzer's clothes -- and the only thing that found it was
injecting a defect and noticing that nothing happened.

The seed is `seed-document-saved-networks.bin`, made with `ncfg show --json`
on a config whose network carries `config`, `routes` and a `dns` block. The
reproducer the control produced is `routes-past-the-count.bin`, and both are
committed, so `make check` runs them through `client-test`.

### And the harness's own undefined behaviour

The first version dispatched through a table of twenty-one `{reader, free}`
pairs with `out` cast to `void *` -- four lines instead of eighty, and
**undefined behaviour**: calling a function through a pointer of another type
is UB whatever the ABI does, and `-fsanitize=function` says so. It said so
within seconds of the first run.

So the dispatch is a macro over a switch now: each case names the real type,
calls the real function and frees with the real free, with no cast anywhere
and the compiler checking all three against each other. **The sanitizers found
a bug in the thing built to find bugs**, which is the argument for pointing
them at the harness and not only at what it drives -- and for preferring
eighty lines the compiler checks to four it cannot.

## 10.509 A client could write its own configuration, by naming a key

"now fuzz the shim's dictionary reader too", the copyright holder, 2026-10-21.
It found a configuration injection in `nmc_block_render`, which 0278 records
and which is fixed with two regression tests and a corpus input.

### What a client could do

`AddConnection` takes `a{sa{sv}}`. The renderer writes a drop-in under
`/etc/netcfgd/conf.d` and the daemon compiles it, and the dropped-settings
note -- which 0034 requires, naming every setting netcfgd cannot express --
wrote the client's group and key names into a comment **verbatim**. A key name
carrying a newline therefore ended the comment:

    #   connection.x"
    }

    network "injected" {
    	ssid = "anything"
    	wifi { open = true }
    }
    #

    network "Victim" {
    	wifi { open = true }
    }

Everything after the newline is configuration the client chose. The second
site was `dns-search`, whose entries went into `search = [...]` with no check
at all and could close the list, close the block and open another.

**The permission this converted.** `AddConnection` authorizes the caller by
uid, so the client was one allowed to add a wifi network. What it got was the
ability to write any configuration netcfgd will compile -- a different
permission, and a much larger one. Addresses and routes were never exposed:
both go through `is_address`, which is why this is two sites and not twelve.

### The fuzzer did not find it, and the honest version of that matters

No crash. The renderer never crashed in millions of executions and still does
not. What happened is that a target assertion fired on a NEAR MISS: the
assertion said the credential must appear nowhere in the block text, and an
input turned up whose passphrase was `802-11-wireless` -- a legal passphrase
length, and a string the note lists because it is a group name. That was a
false positive in my own assertion, and reading the output to understand it is
what showed the note echoing client text into the file.

So: **fuzzing put the output in front of somebody, and the defect was found by
reading it.** The injection itself had to be reproduced by hand, because the
structure-aware generator only emits printable ASCII -- it cannot produce a
newline, by design, since libdbus refuses a string that is not valid UTF-8 and
a generator feeding it arbitrary bytes would report its own bug every run.

The assertion that was too strong is now the sound one: the credential must
never be the VALUE of `psk`, which is what 0042 and 0229 actually require and
which has no false positives.

### What makes the class mechanical from here

`fuzz/shape.c`: after every successful render, the text must be a block this
renderer could have written -- exactly one `network "..." {` header, and every
other line blank, a comment, tab-indented, or the closing brace. Injection
breaks it immediately.

Proved both ways, which is the only thing that makes an invariant worth having:
against the unfixed renderer the seed aborts with `2 network blocks, not one`;
against the fixed one the whole corpus replays clean. The seed is
`corpus/dictionary/seed-newline-in-a-key-name.bin`, produced by the committed
generator, so `make nm-c-test` runs it for ever.

### Two targets, because each is blind where the other is not

This was measured rather than assumed, and the measurement changed the design.

    dictionary   the real boundary: bytes, `dbus_message_demarshal`, render.
                 It reaches the renderer's key comparisons -- libFuzzer infers
                 `"ipv4"`, `"gateway"`, `"owe"` as dictionary tokens, which it
                 could not do otherwise. **And with an injected overflow in
                 `read_text` it found nothing in 2.7 million runs**, because
                 lengthening a string in a D-Bus body means editing four
                 length prefixes at once and a byte mutator produces a message
                 that fails to demarshal instead.
    settings     the dictionary built from the bytes: which group, which key,
                 which type, how long. The same sabotage, and it reported a
                 stack-buffer-overflow in seconds.

A target that cannot reach a bug class is not a weaker target, it is a blind
one -- and the only way to find out which classes it is blind to is to inject
one and watch.

### And a near-miss worth keeping

`read_text` is bounded twice -- the length check and a bounded copy -- so the
sabotage above needed two edits to produce a crash. The comment above the
second bound says why it is there: "a copy into a credential buffer whose only
bound lives in another function is one a later edit breaks without anything
saying so." That is defence in depth working exactly as described, found by
trying to break it.

## 10.508 A fuzzer explores; the corpus is what remembers

"now fix the fuzz gate too", the copyright holder, 2026-10-21, after the
budget gates. 0277 records the arrangement. `make fuzz` fuzzes the C parsers,
`make fuzz-rust` is the old cargo-fuzz path, and **the half that runs every
time is a replay rather than a fuzzer.**

### What was actually wrong, which was not "the gate points at Rust"

It did point at Rust -- five targets under `fuzz/fuzz_targets/` fuzzing five
Rust parsers that stopped being what runs when 0266 shipped the C -- and
pointing them at the C would have fixed the smaller half of the problem.

**A fuzzer explores and does not remember.** Run it again with another seed, or
on another machine, and it goes somewhere else; so "that crash is fixed" is a
claim nothing re-checks, and a defect found on a laptop in October gets
rediscovered by somebody else in March or never. Design section 12 asked for
fuzzing "as part of CI, not as an occasional exercise", and a fuzz target on
its own cannot answer the second clause however good the first is.

So there are two drivers over one function. A target is a plain
`ncfg_fuzz_one()` over bytes; `fuzz/fuzz_libfuzzer.c` hands it to clang and
`fuzz/fuzz_replay.c` walks a committed corpus with the ordinary compiler. The
second is in `make -C c test`, so in `make check`, on a machine with no clang
and no nightly -- **which is the machine a regression actually arrives on.**

### Five targets, parser for parser with the Rust's

    config_parse     the DSL through to a canonicalised document
    document_json    the document /run holds, round trip asserted
    netlink_wire     the kernel's messages: a privileged reader of lengths
                     it must not trust
    backend_ipc      wpa_supplicant and hostapd replies -- a lower-trust
                     boundary than the kernel's
    socket_message   the control protocol's framing and its messages

`netlink_wire` asserts **termination** as well as safety, which is the half no
sanitizer can see: a length that makes no progress is an infinite loop that
looks like a slow input from outside. Every walk is counted and the bound
aborts, which is what the Rust target's `take(10_000)` was for.

### What was proved, because a detector is the thing most worth distrusting

**A fuzzer that finds nothing looks exactly like a broken one.** So:

    finds coverage      50,000 runs per target added 1,145 new units for
                        config_parse, 1,104 backend_ipc, 688 document_json,
                        255 netlink_wire. A target that returned early
                        would add none
    finds a defect      one bounds check removed in a scratch copy -- the
                        `len > remaining` refusal in `ncfg_wire_attrs_next`
                        -- and it reported a heap-buffer-overflow in
                        `ncfg_wire_attr_string` in about 220 executions,
                        with the line and a nine-byte reproducer
    keeps it            that reproducer is corpus/netlink_wire/attr-longer-
                        than-the-area.bin, it replays clean against the real
                        code, and it runs on every `make check` from now on
    clean under ASan    `make -C c SANITIZE=1 fuzz-replay` passes over every
                        committed input, not just the -Os build
    refuses emptiness   a corpus directory with no files fails by name; the
                        replay binary refuses zero arguments with rc 2

The second and third together are the loop this exists for, demonstrated
rather than described -- sabotage, find, keep, replay.

### Two target bugs, and the first is the instructive one

**`ncfg_config_sources_free` aborted in `free()` on the first corpus file.**
The target had built its source set the way the unit tests do -- a
`ncfg_config_file_t` on the stack, `at` pointed at it, never freed -- and then
called the real free function, which walks the array and frees the array
itself. A test that never frees can do that; a fuzz target that runs a million
times cannot, because it would leak. The set is on the heap now and the free
path is fuzzed with everything else.

That is worth writing down because the stack version LOOKS like the
established pattern: five call sites in `c/tests/` do exactly that, correctly.
**A pattern copied across a boundary where its precondition changed** is the
shape, and the precondition here was "nobody frees this".

The second was ordinary: `NCFG_ERROR_MAX` and the hook sink live in headers the
targets had not included, which the compiler said plainly.

### What clang sees that gcc does not

The instrumented build is clang's, and it emitted five `-Wsign-conversion`
warnings the gcc build never has -- `src/plan/link.c:440`,
`src/plan/model_json.c:207`, `:215`, `:240`, `src/plan/write.c:268`, each an
`int` assigned to an enum. Not crashes and not fixed here; recorded because
**a second compiler is a second opinion about the same source**, and this tree
had only ever heard one.

### What this does not claim

Nothing runs a fuzzer on a schedule -- CI is declined for cost -- so the
*corpus* is continuous and the *fuzzing* is a person typing `make fuzz`.
Section 12 now says that in those words instead of claiming the stronger
thing. The sanitizers are still not gated. And the NetworkManager shim's
dictionary reader, which takes `a{sa{sv}}` from any client on the system bus,
is not fuzzed: it needs libdbus to build and is its own piece of work.

## 10.506 The linkage gate was about a binary nobody installs

The copyright holder, 2026-10-21: "fix the linkage gate too", after it was
reported as a finding from retiring the Rust. `make linkage` built
`target/release/netcfgd` with cargo and read that binary's `NEEDED` list, while
its own comment said **"what the shipped binary is allowed to link"**.

**It is the fourth member of a family 0266 named and did not finish naming.**
That record lists `size`, `rss` and `footprint` as gates measuring a binary
nobody ships, and left them pointed there on purpose -- a budget is a
calibrated number and moving it in the same change that moves what it measures
is how a ratchet stops ratcheting. `linkage` is not calibrated. It is an allow
list, so re-pointing it costs nothing but naming what the C actually links, and
there was no reason for it to be in that list except that nobody put it there.

**A gate whose comment describes the right artifact is worse than no gate**,
which is the transferable part. The sentence is what stops anybody looking:
three sessions read "the shipped binary" in that comment while the recipe two
lines below it said `target/release`, and the mismatch was found by asking what
every Rust-era claim in the tree was about rather than by reading the gate.

### Two binaries, two lists, because they are two claims

    c/netcfgd                        libc.so ld-linux
    adapter/netcfgd-nm/c/netcfgd-nm  libc.so ld-linux libdbus-1.so
                                     and libdbus-1.so REQUIRED

The daemon's list is constraint 3: libc and the kernel. As built it has exactly
one `NEEDED` entry, `libc.so.6`. The shim's is 0264's answer -- the D-Bus stack
the core must not have, taken from the system rather than vendored -- so it is
libc plus `libdbus-1` and that is the whole of it.

**The shim's list carries a positive control**, which is the half an allow list
cannot do on its own: `libdbus-1` is *required* to be there. Without it the
check would pass most loudly on a shim that had stopped linking D-Bus
altogether, which is the vacuous pass this tree keeps finding. It pairs with
`nm-containment`, which asserts the shim HAS that stack (10.504); this asserts
the core has not acquired it and the shim has acquired nothing else.

### What came off the list, and the sharper of the two cases

`libncursesw` and `libtinfo` were allowed because `ncfg tui` is a default
**cargo feature** and design section 10.2 lists it as removable. The C's TUI
writes its own escape sequences -- `c/src/cli/tui_term.c` argues it at length
against binding ncurses -- so the shipped daemon links neither.

**`libgcc_s` is the case worth keeping.** Nothing decided to drop it; the C
simply does not pull it, and it sat on the list because the Rust did. An allow
list naming a library the binary does not link is a gate that would not notice
that library arriving -- so a list is not only a statement about what is
forbidden, it is a claim about what is present, and the two rot differently.

### Five arms, each seen to fail

    a library not on the list      the Rust binary against the core's list,
                                   which names libncursesw and libtinfo
    the positive control           the daemon against the shim's list, which
                                   reports "passing for the boring reason"
    a static binary                no NEEDED entries at all, which the gate
                                   refuses rather than calling a pass
    a binary that is not there     "so this would check nothing"
    libdbus absent                 a stub `pkg-config` that fails: the core's
                                   half still runs and the skip is said aloud

The skip matters for the reason every guarded gate here is guarded: a machine
with no libdbus headers cannot build the shim, so it cannot link anything it
should not either -- but a silent skip is how a gate stops being a gate.

### What it stopped covering, named rather than left

Nothing now reads the Rust binary's `NEEDED` list. That is correct and it is
still worth saying: it ships nowhere, and `deny` governs its crate graph. The
link-level question the old gate answered -- a crate that links a C library, or
a build script that finds one, adding an entry with nothing for `deny` to
object to -- no longer has an answer for the Rust, and does not need one. For
the C there is no graph and no build script, so an entry arrives only because
somebody wrote `-l` or included a header pkg-config knows about.

~~`size`, `rss` and `footprint` are still pointed at the Rust. They are 0266's
open item, not this one.~~ **Wrong when written, and wrong by the same
mechanism this entry is about.** All three had already been re-pointed at the C
-- `size` reads `c/netcfgd`, `rss` runs `./c/netcfgd`, `footprint` runs
`./c/ncfg`, and each recipe says so in its first comment. The sentence came
from 0266's *What this leaves wrong* section, quoted rather than re-derived, in
an entry whose whole subject is a gate that rotted because its comment was
believed over its recipe. A record is not editable and does not have to be:
reading the Makefile would have taken one grep. 10.507 has what was actually
left to do.

## 10.504 The Rust shim is retired, and what went with it

The copyright holder, 2026-10-21: "retire the Rust shim, <- the less code we
have, the less bug surface to maintain." 0276 records it. `adapter/netcfgd-nm`
has one implementation now, `make nm` and `make install-nm` build and install
the C one, and 10,034 lines left the tree in one commit -- 8,736 of Rust across
sixteen files, a 102-crate lockfile, a `deny.toml`, and the 174-line
differential oracle.

**The condition was 0264's and it was met the day before**: `tests/live/nm.sh`
at 124 of 124, the guest tier at 214 of 214 (10.503). The C shim's own Makefile
had carried the sentence "the Rust goes on shipping until this passes" since
the port began, and the report that it passed sat beside it for one day.

### The saving is not in the line count, and saying so is the point

    the Rust shim     8,736 lines, 16 files, 102 crates in its lockfile
    the C shim       12,909 lines of src and include, 1,615 of tests
    shipped          224 KB, linking libdbus-1 and libc

**The C is about 1.5 times the source for the same bus surface.** That is what C
costs here and 0266 measured the same ratio for the daemon. What retiring the
Rust buys is one program to fix instead of two, and a D-Bus stack of 102 crates
replaced by a system library the distribution maintains. An entry claiming a
line win would be a comfortable number standing in for the real one.

### The package stopped needing a Rust toolchain at all

This is the consequence nobody asked for and the largest one.
`debian/control` carried `cargo (>= 1.85), rustc (>= 1.85)` with a comment
saying they were "for `adapter/netcfgd-nm` and nothing else since 0266", and
10.384 had already measured that one module as the sole reason the package
needed them. Both are gone; `libdbus-1-dev` is in, because zbus was a crate
that brought its own D-Bus and the C shim links the system's.

**One cargo call was left on the package's path and it was not obvious.**
`override_dh_auto_clean` runs `make clean`, whose first line was
`$(CARGO) clean`, so dropping the toolchain would have failed the package build
at the clean step rather than the build step. It skips loudly where cargo is
absent now -- `if command -v; then ...; fi` and not `cond && run || echo`,
which would report the skip for a cargo that is present and failed. Both arms
were run: absent prints the skip and continues, present-and-failing fails the
recipe.

### Two gates had the Rust as their source of truth

**`tool/dbus_policy_gate.py` parsed `#[zbus::interface(name = "...")]`.** It
reads the C tables now, anchored on the type rather than on a string that looks
like an interface name: a served interface is a value of type
`nmc_interface_t`, which is what the dispatcher routes with and what the
introspection renderer walks. That is what makes 0264's miss impossible rather
than merely fixed -- `org.netcfgd.Compat` is an `nmc_interface_t` and cannot be
overlooked, and `SecretAgent` is a `#define` the shim builds a call from and
cannot be counted as served.

**The two extractions were measured against each other on the one day both
existed**: the same 18 interfaces, plus `org.freedesktop.DBus.ObjectManager`,
which the C declares in its own tables because libdbus generates nothing and
zbus did. That measurement cannot be taken again, which is why it is written
here rather than left as a passing remark.

It was kept static rather than made to ask the program. `nmc/bus.h` said
`nmc_bus_introspect` was "exposed because the policy gate reads the served
interface names", and nothing had ever wired that -- an intention that read as
a fact. Running `netcfgd-nm --interfaces` would be the more decisive
instrument, and it would add code to the shim for a gate's benefit and make the
gate skip on a machine with no libdbus, which is exactly the machine where a
missing grant is found by an operator with no network rather than by CI. The
comment was corrected to say what the function is for: `tests/bus_test.c`.

**`nm-containment`'s second half asserted the adapter's lockfile held at least
twenty crates**, on the grounds that "the core does not have the adapter's
dependencies" proves nothing if the adapter has none -- this tree's vacuous
pass, guarded against. There is no lockfile to count. It asserts two things
now: that the shim still takes D-Bus from the system
(`pkg-config --libs dbus-1` in its Makefile), and that no adapter has acquired
a `Cargo.lock` again, which is the only route by which the old leak could come
back. Both arms were seen to fail -- the second one fired for real, before the
Rust was deleted, which is as good a positive control as a gate gets.

### What was lost, named because it is not recoverable

`tool/nm-compare.sh` brought both shims up against `nm.sh`'s own fixture over a
private bus and diffed what `nmcli` saw. Every defect it found was invisible
from the properties: a wifi card served as an ethernet, a `Strength` formula
its unit test agreed with because one hand wrote both, a `GROUP_CCMP` colliding
with `KEY_MGMT_PSK` so a WPA3 network rendered as "WPA2 WPA3". **There is no
second implementation to measure a C regression against any more.**

What remains is evidence of a different kind and all of it was already running:
`nm.sh`'s 124 checks through libnm, `bus_test`'s 178 over the tables and
contracts -- 115 when 10.396 counted them, and the figure is re-read here
rather than quoted -- and the guest tier's 214. The distinction worth keeping is that the
oracle answered "where do these two differ", which is a question about an
implementation, while these answer "can a client do this", which is a question
about the product -- and the second is what mattered at the end. The last
twelve defects of this port were found by libnm refusing something, not by a
diff.

## 10.503 RequestScan, and the only honest thing a request can be

The last failure in `nm.sh`. `RequestScan` was not a method at all, so
`nmcli device wifi rescan` got the dispatcher's
`this interface has no such method in this build` -- which is 10.486's lesson
about a tier advertised and half served, met one method along.

### A request returns, and the scan happens afterwards

NM's method returns at once and the results arrive as the access point list
changing. That is not a convention to copy for its own sake: a radio takes a
second or two to sweep the band, and this shim answers nothing while a handler
runs, so a scan inside the call would stop every other client for the duration.
The Rust posts a job to its main loop; this records the request on the device
slot and the tick performs it.

**Every pending scan on every tick, rather than one device per tick.** The
round-robin cursor exists because reading one device's thirty-one properties is
expensive (10.396); testing a flag is not, and a client that asked should not
wait a second for each device ahead of it. Nothing happens on a machine where
nobody asked.

**Taking the request clears it**, so a client that asks twice before the loop
comes round gets one scan. That is what a request means, where a queue of them
would have the radio sweeping for as long as somebody held a button down.

**And the sweep asks netcfgd directly rather than through the windowed
accessor**, which would answer from this tick's cache if a property read had
already filled it -- serving a request for a FRESH sweep out of a cache would
make the method a no-op exactly when a client had reason to call it.

### Not authorized, which is the existing position rather than a new one

A scan is not a write: 0264's rule is about changing the operator's
configuration. And reading the access point list already asks netcfgd for a
scan today, with no check, because that is how the list is built -- so adding
this adds no exposure that was not already there. What bounds it is the tier
netcfgd grants this shim's own socket, which is where every other observation
is bounded.

The options argument is read and dropped. NM carries `ssids` there for a
directed scan at hidden networks and netcfgd's scan takes no hints, so the
honest answer is to sweep and let the list say what was found: a client asking
about one network gets a full scan, which is a superset of what it asked for.

### What the host rig could and could not show

It showed the method returning `()` in zero seconds, and a `SCAN` reaching the
fake supplicant afterwards. **It could not show that the second was caused by
the first.** The tick polls a radio's access point list as it comes round, and
that read performs a scan of its own -- so a scan arriving within a tick of the
request is consistent with either cause, and the reading says only that scans
happen.

Recorded rather than papered over, because it is the session's recurring shape:
a control that cannot discriminate between two explanations is not evidence for
either. Distinguishing them needs a fixture whose reads do not scan, which is
not this one. What the live check asserts is the thing that was actually broken
-- that a client asking produces no error -- and that is now true.

### The band is closed, and what that is and is not

`nm.sh` goes from 123 and 1 to **124 and 0**, and the guest tier as a whole to
**214 of 214 with seven scripts of seven** -- the first run of `make
vm-skipped` this session to exit 0.

**That is 0264's acceptance test, passing.** The adapter's Makefile has said
since it was written that "the Rust goes on shipping until this passes
`tests/live/nm.sh`, which is 0264's acceptance test and is the holder's call to
act on." The condition is met; the call is not this session's to make, and
nothing here has acted on it. The Makefile records that the condition is met
and leaves the sentence about whose decision it is exactly where it was.

What the suite proves is what it drives: 37 interfaces reached through a real
`nmcli`, a real `dbus-python` secret agent, and netcfgd itself, with every
profile write, the credential bridge, both IP families in both directions, and
the activation path. What it does not prove is anything no client in it asks
for -- and this session found four such things by asking: a group `GetSettings`
did not report, a key written where the language does not take it, a property
answering zero that no client had reason to read, and a rig whose apply had
never run.

## 10.502 The device-to-activation pair: one blank column, three layers

The last two failures in `nm.sh` outside `RequestScan`, and they were one
fault: `nmcli connection down HomeFiber` printed nothing and did nothing
because there was no active connection of that name to take down -- which is
the same thing the other check reports as a blank `CONNECTION` column.

### A blank column reads the same whichever layer is silent

Three answers could produce it, and the check printed only
`expected HomeFiber, actual ""`: netcfgd not reporting the association, the
shim not naming an activation for it, or that object not carrying an id. So
the check prints the chain now, at **two moments** -- after the activation and
after the deactivation -- because a reading taken only at the end cannot tell
"never recorded" from "cleared by the down" either, and those call for opposite
fixes. The first version of the diagnostic made exactly that mistake and had to
be rerun.

With all three speaking it took one run:

    --- after the activation
    netcfgd on the radio: radio0 COMPLETED     HomeFiber (00:11:22:33:44:55)
    the shim's activation: /org/freedesktop/NetworkManager/ActiveConnection/5
    its Id: Failed to get property Id ...: no such object; it may have gone
            since the path was handed out

netcfgd records the association, before and after the down. The device names an
activation. **That object does not resolve.**

### A radio's association is in the wifi status, not on its link

`ncfg_link_t.network` is empty for a radio declared over a dummy, because the
kernel does not call that link wireless -- while `ncfg wifi status radio0` says
`COMPLETED HomeFiber` at the same moment. The shim read only the link, so it
reported no network for a radio plainly on one, and `nmc_active_profile_of`
then had nothing to name: a radio's `interface` block is deliberately not
served as a profile, so the fallback finds nothing either.

It asks the wifi status now, and only for a radio whose link says nothing,
because that answer costs a socket round trip per window -- 10.396 is this
adapter's tick taking a second over a wifi fetch and starving the dispatch
loop. `facts.wireless` is the test, which `facts_for` already makes with its
own comment about why the kernel's radio list is the wrong source.

### And the device handed out a path its own subtree refused

`Device.ActiveConnection` named `/ActiveConnection/<n>` whenever the device was
addressed; the subtree's resolver requires addressed **and** a profile to be an
activation of. A radio that is addressed and has joined nothing satisfies the
first and not the second, so a client was handed a path and then told
`no such object; it may have gone since the path was handed out` -- the
stale-path answer, for a path it had just been given.

It calls `nmc_active_exists` now, which is the resolver's own test. **Two
conditions that have to agree are better replaced by one that is asked twice**,
and the `NMC_OWN` macro keeps the addressedness test it was right about for the
two IP config objects.

### The band, down to one

`nm.sh` goes from 121 and 3 to **123 and 1**. The one left is
`a client can ask for a scan`: `RequestScan` refuses, which 10.486 records
along with why `wifi_scan` stays in the compat map anyway -- reading what a
scan found is what that tier is about and all of it is served.

## 10.498 The connection group, and the two conversions put side by side

The three per-connection options a settings panel offers beside the address --
whether a network joins by itself, how it ranks, and whether its data costs
money -- plus the `hidden` flag in the group next door. Same fault as 10.497 in
a different group: a client that cannot read an option writes its own default
back over it, so every edit of a ranked network unranked it and every edit of a
metered one made it unmetered.

### The scaling's two halves are in one file now

`autoconnect-priority` is netcfgd's metric inverted and scaled into NM's
0..999, and 0207 is the record of what happens when the two directions
disagree: a profile a desktop client reads and writes back walked upward every
trip -- 100, 103, 107, 111, 115, 119, 124 -- until it crossed another network's
metric and the machine preferred a network the operator had not chosen,
silently.

The write direction was already in `block.c`, carrying the half-band that makes
the trip a fixed point. The read direction went in beside it rather than with
the rest of `GetSettings`, which is the point worth recording: **two
conversions that must be inverses belong where a reader can check them against
each other**, and the alternative is one copy of the ceiling in each of two
files and a drift nothing announces.

### The property, asserted over the band rather than at a point

`nm.sh` asserts the round trip at one priority, and its own comment says why it
does not assert the metric: a number read off the code it checks goes stale in
silence, which is how its `metric = 3924` sat failing from 0207 until this
session.

With both directions in one file the stronger question is cheap, so the unit
suite asks it: **every priority NM can hold, scaled up into a metric and back
down, and none of them may move.** 999 trips in one check.

**It is also the only form of the question that cannot be satisfied by two
functions agreeing with each other instead of with the model.** Either scaling
alone passes any test written from itself. Proved able to fail by removing the
half-band -- the 0207 defect exactly -- which moves 997 of the 999.

### `autoconnect` is written where netcfgd will not take it

Found by writing a profile with it: a block carrying `autoconnect` at network
level does not compile --

    nm-Opts.conf:10:2: unknown network key `autoconnect`

-- and `AddConnection` therefore fails whole, because the daemon compiles back
and keeps nothing that will not compile. `hidden`, `metered` and `metric` are
accepted at network level and `autoconnect` is not.

**This entry first blamed the daemon's compiler, and that was wrong.** The key
belongs inside the `wifi` block, the lowering has always had an arm for it
there, and the renderer was writing it in the wrong place -- measured and
corrected in 10.499, which also says what made the wrong answer plausible: the
model's field list does carry `autoconnect` at network level, because the JSON
surface and the language are not the same surface and are not required to
agree.

What stands from the original is the cost and the reason nothing caught it: the
renderer has written the key since the day it was written, `nm.sh` has no
profile that asks for it, and the round trip was unharmed in the meantime
because the key is only written when the value is false while every network's
default is true.

### The band, and the lens retired

`nm.sh` goes from 104 and 17 to **108 and 13**, four removals and no
additions: the metric scaled into NM's range, whether the network is metered,
whether it joins by itself, and the priority that went in coming back out.
Predicted as 13 before the run from the four checks the group feeds.

What is left is three groups and three strays. **Six are the secret agent and
the activation that needs one** -- netcfgd asking a NM agent for a credential,
which is `agent.c`'s path. **Four are the `IP4Config` pair reporting what was
APPLIED** rather than what was asked for, which is 0032's other half and reads
the observation rather than the document. And `Save`, `ClearSecrets` and
`RequestScan`, each an NM operation netcfgd has no state for or no answer to
yet.

**Every group `GetSettings` serves is now complete**, which retires the lens
three entries have been following: a group it does not report is a group the
next edit deletes, and there are no unreported groups left for a wifi profile.

## 10.497 Both IP groups, and the client call that could not ask for them

The ask was the symmetric `ipv6` group beside the `ipv4` one. What it needed
was three fields in the client library, and what it fixed was silent data loss
in the write path 10.496 had just opened.

### What a client was told, and what it wrote back

Measured before anything was changed, with a static wifi profile this shim had
just written and the read-modify-write a real client makes:

    network "Static" {                        network "Static" {
        ssid = "53746174"                         wifi { open = true }
        wifi { open = true }          ->          hidden = true
        config = ["192.0.2.5/24", "slaac"]    }
        routes = ["default via 192.0.2.1"]
        dns { servers = ["1.1.1.1"] }
    }

The address, the gateway and the nameserver are gone, and the client asked for
none of that: it changed one flag and sent back what it had been given.

**And it is worse than deletion.** libnm fills in its own defaults for a group
it was told nothing about, so what reaches the shim is not an absent `ipv4`
group but `method = auto` -- a static network comes back as DHCP. There is no
reading of the dictionary that recovers the address, because the client is not
reporting what it was told; it is reporting what it believes.

### The read direction could not answer, and the wire always could

`get_settings` served IP groups for `interface` profiles only, which is also
where the asymmetry the ask names comes from: one group, for one kind of
block, and none at all for the other. `ncfg_saved_network_t` reported a
network's name, security, ranking, autoconnect and hidden -- and nothing about
what the network configures.

**The `show` response had carried all of it the whole time.** `addressing`,
`routes` and `dns`, in the same shapes `ncfg_interface_config_t` already
models, from the same document. So this is a parse the client library never
wrote rather than anything missing from the protocol: `read_sources`,
`read_routes` and `read_dns` are decoupled from the interface struct and fill a
saved network's own lists now.

They take no `unmodelled` sink when they do. That field exists to stop a FORM
overwriting content it cannot show, and a saved network has no form here --
whatever reads it composes a whole block or refuses to, which is the same
judgement by a different route.

### Both groups, both kinds, and the family split made twice

`put_ip_group` is the old `put_ipv4_group` with the family as an argument and
a view of the three lists instead of one struct, so one function serves an
interface block and a network block alike.

**Both groups are reported even when a family has nothing.** That is the
lesson above stated as a rule: a client given no group fills in its own
defaults, so `ignore` is a fact and silence is an invitation to guess.

The family split has to be made by the group rather than read off the
document, because the document does not label a source's family --
`config = ["10.7.7.1/24", "2001:db8:7::1/64"]` is two `static` sources and
nothing else. That was already true of addresses, where the first version put
both in `ipv4`; it is equally true of a gateway, a route destination and a
nameserver, and each is filtered the same way now.

Beyond the ask, because the group is either complete or it is another instance
of the same fault: `route-data` carries the next hop and the metric it was
dropping, and both groups carry `dns-data`, the packed `dns` and `dns-search`
-- the packed IPv4 word in network byte order, which `ipconfig.c` already says
is not negotiable and which `block.c` reads back the same way. The
nameservers go only where the method allows them: libnm validates the whole
dictionary before it will activate anything, and `dns` beside
`method = disabled` is invalid, so a family with nameservers and no addressing
would have made a profile no client would connect with.

### The lens, and this is its third instance

**A group `GetSettings` does not report is a group the next edit deletes.**
10.496 was the security group; this is the two IP groups. The population is
every group NM defines that this shim does not serve, and the test is neither
direction on its own but the round trip: read, change one key, write, and
compare the block with what it was.

That is now a check rather than a lens: `nm.sh` reads back the static network
it just wrote, through `nmcli`, and asserts the address it asked for comes
back. A write half and a read half that each pass their own assertions can
still lose everything between them.

### What the live script asks now

Three checks on probe0's `ipv6` group beside the four on its `ipv4` one, and
the third is the discriminating one: **no IPv6 gateway**, because the
document's only default route is v4 and a v4 next hop appearing there is the
family filter failing in the direction the first version failed in.

### The group that made a profile libnm would not activate

**Two checks that had passed seven runs running failed on the eighth**, and
both were in the activation band rather than anywhere near the groups. The
counts said `expected 1, actual 0` about words in the fake supplicant's log,
which reads the same whether the shim forwarded nothing, netcfgd decided there
was nothing to do, or the fake had stopped writing.

The first theory was a race -- `connection up` returns when the shim has asked
netcfgd, netcfgd applies asynchronously, and these two checks sample the log
at once where every comparable check in the script has a bounded wait. It was
wrong, and the diagnostic said so in one line:

    Error: device 'radio0' not compatible with connection 'HomeFiber':
    ipv4.gateway: gateway cannot be set if there are no addresses configured.

**libnm refused the profile locally and never called the shim.** The new
`ipv4` group said `gateway = ""` for a DHCP network, and libnm's rule is that
a gateway cannot be set without an address -- where "set" means the property
is non-NULL, so an empty string fails it. The old group said this
unconditionally too and got away with it, because the only profiles it served
were interfaces with static addresses.

So the key is written only when there is one, and the two empty lists beside it
went the same way: an absent key is a profile that says nothing about
addresses, and a present empty one says the same thing with more rope. **The
comment warning about exactly this was ported in the same commit**, about
nameservers beside `method = disabled` -- libnm validates the whole dictionary
before it will activate anything -- and then the same mistake was made one key
along.

Two things worth keeping. **A count makes a good assertion and a poor
diagnostic**, which this script says of itself and had not applied here: the
two checks now print the supplicant delta beside nmcli's words, and that is
what turned a wrong theory into a one-line answer. And **the failure was
nowhere near the change**: a settings group that reads correctly can still be
a dictionary no client will act on, so the test that matters for a read
direction is one that makes a client *use* what it read.

### The band

`nm.sh` goes from 97 and 20 to **104 and 17**: three checks recovered that the
groups fix -- a network's nameservers, their packed form and its search
domains -- and four new ones, with nothing else moved. The diff against the
run before this change is three removals and no additions.

The four new ones are the ipv6 group's method, its address, its absent
gateway, and the round trip through `nmcli`. The last is the one that would
have caught the fault this entry opens with, and the third is the one that
would have caught the family filter failing.

## 10.496 Update, and the flag that makes editing a secured network possible

The last write. `Update`, `Update2` and `UpdateUnsaved` shared the read-only
refusal; the first two now change a profile this shim wrote, and the third has
the sentence that actually applies to it.

### One flag, and the reason it cannot be inferred

A client editing a profile sends back what `GetSettings` gave it, and that
never contains the passphrase (0029, 0031). So a change to a hidden flag on a
secured network arrives as `key-mgmt = wpa-psk` with no `psk`, which the create
path refuses by name and must: a block referring to a credential that was never
stored is a network this machine will try to join and cannot.

`nmc_block_render` therefore takes `stored`, which only an update can answer.
With it, the block keeps the `@secret:` reference it already had and
`has_secret` stays 0 -- nothing is handed to the secret provider, there being
nothing new -- and a passphrase that *does* arrive with an edit is a password
change and goes, replacing.

**The answer comes from the block netcfgd is holding, not from the secrets
directory.** The Rust asks `has_secret(id)`, which stats
`<config_dir>/secrets/<id>`; this reuses what `ours` already read for a
different question -- whether the drop-in's text carries `"@secret:<id>"`. The
two differ where it matters: a value stored under the profile's name that the
block does not refer to would let a psk-less edit through on the Rust's
question and not on this one, and the reference is what the file will actually
resolve.

### A rename is refused, where the Rust performs it and loses the credential

The block's label is the profile's identity and the filename is derived from
it, so changing `connection.id` is a remove and a create. `store.rs` does
both: it removes the old profile and writes the new one.

**For a secured profile that destroys the credential.** `store::remove` takes
the old secret with the old file; the new block refers to a secret under the
new name, and nothing can write it -- the value cannot be read back (0029,
0031) and a client editing a profile never sends it. So the rename leaves a
network that refers to a credential that does not exist, silently, and the
operator finds out when it will not join.

Refusing says so instead, and names the two steps and the one consequence: the
passphrase will be asked for again. **That is a finding against the oracle
rather than a divergence to reconcile** -- 0266 makes the Rust the comparison
and this is a case where the comparison is wrong.

### The order is the create's, reversed, and for the same reason

A create stores the value and then writes the block that refers to it. An
edit's reference already exists and is not what changes, so the file goes first
and the credential second: the write that can fail without breaking anything
goes last. The cost is visible rather than silent -- the settings are taken and
the passphrase is not changed, which is a sentence a client can show and a
retry can fix.

### The ledger, now that three of eight methods are served

`bus_test` carries the connection interface's whole disposition: every method,
and whether it is served, refuses in its own words, or shares the read-only
refusal. It fails if the count moves, if a method is missing from the list, if
a read-only one drifts onto another handler, or if a served one is wired to the
refusal.

That is the third version of this check in two days and the first that
asserts what it claims. The original compared each handler against
`methods[0]` -- which IS `GetSettings` -- so it caught only a write wired to
the getter, and `Delete` landing did not make it fail. Replacing it found
`GetSecrets`, which must not share the read-only sentence because its own is a
security property; writing it as a table found `UpdateUnsaved`, which wants a
third sentence again, there being nowhere to put a profile that is not written
to disk.

**Proved able to fail**: claiming `Save` is served fails exactly one check.

### A sabotage and its revert inside one second is the sabotage's verdict

Worth recording because it looked like a real failure and is the session's
third stale-artifact incident in a different costume. The control above was
run by editing the ledger, building, reverting, and building again -- and the
suite still failed, because the revert landed in the same second as the
object file. Make compares mtimes and treats "not older" as up to date, so
`bus_test.o` was never rebuilt: the binary that reported the failure was the
sabotaged one, relinked.

`touch` on the source cleared it. The rule is the one
`build-and-commit.md` already states -- never read a verdict off a binary the
build did not rebuild -- with the part nobody expects: **the build system
itself can be the thing that did not notice**, at one-second granularity,
which is exactly the window a positive control runs in.

### The fault the guest tier found and the host rig could not

**The prediction was 97 and 20 and the run said 96 and 21.** The check this
slice was for started passing; one I was not watching stopped -- `and the
credential too, rather than leaving it for nothing`, three checks later and in
the delete band.

The cause was not in `Update`. `GetSettings` left the `802-11-wireless-security`
group out of its answer entirely, so a client sending the settings back -- which
is what every edit is -- sent back no security group at all. `security_of` read
that as an open network, exactly as it should, and rewrote the block without its
`psk` line. **An edit to a hidden flag silently removed a network's
passphrase.** The deletion then had no reference to follow and left the
credential behind, which is the check that failed.

**The two checks around it passed.** `editing a generated profile does not need
the passphrase again` greps for `hidden = true`, which was there; `and the
secret it never sent is still there` reads the secrets directory, which an
update never touches. Between them they describe the operation and neither can
see the thing that went wrong, so the failure surfaced in another band -- which
is the argument for running the whole script rather than the checks a change is
about.

**And the host rig could not have found it, because its fixture was more
generous than the client.** Every dictionary it built carried a security group,
so the case nmcli produces was the one case never tested. That is
`evidence.md`'s *a control has to be able to fail the way the thing it controls
for fails*, met from the fixture side: a hand-built input tests the code
against the author's model of the client, and the model was wrong in the one
way that mattered.

The replacement is a read-modify-write in dbus-python: `GetSettings`, change
one key, `Update2`, which is what `nmcli connection modify` does. It reads
before it writes, so it cannot be more generous than the read direction is.

### The read direction was the fault, and its own comment said so

`GetSettings` left the group out "because secrets are not in `GetSettings`
even in NM" -- true of the passphrase and not of the group, and the two are not
the same thing. NM carries `key-mgmt` and `psk-flags` there and the value in
`GetSecrets`; the Rust shim does the same. So the group is reported now, with
`psk-flags` 0 for system-owned, and `802-11-wireless.security` naming it the
way NM cross-references the two.

**`refuse_secrets` has been claiming this mechanism all along**: its comment
says `psk-flags` already tells a client the daemon owns the credential, so it
does not prompt. There were no `psk-flags` to read. A comment describing what
the code would do if it did the thing is the hardest kind to catch, because it
is right about everything except whether it happens.

It costs a second thing nobody had noticed either: **a client could not see
that a network was secured.** A panel listing netcfgd's networks showed every
one of them as open.

### One lossy round trip, recorded rather than solved

`key-mgmt` takes exactly one value, so a network that accepts both PSK
generations is reported as `sae` -- a WPA2-only client then refuses a network
it could have joined, where reporting `wpa-psk` would have a WPA3 client
silently downgrade, and the first is the better failure. The Rust makes the
same choice.

What that costs on the way back is new here: a client reading `sae` and writing
it back pins `proto = "wpa3"` on a network that had accepted both. The document
can say "both" and NM's field cannot, so the round trip narrows it. Nothing in
the tree does this today -- no network in the fixtures accepts both -- and the
fix would need a spelling NM does not have.

### The signal nobody was sending

**`Updated` was declared in the table, advertised in the introspection, and
never emitted.** That did not matter while nothing could change a profile. It
matters now, and nothing else can carry the news: every declared property on a
connection is constant -- `VersionId` is deliberately 0, netcfgd having no
revision to publish -- so the change poll compares equal values for ever. A
panel holding a profile open would have gone on showing what it read before
the edit, and a client waiting for the signal it was promised would have
waited for ever.

`nmc_emit_plain` is the missing shape: a signal with no arguments, beside the
one that carries a path. Emitted only on a successful edit, which the rig
confirms by counting -- two `Connection.Updated` for the two edits that took,
and none for the rename, the in-memory flag or the hand-written block.

This is *an interface is only as wired as its least-used method* arriving one
layer up: the method was the thing being ported, and the signal that makes it
observable was not part of it until the question was asked.

### The band, and the whole write path served

`nm.sh` goes from 96 and 21 to **97 and 20** -- and the diff against the run
before `Update` is one line long: `editing a generated profile does not need
the passphrase again` passes and nothing else moved. The second run was needed
because the first had the fault above in it, and comparing the two failure
lists rather than the counts is what showed that the credential check had come
back rather than being traded for the new pass.

**Every write a client can make on a profile is served now.** Create, create
with a credential, edit, edit without being asked for the credential again,
and remove. What remains of `nm.sh` is six checks for the secret agent and the
activation that needs one, eleven read halves -- `GetSettings`' connection
options and the `IP4Config` pair -- `Save` and `ClearSecrets`, which are NM
operations netcfgd has no state for, and `RequestScan`.

## 10.493 AddConnection writes, for everything but a passphrase

10.492 scoped this and defined the subset; this is that subset, built. The
renderer is `adapter/netcfgd-nm/c/src/block.c` -- 1,155 lines against
`emit.rs`'s 1,177 -- and `settings.c` authorizes the caller, calls it, and
hands the text to `config_put`.

### What it writes

Everything the Rust renderer does except the credential: the `network` block
and its label, `metered`, a `metric` scaled from `autoconnect-priority`, a hex
`ssid` when the SSID is not the label, `wifi { open = true }` or
`owe = true`, `hidden`, `autoconnect = false`, `config` from both families'
methods and static addresses, `routes` from each family's `gateway` and
`route-data`, a `dns` block from either spelling of the nameservers, and the
comment naming what netcfgd cannot express (0034).

The write itself is `ncfg_client_config_put`, which is where netcfgd's own
rules do the work: 0127 makes the daemon the only writer of `/etc/netcfgd`,
and the daemon compiles the configuration back with the new file in it and
restores what was there if the result will not compile. **So the twelve lines
`store.rs` spends undoing a bad write do not exist here** -- a block that
redefines a network another file already defines is refused as a failed
`AddConnection` rather than leaving a machine whose next reload changes
nothing.

### The boundary is the secret, and it refuses rather than drops

**Closed by 10.494, which is the slice after this one**; what follows is what
this commit did and why the boundary was drawn there rather than somewhere
cheaper.

A `key-mgmt` of `wpa-psk` or `sae` is refused by name, telling the caller to
use `ncfg wifi add`. 10.492's argument, unchanged: a method that wrote the
open case and silently dropped a `psk` would hand a client a secured network
with no credential and no error. OWE writes, because OWE carries no secret --
which is the line being drawn, security without a credential rather than
security.

The refusal never quotes the passphrase back, and that is a check rather than
a habit: a refusal crosses the bus and lands in a client's log, and 0042 calls
a credential the one thing on a machine nobody can get back.

### `AddConnection2` is the method `nmcli` actually calls

`Update2` taught this once already, on the connection interface, and the
comment there says it: with only `Update` declared, a modify got
`this interface has no such method in this build` from the dispatcher and the
refusal never ran. The settings interface declared only `AddConnection`, and
`compat.c` claims NM 1.44.0, so libnm takes the newer path every time.

Its flags are read rather than dropped, because one of them changes the
answer. `AddConnection2` carries NM's choice of where the profile lives, and a
client asking for one that never touches the disk is asking for exactly what
`AddConnectionUnsaved` is refused for -- so the in-memory bits refuse with the
same sentence, which is now one constant both share.

### The announcement is the write's other half

**`nmcli` reported `operation succeeded but object /Settings/8 does not exist`
while the file on disk was correct and all five of its content checks passed.**
libnm learns what exists from `ObjectManager` and nothing else, and it reads
the returned path the moment it has it -- so the loop's next membership tick is
too late. The fix is to announce `InterfacesAdded` and `NewConnection` from the
handler, before answering, which is what the Rust's `republish` call does and
what its comment names with the same sentence.

Worth keeping because the diagnosis was handed over by the shape of the
failure: one check failed and the four below it passed, which is the opposite
of the usual arrangement and said at once that the renderer was right and the
reply was not.

### And the fix was read as not having worked, because the guest ran the old binary

**The second guest run reported the identical error, and the announcement was
not in the binary it ran.** `make test` in the adapter relinks
`tests/bus_test` and not `netcfgd-nm`, the repository is mounted into the
guest read-only over 9p, and `vm-skipped` built `c/examples` and nothing else
-- so the guest drove whatever program was sitting in the working tree, which
was the one from before the fix. Twenty minutes, and a conclusion that the
announcement had not helped.

`build-and-commit.md` names this exactly -- never conclude a test's verdict
from a binary the build step did not rebuild -- and it names the cure the
convention costs: a fast default build has to be paid for by the dependencies
being right. Here the dependency was missing from the target rather than from
a rule, which is the version of it that no `.d` file can catch.

So `vm-skipped` builds the shim now, guarded on `pkg-config --exists dbus-1`,
which is the shape `live` already uses for `c_nm_signals.sh` and for the same
reason. **What found it was a rig on the host**, which is the other lesson:
`nm.sh` needs `nmcli` and this machine has none, but `gdbus` and a private
`dbus-daemon` are enough to call `AddConnection2` and watch what the shim
emits -- 20 seconds a cycle against the guest's twenty minutes, and the
monitor showed no signals at all where the code plainly sent two.

### The fact window had to be reopened, and that is new

`state.h` argues that a cache scoped to one dispatch cannot go stale, and that
is true of every read-only dispatch -- which was all of them. This one writes,
so a getter that had fetched the saved list earlier in the same dispatch would
leave the lookup after the write reading the list from before it: the network
would not be found and a client would be told its write failed with the file
already on disk. Nothing fetches it that early today, which is the point --
the call order was the only thing keeping it true, and `nmc_window_end` then
`nmc_window_begin` does not depend on the call order.

### Four places it differs from the Rust deliberately

- **`replace` is false.** `store.rs` passes `replace: true`, because its one
  write serves `AddConnection` and `Update` alike. Add alone must not
  overwrite: the uuid is derived from the id, so two profiles of one name are
  one profile here, and overwriting would hand a client two paths to one file.
  The file it would clobber may also be one an operator wrote by hand.
- **An unrecognised addressing method is refused.** `addressing()` in Rust
  ignores what it does not match, so `ipv4.method shared` -- address
  translation for other machines -- writes a profile with no `config` line and
  no complaint. That is 10.491's wrong-family fault from the other side: a
  file that looks complete and is not.
- **An empty string counts as absent.** The Rust reads `Some("")` and then
  fails the address parse, so a client sending `gateway: ""` is told its
  gateway is malformed. Saying once that an empty value is not a request is
  clearer than three refusals that each have to explain themselves.
- **No `dropped` note for a group it cannot read.** Both refuse what they
  cannot express; the C list is the Rust's `UNINTERESTING` table verbatim, so
  the note names the same settings.

### The test builds the message rather than a struct

`bus_test.c` said marshalling needs a live bus. That is true of what the
program WRITES and not of what it READS: a `DBusMessage` is created and
appended to with no connection at all, so a client's settings dictionary --
a variant inside a container inside a container -- can be built in the unit
suite, and the renderer is a pure function of it. 25 checks, of which the one
that matters compares **the whole block** against a literal, because the live
script greps the generated file for four of its lines and a renderer with the
right shape and the wrong spacing would pass every check keyed on a fragment
and write a file netcfgd refuses -- which, the loader compiling the drop-in
directory as one document, would take every other network down with it.

Proved able to fail: `open = true` to `open =true` fails exactly that check
and no other.

The metric check asserts the round trip rather than the number. `nm.sh`'s own
version of it said `metric = 3924` and had been failing since 0207 moved the
arithmetic, because an assertion read off the code it checks goes stale in
silence -- so this one scales the written metric back down and asserts it
returns the priority that went in.

### `Filename` is a path the shim invents, and it is wrong twice

Found by the host rig rather than looked for: the `Filename` property reported
`/etc/netcfgd/conf.d/nm-Office.conf` for a profile written into a work
directory. `say_filename` builds that string from a hardcoded prefix and the
raw id, so it is wrong whenever `NCFG_CONFIG_DIR` is not the default -- which
is every test rig -- and wrong again for any id a filename cannot carry, since
it does not sanitise. `store.rs` gets both right through its `config_dir()`
and `path_for`.

It predates this change and nothing asserts it, which is why it is recorded
rather than fixed here. The cheap answer is to read `NCFG_CONFIG_DIR` and
share `block.c`'s stem rule, and the right one is to ask the daemon:
`ncfg_client_configs` already answers with each drop-in's `file`, so the path
would be netcfgd's own rather than a second guess at its layout.

### A narrow edge, recorded rather than closed

An id of 62 bytes or more makes a stem of 65 or more, and the daemon's name
rule stops at 64 -- so a network `ncfg wifi add` would accept is refused here,
with netcfgd's own sentence quoted inside the shim's. The `nm-` prefix is what
costs the three bytes. Left alone: the refusal is legible, and the alternative
is a second naming scheme for long ids.

### Where it leaves the band

`nm.sh` in the guest tier goes from 76 and 42 to **87 and 30** -- eleven more
checks passing and twelve fewer failing, the twelfth being
`a client can write a static profile at all`, which prints nothing when it
passes because it is a guard on the command rather than a check on a value.

What remains is three bands rather than a list. **Fifteen are downstream of
the credential**: the `Roaming` profile and every agent check after it, which
need the secret half this slice refuses. **Eleven are the read direction** --
`GetSettings` does not yet report `metered`, `autoconnect-priority` or a
profile's nameservers, and the `IP4Config` pair does not report what was
applied -- so the write half of each of those passes now while the read half
does not, which is the pair 0207's fixed point lives between. The last four
are the activation and scan checks already recorded in 10.486 and 10.490.

**The write direction was checked twice, by different instruments.** The
guest tier drives a real `nmcli`; the host rig drives `gdbus` against the same
shim, bus and daemon, and the two agree on the Office block, the dropped note
and the refusal. That is worth saying because the first is slow and the second
has no `nmcli` on this machine -- so neither is a substitute for the other,
and the cheap one is what made the twenty-minute one worth starting.

## 10.491 The gateway nmcli shows is unavailable to the shim, three ways out

Asked to fix it. The diagnostic settles where it is lost, and the answer is
that the shim cannot have it:

    kernel:  default via 10.7.7.254 dev probe0 proto 110
    nmcli:   IP4.GATEWAY = [--]

netcfgd installed the route -- `proto 110` is its own marker -- so this is not
an apply that did not happen. `ipconfig.c` serves `say_no_gateway` on purpose
and says why: **`ncfg_link_t` carries WHETHER a link holds the default route
and not what the next hop is**, so "empty is NM's unknown and `0.0.0.0` would
be a claim -- a client showing a gateway of `0.0.0.0` has been told something
false, where one showing none has been told nothing."

That is also why addresses project and routes do not: `facts_for` reads the
same `ncfg_link_t`, which carries addresses and one boolean for the route.

**Measured rather than assumed: the client API has no observed-routes
accessor.** Fifty-nine `ncfg_client_*` verbs, and the only route data is
`ncfg_client_interface_config`, which is the DOCUMENT's routes, and
`ncfg_client_status`, which is the whole observation as JSON. 0032 settles
which of those may feed a details panel -- the panel is the observation -- so
the document's copy is not an answer even though it has the next hop in it.

### The options, their costs, and whose each is

**A. Parse `ncfg_client_status`'s JSON in the shim.** In scope without a core
change, and semantically right since that blob is applied state -- which
`nm.sh` itself polices one check over, "the nameservers come from what was
applied, not from the config". The cost is architectural: it fetches the whole
observation to answer one property, and it introduces a second access style
beside the seven typed accessors the shim uses for everything else. The
adapter would be hand-parsing what the core could type.

**B. Give the observation the next hop** -- a field on `ncfg_link_t`, or a
typed `ncfg_client_routes`. The natural fix and the one that makes every
future client's answer cheap. It is also **a core change wanted by an
adapter**, which 0271 refuses unless the concept is independently something a
local operator wants: `ncfg status` already shows routes, so the local
justification is weak and would have to be made rather than assumed. Whose:
the holder's, and it is the question 0271 exists to route.

**C. Leave it.** The present behaviour is principled rather than lazy, and the
comment is the argument: an unknown gateway reported as unknown is honest. The
cost is a settings panel with an empty gateway field, and two checks in
`nm.sh` that cannot pass -- `and the gateway is the next hop of the default
route`, and the route-table one beside it, since 0033's split gives NM the
default's next hop as `gateway` and the rest as routes.

**Settled by the copyright holder: B.** And it cost far less than this entry
priced, which is the correction worth keeping.

**B is not a protocol change at all.** `link_has_default_route` has been
walking the observation's `routes` array client-side since the flag existed,
to compute the boolean -- so the next hop was already on the wire and the
client library simply did not expose it. `ncfg_link_t` carries `default_via`
now: no daemon change, no socket change, no extra round trip, and an addition
to netcfgd's own client library rather than to its interface.

That also strengthens the 0271 justification rather than straining it, and it
is written beside the field instead of assumed: the boolean answers "is this
the way out" and the new field answers "out through what", which an operator
reading one link must otherwise get by cross-referencing the routes section by
hand.

**The old reasoning is kept where it still holds**, in three places rather
than deleted as superseded. NULL and not `0.0.0.0`, because a link with no
default route has no next hop and a zero would be a claim. Empty for an
on-link default, which has a route and no hop to name. And the **v6**
`Gateway` stays stubbed, with the original argument now guarding that case:
`default_via` is the IPv4 default's next hop, so serving it for v6 would be
the wrong family rather than a missing value, which is worse than empty.

Measured: `and the gateway is the next hop of the default route` passes, and
`nm.sh` moves to 72 and 46.

### And the profile's `ipv4` group, which was absent rather than incomplete

Four checks beside it read the CONNECTION's `ipv4` setting through
`nm_setting.py` rather than the device's `IP4Config`, and all four were empty
because **there was no `ipv4` group at all** -- so a panel opened on a static
interface was told it had no method, no address, no gateway and no routes.
`settings.c` emits one now and all four pass; `nm.sh` is 76 and 42, from 66
and 51 when this thread started.

**From the document and not the observation, which is the opposite of
`IP4Config` and is the point rather than an inconsistency.** 0032 puts the
details panel on the observation because it answers what the machine is doing;
a profile answers what was asked for, and a client editing one must see its
own request rather than the result. `ncfg_client_interface_config` is that
