view and already types the routes with destination, via and metric.

**0033's split is NM's and not netcfgd's**: netcfgd keeps one `routes` list
with the default as an entry, NM wants the next hop in `gateway` and the rest
in `route-data`, so the default is deliberately absent from the table --
reporting it in both draws a duplicate row in every panel, which is what the
check asserts.

**`method` has no honest mapping and the editable answer wins.** netcfgd
allows several sources on one interface and NM's `method` is one enum, so a
static address makes it `manual` even with a lease beside it: that is what a
panel can edit, where `auto` would hide the address the document states. A
judgement, and a real client acts on it.

### The document does not label a source's family, and the first version did not either

`config = ["10.7.7.1/24", "2001:db8:7::1/64"]` is two `static` sources and
nothing more -- netcfgd's model does not split families because an interface's
addressing is one list, and NM's does. So the group must tell them apart, and
the first version did not: it reported a panel's **IPv4** addresses as
`10.7.7.1/24 2001:db8:7::1/64`.

That is the fault `ipconfig.c` names one layer over about the v6 gateway --
**a wrong-family answer is worse than a missing one**, because empty reads as
unknown while a populated field reads as a fact -- argued there an hour before
being walked into here. A colon test now filters addresses, route
destinations and the next hop alike, and it also stopped an IPv6-only
interface claiming `manual` for addresses it has none of in that family.

**The symmetric `ipv6` group is deliberately not added.** Nothing reads it, so
it would be an untested projection of exactly the kind that just failed --
guessing at property names and family handling at once, with no check to catch
a mistake. `ipv4` served and `ipv6` absent is a visible gap rather than a
false claim.

## 10.486 nm.sh's 51 failures are the C adapter's unported activation surface

Asked what `nm.sh` was failing for. It is not a broken subsystem and it is not
fifty-one defects: **66 checks pass**, and the passing set proves the shim
works -- it refuses to run without netcfgd, serves every link netcfgd reports,
takes MTU and hardware address from the observation, refuses a second claim on
the bus, serves WireGuard devices with their listen port and the key the kernel
derived, serves VLANs with tag and parent, maps scan signal onto NM's scale
against values a real daemon reported, and names the access point the radio is
on. The fixture has a radio with an association, so the failures are not for
want of one.

### The first failure named itself once it was allowed to

    Error: this interface has no such method in this build.

The check reporting it had been `grep -c Error`, so its whole evidence was
`actual: 1` and the sentence was discarded -- the same fault as five bad counts
earlier in this session and as the `2>/dev/null` in 10.485. It carries nmcli's
words now.

### What is established

`RequestScan`, `ActivateConnection` and `DeactivateConnection` are **not
implemented in the C shim**, and `nm.sh` tests the C shim --
`${NCFG_NM_SHIM:-$repo/adapter/netcfgd-nm/c/netcfgd-nm}`. The Rust shim has
all three: `request_scan` at `src/device.rs:982` and `src/state.rs:300`,
`activate_connection` at `src/manager.rs:134`, `deactivate_connection` at
`src/manager.rs:209`. The C shim's method table has `AddConnection`, `Update`
and `Delete` and nothing else of that family -- **and having them in the table
is not implementing them**, which this sentence first read as. Their handlers
are `refuse_add` and `refuse_write`: they authorize the caller and then say the
write is not built. So the write failures in this band have the same cause as
the activation ones rather than a different one, and 10.487 has the order that
is deliberate about.

So this band is a **port gap in the adapter**, measured rather than inferred,
and `make vm-skipped` is the only thing that measures it. It is invisible to
0263's register, which is the planner's `warn_unported` and says nothing about
`adapter/`.

### Giving the checks their messages found a second defect under the first

Most of the 51 needed nothing: **43 of them already reported `actual:` empty**
against a concrete expectation -- `connected`, `9.9.9.9`, `600`, `42` -- which
says the property is ABSENT rather than wrong. Forty-three wrong values would
be forty-three bugs; forty-three absent ones are one thing not happening. Only
eight reduced to an opaque count, and three of those had their messages
already written to files nobody printed: `nmcli connection up` redirects into
`$work/up.log` while the check asserts a `grep -c` over the supplicant's log.
`check_saying` keeps the count as the assertion and adds the file as the
diagnostic.

What it printed was not what this entry first predicted:

    Error: device 'radio0' not compatible with connection 'HomeFiber':
      The connection was not valid: 802-11-wireless.ssid: property is missing.

**A real and separate defect, now fixed.** `settings.c` emitted
`ssid-text` -- a key NetworkManager has never had -- where `802-11-wireless`
requires `ssid` as `ay`. So libnm refused every wifi profile in the CLIENT,
before any method was called, and the comment directly above that code already
said the group "carries a mode and an SSID". `settings.rs` carries the same
requirement in prose and emits the octets, which is what the fix is a port of.
Measured after it: `up.log` no longer carries an error.

**It was masking the original diagnosis rather than replacing it.** This entry
first said the band was unported activation; the `ssid` error made that look
wrong, and it was not. The C shim has no `ActivateConnection` anywhere -- its
manager interface serves `GetManagedObjects` and the word appears in no method
table -- so the fix moves the wall from libnm's validator to the absent
method, which is why the count is still 51. Necessary, not sufficient.

### And the compat interface advertises what this build has not got

`compat.c`'s `SUPPORTED[]` names `activation` and `wifi_scan` among the tiers
it serves. There is no `ActivateConnection`, and `RequestScan` answers
`this interface has no such method in this build`. The convention it breaks is
stated in its own comment, three lines above the list: **"a build that cannot
activate a connection omits `activation` rather than saying false"**. So a
client asking what this shim supports is told yes and then refused, which is
worse than being told no -- and `nm.sh` asserts the list is served without
asserting it is true, so nothing catches it.

**Settled by the copyright holder 2026-10-17: omit `activation`.** It is out,
verified in the artefact rather than inferred from the build -- `strings` on
the shim shows the key gone and the other nine tiers intact -- and the guest
tier is unchanged at 66 and 51, so nothing depended on the claim. The comment
records when it returns: in the same commit as `ActivateConnection` and not
before, which is 0263's register rule applied to an advertised capability
rather than to a planner's arm.

**`wifi_scan` stays, and the asymmetry is written down rather than left to
look like an oversight.** `RequestScan` refuses here too, but what that tier
means to a client is reading what a scan found -- the access point list, each
signal mapped onto NM's scale -- and all of that is served and checked.
Removing the key would say the results are unavailable when they are there.

**And it is pinned, because the hole was never the wrong key.** `nm.sh`
asserted the tier list was SERVED and never that it was TRUE, which is why a
build advertised an activation it could not perform for as long as it did. A
check asserts the absence now, in the direction the build is in, so returning
the key without the method fails. Controlled both ways in the guest: with
`activation` restored the check reads FAIL, with it removed `ok`.

What stays open is the general form. Proving every advertised tier is one the
shim can serve is a different problem from grepping one key -- `secret_agents`
and `connection_options` have no one-line equivalent -- so one tier is held
and the rest are still only served.

### 0265's record of this script is stale in the good direction

It lists `nm.sh` as "4+ failed" with "the loopback is a loopback, not an
ethernet". That check **passes** now: the payload's own header records running
all nine bare having put `nm.sh` on the guest's real network instead of the
namespace its header documents, and `needs_netns` fixed it. So the recorded
failure is cured and the recorded count was never the whole set.

## 10.484 What bluetooth would cost, four ways, and whose each one is

Asked for the costs rather than a proposal, so each option below carries its
price and who owns it. `working-practice.md` warns that describing a mechanism
thoroughly is a way of proposing it, so the longest entry here is not the
recommendation and the recommendation says so.

### What already exists, measured rather than assumed

  * **The document accepts the block.** `ncfg_bluetooth_device_t` carries
    `id`, `address`, `profile` and `autoconnect` -- and its comment already
    settles the hardest question: no pairing state and no codec, because
    whether a device is paired "is a fact about the adapter's key store,
    established interactively, and writing it here would be a second source of
    truth for something netcfgd does not own."
  * **Observation is done.** `ncfg_observe_bluetooth` lists
    `/sys/class/bluetooth`, names each adapter and resolves its rfkill switch.
  * **There is a live script.** `tests/live/bluetooth.sh` makes a virtual
    controller through `/dev/vhci`, needs real root, reads sysfs only, starts
    no daemon, and says in its own header that pairing and audio are beyond
    its rig because one virtual controller has nobody to talk to and Debian's
    bluez ships no `btvirt`.
  * **Nothing acts.** `plan/build.c` warns that nothing pairs the device,
    connects it, or brings a `pan` link up. That arm is the whole gap.

Two facts about this machine that decide more than they look like:
**`bluetoothd` is not installed** (`bluetoothctl` and `btmgmt` are), and **the
C core contains no D-Bus code at all** -- `grep` for it over `c/src` and
`c/include` returns nothing. What D-Bus this project has lives in
`adapter/netcfgd-nm`, a separate Rust binary.

### A. Remove the block

Cost: a configuration that uses `bluetooth` stops compiling, so it is a
breaking change to the language for anybody who wrote one. Buys honesty at
once and the smallest surface. Whose: the holder's, as a scope decision.

### B. Keep observation, and say that is all it is

The warning promises a future -- `warn_unbuilt` is the register 0263 requires
an arm to leave when a pass lands, so a sentence sitting in it reads as owed
work. If netcfgd observes adapters and never pairs or connects, that arm
becomes a statement of intent rather than a debt, and `bluetooth.sh`'s
"a green run here must not be read as Bluetooth works" becomes the documented
boundary rather than an apology.

Cost: one comment, one warning's wording, one decision record. No code, no
dependency, no new test rig. Whose: the holder's, and it is the only option
that costs nothing to reverse later.

### C. Connect an already-paired device, and only that

This is the option that inherits the document's own pairing decision instead
of fighting it: the operator pairs, netcfgd honours `autoconnect` and
`profile` on a device the adapter already has keys for. It splits by how
netcfgd reaches bluez, and the two halves have very different prices.

**C1, through `org.bluez` over D-Bus.** The correct interface, and it would be
**the first D-Bus dependency in the C core**. That is a dependency decision
rather than a feature one: it reaches the build, the packaging, the static
archive, and every machine the daemon runs on. It also needs `bluetoothd`
running, which is a second daemon netcfgd does not supervise and cannot start
on a machine that has not installed it.

**C2, by driving a program.** `bluetoothctl connect <address>` fits the
pattern every other backend here uses -- `backend_run.c` spawns a program,
watches a pid, reads a marker -- and adds no dependency to the core. The price
is the interface: `bluetoothctl` is a REPL written for people, its output is
not a contract, and a parser over it is the thing this project has refused
elsewhere. `btmgmt` is the lower-level sibling and is present here too.

Cost either way: a backend kind, a plan arm, an executor arm, an observation
arm, and the ownership discipline the other nine carry. Link-local was that
shape and took a day with a clear upstream contract; this has no equivalent of
`-D -w --force-bind`. Whose: C1's dependency question is the holder's; the
shape of C2's interface is a design question worth settling in
`doc/decision/` before code.

### D. Pair, connect, and bring up `pan`

Pairing needs an **agent** -- the thing bluez calls back to answer a
passkey -- and consent is interactive by nature, which is what the document's
own comment declines to own. A daemon reconciling unattended has nobody to
ask. `pan` adds NAP against PANU, which is a network role rather than a
connection.

Cost: the largest, and it is the only option that contradicts a decision the
tree has already made in writing. Whose: the holder's, and it would want the
pairing comment in `document.h` revisited first, because implementing D means
that sentence is no longer true.

### What none of them can be tested against here

`bluetoothd` is absent, so C and D cannot be exercised on this machine at all,
and `bluetooth.sh` already states its rig cannot reach pairing. That is the
same shape as `sandbox_writes.sh` -- a check the host cannot answer -- and the
answer there was the VM tier. So any option past B carries a guest with bluez
installed as part of its price, not as an afterthought.

### The recommendation, and it is the short one

**B.** It costs a comment and a decision record, it makes the register honest
about a gap that is a choice rather than a debt, and it matches the pairing
decision `document.h` already took. C2 is the natural second step if netcfgd
should act, because it inherits that decision and adds no dependency; C1 and D
are both larger than the feature, for different reasons -- one reaches the
build, the other reaches the document's own stated intent.

**Settled the same day, and B was taken.** Decision 0272 records it: netcfgd
observes adapters and does not pair or connect, the block stays in the
language, and the warning says so by decision rather than for want of a pass.
The arm left `warn_unbuilt`'s list in `plan/build.c`, which was its last --
the first time an entry has left that register by a decision instead of by a
pass landing.

So the costing above is now the record of options rejected rather than a
question, which is what `working-practice.md` asks for: C2 is where a later
decision to connect a paired device would start, because it inherits 0272's
reasoning instead of contradicting it, and it would want a guest with bluez
since `bluetoothd` is absent here.

## 10.480 Link-local wired, and a loop bound that had been short for two kinds

The feature 10.479 designed is landed: the tenth backend kind reaches the plan
from the document's addressing, the executor from the plan, and the observation
from the machine, and `tests/live/link_local.sh` checks the three are joined
rather than merely present. What the wiring turned up is worth more than the
wiring.

### `--supported` had been reporting eight backend kinds of nine

The dump enumerates each taxonomy so that an operator can ask the build what it
can do. Its backend loop was

    for (kind = 0; kind <= (int)NCFG_BACKEND_DNS; kind++)

which was correct the day it was written and went short the day
`router_advert` was appended after `NCFG_BACKEND_DNS`. Nobody noticed, because
nothing compares the dump to the enum: `ledger_gate.py` reads the frozen
witness and asks the C to answer for every name in it, which is the
witness-to-C direction only, so a kind the C has and the witness does not is a
kind no gate is looking at. Adding `link_local` made it eight of ten.

Three of the four loops in that function were bounded by a named member rather
than by a count. `NCFG_OP_COMMIT_REVERT` and `NCFG_KIND_IFB` were still the
real last members, so only the backend loop had actually rotted -- but all
three carried the same hazard, and they are bounded by their name tables now.
`ncfg_backend_kind_name` and `ncfg_interface_kind_name` return NULL past the
end of the word table they read, and `ncfg_op_name` returns the empty string,
so each loop grows with the enum it walks.

### The test that should have caught it was a copy of the loop's own bound

`main_test.c`'s completeness ledger asserted

    backends == ((size_t)NCFG_BACKEND_DNS + 1u) * 3u

against a loop bounded by `NCFG_BACKEND_DNS`. Both sides read the same
constant, so neither moved when a kind arrived, they went on agreeing, and the
check printed `ok` directly above a dump that was missing a kind. This is
`evidence.md`'s *a gate that compares an artifact to its generator tests
agreement*, in four lines.

The fix is not to make the expectation cleverer. It is that the same
hard-coded member is a defect in the generator and the whole point in the
check: now that the loops read their tables and grow on their own, the named
constants below them cannot track what they are watching, so the next kind
appended to an enum makes the dump emit one more, leaves the number unchanged,
and fails the check. Confirmed by control -- pointing the expectation at
`NCFG_BACKEND_ROUTER_ADVERT` fails exactly that one check and nothing else.

It is also the only thing holding `backend_kind_words` to
`ncfg_backend_kind_t`. `word_table_gate.py` reads the renderer's language
tables, and `observed.c`'s model tables are not among them, so a kind appended
without a word would shorten the now table-bounded loop instead of lengthening
it. The same check fails for that, from the other side.

### The permissive default would have left the client running for ever

`backend_wanted` in `plan/backend.c` answers "wanted" from its `default` arm
for any kind no pass names -- the safe direction for a kind nothing starts, and
the wrong one for a kind something does. The `pppoe` arm is in that switch
because `pppd` held a line up with `persist` and `maxfail 0` after its device
was deleted; an IPv4LL client left running keeps a `169.254/16` address nobody
asked for, and `--force-bind` means it keeps it beside whatever replaced it.
Three cases in `plan_gaps_test.c` cover it, and all three fail with the arm
removed.

`addressing_asks_for` was the other half and was a latent wrong answer rather
than a missing one:

    int source_kind = kind == NCFG_BACKEND_DHCP4 ? NCFG_ADDRESS_SOURCE_DHCP4 :
        NCFG_ADDRESS_SOURCE_DHCP6;

Anything that was not `dhcp4` answered for *dhcp6*. Correct while only the two
DHCP clients reached it, and a wrong answer waiting for a third -- which is
what makes a two-valued mapping worth spelling as a switch even when it has two
values. It has a `default` that answers no rather than guessing.

### The seam, and a refusal that named the wrong program

`service.autoip_program` was declared and read and assigned by nothing, so it
was always NULL -- which the header documents as "find the conventional name",
and is right for the daemon's own path. It left no way to substitute a
stand-in, which is how the other three backend programs are tested, so
`NCFG_AVAHI_AUTOIPD` is wired through `ncfg_main_world_where_from_environment`
and reaches the client's executor as well as the daemon's, both going through
`cli_machine.c`.

With an explicit path that is not installed, the refusal named
`avahi-autoipd` rather than the path asked for -- which sends an operator who
pointed the seam somewhere to look at a machine that may well have a client
installed.

### Two of my own checks were asking nothing, and a third asked the machine

The case for that refusal used `/nonexistent/avahi-autoipd` and asserted the
message contained `avahi-autoipd`. The path contains the string, so it passed
against both messages: a fixture that cannot reach the thing it is about. A
basename sharing no text with the constant is what makes the two separable.

Replacing it, I wrote a second check for the other branch -- no path given, so
the conventional name is looked for -- and it would have spawned a real IPv4LL
client from the unit suite on any machine that has one.
`ncfg_backend_find_program` searches `/usr/sbin` before `PATH` deliberately, so
a stand-in on `PATH` is found only where nothing is installed. The check passed
here because this machine has no `avahi-autoipd`, which is a verdict about the
machine rather than the source. It is gone, with the reason written where the
next person will reach for it.

And in the live script, `grep -c '"kind":"link_local"'` found nothing and
reported the observation broken. The daemon's JSON is pretty-printed, so the
text is `"kind": "link_local"`. Reading `status --json` directly settled it in
one run: the observation was correct and the pattern was not. Three check
faults against two code faults, in one piece of work, all three found by
looking at what the check could distinguish rather than at whether it passed.

### Where it stands

`make -C c test` is green, `make style` passes both modes, `make ledger`,
`make packaging` and the seven standalone gates pass, and
`tests/live/link_local.sh` is 19 checks, all passing, under a second, named in
`make live`. The live suite is 84 scripts now.

**And the whole suite was run after the wiring, which is what 0263 asks for
rather than the script on its own**: 79 scripts reported a summary, every one
of them passing, `link_local.sh` among them in-suite rather than only
standalone, and no `FAIL` line anywhere in the log. `make` still exits
non-zero, and on this machine it always will -- `sandbox_writes.sh` is the
last invocation in the target and refuses under `NCFG_LIVE` because there is
no systemd here to impose the unit's sandbox, which `make vm-sandbox` exists
to answer. So the suite's exit code is not the acceptance signal on a sysvinit
host and the absence of failing checks is.

**One thing the suite cannot establish, said here because the check looks as
though it does.** `link_local.sh` asserts the exact argv netcfgd passes -- `-D
-w --force-bind <iface>` -- against a stand-in that accepts anything, so both
sides of that comparison were written in one sitting by one hand. It is a
regression pin and not a validation, and the flags themselves came from
`avahi-autoipd`'s upstream documentation because the client is not installed
here and has no local man page. Only a real client can confirm them.

What keeps that an acknowledged gap rather than a hidden one is that a wrong
flag cannot be quiet. `ncfg_autoip_start` turns a non-zero exit into the
client's own complaint lines, and an exit of 0 with no process carrying
netcfgd's markers into a refusal saying netcfgd has nothing it could stop
later -- which is the arm a careless version would omit, because that is the
one where the program appeared to work. So the failure mode of being wrong
about upstream is a refused apply with a reason attached.

**That last script was then run where it can run**, rather than left as a
pointer: `make vm-sandbox` exits 0 with `sandbox_writes.sh: all checks passed`
in the Debian guest, and the three checks it adds there are its own controls --
the write that cannot be refused without the unit's `ExecPaths=`, the signal
that cannot cross a uid without its `CAP_KILL`, and the probe's own positive
control showing a sandbox where `rw` would mean something different. So the
acceptance after this feature is whole across both tiers rather than whole on
the host and pointed at elsewhere.

## 10.479 Link-local: the client's own interface decides the design

With 10.474's invented blockers gone, the feature is landable C-only and the
next input is the client's actual command line. `avahi-autoipd` is not
installed here and has no local man page, so this came from upstream
documentation rather than from memory -- which matters, because the design
turns entirely on it:

    avahi-autoipd [options] interface
    avahi-autoipd --kill interface
    avahi-autoipd --check interface

    -D, --daemonize    daemonize after startup; implies --syslog
    -w, --wait         wait until an address is acquired before detaching;
                       only valid with --daemonize
        --force-bind   acquire an IPv4LL address even if a routable address
                       is already configured on the interface

    no --pid-file, and the action script is fixed at
    /etc/avahi/avahi-autoipd.action

### The obvious shape is unusable, and that is the finding

`--kill interface` and `--check interface` act on **whichever** client is on
that interface. There is no pid file to point somewhere netcfgd chose. So the
delegation this tree uses everywhere else -- start it, record where, and prove
ownership before signalling -- has nothing to prove ownership with, and
`--kill` would stop an operator's IPv4LL client as readily as netcfgd's.

That is the thing this project refuses to do, and it has the rules to say so:
0141 on not spawning beside a running client, `ncfg_dhcpcd_whose` on telling
ours from theirs, and `ra.h`'s own standard -- the marker is a path netcfgd
chose, so "an operator's own radvd cannot match that, which is a stronger
claim than `not by name`".

### What makes it possible is the flag the semantics already require

`document.h` settles that IPv4 link-local **coexists with routable addresses
rather than being a fallback**. `--force-bind` is exactly that behaviour:
without it the client declines when a routable address is present. So netcfgd
must pass it on correctness grounds -- and a cmdline carrying `--force-bind`
beside the interface is then netcfgd's marker.

**It is weaker than radvd's and the header will say so.** An operator who
passes `--force-bind` themselves is indistinguishable, where a radvd pointed at
a path under `/run/netcfgd` cannot be. It is the same strength as the udhcpc
adoption this tree already accepts -- "by the `-p` it was started with and the
privilege it runs with" -- and it is strictly better than `--kill`, which
asserts nothing at all.

### So the design, settled

  * **Start** `avahi-autoipd -D -w --force-bind <iface>`. `-w` makes the start
    synchronous: it stays in the foreground until an address is acquired, so
    `ncfg_backend_run` waits and gets a real status, which is the shape
    `dhcpcd -b` already has here.
  * **Record** the pid under `<run>/autoip/<iface>.pid`, found by the marker,
    because the client writes no pid file of its own.
  * **Stop** by reading that pid, checking `/proc/<pid>/cmdline` still carries
    the marker, and terminating it. Never `--kill`, which would reach
    somebody else's.
  * **No new op**: `backend.start` and `backend.stop` carry a kind, and the
    tenth kind is the C's own.

## 10.478 OPEN: `profile save` through the C daemon refuses its own snapshot

Found by running the suite on a machine with inotify available, which this one
had not been for the whole of the work above.

`tests/live/c_daemon_answers.sh` fails two checks. The transcript names the
sides: `expected:` is the Rust's and `actual:` is the C's, and what the C says
where the Rust saves is

    ncfg: saving `saved` would not reproduce what this machine is running, so
    nothing was kept. That is a fault in the snapshot rather than in your
    configuration; write the profile by hand and please report it. The two
    differ in a block this cannot name.

So the C's daemon renders the running document, recompiles it, finds the result
unequal and rolls the whole save back -- about a configuration the Rust saves
without complaint. The message asks the operator to report it, which is this
entry.

**It is the daemon path, not the CLI path.** `tests/live/profile.sh` passes and
covers `ncfg profile save` run locally; this one goes over the socket, where
the document being reproduced is the daemon's own `desired` rather than a fresh
compile. That distinction is why two days of renderer round-trip work did not
touch it.

**The polling fallback was hiding it.** Measured across three full runs, same
tree:

    run 4   config watcher polling    c_daemon_answers.sh  all checks passed
    run 5   config watcher polling    c_daemon_answers.sh  all checks passed
    run 6   config watcher inotify    c_daemon_answers.sh  2 check(s) failed

And it reproduces standalone on the inotify path, so it is deterministic here
rather than a race inside a long run.

### Reproduced in forty lines, and the condition is exact

`sh -x` on the script named the step a hand-built reproduction was missing --
`ncfg wifi add TestNet --open`, immediately before the save -- and with the
script's own shape (its own config directory, a run directory beside it,
`--no-apply-on-start`, the five verbs in order) a local probe refuses
identically.

Bisected by omitting one verb at a time:

    all five verbs                     refuses
    without the `extra0` drop-in       saves
    without `secret set`               refuses
    without `wifi add TestNet`         saves

**So it takes a declared device with no interface AND a network, together.**
Either alone round-trips. The secret is irrelevant.

### Three plausible causes ruled out

  * **A stale daemon document.** The daemon's `desired.json` and a fresh
    `ncfg show --json` of the same directory are identical, key for key -- so
    the snapshot is not being rendered from a document that has drifted from
    the configuration.
  * **The writing verbs themselves.** put/rm/put, `secret set` and `wifi add`
    through the daemon do not break it without the device block present.
  * **A bare `device` block alone.** It renders and recompiles cleanly on its
    own, with or without the network's absence.

### Root-caused: the daemon's document is stale, and nothing promised otherwise

Instrumented `write_profile_snapshot` to print the counts, which is the step
this entry named:

    running: nets=0 devs=2 ifaces=1 | to_write: nets=0 devs=2 ifaces=1

**The document handed to `profile save` has no networks**, while
`desired.json` on disk has one and the configuration directory carries
`conf.d/wifi-TestNet.conf`. So nothing downstream is misbehaving: the renderer
is right, `copy_json` is right, `ncfg_render` correctly fails on a refusal and
did not refuse, and `profile save` honestly refuses because a snapshot of a
document without the network cannot reproduce a directory that has it. The
message is accurate; the input was wrong.

Confirmed by changing one thing:

    wifi add, then save                     running nets=0   refuses
    wifi add, then `ncfg reload`, then save  running nets=1   saves

**`ncfg wifi add` writes the drop-in through the daemon and does not make the
daemon re-read it.** Nor does `config put`: both leave it to the config
watcher, which is asynchronous. `config put` gets away with it here only
because three other verbs separate it from the save, while `wifi add` is
immediately before it -- so this is a race between the watcher and the next
request, not a property of either verb.

And the client already claims otherwise: `config put` prints *"stored `extra`
and re-read its configuration"*, which is a promise nothing enforces.

**The operational consequence is not confined to the suite.** A script writing
`ncfg wifi add X && ncfg profile save P` is racing the daemon, and the two
outcomes are a refusal -- which is the good one -- or a profile saved without
the network, depending on whether the watcher has fired.

### Fixed: `ok` now means in force

`wrote_configuration` in `daemon_answer.c` wraps the six kinds that write
something the compiler reads -- the two `config` verbs, the two `wifi` ones and
the two `profile` ones -- and re-reads before the reply goes out. Six, not the
four this entry first named: `profile set` changes the selection and `profile
save` writes a snapshot and a selection, and both change what compiles.

Secrets are deliberately outside it. A `@secret:` reference is a name in the
document and the store holds the value, so writing one changes nothing the
compiler reads.

**The hazard I flagged dissolved on measurement rather than being accepted.**
The worry was that a reload re-materialises every hook, which is the mechanism
behind 10.470's silently disarmed hash control. But the watcher reloads on the
same write a moment later -- measured, `desired.json` ends with the network
even when the save was refused -- so this changes **when** the reload happens
and not **whether**. It adds no recompile and no re-materialisation that was
not already coming, and 10.470's reload was spurious where this one is not:
the configuration really did change. `hooks.sh` passes with the fix in, which
is the check that matters for 0063.

A reload that fails is logged rather than turned into a failed write: the file
is on disk either way, `reload` keeps the previous desired document when the
new one does not compile, and calling the write failed would be the one untrue
answer available.

    c_daemon_answers.sh   all checks passed   (was 2 failed)
    hooks.sh              all checks passed
    config_arrives.sh     11 of 11
    profile.sh            all checks passed
    make -C c test        0 failures

Confirmed suite-wide afterwards: a full `make live` with zero failing checks,
73 scripts passing, and nothing left in `/tmp` by the suite.

### And the lens this defect suggests comes up clean

The shape worth generalising is **a message asserting a fact the code does not
establish** -- "stored `x` and re-read its configuration" was true of neither
half until now. Swept for other success messages making a checkable claim, and
the three sharpest are all honest:

  * *"and removed the credential `%s`, which nothing refers to now"* --
    `wifi_profile.c` recompiles **after** the removal, asks
    `ncfg_secret_referring_to` of the whole document rather than of the other
    networks, and fails closed: a configuration that cannot be read back keeps
    every credential, because removing one on a guess is unrecoverable (0042).
  * *"stored <path> (0600)"* -- measured: the file is 600 and the directory it
    goes in is 700.
  * *"nothing in the configuration refers to `@secret:x` yet"* -- the same
    reference check, run in the other direction.

So this was an isolated claim rather than a habit, which is worth knowing
before anybody sweeps the messages again.

### What was unnamed before this, kept for the method

Which block differs. The Rust's successful snapshot is on record in full and
emits, in order, `override interface dd0`, `override network "TestNet"`,
`override device dd0`, `override device extra0` -- so whatever the C writes,
that is the shape that compiles back. The C's own snapshot was not captured: it
writes, recompiles, compares and removes faster than a 10ms poll of the
directory catches, so the next attempt wants the file held open or the compare
instrumented rather than the directory watched.

The suspicion worth testing first, from `profile_save.c`'s own order: the fold
comes out of `conf.d` before the overrides are collected, so a device declared
*only* in a folded drop-in is no longer declared in the base when
`collect_overrides` runs -- and the `!declared` skip added for 10.418's
invented devices would then drop it. A document carrying a network is what
makes that reachable, and why is the part not yet understood.

## 10.477 The inotify exhaustion is not this suite's, and what it costs here

Two of this session's hardest diagnoses turned on one environmental fact -- the
config watcher falling back to mtime polling -- so the fact itself was worth
measuring rather than accepting. **It is not netcfgd's doing**, and that is
established rather than assumed.

    165   orphaned `dbus-daemon --session` processes owned by this account
    363   MB resident between them
    100   of the machine's 128 inotify instances, held by those 165
      2   netcfgd scripts start a bus at all

**Measured, not inferred.** `c_nm_signals.sh` starts one with
`dbus-daemon --session --print-address=1 --print-pid=1 --fork`, so it
daemonises and is never the script's child -- which is why `wait` was correctly
excluded for it in 10.476. Counting orphaned buses either side of a full run:
165 before, 165 after. Its cleanup kills the printed pid and the kill works.
`nm.sh` is the only other starter and it skips here for want of nmcli, so it
cannot leak on this machine.

The cause is the workspace-level session-bus leak that
`claude-guidelines`' own signal list already carries, together with the
holder's fix of setting a bus address in `~/.screenrc`.

### What it costs netcfgd specifically, which is the part worth knowing

With 100 of 128 instances held, `ncfg_watch_open` gets no inotify descriptor
and the daemon falls back to the 5-second tick. That is not a cosmetic
difference:

  * it is why the hook-materialisation defect in 10.470 was invisible -- the
    spurious reload it caused only happens on the polling path;
  * it is why `confirm.sh`'s two `sleep 3` checks failed, measuring 4.53s
    against a 3-second wait (10.472).

So a machine with no spare inotify instance does not merely run the suite more
slowly, it runs a **different** netcfgd -- and both defects that produced were
real, which is the uncomfortable half: the degraded machine found two faults a
healthy one would have hidden.

**The reaping was held off here and has since been done.** The reasons for
holding off were sound and are kept: 165 processes belonging to this account
are not a netcfgd question, killing a bus a live session is using would break
that session, and `evidence.md`'s PID-reuse hazard applies to any sweep of
them -- a pid recorded as a dbus-daemon has already, once in this workspace,
become a live worker by the time the kill landed, which is why the sweep that
was eventually run re-read each `/proc/<pid>/cmdline` immediately before
signalling and skipped anything that had stopped being a bus.

Only the clientless ones were taken, which is what made it safe to take any:
165 reaped, and the measurement either side is the whole of the evidence --
126 of 128 inotify instances in use before, 27 after. Re-measured on
2026-10-13, after a `make live` and several days: **32 of 128 in use.** So the
headroom holds rather than merely having been won once.

**The bus count in the first version of this correction was wrong, and the way
it was wrong is the point.** It said one bus on this account and none
orphaned, from `grep -c 'dbus-daemon --session'` -- a pattern requiring
`--session` to follow the program name immediately. These are launched
`dbus-daemon --syslog --fork --print-pid 4 --print-address 6 --session`, with
the flag last, so the pattern matched none of them and the shortfall read as
good news. Asking for both words anywhere in the argv instead: **seven buses,
six of them this account's and parented to init**, two of those started during
the session that wrote the sentence.

So the leak recurs, which is consistent with what this entry already says
about whose it is -- it arrives with session starts rather than with anything
netcfgd runs -- and six buses are not what cost the inotify headroom, since
the headroom is fine with them alive. What the reaping bought was the
hundredfold case, and that is what holds. A count is not a trend, and a
pattern that cannot match the thing it is counting is not a count at all.

### And the healthy machine stopped testing the path the sick one did -- end to end

With instances available, `ncfg_watch_open` succeeds here, so the slower path
stops being the one the suite runs. That is the uncomfortable corollary of the
paragraph above: a machine with no spare instance runs a different netcfgd
rather than a slower one, and both defects this entry credits to the degraded
machine would be invisible on a healthy one.

**The first version of this section said the fallback was exercised by nothing
here, and asked for a seam. Both halves were wrong, and the tree had answered
it twice.** `watch_test.c` makes `ncfg_watch_open_polling` public and asks both
mechanisms the same assertions, with its header giving the reason in the terms
this section was reaching for -- the fallback runs only once something else has
gone wrong, "which makes it exactly the code nobody has ever seen work". And
the daemon carries `--poll-config`, in `--help`, which forces the same path
from outside. So the seam existed at both levels and the unit tier covers it on
every `make -C c test`, whatever the machine's inotify headroom.

**What was actually missing was narrower and is now closed.** Nothing in
`tests/live` used `--poll-config`, so the DAEMON on the polling path -- the
5-second tick, which is what changed the timing in both of those defects -- had
no end-to-end witness. `config_arrives.sh` takes `NCFG_LIVE_DAEMON_FLAGS` now
and `make live` runs it twice, which puts its eleven questions to both
mechanisms for the cost of one line.

It proves which mechanism it got, from the daemon's own `watching ... via ...`
line, because a flag silently dropped would otherwise produce a second inotify
run and twelve passing checks. Asserted strictly only under the flag: without
it the mechanism is the machine's answer and pinning `inotify` would fail this
file on exactly the exhausted host this entry is about. Controlled by pointing
the strict assertion at `inotify` while the daemon was told to poll -- 1 of 12
failed, and it was that one.

**Three times in one session a question was handed over that the tree had
already decided somewhere else**: this, `sandbox_writes.sh` (answered by the
`vm-sandbox` target's own comment), and the cast sweep in 10.481 (which did not
exist). `working-practice.md` says a wrongly-deferred question is caught by
nothing, and the common thread in all three is that the answer was in a
comment at the place doing the work rather than in a document -- which is also
what that rule says to go looking for.

## 10.476 The live suite's cleanups raced the daemon they had just killed

Found by the sweep `running-code.md` asks for after a run, which is also how
10.471 was found: three directories in `/tmp` after a `make live` whose every
script had passed.

    /tmp/ncfg-qdisc.*    /tmp/ncfg-rules.*    /tmp/ncfg-switch.*

Each holding `run/observed.json` -- netcfgd's own state, not the script's.

### The cleanups were already careful, and that is what hid it

These scripts do not forget to clean up. Their traps kill the daemon, then
retry the removal for five seconds, then **say so** if it has not worked:

    note: /tmp/ncfg-switch.FHIE3I outlived five seconds of trying to remove it

One of the three said that. The other two said nothing and leaked anyway,
which is the part worth the entry.

**`sh -x` settled it in one run.** The trace shows the first `rm -rf` fail, the
retry succeed, the loop break, and the final `[ -d "$work" ]` test come out
false -- so at the moment the trap finished, the directory was gone and there
was correctly nothing to report. It is there now. **The daemon re-created it
after the trap had finished**, because `kill` returns when the signal is sent
and nothing waited for the process to go.

So the retry loop covers the case where `rm` *fails* and is blind to the case
where `rm` *succeeds and the writer comes back*. The comment above it names the
right hazard -- "a signalled daemon writes on its way out" -- and the remedy it
chose can only see one half of it.

### 28 of the suite's scripts already had the answer

`wait "$daemon" 2>/dev/null || true` after the kill, which is `drift.sh`'s shape
and `adopt.sh`'s and twenty-six others'. **Twenty did not**, and the correct
pattern being the majority in the same directory is this project's recurring
lesson: a working sibling explaining itself is a cheaper source of a decision
than any document.

Proved on the reproducible one before touching the rest: `rules.sh` leaked on
every run, and with the wait added it leaked on neither of two.

**Nineteen fixed, and `wait` only where the pid is a direct child.** A blanket
insert would have claimed a fix that does nothing: `wait` works on children of
the current shell, so a forked `dbus-daemon` whose pid came from
`--print-pid`, and the adopted clients `udhcpc_orphan.sh` finds by pid file,
are killed without being waited for -- correctly, since neither writes the
state files this race is about. `sim_select.sh` is the twentieth and is left
alone deliberately: it `pkill`s a `gpioset` stub by pattern, which is not a
child and writes nothing into the work directory.

### Proved suite-wide, not only on the one that reproduced

Two full `make live` runs, same machine, same 73 passing scripts and no failing
check in either, differing only by these nineteen files:

    before   3 directories left in /tmp   qdisc, rules, switch
    after    0

### Why it went unseen, which is 10.471's answer again

A green suite, directories in `/tmp` rather than in the tree, and `df` in a
source tree answering for the wrong filesystem. What is new here is that the
cleanup *reported* in one case out of three -- so the signal existed, in the
log, once, and nothing was watching for it. A note on stderr in a 400-line run
is not a mechanism.

## 10.472 The suite's waits, and the negative checks that were vacuous

Settled 2026-10-11: fix them. `make live` stopped at `confirm.sh`, and 10.470
established why -- a 3-second wait against a 5-second tick on a machine whose
config watcher has fallen back to mtime polling. This is the fix, and the half
that was not expected is the more interesting one.

### The rule was already in the file, twenty lines above the cases that broke it

`confirm.sh` carries it in a comment over `await_window`:

> **Wait for the outcome, do not sleep for it.** [...] A fixed sleep shorter
> than the thing it waits for is a test that reports on the load average.
>
> These are for asserting that something *did* happen. Asserting that something
> did **not** still wants a fixed sleep: there is no outcome to wait for, and
> returning early would only mean not having looked long enough.

That is the whole doctrine, correct, and paid for by an earlier case that
"passed every time it was run alone and failed inside the full suite". Cases 14
and 15 were never converted to it. **A working sibling explaining itself is a
cheaper source of a project's decisions than the document is** --
`working-practice.md` says so, and here the sibling was in the same file.

### The negative checks were the worse half

Each of those cases pairs a positive assertion with a negative one:

    sleep 3
    check "an identical rewrite over drift arms nothing"   <- negative
    check "and the drift was still corrected"              <- positive

The positive one failed, which is what sent anybody looking. The negative one
**passed, and could not have failed**: at 3 seconds the daemon had not yet
looked at the rewrite, so no window existed to find whatever the guard did.
Any implementation passes that, including one with the guard deleted -- which
is `evidence.md`'s vacuous pass, arrived at by timing rather than by an empty
file list.

The fix is an ordering and it is not arbitrary: **the pass that corrects the
drift is the pass that would have armed the window.** So wait for the
correction, then ask about the window, and both answers are about the same
pass. Case 15 is the same shape -- the pass that declines to arm is the pass
that logs why -- and case 9's control was the same again, `sleep 2` then "arms
nothing", now waiting for the address that pass also produces.

**Case 9's other sleep stays, and that is the distinction working.** Its
`sleep 7` waits for a window that should not exist to fail to expire. There is
no outcome to wait for, so it is a fixed sleep, and it is where that case's
teeth are.

### `config_arrives.sh`: the count that proved nothing

It asserts a broken configuration is complained about once rather than per
pass, after two touches a second apart. On a 5-second tick the daemon need not
have read either, so a count still reading 1 was consistent with no
de-duplication at all. Six seconds each instead: it still reads 1, so the guard
is real and the check now exercises it. Nothing to wait for here either -- the
claim is that a second line never appears -- which is why this one had to get
longer rather than smarter.

### What was deliberately left alone, and the criterion

Of **295** fixed sleeps in the suite, **40** sit immediately before a check in
a script that runs a daemon. Four scripts' worth were wrong. All the rest are
one of two things that are not:

  * **a non-event assertion** -- "is not a roam", "provokes nothing", "is not
    adopted", "does not run the portal", "everything else is still dropped".
    Converting these to a poll would make them return as soon as the answer is
    the one wanted, which for a non-event is immediately and always.
  * **a wait on an event-driven path** -- `roam.sh`, `wifi_trouble.sh` and
    `drift.sh` wait on supplicant control-socket events and netlink, which
    arrive in milliseconds. No tick is involved and a second is generous.

So the criterion is not "is this sleep short" but **"is the thing being waited
for produced by a poll"**. Only the configuration watcher and a sysctl the
kernel announces no event for are, and they are what the four scripts touched
here were waiting on.

### Verified both ways

    confirm.sh        C: all pass (was 2 failed)   Rust: 1 failed (was 3)
    adopt.sh          C: all pass                  Rust: all pass
    altname.sh        C: all pass                  Rust: all pass
    config_arrives.sh C: 11 of 11                  Rust: 4 failed, pre-existing

**The Rust's remaining `confirm.sh` failure is not a timing fault and the C
passes it.** "The windowed apply set the MTU" expects 1400 and the Rust leaves
1500. That was one of the three it failed before this change and is the one the
other two were hiding; under 0263 it is the port being ahead rather than
behind, and it is unexplained here.

### And a second place the C is ahead, found by running the oracle at all

`config_arrives.sh` had never been run against the Rust -- the sweeps that
produced 10.469 and 10.470 drove the C, and the oracle was only brought out for
the scripts that failed. It fails **4 of 11** against the Rust and passes 11 of
11 against the C, and the cause is one thing: **the Rust's daemon never logs
that a configuration does not compile.** Every check that counts that line, or
the file name in it, or the recovery line that follows it, reads zero.

**Not caused by this change, and the reason is structural rather than a
judgement.** The first of the four is reached through `awaits 'grep -q "does
not compile" ...'`, a helper this commit does not touch, and it fails before
execution reaches the sleeps that were lengthened. A longer wait cannot
manufacture a line the daemon does not write.

What it says about method: **the oracle is only an oracle where it is
consulted.** A script that passes against the C was never compared, so a port
difference in the C's favour sat unrecorded -- and the asymmetry matters,
because a difference the C *loses* shows up as a failing check whereas one it
*wins* shows up as nothing at all.

## 10.470 The four port gaps, and what each turned out to be

Settled 2026-10-10: fix the four 10.469 measured. All four are closed and the
scripts pass. Not one of them was the thing its failing check appeared to name,
and two were caused by this port's own earlier work.

    exec_refused.sh    10 checks   two faults, plus a variable nothing read
    hooks.sh            2 checks   a spurious reload, from a writability probe
    profile.sh          3 checks   three block kinds a list had never named
    dhcpcd_orphan.sh    1 check    10.468's fix, silencing more than its target

### `exec_refused.sh`: the reason was computed and thrown away

Two faults in one loop. `ncfg_dhcp_start` tries dhcpcd, udhcpc and busybox in
order; `program_for` returns NULL for *both* "not installed" and "installed and
unusable", so the loop's `continue` discarded the distinction and the tail said
one generic sentence naming none of the three. An operator holding `no DHCPv4
client found` could not tell a machine with nothing installed from one whose
dhcpcd is mode 0644 -- and `ncfg_process_exec_refusal` already produced exactly
the sentence that tells those apart (0178/0182), with nobody calling it from
here.

The second was the dhcpcd hook check, which `return`ed and so **refused the
start before a client was ever looked for**. The hook is dhcpcd's alone and
udhcpc never runs it, so a machine whose working client is busybox was refused
its lease over a file that would not have been used. Worse for the script
itself: in an uninstalled tree every check in it read back a message about the
hook instead of the one it was written for, which is what its own header says
it exists to avoid.

So the loop accumulates a reason per candidate -- absent names collected into
one sentence, an `access(X_OK)` refusal reported through the refusal helper that
distinguishes a missing executable bit from a `noexec` mount, the hook asked
once before the loop and disqualifying dhcpcd rather than failing the start --
and the "install dhcpcd, udhcpc or busybox" line is emitted **only where
nothing was found to run**. Telling an operator whose dhcpcd is 0644 to install
dhcpcd sends them to `apt` for a fault a `chmod` fixes, and it is the sentence
they read first because it is the one naming an action.

### And underneath it, two environment variables the C never read

`NCFG_DHCPCD_HOOK` and `NCFG_DHCPCD_RUN_DIR` are how an uninstalled tree is
driven at all: the hook ships to `/usr/libexec`, so **six** live scripts set one
or both -- five of them pointing the hook at `packaging/hooks/dhcpcd-hook` in
this tree, and the sixth the run directory. The Rust reads both. `ncfg_dhcp_machine` filled its members from the
compiled-in defaults and looked at nothing, so every dhcpcd check in those six
was answered about a hook nobody had installed.

`dhcp.h` says of that struct that nothing in it has a default and no function
taking it reads the environment -- which is right and stays. The reading goes
in `ncfg_dhcp_machine`, the one function whose job is "what this machine is",
beside where the daemon resolves its run directory, and the header now says so
rather than describing an arrangement its own constructor did not keep. Three
callers wanted the same answer; one place looks.

### `hooks.sh`: a writability probe disarmed 0063's hash control

The check is that a materialised hook edited after the configuration was
compiled does not run: the document carries its content hash, and the executor
refuses a file that no longer matches. The C ran the hook and reported success.

The hash check was present and correct. What happened is that **the file was
rewritten with its original contents before the hash was read**. A `sha256sum`
either side showed it: tampered going in, pristine coming out.

Three theories, all wrong, and each cost a run: a reconcile pass woken by the
`ip link set up`; the confirm path recompiling to find its revert target; the
apply request reloading. A `sleep 2` with no apply showed the tamper surviving,
which killed the first; reading `ncfg_confirm_may_arm` and
`ncfg_daemon_apply_request` killed the other two. One `strace -f -e
trace=openat,unlink` on the daemon answered it in a single run:

    openat(".../etc/.netcfgd-write-probe.4659", O_WRONLY|O_CREAT|O_EXCL) = 12
    unlink(".../etc/.netcfgd-write-probe.4659")                          = 0

`report_writability` probes the configuration directory with a real
`open(O_CREAT|O_EXCL)` and an `unlink`, because `access(2)` walks straight past
a read-only *mount* and that is the case it exists for (0178 one layer up). The
probe is right. It ran **after** `ncfg_main_watchers_open`, and creating and
removing a file bumps the containing directory's own mtime -- which is part of
the polling watcher's baseline. So the baseline was one modification behind the
directory from the moment it was taken, and the first tick reported a
configuration change that had not happened. The reload re-materialises every
hook under `<run>/hooks/`, putting the original back.

**The cost is not the test.** On any machine whose inotify instances are
exhausted -- or anybody running `--poll-config` -- the daemon recompiled on its
first tick, every start, and 0063's hash control was silently disarmed. Nothing
said so: a successful reload logs nothing, which is correct and is also why this
hid.

The fix is the ordering, and the invariant is written at both ends: **nothing
this daemon does may write into a watched directory after the watchers open.** A
refresh after the fact was the other candidate and is worse -- it would hide a
real edit made while the daemon was starting, which is the opposite mistake.

Measured before and after with nothing touching the config: two reloads in five
seconds became one, the one at startup.

### And the journal over the socket was printing the whole document

Found in the same output while reading it. `ncfg apply --confirm-within N` is
the daemon's to carry out, and the client prints the journal it answers with --
as, measured:

    doneid1opaddr.delinterfacehooked0reasoninterfacehooked0fieldenabled...

`ncfg_json_string` hands out **counted, not terminated** bytes, and says so in
as many words; `say_journal` passed NULL for the length and used `%s` and
`strcmp`. Every string ran to the end of the buffer, so the `strcmp` against
`"done"` failed, the outcome lookup fell through to the raw bytes, and `%s`
printed the rest of the document. Only the last record came out right, its
value being the one that happens to sit at the buffer's end -- which is why the
one `Done hook.run` in the output looked like the shape working.

Matched with `ncfg_json_string_equals`, which exists for exactly this, and
printed with `%.*s`. It reads as the Rust's does now.

### `profile.sh`: the third time this list fell behind the renderer

`ncfg profile save` renders the running document beside the base, so a block the
base defines has to be restated as `override`; `collect_overrides` says which
those are. It named interface, network, device and bluetooth. The renderer opens
**seven** kinds, and `rule`, `access_point` and `linkset` were never in the
list, for as long as it could write them. The base in that script defines `rule
profile-probe`, the snapshot restated it bare, and the save rolled itself back
with *"that would stop the configuration compiling"* -- about a faithful
snapshot. The verb was unusable on any machine with a rule, an access point or a
linkset in its configuration, which is every machine running an access point.

Three recurrences of one omission is a class: `device` was counted when it
should not have been, `bluetooth` was missed when the renderer learned it, and
now three at once. `tool/override_coverage_gate.py` reads the kinds out of the
renderer's own `ncfg_render_opening` calls and out of `collect_overrides`, and
fails in both directions. Seen to fail both ways before being trusted. A round
trip cannot cover this: it renders a document with no base to collide with.

### `dhcpcd_orphan.sh`: 10.468's fix was broader than its target

The check reads `adopted the dhcp client already running on ...` from the apply
output, and it is **the only discriminator there is**: a second `dhcpcd -b`
against a running one is a silent no-op, so the client count is 1 whether
netcfgd adopted or blindly re-ran. A silent adoption is indistinguishable from
netcfgd having started a second client.

The message was there, at `INFO`, and two things of this port's own making
stopped it. 10.468 bracketed the CLI's `ncfg_apply` with
`ncfg_log_accept(NCFG_LOG_CRITICAL)` to stop the engine's per-action line being
printed beside the journal that already says it -- and that silences **every
line the backends emit while the plan runs**, not the engine's. And `main.c`
imposed a `WARNING` floor for the same duplicate, which is two steps stricter
than the Rust, whose default is `Info`: so even unbracketed, no `INFO` line a
backend emits reached an operator of the C.

Both are gone. `ncfg_apply_silently` is the duplicate's actual fix -- the engine
withholds *its own* narration for the one caller that renders the journal, and
takes nobody else's lines -- and the floor had no remaining reason, so the two
builds' default levels agree. `ap.sh` and `acl.sh`, the two scripts 10.468 was
fixing, still pass.

**A severity floor silences by level what wanted silencing by author**, and the
blunt instrument was mine. The narration belongs to the caller; that is what the
two function names say now.

### The whole suite re-run afterwards, because one of these fixes is broad

Removing the `WARNING` floor changes what every `ncfg` command prints, so the
83 scripts were run again end to end. **Two fail, and they are the two that
failed against both builds before any of this.** The rest:

    70  pass          67 saying "all checks passed", 3 wording it their own way
     8  cannot run    no /dev/vhci, no mac80211_hwsim, no systemctl, no nmcli,
                      no odhcp6c, and two wanting an artefact built first
     3  not tests     control_helper.sh and the two fake modem CLIs are
                      fixtures the others drive, and say so when run alone
     2  fail          confirm.sh, control_exposure.sh -- shared, see below

**My own tally was wrong first, by its own detector.** It counted lines whose
first field was `FAIL`, and the sweep writes the failing check names underneath
the script's verdict line -- so two failing scripts and three failing checks
read as five failing scripts. A count inherits its detector, in a script I
wrote to count.

**And `gui_wifi.sh` passes.** 10.469 recorded it running to the 180-second
timeout on two separate sweeps, the one entry in that table that was neither a
pass, a failure, nor a statement about the machine. It now passes bare and
under `NCFG_LIVE=1`, which is the condition it hung in. Recorded rather than
claimed: nothing here was aimed at it, and I have no mechanism connecting any
of these five fixes to it. If it hangs again that is the thing to know first.

### The two that fail against both are this machine, not either build

Re-measured 2026-10-10 because a "shared failure" is a claim about the other
build and goes stale the moment either moves: both still failed on both.
**Diagnosed 2026-10-11, and neither is a defect in the C or the Rust.** Each is
a premise the script needs that this machine cannot supply, and "it fails on
both builds" was the clue -- two independent implementations agreeing on a
failure is usually a statement about the third party in the room.

**`confirm.sh`'s two are a 3-second wait against a 5-second tick.** Cases 14 and
15 edit the configuration and check a consequence after `sleep 3`: that drift was
still corrected, and that the daemon logged why it would not arm a window. Both
depend on the daemon noticing the configuration changed, and
`NCFG_MAIN_TICK_MS` is 5000 -- so on a machine where the config watcher has
fallen back to mtime polling, the news arrives on the next tick rather than at
once. This machine is that machine: its inotify instances are exhausted, which
is the same condition that hid the hook defect in 10.470.

Measured rather than inferred, by replaying each case with the wait
instrumented instead of fixed -- the daemon reporting `via mtime polling` in
both runs:

    case 14   forwarding back to 1        after 4.53s   script allows 3s
    case 15   "the last-good ... empty"   after 4.53s   script allows 3s

So the behaviour both builds are accused of losing happens, 1.5 seconds after
the script stops looking. **Naming the experiment and running it is the whole
of this entry**: the environmental story was available from the first reading of
the tick constant, and a comfortable explanation that ends an investigation is
worth less than no explanation -- so it was tested, and it held.

**~~`control_exposure.sh`'s one cannot pass under `unshare -rn` at all.~~ It
was never failing: my sweep invoked it wrongly.** The diagnosis below is
correct about the namespace and wrong about mattering -- `make live` runs this
script **bare on the host**, where `id -Gn` offers `dialout` and the chgrp
works. Run as the Makefile runs it: all checks pass. Corrected 2026-10-11,
hours after being written here.

What the namespace does to it, kept because the mechanism is real and the next
sweep will meet it again: the script asserts that a remote socket configured
with `agent = "group:<g>"` is chgrp'd to that group, and picks `<g>` as the
first entry of `id -Gn` that is not the primary group -- deliberately, because
a socket is already created owned by its creator's primary group and asserting
against that would pass with the chown reverted. In a user namespace made by
`unshare -r` the gid map has exactly one entry, so the only secondary group on
offer is `nogroup`, which is unmapped:

    gid_map:  0  1000  1
    id -Gn:   root nogroup
    chgrp nogroup <file>  ->  Invalid argument

**And that is the invocation error 10.469 wrote a paragraph about, made again
by the same sweep runner.** `make live` runs 23 of the 83 scripts bare on the
host; my sweep ran 3 of those bare and wrapped the other **20** in `unshare
-rn`. For most it costs nothing -- a pass in a stricter environment is still a
pass -- but a FAIL from that sweep is not evidence until it has been re-run the
way the Makefile invokes it, and the one failure I did re-run that way
evaporated. So **the sweep's passes stand and its failures were never
load-bearing**, which is not what either sweep's tally implied.

**`make live` could not complete on this machine until one of those moved**,
since the target stops at the first failing script and `confirm.sh` is the
tenth thing it runs. Three ways out were open: wait for the condition rather
than sleeping a fixed three seconds (the suite already has `await` helpers, and
it would make the scripts correct on any machine without a spare inotify
instance); raise `fs.inotify.max_user_instances`, which is 128 with 126 in use;
or reap the orphaned session buses holding most of those.

**The first was taken, on the holder's instruction -- 10.472 has it**, and it
turned up more than the two failures: the negative half of each case was
vacuous, passing at a moment no implementation could have failed it. With
`confirm.sh` passing and `control_exposure.sh` never having been a blocker,
the target went on to run the whole suite -- 10.473 has the three runs and
where each stopped.

**And `confirm.sh` separates the two builds the other way.** It fails three
checks against the Rust and two against the C -- the Rust also fails "the
windowed apply set the MTU". Recorded because the next reader of "fails against
both" should know the counts are not equal; whether the Rust's third has the
same timing cause is unmeasured.

### What this cost, and the two habits that cost it

**Theorising about a mechanism before reading the input cost three runs** on the
hooks defect. Every theory was about which of netcfgd's own paths reloaded, and
the answer was a syscall nobody had looked for; one `strace` was cheaper than
all three. `evidence.md` has this as *read the input before theorising about the
mechanism*, and the shape to recognise is that each theory was plausible, each
was testable, and testing them one at a time is the expensive way to search.

**And `kill "${daemon:-0}"` in a trap signals the process group.** My first
probe exited before the variable was set, the trap fired, and the whole group
including `timeout` took the signal -- which read as a 180-second hang in the
thing being probed. A default of `0` in a `kill` is not a no-op.

## 10.467 Three live-suite checks the C fails and the Rust passes

0263 says a module of the C port may replace its Rust half "only once it passes
the Rust's own tests for the same behaviour", and names the 83 scripts under
`tests/live/` as the whole of that suite -- the Rust's 536 unit tests cannot be
pointed at another binary, and these can. **Nobody had run them against the C
recently, and three checks fail.**

The comparison, same script, same `unshare -rn`, same `NCFG_LIVE=1`, differing
only in `NCFG_LIVE_BUILD`:

                    the Rust            the C
    acl.sh          all checks passed   1 check failed
    ap.sh           all checks passed   2 checks failed

So these are port gaps and not tests that are wrong for both, which is the one
thing the comparison settles and reading could not.

    acl.sh   "and says which of the two states it found"
             `did not answer its control socket` expected once, said twice
    ap.sh    "and named hostapd rather than the action"
    ap.sh    "quoting what hostapd said"

All three are about what the operator READS on a failed apply, and the Rust
gets them right. The first has a diagnosis started: `ncfg_plan_wedged_backends`
has one emission site and `ncfg apply` builds one plan, so the duplicate is
most likely the same backend appearing twice in `observed->backends` rather
than two warnings. Confirming that needs the observation instrumented inside a
live run, which is where this stops rather than guessing.

### The suite is runnable without cargo, which is how this was found at all

`make live` builds the Rust workspace and runs three Rust test binaries beside
the scripts, so it looks like the scripts need cargo. They do not: each is
standalone shell that takes its binaries from `$build` and runs under
`unshare -rn` on its own. One script took three minutes to try.

### What the Makefile said about this, and what is true

Its "WHICH BUILD THE SCRIPTS DRIVE" block said the scripts default to
`target/debug` and that `NCFG_LIVE_BUILD=$PWD/c` opts into the C. **Counted:
69 of the 83 take `${NCFG_LIVE_BUILD:-$repo/c}`, none defaults to
`target/debug`, and 14 need no binary.** The default flipped to the C and the
block did not notice, so a reader following it would believe the acceptance
suite still tests the superseded implementation. Rewritten with the count, and
with the inverse spelling -- pointing the suite at the Rust is what takes a
variable now.

### Two flaws in my own sweep, which is why no total is quoted

I globbed `tests/live/*.sh` and ran every one without `NCFG_LIVE=1`. Both are
wrong:

  * **the glob includes helpers.** `fake_mbimcli.sh` and `fake_umbim.sh` are
    fakes other scripts invoke; run alone they exit non-zero ("nothing asked
    for"), and I counted them as failures.
  * **`NCFG_LIVE` inverts skip semantics.** The scripts read it, and with it set
    a skip becomes a loud failure -- which is the right design, since asking
    for the live tier and getting a skip is a result worth a red line. Without
    it they skip quietly, so my six SKIPs are not what the project's own run
    would report.

Stopped at 31 of 83 rather than finished: scripts began hitting the 150-second
timeout, the remainder would have taken an hour, and the count it produced
would not have been comparable to anything. The three confirmed failures were
each re-run under the project's own invocation before being believed.

**Also reported as failures rather than skips**: `bluetooth.sh` without
`/dev/vhci` and `c_daemon_tryout.sh` without systemd, where `association.sh`,
`c_dns_delivery.sh` and `c_nm_signals.sh` say "skipping: <reason>" for the same
kind of absence. Same class as 10.465's inotify fix, in the live tier, and not
touched here.

## 10.460 Coverage as the lens, after the invented ones ran out

Fifteen lenses in, each new one was finding less, and the next would have been
invented rather than derived. So: measure what the suite does not execute, and
let that be the list.

`gcov` over the whole C suite, built from `git archive HEAD` with `-O0
--coverage` in a scratch tree:

    render.c          94.88% of 586 lines
    render_link.c     95.55% of 427
    render_device.c   97.97% of 444

**The unexecuted lines sort cleanly into two kinds**, which is what made the
measurement worth taking:

  * **allocation failures and NULL-argument guards** -- `return NULL` after a
    failed `malloc`, "an override was recorded with nowhere to put it",
    `missing->failed = 1` where recording a refusal itself failed. Almost all
    of `render.c`'s thirty are these. Reaching them needs allocation injected,
    and they are the error paths of a library that is not allowed to crash;
    uncovered is the honest state.
  * **refusals nothing exercises.** About nine, and these are behaviour with a
    sentence nobody has ever read back.

### One of them was mine, added without a test

`render_link.c:183` is the static address `peer` guard from 10.454. I tested
the address beside it and not the peer. It had never run.

That is the sharper half of this measurement: coverage did not find a gap in
somebody else's old code, it found a guard I had added four passes earlier and
believed tested because its sibling was.

### Six are tested now, and what the others are

    a `peer` that is not an address              now tested
    a delegation's `index`                       now tested
    an advertised prefix's `index`                now tested
    an advertise backend of `exec`                now tested
    an advertise block with no prefix             now tested
    a wireguard key that will not render          measured, not testable

`render_link.c` goes 95.55% to 98.59% on that. The `index` pair is the
interesting one: the member exists in the model and `@pd:` has no spelling for
it, so a document read from JSON can say which delegation it means and the
language cannot -- two separate sites, two separate refusals, neither ever run.

**The wireguard one cannot be reached from a document and the test says so.**
`ncfg_key_render` refuses only on a buffer too small, and a key of every bit
set still renders -- base64 has no invalid byte -- so the refusal is a caller's
bug and not a document's. The case asserts that the all-ones key renders, which
is a fact that can fail, rather than asserting the refusal, which cannot fire.

**And the first draft of that case was vacuous.** It read
`check(!renders(document) || 1, ...)` -- a tautology, written while reaching
for "accepted or refused, either is fine". A check that cannot fail is the
thing this file has been complaining about for ten entries, and I wrote one.
It is the assertion above instead.

### The method, because repeating it has a trap

`CFLAGS` given on the make command line **overrides the makefile's `+=`**, so
`make CFLAGS="... --coverage"` silently drops `-Iinclude -I../client` and the
build fails on a missing header three files in. The flags have to be passed
whole:

    make -C c CFLAGS="-std=c11 -O0 -g --coverage -D_DEFAULT_SOURCE \
        -Iinclude -I../client -MMD -MP" LDFLAGS="--coverage" test

## 10.454 The string half, which is wider than the numeric one, and a silent truncation

10.453's sweep reads **numeric** leaves. The vxlan family pair in 10.452 was a
pair of STRINGS and was found by hand, so the string half of the class was
untested. It is much the larger half.

### Five found by hand first

A device's `name` is `NCFG_F_STR` in the field tables, which carry no shape at
all. Set to `eth 0`, to the empty string, to one with a newline, or to 64
characters, each rendered cleanly and then failed its own round trip on the
lowerer's words -- and so did a static address set to `not-an-address`.

Two that do NOT fault are worth recording: a device named `global`, which is a
block keyword, and one named `a{b`. **Quoting already covers the lexical
half** -- the renderer writes the label quoted, so the lexer reads it back
whole. What quoting cannot cover is the semantic half, which is the lowering's
name rules, and that is the gap.

**Both validators already existed and were already public.** `ncfg_usable_name`
is in `document.h` and the supplicant backend calls it; `lower_value.c` wraps
it as `ncfg_name_ok` only to attach a span and a sentence. `ncfg_address_canonical`
takes CIDR and bare alike. Nothing needed extracting into the model, which the
three fixes before this one each did -- the separation was already there and
the renderer simply never called it.

**One pass, not fifteen guards.** The names are spread over three files and a
tagged union; a check per site is fifteen places to forget. `render.c` checks
them all once before the walk, and the list's obligation is to track what the
LOWERING validates: `ncfg_require_interface_label` for a block's label, the ten
`ncfg_as_interface_name` call sites, and the per-word check in `lower_kind.c`.
`ingress_redirect` is deliberately absent, being a name the lowering does not
validate -- refusing it would stop a profile saving over something the language
reads back perfectly well, which is the band-6 lesson from 10.451.

### Then the sweep was extended, because the lesson was to exercise rather than read

10.453's own conclusion was that an enumeration of a behaviour has to come from
exercising it. So the sweep learned about string leaves -- whitespace, empty,
over-long -- and found **113 fault lines over fifteen distinct constraints**,
against six for the whole numeric half:

    a secret reference needs a name        a `network` block needs a name
    is not a route destination            cannot be a network name
    is not an absolute path                is not a regulatory domain
    is not a Bluetooth address             is not an IPv6 address
    is not an `http://` URL                is not a hostname
    is not a duplex setting                is not a band
    is not an address or keyword           needs a name after it
    an APN cannot be empty

**Pinned rather than disabled.** Fifteen guards at once would be fifteen rushed
guards, so they are a baseline the sweep carries: the set cannot grow, and each
entry is a named piece of work with a reproduction. That is the agree gate's
`SAVE_AHEAD` idiom, which pins what is known-open so a new one fails.

Keyed on the **compiler's reason** and not on the JSON key, because a key is
shared: `name` here is a secret reference's, while a device's `name` is guarded
by the pass above -- a pin on `name` would have masked that guard's removal. And
held in both directions: all fifteen are asserted to still fire, so a pin left
behind after a fix fails rather than going quiet.

### The one fault that was not a refusal

Fourteen of the fifteen say "does not compile". One said **"compiles to a
DIFFERENT document"** -- the renderer wrote something that compiles and means
something else, which is worse than anything else here.

It is a silent truncation, in two places. A delegation source is copied into a
fixed buffer:

    if (length >= sizeof(name)) { length = sizeof(name) - 1u; }

So `@pd:` with 64 characters and `@pd:` with 70 both became the same 63, and
**two configurations naming different delegations compiled to one document**,
with the prefix taken from a name nobody wrote. Reachable from a configuration
file, not only from JSON -- measured with both lengths and the same stored
result. The advertised-prefix source was not validated as a name at all either,
so `@pd:eth 0` and a bare `@pd:` were accepted.

Both refuse now. The advertised source goes through `ncfg_name_ok` like every
